"The team, the baggy green, the mateship and all that stuff - that was what playing Australia was like, so for an Australian team to say, 'no, it's just those three' when it was never going to be just those three [is surprising]."
'Worst of both worlds from Cricket Australia'
Hussain's fellow analyst, Michael Atherton, is currently in Australia ahead of England's white-ball tour of the country, which begins with the first ODI in Perth on Friday (3.30am UK time).
Atherton will attend what he anticipates being a "circus" of a press conference on Thursday as Australia white-ball captain Mitchell Marsh - the only player to have figured in the Newlands Test in 2018 in the hosts' squad to tackle England - fronts up.
Usual ODI skipper Pat Cummins has been rested, along with Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, all three of whom were involved in the sandpaper Test and released a joint statement back in 2021, with spinner Nathan Lyon, denying prior knowledge of the plot.
Sky Sports pundit Atherton was critical of Cricket Australia's handling of the situation eight years ago, saying it was always "going to come back to haunt them".
Smith and Warrner were banned for a year after 'Sandpapergate' with Bancroft suspended for nine months.
Atherton, who does not see a need for a new investigation to be opened following Khawaja's claims, said: "It was almost like the sandpaper was the straw that broke the camel's back.
"It was on the back of the team having become, and Khawaja talks about it in his book, slightly out of control, a bit unlikable and with a kind of win-at-all costs mentality.
"Then it was the worst of both worlds.
"They handed down unbelievably heavy sanctions - I thought hard-to-justify sanctions - and left three players to take the rap. But it left questions unanswered, left the door open for it to come back to haunt them, which it is doing now.
"It was eight years ago and there will be a weariness around the story eventually, because it's all over every newspaper, podcast, whatever.
"But I do think the particular point about not having people's backs is the thing causing the most disquiet [in the Australia public] and will rumble on for a while yet."
Atherton: Cracks in the Australia team
Australia have also toiled on the field, losing 2-1 in South Africa in their first Test series in the country since the ball-tampering scandal, with the out-of-form Marnus Labuschagne now dropped for the impending home clashes with New Zealand.
Amid a relentless Test calendar that then features a five-match assignment in India, the day-night 150th anniversary Test against England in Melbourne in March, and an away Ashes series in June and July, Atherton feels the Baggy Greens are in a tough spot.
He added: "The schedule is brutal and unforgiving and already there's cracks in that team.
"It doesn't feel as though the team is robust enough to get through this period.
"This [the ball-tampering claims] is adding a little bit more fuel to the fire."

After 40 years, Chilean mother reunites with two children stolen during dictatorship
Teresita de Jesús Padilla has reunited with her two sons after they were taken from her in Chile four decades ago
SANTIAGO, Chile -- Four decades after a brutal separation, Teresita de Jesús Padilla was able to embrace two of her children again, after they were taken from her native Chile by hospital workers in one of the thousands of illegal adoptions under the late Gen. Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship.
“God gave me back my children, whom I thought I had lost forever,” Padilla said moments after meeting Tim Rolnick and Travis Murdoch, 41 and 37, respectively, during their reunion in Santiago, Chile's capital.
The brothers, along with Travis's twin, were taken from their biological mother while she was still in the hospital. Their case is part of one of Chile's darkest chapters when child-trafficking coincided with many other human rights violations during Pinochet's 17-year reign. During the dictatorship, at least 3,095 people were killed or forcibly disappeared, according to government figures, and tens of thousands more were tortured or jailed for political reasons.
Both of Padilla's children grew up in the United States. They knew they were adopted but were unaware of the shadowy history behind their origins.
“It felt almost like I've known Teresita my whole life. I just felt a connection,” Rolnick said after reuniting with his biological mother. “It’s definitely something I will remember for the rest of my life."
Rolnick discovered in 2020 that he had an entire family in Chile who never stopped thinking of him. He also learned he had two brothers living just a few hundred miles from his home in Maryland.
“It all started when I was trying to find out about my medical history” through a MyHeritage DNA test, he explained.
Soon after, distant cousins and social organizations dedicated to investigating and reuniting families who had been illegally separated began contacting him. “And then it was like opening up Pandora’s box."
As he continued searching for answers, Rolnick discovered not only that he and his two brothers had been trafficked to the United States, but that he also had another sibling who remained in Chile.
Four years after Rolnick was illegally taken from his mother’s arms, his brothers, twins Travis and Chris, suffered the same fate and were also adopted by an American couple. Rolnick decided to reach out.
“I always wanted a brother, so I got three!” he said.
Today, the brothers share a close bond. Murdoch recalled being nervous and wondering whether his brother would show up.
“Then we met and he looked just like me and I was, like, this is super weird, very surreal," he added. “We started talking and getting to know each other and we clicked pretty quickly. Hanging out with him now feels like we’ve known each other for our entire lives.”
Six years after that initial contact, the two brothers were finally able to share their first embrace with Teresita in the Chilean capital. While Travis flew to Santiago, Chris was severely injured in a car accident in 2013 and was physically unable to make the long journey.
“A lot of nerves, I think more nerves for her than for me,” Murdoch said about the reunion. “I think for her it’s nice to finally meet us and move on from all this."
According to Chilean judicial reports obtained by The Associated Press, approximately 20,000 cases of forced or criminal adoptions took place during the 17 years of Pinochet’s military regime. However, civil society organizations such as Nos Buscamos estimate that more than 50,000 Chilean families have been affected.
“We still haven’t been able to identify the actual number of children who were taken out of Chile," Constanza del Río, the NGO’s director, told AP.
Del Río explained that the most vulnerable women, particularly those from Chile’s poorest regions, were the main targets of a child-trafficking network made up of social workers, doctors, judges and lawyers who arranged for children to be taken out of the country. In the 1970s, Chile was the third-largest exporter of children for illegal adoptions, after China and South Korea.
Padilla, now 66, was one of these women. Her father died when she was four and her family struggled with poverty since.
When she became pregnant, she saw the hospital as a refuge that could help her find a better life for her babies. However, she never expected that they would be violently taken away from her not just once, but twice.
“These women took my children away from me under threats, through sheer terror, and I suffered because of it my entire life,” Padilla said.
Despite the bittersweet feelings surrounding a reunion that finally took place after 41 years of pain and anguish, mother and sons share a common desire: to rebuild a fragmented family, create new memories and write the next chapters of a future that is only beginning.
“There’s no reason to look into the past too far and from here we can work toward the future,” Murdoch said.

Why a US-Russia showdown left Morocco celebrating
- Published
Morocco has welcomed the end of a decades-long UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a diplomatic showdown between the US and Russia left the Security Council unable to agree on its future.
The council failed on Friday to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso) after Russia vetoed a US-backed proposal. A rival Russian draft to extend the mission also failed to secure enough votes.
The decision raises questions about the future of Africa's longest territorial dispute and the fragile ceasefire between Morocco, which claims Western Sahara, and the Polisario Front which has been fighting for the territory's independence for more than 50 years.
Here is what you need to know.
Why is Western Sahara disputed?
Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.
As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory.
The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.
Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.
Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.
The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.
Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.
Algeria became Polisario's main regional ally, providing military support and hosting its leadership and thousands of Sahrawi refugees in camps near the city of Tindouf.
The North African country says its position is based on the right to self-determination, while Morocco sees Western Sahara as an integral part of its territory.
Morocco and Algeria fought a brief border war in 1963 over disagreements about territory inherited from French colonial rule. Their relationship has remained tense, with Western Sahara at the centre of their dispute.
What was the UN's mission role?
After 16 years of fighting, Morocco and Polisario agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991, with the territory divided by a sand wall, or berm, to keep the rival forces apart.
The UN established Minurso to monitor the ceasefire and organise a referendum on the territory's future. Sahrawis were meant to choose between independence and integration with Morocco.
The vote was scheduled for 1992 but never took place. The two sides could not agree on who would be eligible to participate, with disputes over voter identification becoming a major obstacle.
In 2007, Morocco put forward a proposal for autonomy, which would see Sahrawis managing their internal affairs, while Rabat retained control over defence and foreign relations.
The Polisario Front and Algeria rejected the plan, insisting on a referendum that included independence as an option.
Years of UN-sponsored negotiations failed to produce a breakthrough.
The ceasefire broke down in November 2020, when Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle.
But following a long diplomatic campaign by Morocco, the UN Security Council voted in 2025 in favour of a resolution backing the autonomy plan as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.
While most Sahrawis live in the part of Western Sahara controlled by Morocco, tens of thousands are estimated to be in refugee camps in Algeria.
What happened at the UN?
The US proposed extending Minurso's mandate for another year, but its draft went beyond the usual renewal.
It would have removed the word "referendum" from the mission's name and made Morocco's autonomy proposal the sole basis for further negotiations.
The draft received the support of 11 of the Security Council's 15 members, including France and the UK but Russia vetoed it, arguing that it was too favourable to Morocco.
Russia then proposed extending Minurso's mandate without changing its terms. That draft also failed, receiving only two votes in favour.
Minurso's mandate expired at the end of Saturday, 31 October. The UN said the following day that the mission had entered a liquidation period, with a reduced team overseeing the transfer of military equipment and other assets.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination must be respected and warned of the risk of renewed hostilities.
The Polisario Front condemned the US proposal. Its representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing it, saying it would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and threaten regional and international peace.
Morocco, meanwhile, said the mission's personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days, arguing that Western Sahara issue should no longer be considered by the Security Council.
Minurso had 155 military personnel and was expected to cost $62m (£46m) in the financial year beginning in June, according to a UN report.
Why is Morocco celebrating the end of the UN mission?
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.
In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI.
"The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.
He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.
The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.
Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR).
But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.
In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel.
France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.
Morocco rejoined the African Union in 2017, more than three decades after leaving its predecessor, the Organisation of African Unity, in protest at the SADR's admission.
Since returning, Rabat has sought to build support for its position from within the organisation. At least 10 African countries have opened diplomatic missions in the territory in support of Rabat.
"Morocco is not necessarily seeking to abandon the UN process, but to change the framework for negotiations and draw greater support from regional organisations," says Laaroussi.
Addressing a special joint session of parliament on Monday, House of Representatives Speaker Ahmed Touizi hailed the end of Minurso as a victory for the country's diplomacy.
He said the country should now move from "managing the dispute to implementing its autonomy plan under Moroccan sovereignty, while pressing ahead with development projects in the territory."
Could this lead to a renewed war?
The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.
The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation.
Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.
Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps.
"Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.
The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online.
Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.
In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.
Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."
Polisario has not said what it will do next.
Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), both countries significantly increased military spending last year, with SIPRI citing their dispute over Western Sahara as a key driver.
Algeria spent an estimated $25.4bn, more than four time Morocco's $6.3bn.

- Dark Souls 2 and 3 online servers are back after nearly 12 days of downtime.
- FromSoftware confirmed it has completed the investigation and responsed to the server issues.
- Players can once again access online multiplayer features, including co-op and PvP invasions.
FromSoftware has finally restored online services for Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 on November 11, 2026. The online servers were taken offline nearly 12 days ago on October 30 due to an unspecified issue, which the developer later confirmed involved security vulnerabilities.
According to the official FromSoftware support X account, the developer has completed its investigation and response to the server issues. With that done, it has restored online services for both games. The company also apologized to players for the inconvenience and thanked them for their patience during the downtime.
Initially, FromSoftware did not reveal the exact reason behind the sudden shutdown. However, on November 2, the developer confirmed that the servers were taken offline due to security vulnerabilities. At the time, it did not provide an estimated date for restoring online services.
The situation raised concerns among fans because of a similar incident in 2022, when a serious Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability forced FromSoftware to shut down the Dark Souls PC servers for several months. However, this time the servers were restored in less than two weeks.
While FromSoftware has not disclosed the exact nature of the vulnerabilities, the relatively quick restoration is a welcome development for players. The incident also comes amid broader gaming security concerns, including the recent PlayStation jailbreak controversy.
Nevertheless, online services have now resumed. Players can now once again enjoy co-op multiplayer, PvP invasions, player messages, and other online features in Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 on supported platforms.

12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న 4వ జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లో పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను తగ్గించడం/మాఫీ చేయనున్నారని చెబుతూ ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో విస్తృతంగా ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న 4వ జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లో పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను తగ్గించడం/మాఫీ చేయబడతాయి.
ఫాక్ట్: ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను మాఫీ చేస్తున్నట్లు జాతీయ లేదా రాష్ట్ర లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీలు ఎక్కడా ప్రకటించలేదు. అయితే, 2026లో కర్ణాటక, బీహార్, ఒడిశా వంటి పలు రాష్ట్రాలు పెండింగ్ చలాన్ల చెల్లింపులో రాయితీని కల్పించాయి. తెలంగాణ, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ రాష్ట్రాలు గతంలో ఇలాంటి రాయితీలు ఇచ్చినప్పటికీ, డిసెంబర్ 2026లో జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లో మాత్రం ఎలాంటి రాయితీని అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా ఈ విషయం గురించి జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించే నేషనల్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీ (NALSA) అధికారిక వెబ్సైట్ను పరిశీలించగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న దేశవ్యాప్తంగా పలు రాష్ట్రాలలో లోక్ అదాలత్లు నిర్వహిస్తున్నట్లు తెలిసింది. దీనిలో భాగంగా విచారణలో ఉన్న సివిల్, క్రిమినల్, చెక్బౌన్స్ కేసులు, కాంపౌండబుల్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్ కేసులు, మోటారు వాహన ప్రమాదాలు, కుటుంబ తగాదాలు మొదలైనవాటిని రాజీ మార్గం ద్వారా పరిష్కరించుకునే అవకాశాన్ని ఈ లోక్ అదాలత్లు కల్పిస్తాయి. అయితే, పెండింగ్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను 100% మాఫీ చేయనున్నట్లు ఇందులో ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు.
ఇదే విషయమై తెలంగాణ స్టేట్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీ (TSLSA) వర్గాలను సంప్రదించగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న తెలంగాణలో జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లకు మాఫీ/ డిస్కౌంట్ ఇస్తున్నట్లు తాము ఎక్కడా అధికారికంగా పేర్కొనలేదని స్పష్టం చేశారు.
అంతేకాకుండా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో తెలంగాణ వ్యాప్తంగా పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లను రాయితీపై చెల్లించే అవకాశం కల్పించడం లేదని తెలంగాణ పోలీసులు కూడా మాకు ధృవీకరించారు. మార్చి 2026లో కూడా ఇటువంటి వార్తలే వచ్చినప్పుడు వారు దీన్ని ఖండించారు. మరోవైపు, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ లీగల్ సర్వీసెస్ అథారిటీని, పోలీసులను సంప్రదించగా వారి స్పందించలేదు. అయితే, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ పోలీసులు కూడా పెండింగ్లో ఉన్న ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లపై రాయితీ కల్పించే విషయం గురించి ఎక్కడా అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు.
అయితే కర్ణాటక, ఒడిశా, బీహార్ వంటి పలు రాష్ట్రాల్లో 2026లో ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లకు రాయితీ కల్పిస్తూ సెటిల్మెంట్ చేసుకునేందుకు వీలుగా ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించిన సందర్భాలు ఉన్నాయి. గతంలో హైదరాబాద్ ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు కూడా ఇలాంటి లోక్ అదాలత్లను నిర్వహించారు. 2016, 2017 సంవత్సరాల్లో హైదరాబాద్ ట్రాఫిక్ పోలీసులు గోషామహల్లో లోక్ అదాలత్ నిర్వహించి, 50% రాయితీతో పెండింగ్ చలాన్లను చెల్లించే అవకాశం కల్పించారు. అయితే, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరగనున్న లోక్ అదాలత్లలో తెలంగాణ, ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ రాష్ట్రాల పోలీసులు లోక్ అదాలత్ ద్వారా ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లపై రాయితీని కల్పించే పథకాన్ని అధికారికంగా ప్రకటించలేదు.
చివరిగా, 12 డిసెంబర్ 2026న జరిగే జాతీయ లోక్ అదాలత్లో పెండింగ్ ట్రాఫిక్ చలాన్లు 100% మాఫీ అవుతాయని సోషల్ మీడియాలో జరుగుతున్న ప్రచారంలో నిజం లేదు.

Nobody gets to choose the season they are living in. Right? We all are well experienced that how a promotion arrives just as a parent falls ill. A friendship ends in the same month a new one begins. In short, some years give, and some years take, and neither asks our permission. Our life itself moves through various cycles, where there are times of joy and times of sorrow, beginnings and endings, expansion and withdrawal. But the fact remains, we cannot hold on to one season forever. The wisdom thus lies in learning how to remain centered while the seasons change. But staying centered is not something we can do in the middle of the storm if we have never practiced it in calm weather. Perhaps that is why silence becomes so powerful. When we sit quietly, even for a few moments, we step away from the noise of the world and return to the point within ourselves where there is stillness. In that stillness, we do not have to prove anything to anyone. We do not have to compete with anyone. We simply have to be who we are. And from that place, we can see things more clearly. We can ask ourselves: What really matters to me? What am I holding on to unnecessarily? Which relationships of mine need more love? Which expectations need to be released? Am I living according to my values, or merely according to what the world expects from me? These questions rarely get answered in a hurry. But even asking them honestly begins to loosen things that have remained tight for years.
The art of balance is not about creating a perfect life. It is about creating a stable center point within an imperfect life. When I know who I am, I don’t need the world to constantly remind me of my worth. When I experience peace within, I don’t have to demand that every circumstance outside me be peaceful. When I know my inner value, I can appreciate success without becoming arrogant and face failure without becoming broken.A tree does not stop the wind. It simply grows roots deep enough so that the wind passes through without uprooting it. Similarly, our circumstances will keep changing, as they always have. What we can build is the depth beneath them. So let the seasons turn. Let some be generous and some be hard. The one thing worth working on, every single day, is the ground we stand on while they do.

BSE SME listed Veefin Solutions has migrated to the main board of the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and the BSE, more than three years after its SME IPO. Veefin's shares opened for trade on the BSE mainboard at ₹249.75 (2.5% higher than previous close) and at ₹250.84 on the NSE. Veefin’s market capitalisation as of 13:20 IST stood at ₹633.76 Cr ($67.61 Mn). Shares of Veefin were trading 1.2% higher at ₹249 apiece on the BSE and 1.2% higher at ₹246.65 apiece on the NSE around 13:30 IST. Veefin listed on the BSE SME platform in July 2023 at ₹86.05, a near 5% premium from its IPO price. The company's ₹46.73 Cr IPO comprised about 57 Lakh shares, with equal parts of fresh issue and offer for sale shares. Its mainboard debut comes on the heels of the company solidifying its financial position over the recent quarter. Its operating revenue for the first half of the ongoing fiscal year (H1 FY27) doubled to ₹238.8 Cr while its consolidated net profit zoomed 127% YoY to ₹24.9 Cr. Veefin reported a 127% year-on-year (YoY) increase in consolidated net profit to ₹24.9 Cr in H1 FY27 from ₹11 Cr in the corresponding period last year. Net profit was also up 9% from ₹22.8 Cr in H2 FY26. In Q2 FY27, Veefin's net profit rose 61% sequentially to ₹15.3 Cr from ₹9.5 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue increased 9% sequentially to ₹124.7 Cr from ₹114.2 Cr, while total income stood at ₹125.7 Cr. The company also reported a deal pipeline of around ₹920 Cr alongside its half-year results. Around 84% of the pipeline comprises opportunities from banks and financial institutions outside India, with Southeast Asia emerging as a key market. The mainboard listing is expected to widen access to Veefin's shares among retail and institutional investors. Unlike the fixed trading lots on the SME platform, the main boards allow investors to buy and sell shares individually. Veefin Bets On AI Employees In a statement, the fintech SaaS company said that it will now look at expanding beyond fintech with an AI platform that enables businesses to deploy digital employees for defined roles. Alongside the listing, the company announced a rebranding from veefin.com to veefin.ai, reflecting the growing role of AI in its products and growth strategy. Its next growth opportunity is through the Veefin AI Operating System (AIOS), a platform designed to help businesses create, deploy and supervise AI employees for defined roles. Veefin has developed more than 1,000 reusable AI skills and has started deploying AIOS internally across three functions: customer implementation, customer support and software testing. The company is using these deployments to improve productivity and build experience before offering the platform to customers. The company sees an opportunity to cross-sell the platform to its current customers and reach enterprises beyond the financial services sector. “We listed on the SME platform three years ago as a supply chain finance technology company. We come to the main boards as a multi-product company whose revenue has more than doubled in the past year, and with many more investors able to take part in what we build next,” Gautam Udani, vice chairperson, cofounder and COO of Veefin Group, said. Founded in 2020 by Udani and Raja Debnath, Mumbai-based Veefin develops lending, supply chain finance and transaction banking software for banks, NBFCs, fintech companies and enterprises. The company began with supply chain finance and has since expanded into trade finance, cash and liquidity management, loan origination, loan management, collections, and corporate and retail digital banking. Its customers use its technology through complete applications, platforms or individual components integrated into their own systems. Is honesty always the best policy? When to speak up — or stay silent
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Should you tell your partner how you really feel about their casserole? Offer a colleague feedback about their subpar interview performance? Let a stranger know she has toilet paper on her shoe?
Life Kit
How honest should you really be? Tips for sharing good and bad news
Sometimes the hardest part about talking to other people isn't finding the right words to say — but deciding if you should say anything at all, says social psychologist Vanessa Bohns.
"There are times when honesty is the best policy," she says. "On the other hand, honesty is not the best policy if whatever we say is going to be honest without any instrumental value."
Bohns is the author of Should I Say Something? The Science of What to Share—and What to Keep to Yourself, published in October. The book provides research-backed strategies to help you figure out when to share the truth or a personal opinion. It also offers advice on when to share good news, say sorry or be vulnerable.
There's a reason why giving difficult feedback or even loving criticism can feel like a dilemma. "It pains us to embarrass or hurt other people," Bohns says. So we don't tend to like doing it. In fact, there's a name for the phenomenon — the MUM effect, or minimizing unpleasant messages.
But with care and intention, it's possible to make informed choices about when to speak up or stay quiet, no matter how small or big the situation. Bohns shares three questions to ask yourself before sharing an opinion.
Is this information helpful?
When you decide to tell someone something, remember you're sharing two things: the message itself, and the fact that you are choosing to speak up at all, Bohns says.
People often spend far too much time worrying about the content of their messages, she says. "But the choice of saying something at all communicates so much. It says, 'I see you. I care about your suffering. I want to help you in some way.'"
So, before telling your boss/spouse/mother-in-law how you really feel about that new haircut, Bohn says to consider whether your feedback is actionable.
Honesty is only the best policy if your opinion is going to help someone "perform better or avoid embarrassment or learn something about themselves." If your feedback is mean-spirited, unrelated to the matter at hand or simply can't be enacted, you're probably better off holding your tongue.
For example, flat-out telling your roommate the cake she baked for your birthday tastes terrible? That's just mean. But if she bakes that same cake to enter into a baking competition? It would be mean not to offer her some feedback!
Would I want to hear this?
Just because you don't want to share the truth doesn't mean the person on the receiving end shouldn't or wouldn't want to hear what you have to say.
A 2022 survey, for example, found that people consistently underestimate others' desire for feedback. In the study, researchers put visible smudges of lipstick, chocolate or marker on their faces. Then, without acknowledging those smudges, they went out on the street asking random people to participate in a survey on a different topic.
Less than 3% of the survey participants spoke up, even though the smudges were something the researchers "clearly could have done something about and would have wanted to know," says Bohns.
So, if you choose to stay silent when your new co-worker keeps mispronouncing the name of the company CEO, for example, reflect on your own motivations. "Are you being kind, or are you avoiding your own discomfort?" writes Bohns in her book. Speaking up may help your colleague in this instance.
Do they want your feedback?
Has anyone ever given you advice about a topic you knew more about than they did? Or misjudged how much you knew based on how you looked?
When in doubt, don't assume you know what information the other person wants or needs from you. Pre-assessing how valuable the truth is to someone else, or their ability to handle it, can quickly make well-meaning feedback sound patronizing, writes Bohns in her book.
So just ask the other person if they want the feedback you have to share. "Give them the autonomy, then respect their decision, whatever it might be," she says.

: Fresh CCTV footage of the murder of former Tech Mahindra regional business head Paramjeet Dhankhar has emerged, capturing the chilling sequence of events in which his neighbour allegedly chased him and fired multiple rounds at him, even after he fell to the ground.
The footage shows the accused, Mohan alias Monu Sharma, engaging in an argument with Dhankhar for around four minutes before opening fire at him. Even after Dhankhar fell to the ground, the accused continued shooting.

A woman relative of Dhankhar attempted to intervene and stop the accused, but he continued firing on the road while hurling abuses. The footage also shows him reloading his weapon with another magazine.

Dhankhar, who was based in Singapore, had returned to Faridabad just two days before the incident to attend his nephew's wedding. He had earlier served as the regional business head of Tech Mahindra's Asia-Pacific operations and was working as senior vice-president at FPT Software at the time of his death.
Police investigations have pointed to a prolonged dispute between the two families over vehicle parking. Investigators are also examining whether an earlier disagreement involving a pet dog contributed to the escalation.

Google has announced a “super network” upgrade for its Fi cell service. For the past few years, Google Fi has operated exclusively on the T-Mobile network, but now it’s adding support for a second 5G network. Oddly, Google refuses to say which one.
Google’s MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) launched in 2015 as Project Fi with support for both T-Mobile and Sprint service. The service initially only worked on Google’s Nexus phones, which would switch between networks based on signal strength. After T-Mobile absorbed Sprint, Fi switched to being a single-network service in the US while continuing to hop between networks for international travel.
With the super network, Google Fi is again a dual-carrier service stateside. Phones connected to Fi will be able to hop between T-Mobile 5G and a different 5G network to provide the best possible connectivity. Google’s blog post announcing the change conspicuously doesn’t mention either network, saying only that it supports “two of America’s best 5G cellular networks.”
We know one of them is T-Mobile, and the other must be either AT&T or Verizon. When reached for comment, a Google spokesperson declined to name the second network, which is odd. Looking at the Fi coverage map, my best guess for the super network partner is Verizon. The shape of unserved regions is a closer match than AT&T, but carriers do tend to fudge the fine details of these maps.

Leader, role model, extraordinary - how Kane's 'fairytale' came true
- Published
"It's great when fairytales come true," England boss Roy Hodgson said after 21-year-old Tottenham striker Harry Kane scored 79 seconds into his international debut back in 2015.
"Let's hope it's the start of a good and long England career for him."
Eleven years on, Kane will make his 126th appearance for his country and become the most-capped men's player in Three Lions history when England play Croatia in the Nations League at Wembley on Thursday (19:45 GMT).
Peter Shilton, who served England as a goalkeeper, won 125 caps between 1970 and 1990.
"It's not about me - it's about the team," said Kane, scorer of 91 goals in 125 appearances for his country, about his landmark moment.
"I love coming to every England camp, I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible."
Kane, 33, has gone through every emotion playing for his country.
He fought back tears after missing a penalty in the World Cup quarter-final defeat by France in 2022, and sang Wonderwall with fans following the win over Croatia at this summer's World Cup - which he labelled one of his "favourite ever moments" in a Three Lions shirt.
London-born Kane is the boy who grew up in Chingford to captain his country, become England's record goalscorer and win the 2026 Ballon d'Or.
Now the Bayern Munich striker stands on the brink of making more appearances than any other man in England's football history.
"He wins the Ballon d'Or, and deservedly so, and in the next game for England he gets the all-time record with 126 matches," England boss Thomas Tuchel said about Kane when announcing his squad last week.
"Thursday is a deserved occasion to celebrate an extraordinary player."
Kane: The England fan
Long before Kane made his first senior appearance for his country in a 4-0 Euro 2015 qualifying win over Lithuania at Wembley, he was an England fan.
Aged 12, he remembers the heartache of going out on penalties to Portugal in the quarter-finals of the 2006 World Cup under Sven-Goran Eriksson and failing to qualify for Euro 2008 under Steve McClaren.
"During most major tournaments we would go to the pub to watch England, with the beer garden and the screen," said Kane.
"We loved England, we loved watching England and we were big England fans. I remember many tears being shed after we went out on penalties and things like that."
Kane fell in love with football from an early age.
Aged five, he wrote about his ambition to become a footballer in a school project.
Weekends and holidays were spent playing football in his local Ridgeway Park with his dad Patrick and brother Charlie.
They would use trees as goalposts, with the two brothers taking turns to shoot while Patrick was in goal.
At Larkswood Primary School, Kane and his friends would play football in the playground - where they were only allowed to use tennis balls.
By then, the future England captain was playing for Sunday league team Ridgeway Rovers - whose former players included David Beckham, Kane's idol growing up.
Former Manchester United midfielder Beckham, who won 115 England caps between 1996 and 2009, was playing for Real Madrid when Kane was at Chingford Foundation School.
"He had sent a Real Madrid shirt back to our secondary school," added Kane.
"Seeing Beckham's shirt hanging there growing up and knowing he grew up in the same surroundings as I did was a source of great motivation."
1 of 5
Kane: The leader
Wayne Rooney was England captain and Joe Hart was goalkeeper when Kane came on to make his Three Lions debut 11 years ago.
"My reaction when he first came into the England squad was: 'Alright, who is this guy?'" Hart told BBC Sport of the young Tottenham striker called up after scoring 26 goals in 42 league and cup games in 2014-15.
"Then I was like: 'Oh OK, he's good! Then he kept coming back [into the England squad] and my reaction was: 'Flipping heck, he's getting better!'
"I went to Tottenham during Covid and it got to the point in training where he was that good that I wasn't even diving for his shots. I was thinking: 'I adore you, but you are frustrating the life out of me.'"
Kane has served five different England managers.
As well as Hodgson and current boss Tuchel, Kane won 81 of his 125 caps under Gareth Southgate, played for Lee Carsley when he was interim boss in 2024, and appeared in Sam Allardyce's sole match in charge in 2016.
It was Southgate who recognised Kane's leadership skills and handed him the England captaincy for the first time in 2017, even though Kane was not captain of Tottenham at the time.
"I want people with leadership qualities who are respected by the group, and capable of stepping forward at the right moments and handling responsibility," said Southgate.
When he has started, Kane has captained the Three Lions 97 times - more than anyone else.
Kane: The role model
How long will Kane carry on playing for England? More worryingly, who will lead the attack when he retires?
Despite individual awards and back-to-back Bundesliga titles with Bayern Munich, Kane has yet to inspire his country to a major trophy.
He will be approaching 35 when England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland co-host Euro 2028.
"He aged, but he got better too, like red wine," Lothar Matthaus, West Germany's 1990 World Cup-winning captain, told BBC Sport.
Kane, who has had to adapt his game to stay at the top level, is certainly not ready to talk publicly about retirement dates while he is still only 33.
"From a physical point of view, I feel great," he told BBC Sport recently.
"My numbers are as high as ever, and I've recently reached a new top speed in a game against Borussia Dortmund. I'm going to keep pushing and see what else is possible."
Kane's former Tottenham and England team-mate Hart added: "He's never particularly relied on pace. It's all about his thought process and his brain and how he calculates the game."
The Three Lions have won 83, drawn 22 and lost 20 of the 125 games Kane has appeared in.
His 91 goals for his country include 58 with his right foot, 15 with the left and 18 headers, with three from outside the box. Twenty-six have come from the penalty spot.
Kane's rise from Leyton Orient loan signing to Ballon d'Or winner is well-documented.
His story - the model student and family man who married his childhood sweetheart and became an England great - serves as a reminder to pupils at his old school to never give up on their dreams.
He has not forgotten his roots - or the clubs that helped him on his pathway.
In 2020, Kane sponsored Leyton Orient's shirt. The club's home strip carried a message of thanks to frontline workers tackling the coronavirus pandemic.
Mental health charity Mind and Haven House Children's Hospice also had their logos on Orient's two change shirts as part of the deal.
"I was born and brought up only a couple of miles from Orient's stadium and I'm really happy to have the opportunity to give back to the club that gave me my first professional start," said Kane at the time.
"It also gives me a platform to say a big thank you to the many frontline heroes and charities out there who provide care and support during these challenging times."
Matthaus, who has witnessed Kane's impact at Bayern Munich, added: "He is a good person, a good ambassador, the captain of the English national team playing at a German club."
On Thursday, England's players and fans will salute Kane for breaking another record and making it 126 not out.
"He is superhuman," added Hart.
