Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

- Luxbane is one of the Lord Ravagers in Honkai Star Rail, and is responsible for destroying multiple star systems single-handedly.
- It is nicknamed as the Sun Devourer due to its shape that eclipses even multiple suns with its massive size.
- As per the latest version, Luxbane has been confirmed to be dead.
Honkai Star Rail 4.7 ended up being one of the best finales to a Trailblazing arc thus far. It bombarded players with massive lore drops while also giving us one of the best boss fights. Among all this, Luxbane’s name was mentioned at the very end of Honkai Star Rail 4.7, and it has spurred more questions than answers among players. So, who is Luxbane in Honkai Star Rail? And did the Trailblazer really defeat it? Learn all about HSR Luxbane here.
Who is Lord Ravager Luxbane in Honkai Star Rail?
Luxbane is one of the Lord Ravagers of Honkai Star Rail. Lord Ravagers are the Emanators of Destruction, and they are considered one of the biggest threats to the cosmos. In HSR, Luxbane is also known as Sun Devourer. It has been responsible for multiple cosmos-level extinctions and is seen as a natural calamity rather than a defined person.
According to reports from the Intelligentsia Guild, Luxbane has been credited with extinguishing one-third of the stars in the Yvanna Chain within a period of 300 years.
As per the lore, Luxbane is said to have an indescribable shape, so vast that it eclipses suns, blotting out sky and space alike. This is where the nickname Sun Devourer came into existence. Some theories consider it to be a descendant of the Leviathan species, which has been extinct for a long time.
Lord Ravager Luxbane’s Connection to Oroboros and Voracity
According to Aeon Aha, Luxbane has been after Oroboros, the Aeon of Voracity, for quite some time. Although Oroboros has been dead for a long time, its remains have been sealed in Planarcadia. Eventually, it had nearly merged with the Path of Elation and the original body of Aha to create a monstrosity that the Trailblazer had to defeat in version 4.7.
Now, there have been rumors that Luxbane is either created to confront Voracity or Permanence. As already established, every Lord Ravager has been tasked with destroying a path. With Luxbane’s target not determined, its interest in Orobors makes it seem that it was tasked to target Voracity.
However, during the fight against Voracity, the Lord Ravager Luxbane never made an appearance. This was not expected by players, as they had expected Luxbane to play a major role in the story.
But in a complete twist, at the very end of the mission, we learn that Luxbane has been defeated by the Trailblazer, at the same time as they were confronting the mix of Oroboros and real Aha. This came not only as a shock to players, but also to the Trailblazer themselves.

Jockey O'Brien dies aged 39
- Published
Jockey Tom O'Brien has died at the age of 39 after being diagnosed with cancer.
Irishman O'Brien rode more than 1,000 winners in Britain and Ireland, including two at the Cheltenham Festival and the Welsh Grand National twice.
The nephew of trainer Aidan O'Brien, he was a mainstay of the Minehead operation run by Philip Hobbs, joining as a teenager and remaining until his retirement in 2023.
"He touched countless lives on both sides of the Irish Sea, bringing joy to everyone who had the privilege of knowing him and watching what he did best, on and off the racecourse," said British Horseracing Authority (BHA) chief executive Brant Dunshea.
"Tom was held in the highest esteem and meant so much to so many people across our sport, who benefitted from his kindness and loyal friendship.
"He will be hugely missed and his loss is immensely difficult to process.
"The racing family is distraught, but I know how we will all rally round to provide each other with support, comfort and to remember Tom as we knew him best: a brilliant jockey, a valued colleague, a loyal friend and above all a loving husband and devoted father."
Riding the Hobbs-trained Thyme Hill, O'Brien won the Liverpool Hurdle in 2021 and the Kauto Star Novices' Chase in 2022.
"It's very sad, particularly for his wife Hayley and two young children," said Hobbs, who now shares Minehead with Johnson White.
"He came to our yard from Ireland having not ridden in a race, but it soon became obvious he was pretty talented.
"He was always very reliable and a very good bloke. There's lots of good memories and there were lots of winners.
"I'd kept in touch with Tom since his retirement as he only lived half an hour away. He was only in our yard about three weeks ago."
O'Brien joined the BHA stewarding team after ending his racing career.

MDCalc, a medical reference tool site, Wednesday announced the launch of CrossCover, which the company said is meant to help clinicians trust the answers of medical artificial intelligence chatbots while preserving patient and provider privacy.
Graham Walker, head of AI at MDCalc, said the company sees the tool as an accelerator for clinical generative AI. “We can take away some of the challenges and risks and problems with the technology so that physicians can feel more confident in using it,” he said.
CrossCover takes an approach that contradicts that of medical AI tools from OpenEvidence, Abridge, and electronic health record company Epic, which are trying to incorporate an ever-widening repertoire of patient, provider, and payer information into their recommendations. Rather than requiring clinicians to register with their national identification numbers or trying to mitigate risk by brokering privacy agreements that allow clinicians to enter protected patient health information, MDCalc’s tool focuses on stripping out those types of information from clinicians’ queries.

A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump wrote a social media post chastising Vice President JD Vance, including an order to change the vice president's name, circulated in November.
People on social media shared a purported screenshot of a social media post attributed to Trump that claimed, "I'm hereby signing an EXCLUSIVE ORDER legally changing JD Vance's name to JUDAS DISLOYAL VANCE!"
(X user @miribobs)
The alleged post was dated Nov. 5 and inspired readers to reach out about its authenticity. It circulated after Democrats enjoyed major victories in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
It read in full:
I'm hereby signing an EXCLUSIVE ORDER legally changing JD Vance's name to JUDAS DISLOYAL VANCE!
Nobody gave JD more than President Trump. I took him from the sidelines and gave him the biggest job of his life—and now he thinks he can DOUBLE CROSS THE BOSS and run for President in 2028 without my blessing?
EHHH!
WRONG!
You don't walk into the Trump Family, eat at the table, kiss the ring, and then decide you're the new Boss!
There is only ONE person who can make America Great Again the RIGHT WAY, and everybody knows who that is.
JD, you may have forgotten who made you—but I NEVER forget!
THE PRESIDENT HAS SPOKEN.
The post was fake, however.
A search of the president's Truth Social account and an online archive of his social media posts revealed no such post.
The fake Trump post circulated as an apparent response, likely satirical, to a Nov. 4 X post by Vance addressing the Republican turnout at the polls for the midterm elections. Vance wrote: "The main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026." His post sparked rumors that he's angling for a 2028 bid for the White House.
The engagement metrics displayed on the fake post — 14.3K reposts, 56.7K likes — exactly match those of other debunked Trump posts, suggesting it may have been generated using a template or a fake post generator. Note that the timestamp is written out as "11/5/26," while authentic Truth Social posts show dates written as "Nov 5, 2026."
The president made multiple posts on Truth Social on that date, but nothing about Vance or a rumored bid for the White House.

The alleged espionage scandal involving NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and the growing scrutiny of the chipmaker’s business dealings with China have added another layer of uncertainty to the global AI infrastructure market already facing questions about its financing model. At the same time, political and regulatory resistance to data centre expansion in the US could slow infrastructure investment, putting pressure on companies that have borrowed heavily to build capacity. While unrelated, these developments present two separate risks to the investment model underpinning the AI infrastructure boom. The first is already visible in the American stock market. Investors have been selling shares of US neocloud companies since September, with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN witnessing sharp corrections. The selling intensified through October and into November, as concerns mounted over the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending and the debt these companies have taken on. The selloff has only intensified talk of an AI bubble, and neoclouds in India face the risk of getting caught in the middle. Neoclouds – AI infrastructure providers that offer GPU-as-a-service - have emerged as an important part of NVIDIA's AI ecosystem. They provide GPU compute to customers that may not have the scale or resources to build their own infrastructure. Neocloud business models are capital-intensive, with GPU procurement, data centre capacity, and financing arrangements determining how quickly they can scale up. NVIDIA has played a significant role in supporting this ecosystem through strategic investments and financing arrangements, helping expand the market for its chips beyond traditional hyperscalers. India is increasingly becoming part of this infrastructure buildout. That buildout serves two demand pools. One is subsidised compute for domestic startups, researchers and institutions under the IndiaAI Mission, which had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026. By August, it had approved 237 projects for subsidised compute, with 93.18 lakh GPU hours sanctioned. The other is commercial workloads from customers willing to pay for guaranteed capacity. The first highlights the scale of the government programme, but sanctioned hours do not necessarily translate into sustained usage. To justify their spending, India’s neoclouds are betting on the second. Among the main Indian players, Yotta plans to spend over $7 Bn on AI infrastructure by the end of FY27 and is targeting a $1.5 Bn IPO, partly to repay debt. ESDS went to the market after the cost of the GPU servers it planned to buy rose from ₹25 Lakh to ₹1.8 Cr. E2E Networks, meanwhile, reported a 411% year-on-year jump in Q2 revenue. Besides these, the likes of NxtGen, NeevCloud and Neysa are also building their neocloud infrastructure in India in anticipation of a big adoption wave. US giant CoreWeave is also entering India as the sole tenant of a planned 240 MW AdaniConneX data centre campus. However, any sustained pressure on its financing or expansion plans could have implications for the project. If concerns in the US around data centre build-up trickle down to India, neoclouds will be one of the first to get hit as a lot of their build-up depends on institutional funding commitment. The question is whether Indian companies will continue to enjoy the financial backing and attract customer commitments to withstand the headwinds if and when they come. No Anchor Customers In India The investment case for US AI infrastructure companies is underpinned by large customers such as Meta and OpenAI, whose scale and long-term compute requirements offer some visibility into future demand. These anchor customers make it easier for infrastructure providers to secure financing and justify large upfront investments. Indian neoclouds, however, do not yet have comparable customer base to underwrite their expansion plans. International customers now account for 75-80% of Yotta’s customer base, partly because they are willing to pay more. Within India, however, the IndiaAI Mission is emerging as an important source of demand, although it utilised less than half its FY26 outlay of ₹10,000 Cr, which has directly impacted hardware procurement and deployment timelines, as Neysa mentioned in one of its blogs. A recent Moneycontrol report highlighted a mismatch in the Indian market: some GPUs are underused, while startups and researchers say fragmented capacity, allocation delays and the type of hardware on offer can make suitable compute difficult to obtain. A headline GPU count may therefore obscure both the quality of available clusters and the path from allocation to actual use. The mismatch makes domestic demand hard to read. The demand exists, but it does not always reach the neoclouds that have built capacity for it. Even well-funded companies are waiting. Juspay, which buys GPUs with its own cash, has been “given commitments that it will take three to six months” to receive them, co-founder and COO Sheetal Lalwani said at a media briefing. When large customers buy and run their own hardware, and smaller ones struggle to find suitable clusters, aggregate capacity figures say little about how much will turn into long-term, paying contracts for neoclouds. Can government-backed compute requirements offer the kind of long-term revenue visibility that hyperscaler contracts provide in the US? Or will Indian neoclouds remain dependent on international customers to sustain utilisation and justify their infrastructure investments? GPU infrastructure requires substantial upfront capital, while the returns depend on sustained utilisation, predictable demand and long-term customer commitments. Notably, government-led regulations as well as citizen pushback could limit data centre build; it even emerged as a major factor for voters in the recent US midterm elections. For Indian neocloud players, which are increasingly catering to foreign and especially US-based clients, could suffer a trickle-down effect. Neocloud stocks, those of Coreweave, Nebius and Iren, among others, battered after the Democratic win in the recent elections. Closer home, ESDS and E2E stocks are already suffering from the second order impact of the sharp selloff in US tech stocks, following the mid-term results. On November 9, ESDS closed at approximately ₹1,147.25, against a September 24 high of ₹1,864.35, while E2E Networks ended at around ₹490.50, significantly lower than its October 14 high of ₹769. The NVIDIA Question NVIDIA’s role in the neocloud ecosystem goes beyond supplying GPUs. Its investments, financing arrangements and partnerships with infrastructure providers have helped bring new compute capacity online. But the relationship varies across Indian companies. NeevCloud said its engagement with NVIDIA covers technical planning, GPU availability and deployment readiness. Procurement, financing and customer contracts are separate arrangements. The company acknowledged the concentration risk of relying on a single technology provider, but said it ties investments to customer commitments and available financing. “The market correction reinforces the need for discipline. We assess each project on its commercial viability and phase investments accordingly,” Narendra Sen, founder of NeevCloud and RackBank Datacenters, told Inc42. ESDS said it has no direct commercial or financing relationship with NVIDIA. The company buys systems from OEMs and system integrators such as Supermicro, Dell, Lenovo and WWT. It has also signed a $1.25 Bn, seven-year agreement with Australia’s Sharon AI. Sharon AI owns and operates an 8,000-GPU cluster, which ESDS uses to serve its domestic and global customers. ESDS plans to explore similar partnerships. “I would separate technology dependence from financial dependence,” said Piyush Somani, founder of ESDS. He pointed out that all of ESDS’s deployed GPU capacity runs on NVIDIA. Financing is a different matter. ESDS commits capex only after a customer has paid at least 35% of the project cost, and only then does it place orders with OEMs or system integrators, Somani said. Both companies say financing for neocloud centres is getting more selective. Lenders and investors now favour projects with confirmed customers, predictable revenues and substantial upfront advances. Sen added that older GPUs could face more pricing pressure as newer generations arrive. This is where the economic model gets complicated. NVIDIA has offered neoclouds worldwide a revenue-sharing and credit-support model in July, but later paused some of the deals, as reported by The Wall Street Journal. Yotta is exploring similar structures where partners fund and own the GPUs, while the company installs and operates them in its data centres and signs customer contracts. Gorilla, the Nasdaq-listed British tech company, is one such partner. In April, the two companies deepened their partnership, adding another $2.8 Bn to an agreement that was initially valued at $500 Mn. Such partnership models depend on GPU rental prices holding up. If compute prices fall or older GPUs lose value faster than expected, who absorbs the loss: the neocloud, the customer or the financing partner? The Jensen Huang Overhang NVIDIA’s chips, software stack and partnerships shape how quickly new compute capacity comes online. That is one of the reasons The Economist has called it the “central bank of AI”. This also highlights growing concerns about the AI ecosystem’s dependence on NVIDIA. On November 8, NVIDIA’s board launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be spying for the Chinese government. The NVIDIA board, however, has maintained that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Questions about her alleged links to Chinese intelligence, and what they mean for NVIDIA’s China business, remain open. For Indian neoclouds, the direct exposure is less about a change in NVIDIA’s leadership and more about their dependence on globally-sourced GPUs and NVIDIA’s software ecosystem. The Government of India has said its compute ecosystem currently relies on globally-sourced GPUs and any change in chip availability, export controls, pricing or allocation could affect deployment schedules and project economics. There is no evidence yet that the controversy has affected NVIDIA’s relationships with Indian neoclouds. But any fallout for its leadership, China business or financing strategy would hit an ecosystem that leans heavily on NVIDIA’s technology. There are concerns regarding what a potential wider restructuring of NVIDIA might mean for the neocloud business, especially if the build-up of data centres slows down in the US. Incidentally, NVIDIA is set to announce its third quarter earnings on November 17, 2026, and this will reveal much more about the underlying numbers for the data centre business. Will the corporate governance issues have an overhang on the stock till then? In February this year, the fear was that AI would trigger a SaaSpocalypse. Since then, models have advanced and the opportunities have grown bigger, but the concern now is whether the companies building AI infrastructure can carry the debt and capital commitments needed to keep this boom going.

US President Donald Trump has said that the FBI is investigating the affair. The agency is separately examining whether the 63-year-old Nvidia CEO was targeted as part of a foreign intelligence operation.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had also reportedly briefed Trump about the relationship, according to reports.
Huang has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family in an internal memo addressed to Nvidia employees.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang said in the memo.
The Nvidia chief, however, did not provide details about the relationship.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, has been identified in reports as a former Chinese business executive suspected by US officials of having links to China's Ministry of State Security (MSS).
Huang has acknowledged the affair, but the allegations that Alice was working for Chinese intelligence remain unproven. Beijing has strongly rejected the accusations.

Beau Lamarre-Condon has admitted he threw Jesse Baird’s phone off a bridge to destroy evidence after allegedly murdering him, a court has heard.
The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Sitting in the witness box for a sixth day, Lamarre-Condon was asked what he did with Baird’s phone after the alleged murders.
He told the court on Thursday it was thrown off Tom Uglys Bridge near the Sutherland Shire in Sydney’s south.
“I didn’t want to have any evidence of Jesse’s phone on me … I did throw it off the bridge,” Lamarre-Condon told the New South Wales supreme court.
As part of his cross-examination, crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC put to him: “You did [that to] destroy evidence on Jesse’s phone that might incriminate you.”
Lamarre-Condon responded: “Essentially, yes.”
The former officer did not deny he had contacted his friend Stacey Parker, who lived in Western Australia, and asked if he could send her the phone for her to throw into a body of water.
But he did not end up mailing her the device.
Lamarre-Condon was also asked by Hatfield if he deleted messages between himself and Baird, alongside photos of them together, after his arrest.
“You did that deliberately to remove evidence of your relationship with Jesse Baird,” Hatfield told the court.
Lamarre-Condon said he disagreed and did not believe he had deleted the messages.
‘All these messages are a lie’
Lamarre-Condon and Baird were seeing each other in 2022 and 2023, the jury heard.
Hatfield suggested the former police officer “lied to [Baird] and deceived him numerous times throughout your relationship”. Lamarre-Condon agreed, saying: “On a number of occasions.”
Lamarre-Condon told the court he posted a photo of a bouquet of flowers on a florist’s Instagram page in November to “give the insinuation Jesse did send it to me”.
During that period, Baird was in Melbourne and the photo was captioned: “When he’s in Melbourne but still sends you these.”
The former officer said he and Baird were not in an exclusive relationship and had seen other men.
But Lamarre-Condon had posted it to his close friends story on Instagram, with its settings adjusted so only the man who Baird was seeing could view the post.
“I wanted to see if [the man Baird was seeing] was going to message me saying if he was in a relationship with Jesse or not,” Lamarre-Condon told the court.
The accused then admitted to using Baird’s phone a few days later, blocking the man and deleting the messages they had sent each other.
“I was wrong and I shouldn’t have done that, but I did do it,” he said.
When Baird texted him about the flowers story, Lamarre-Condon replied in a message: “I’m confused why you’re asking me about that.”
Hatfield suggested: “That’s another form of gaslighting isn’t it? Painting yourself as the victim when you’re the person lying?”
Lamarre-Condon responded: “Well no … this is all just me denying it.”
In the messages, Lamarre-Condon then told Baird the flowers were sent from his stepfather to his mother, who had recently injured her ankle.
He ordered a bouquet from the florist that looked exactly the same as the phone he posted, telling the jury he was getting it for his mum.
He then sent a photo of his mother and the flowers to Baird.
The crown prosecutor read further texts between Lamarre-Condon and Baird and accused the former officer of making out that he was being unreasonable by asking questions, to which Lamarre-Condon agreed.
“Yes, all these messages are a lie,” Lamarre-Condon said.
Hatfield suggested to the accused that his problem was “[Baird] didn’t like you anywhere near as much as you liked him”.
“Your unrequited love turned into obsession, didn’t it?” the prosecutor said.
Lamarre-Condon said this wasn’t the case.
When Hatfield asked, “You wronged him in a number of ways, hadn’t you?”
Lamarre-Condon responded: “Yes, I agree, in certain aspects.”
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

A 22-second-long clip shared by X user Vijay Thottathil (@vijaythottathil) showing a massive crowd in a large open area went viral on November 1.
Thottathil posted the video with the caption, “Early in the morning itself Ramlila Maidan is packed #ChaloDilli,” thus claiming that the crowd had gathered for the INDIA’s bloc’s rally on November 1 to protest against electoral irregularities and demand the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Early morning itself Ramlila Maidan is packed ✊🏼 🔥
#ChaloDilli https://t.co/oM5kSpCNoH
— Vijay Thottathil (@vijaythottathil) November 1, 2026
The post by Thottathil, who was till recently a social media manager of Kerala Congress, amassed over 243,000 views and was reshared over 1,400 times. (Archive)
Congress leader Harish Rawat, too, shared the video on Instagram, claiming that the visuals were from the November 1 protest rally.
View this post on Instagram
Various other X handles posted the same 22-second clip, claiming that they are visuals from the ‘Chalo Dilli’ rally held on November 1. A few of them are shown in the gallery below:
Fact Check
In the comments of the video posted by Vijay, X users were quick to point out that the video was not from the November 1 ‘Chalo Dilli’ protest, and instead was from another rally held at an earlier date.
To determine the veracity of these claims, we ran a reverse image search on a few of the keyframes, which led us to a video uploaded by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on December 14, 2025.
This video, captioned “‘वोट चोरी’ के खिलाफ जनसैलाब 🔥🔥” (A public outpouring against “vote theft”), was uploaded during the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhodo” protests of December 2025.
View this post on Instagram
The comparison of certain keyframes of both videos reveals stark similarities, including the backdrop, the size of the crowd, a flag being waved in the front, and even a blue tent visible in the clip. See below:
A deeper dive revealed that Congress leader Harish Rawat had himself shared the video during the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhodo” protests on December 14, 2025. He has now shared the same clip again as scenes from the INDIA bloc rally of November 1, 2026.
To sum up, the viral clip with the massive crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan shared by Thottathil is an old clip from the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhoro” protests that was organised by Congress in December last year. Several users have falsely presented it as visuals from the recent ‘Chalo Dilli’ march on November 1.

Assessing the reasons for Man City's decline in form under Maresca
- Published
The ongoing international break will give Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca much-needed time to fix the growing issues in his squad.
The Italian made a dream start after taking over from Pep Guardiola in the summer, leading the club to a record seven consecutive victories at the beginning of the Premier League season.
But three consecutive defeats have followed as they have fallen six points adrift of league leaders Arsenal, who are looking in imperious form as they aim to retain their title.
In September, it was announced that City had been found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, and matches have continued as the club await the outcome of their appeal.
With possible sanctions hanging over them, is City's recent league form down to psychological issues or are there tactical problems Maresca needs to address?
- Maresca's dream start turns into nightmare as title hopes hit 
  - Published3 days ago
Renowned sports psychologist Dr Paul McCarthy has 25 years' experience working in the industry with top clubs in England, Scotland, Germany and France.
McCarthy works on the personal and professional lives of players and says both contribute to how well they perform on the pitch, with the need to "piece together a jigsaw" when situations become disrupted.
"Players are like everyone else - they talk about what is going on in their own lives and things that are topical, especially about uncertain events," McCarthy tells BBC Sport.
"It generates communication with a lot of stories and rumour and over time if there are enough losses, there often becomes a reduced collective efficacy.
"A collective efficacy is a squad's belief in their ability to do what they need to do [to win] and because of their success in the past, that is often shaken a little by consecutive losses."
'Uncertainty leads to a lack of perceived control'
City were sitting pretty at the top of the table after a flawless start, but have dropped to third - behind Arsenal and Brighton.
After the guilty verdict was announced during the last international break, Maresca's men won their first game back - against 10-man Liverpool at Anfield - then narrowly overcame Ipswich at Etihad Stadium in their following match.
But they have since lost to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest, with defensive issues exposed and individual mistakes proving costly.
In their first seven games of the season, City did not concede any goals because of individual errors - but that has shifted dramatically in the past three matches, with four mistakes from players contributing to goals.
City have conceded 13 goals after 10 league games - their highest total at this stage of a season since 2008-09, when they had let in 16 - and that has prompted questions about their defensive solidity.
Asked if the uncertainty over the ongoing appeal process may affect the focus and attention of players, McCarthy said: "Yeah, that would be a very reasonable human response.
"When people are uncertain about their future, that uncertainty leads to a lack of perceived control, so uncertainty is often more stressful than bad news and the research shows that.
"So while you are waiting and you don't know the outcome, you are uncertain of where you are and there is that lack of control for a lot of people - they come to training, they play their games and it's outside of their responsibility."
'Anderson can't single-handedly resolve build-up play'
While at Chelsea, in a video for NBC Sports, Maresca discussed his tactics - moving counters into a 3-2-2-3 shape before pushing one up to create the 3-1-6 shape.
He explained using six attackers was a tactic he had employed against Inter Milan to outnumber their back five.
This season, he has adopted the 3-1-6 shape more permanently - trading a second holding midfielder for an extra attacking midfielder.
Coaching a team full of quality footballers, there is logic to wanting to play in a more front-footed and imposing manner, but how well tactics are performed depend on the skillset of the players asked to do them.
The big questions come in the form of Elliot Anderson and his midfield partners.
Anderson - naturally more of a roaming midfielder - leans on his physical strengths. At Nottingham Forest, he defended intensely, pressed high and wide, and contributed to attacks. This season, Maresca and his staff have looked to mould him into more of a sitting midfielder after the departure of Rodri in the summer.
Learning that role will take time, as it did for Rodri when he first joined.
It is not problematic in its own right to try to coach a player into a key role, but City have looked exposed through the middle of the pitch more often in recent games.
Anderson, who has largely impressed, has played to his habit - stepping out of a holding midfield position to attempt to press or track opposition players, often looking to win the ball back. Clever opponents have used this to drag him out of position before finding players through the middle.
1 of 2
With City looking to press high and often in a man-to-man fashion, Anderson has had to cover more space with his partners in midfield lacking the physicality required to support him.
When City are in possession, Enzo Fernandez - often one of City's midfield three - makes frequent attacking runs off the ball into the final third. When this happens, City can find themselves with as few as two or three players behind the ball, giving opponents favourable conditions to counter-attack if they can break the initial press.
For Maresca, the issue is less around the shape, and more around losing the ball in the first instance. After the loss to Forest, he said: "You concede transitions when you lose the ball, and when you don't win duels."
Further concerns arise when assessing the skillset of the players behind Anderson.
Gianluigi Donnarumma is not a goalkeeper renowned for his ball-playing ability. The defensive cohort are serviceable on the ball but have made costly errors under pressure, playing out from the back, this season too.
Guardiola's solution to mitigate some of these issues last season came in the form of asking midfielders to shoulder more ball-playing responsibility.
The loss of Rodri and especially Bernardo Silva, who would drop deep and take City from their own goal into midfield alone, have made City's problems more obvious.
As good as Anderson is, he is not a player who can single-handedly resolve build-up play as Bernardo Silva did, but Ayyoub Bouaddi may be somebody that could be used in this manner as we saw him against Brazil's press in the World Cup.

Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
- Published
Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
Demonstrations were also planned later on Wednesday, with the biggest protests expected in Madrid and Barcelona. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."
However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved.
Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads.
The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.
The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.
Rental prices in the capital have soared in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50m sq apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460 (£2,056).
That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform.
Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes.
And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing.
"Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes.

  - Published23 September

  - Published5 October
The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain.
PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election.
Sánchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike."
Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid.
Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights.
The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.
Álvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment.
He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay €1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills.
"It's absolutely crazy… with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."
He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible."
With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible".
However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing.
"This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said.
Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election.
Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector.
Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.

History has a warning for the new Democratic majority
The midterms marked the biggest electoral landslide in more than 50 years. What happened after the others?
We’re a week past the midterms now and the dust has largely settled. Sure, you still have some uncalled House races in a handful of states, and we’re still waiting with bated breath to meet the next senators from Mississippi and Alaska.
But even without those final numbers, we can say a couple things for sure: First, last week’s blue wave was the largest in more than 50 years. And second, Democrats’ real work has only just begun.
This week, the incoming members of Congress — roughly seven weeks out from their official debut — are in Washington, DC, to set up their offices and meet their new coworkers. Democrats still have to choose new leaders or stick with their old ones. And once they’ve reached some sort of consensus on that, they’ll start to confront the final boss: President Donald Trump.
“They’re in control, but they’re really not in control,” Trump told Fox News last week, of the Democrats’ prospects in a split government. “Because they can send over, you know, 50 different great bills that they’re all excited about and I send them back with a nice stamp.”
Fortunately, amid all this jockeying and post-election euphoria, we do have some precedent to fall back on. After all, this blue wave was historically big — but not totally unheard-of. Midterm elections also ushered in huge partisan majorities in the early 1970s and 1990s. And that history suggests that Democrats have won a chance…not a guarantee.
Go a little deeper
You have to go back to the Watergate era to find a blue wave as big as last week’s. The year was 1974, the vibes were alternatingly grim and groovy, and American voters were looking for change after the scandals of Richard Nixon’s presidency.
Democrats already controlled the House and the Senate, but that year’s midterms ushered in a class of even younger and more liberal lawmakers. And these so-called Watergate babies came to play: They helped extend a run of post-Watergate reforms that opened up congressional proceedings, required financial disclosures from senior officials, and strengthened oversight of federal agencies.
But 52 years later, the 1974 blue wave isn’t exactly remembered as an unrivaled success — for the Dems or for democracy. Ronald Reagan became president just six years later, and both he and other presidents since have weakened the reforms of the mid-’70s.
The push to make government more transparent — by inviting television cameras into hearings, for example — also arguably made Congress a more polarized and confrontational place as lawmakers were newly incentivized to be less candid, more performative, and more rigid in their ideology.
Other, more conservative waves have also run up against the limits of congressional power. The political scientist Robert A. Strong points to Newt Gingrich’s 1994 “revolution,” which ended four decades of Democratic House control.
But that Republican sweep, far from delivering Gingrich’s vision of a dramatically smaller government in one fell swoop, triggered bitter confrontations with President Bill Clinton, including debt-ceiling standoffs and government shutdowns. When major legislation did become law, it required compromise: A sweeping welfare overhaul only passed after Clinton vetoed prior versions twice.
In some ways, these challenges are fairly intuitive. Even when one party controls the White House and both chambers of Congress, it still has to reconcile competing factions and navigate procedural hurdles in the Senate. And when control of those branches is split between parties, as it will be soon, you end up with even bigger obstacles — like a veto-happy president.
Given that, Democratic voters might want to temper their expectations just a little. As my colleague Andrew Prokop laid out earlier this month, Democratic bills will — even in this new, blue environment — likely only pass through compromise or fierce confrontation.
Making electoral history is one thing, as history itself shows. But making legislative history is an altogether tougher proposition.

When people think of cancer, factors such as genetics and family history often come to mind. However, for endometrial cancer, everyday lifestyle choices can also play a significant role. Understanding these risk factors can help women make informed decisions about their health.
Endometrial cancer, which begins in the endometrium, that is, the inner lining of the uterus, is one of the most common gynaecological cancers in developed countries. Over the past several years, its incidence has been rising in India. It is mostly diagnosed after menopause, but other conditions can also increase risk.

Tubi users can now create and share playlists of movies and shows available on the streaming service.
Tubi is a free ad-supported streaming television (FAST) service that has both live channels and on-demand content.
Today, the Fox-owned company announced “Mixtapes” as a way for users to make watchlists from Tubi’s “nearly 400,000 movies and TV episodes,” Tubi’s announcement said, adding:
They can give each mixtape a title and description and arrange the entertainment inside in whatever order feels right to them. Viewers can build one entirely on their own, or describe what they’re looking for and let Tubi offer a starting place that they can edit, rearrange, or rebuild entirely. When their mixtape is finished, they can publish and share it with other people or keep it for themselves.
Tubi’s Mixtapes website already features numerous playlists, including: “Millennial Memory Lane”—with movies like Cruel Intentions (1999) and The Fifth Element (1997) and shows such as Everybody Hates Chris (2005–2009) and Degrassi: The Next Generation (2001–2015); and “Bald Baddies”—which includes Fast & Furious Presents: Hobbs & Shaw (2019) and Central Intelligence (2016).
Watching a Mixtape doesn’t require a Tubi account, but making one does.
Tubi’s Mixtapes comes at a time when streaming service providers are seeking a way to address the content fragmentation that’s frequently cited as a frustration among streaming users, as well as users struggling to find something to watch. Gracenote’s “2025 State of Play” report, for instance, surveyed 3,000 consumers in the US, Brazil, France, Germany, Mexico, and the UK and found that “nearly 33 percent of streaming users feel content and service fragmentation negatively impacts their TV experience.”

Farm-fire incidents across six northern Indian states fell by 11.5% to 9,590 since the start of the stubble-burning season on 15 September, from 10,832 in the year-ago period, showed satellite-based data from the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR).
Punjab continued to account for the largest share of farm fires from 15 September to 10 November, reporting 5,002 incidents, followed by Madhya Pradesh with 2,145 and Rajasthan with 1,335. Uttar Pradesh recorded 689 cases, while Uttarakhand and Haryana reported 213 and 206 incidents, respectively.
During the year-ago period, Punjab recorded 4,195 farm-fire incidents, followed by Madhya Pradesh (2,517) and Uttar Pradesh (1,902). Rajasthan reported 1,385 incidents, while Uttarakhand and Haryana recorded 470 and 363, respectively.
Farm-fire incidents across the six states have consistently declined, from 46,399 during 15 September-10 November 2022 to 36,415 in 2023, 17,314 in 2024, 10,832 in 2025, and 9,590 in 2026.
Pollution crisis
The decline in farm fires is significant, given their contribution to Delhi’s pollution. While they account for around 2.25% of the city’s annual pollution, their share rises to 12-40% during the winter stubble-burning season.
The National Capital Region (NCR) grapples with poor air quality throughout the year, with conditions typically worsening between November and February as slower winds trap pollutants over the region for longer.
According to Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data, Delhi recorded its worst daily average Air Quality Index (AQI) of 2026 on 6 November, at 382. The average AQI stood at 376 on Diwali, 8 November, making it the most polluted Diwali in five years.
Delhi’s air quality has remained in the poor to very poor categories so far this month. The city’s AQI stood at 313 at 4.05pm on Wednesday, placing it in the very poor category.
Experts believe the actual number of farm fires is higher than reported. “The actual number of farm-fire incidents is likely to be much higher than the reported figures, as satellite-based monitoring may fail to detect fires when the sky is covered with smoke. This means the available data may not fully capture the scale of stubble burning," said Surendra Kumar Dhaka, professor of atmospheric physics at Rajdhani College, University of Delhi.
He said there is a need for stricter enforcement of existing regulations and stronger monitoring at the ground level to curb farm-fire incidents.
Stubble burning can account for up to 40% of Delhi’s air pollution this year, depending on weather conditions, added Dhaka.
The burning question
There is a need to bring about behavioural change among farmers, said Umendra Dutt, executive director of Kheti Virasat Mission, a non-profit civil society action group that promotes natural and organic farming.
“Awareness and outreach efforts should not be limited to the two months preceding the stubble-burning season. Instead, the government should undertake year-round activities to educate farmers, promote alternative crop-residue management practices and encourage their adoption at the grassroots level.”
A policy paper titled Innovative Approaches for Sustainable Crop Residue Management, published by the National Academy of Agricultural Sciences, New Delhi, says curbing residue burning requires a three-pronged approach focused on avoidance, awareness and adoption.
A sustainable strategy should include crop diversification, with part of the paddy area shifted to maize, supported by assured markets and economic incentives. Developing high-yielding rice varieties that produce less straw and expanding access to crop residue management (CRM) machinery can encourage in-situ residue recycling and ensure timely wheat sowing. Satellite-based monitoring can also improve the tracking of CRM adoption.
Mint's query emailed to the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) remained unanswered.
To curb pollution, Delhi and its neighbouring states have drawn up a coordinated seven-month programme, with a greater focus on public outreach, behavioural change, and preventing crop-residue burning ahead of winter.
The programme, covering September 2026 to March 2027, targets industrial emissions, diesel generator sets, road dust, construction and demolition waste, municipal solid waste, agricultural residue and vehicular emissions.

Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader
- Published
Joseph Kabila was a commander in the rebel alliance that brought his father to power in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1997, went on to succeed him as president and now, at the age of 55, he is a rebel leader once again.
In an even stranger twist, the man he has sworn to topple is the very man he handed power to after 18 years at the helm, and with whom he had formed a coalition government after stepping down. While one of the rebel groups he had fought against as president is part of his new alliance.
His career reflects the ever-shifting nature of politics in DR Congo, where alliances are ephemeral, with the use of force a constant threat.
When Kabila was named leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), earlier this month, it confirmed what many Congolese had long believed – that the former president was working with the M23 rebels, who last year seized much of eastern DR Congo, including the region's main cities of Goma and Bukavu.
Nevertheless, the confirmation sent shockwaves through DR Congo – a vast country two-thirds the size of western Europe, with huge deposits of gold, diamonds and even more importantly minerals used to make everything from the mobile phones to batteries for electric vehicles.
For Kabila, the alliance offers a possible route back to the power he had lost.
For the M23 rebels, his involvement brings the experience and networks of a former head of state to a movement whose military advances have yet to translate into broad national legitimacy.
But it is far from certain that they can achieve their stated goal of ousting President Félix Tshisekedi.
Policy analyst Henry-Pacifique Mayala told the BBC that Kabila had been left with few options for regaining political influence.
"He actually was left with no other choice," he said.
Facing a death sentence after being convicted in absentia of treason, as well as US sanctions over his alleged support for the M23, Kabila may have sought assurances that the partnership could serve his interests, Mayala suggested.
"I'm not sure that he is making this huge leap in the dark without having received considerable assurance," Mayala said, adding that the M23's military strength could give Kabila greater leverage in any future negotiations with the Congolese government.
Kabila's involvement also raises questions about whether the conflict could spread beyond the east.
The M23's territorial gains have been concentrated in the country's eastern provinces, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) from the capital, Kinshasa.
Kabila's political networks could give the rebellion a broader reach, but that does not necessarily mean it has the capacity to extend its military campaign across the country.
And it is not clear how far Kabila's national reach extends.
While he was in power, after being named following the mysterious assassination of his father Laurent in 2001, he was often seen as something of an outsider in Kinshasa. He was far more at home speaking Swahili, the lingua franca of eastern DR Congo, as well as east Africa, rather than the Lingala spoken in Kinshasa.
His father's rebel group actually walked across the country to Kinshasa, also starting in the east, over a period of seven months, before eventually seizing power in May 1996 and ousting long-time ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, who had governed the country as his own personal property for more than 30 years.
There is little suggestion that Joseph Kabila's FRN would try to repeat that feat but earlier this week, he likened Tshisekedi to Mobutu.
"You have a tyrant who wants to impose and dictate what he thinks is right and not necessarily follow the constitution, which is the supreme law of the land," he told Conspiracy Trackers Great Lakes (CTGL), a pro-M23 research group.
Kabila accused the government of using the death penalty, ending the moratorium introduced during his own presidency, to intimidate civilians, politicians and members of the military, as well as himself.
"This is personal," he said.
He framed his confrontation with Tshisekedi as a fight against authoritarianism, invoking Section 64 of the constitution, which calls on citizens to resist anyone who seizes power or exercises it in violation of constitutional provisions.
Tshisekedi is rumoured to be planning to change the constitution to allow him to seek a third term in office, with the C64 coalition of opposition parties named after that same section of the constitution, campaigning against such a move.
But in a sign that he may not get everything his own way, the C64 coalition this week refused to back Kabila's rebellion, saying that Congo's multiple security crises cannot be resolved by military means alone. Instead, it announced plans to seek direct talks with both Tshisekedi and Kabila in pursuit of what it called a "genuine and inclusive national dialogue".
Richard Moncrieff, a Great Lakes analyst with the International Crisis Group think-tank, said President Tshisekedi retained substantial advantages.
"Tshisekedi has strong American backing. He has a lot of money. And he generally controls the political system and, as far as we can see, the military system," Moncrieff said.
In his first public reaction to Kabila being named FRN leader, Tshisekedi was damning: "In my view, it's simply proof that he has never loved this country, and even less its inhabitants," he said last week.
And yet Kabila is widely believed to have helped ensure that Tshisekedi succeeded him, rather than Martin Fayulu, who was the true winner of the 2018 elections, according to leaked results provided by the Catholic Church, which had observers around the country.
Indeed, the former head of the electoral commission who announced Tshisekedi as the winner, Corneille Nangaa, has said as much.
Now one of Kabila's deputies in the FRN, he claimed that Kabila and Tshisekedi had reached a political agreement before the final election results were announced.
"I can confirm that I helped draft the deal," Nangaa told France 24 in September 2023. "Tshisekedi is a liar. He knows there was an agreement and he knows what was contained in the deal."
Tshisekedi has maintained that he won the election legitimately.

After the disputed election, Kabila and Tshisekedi entered a power-sharing arrangement that allowed Kabila's coalition to retain control of parliament even after Tshisekedi took office in January 2019.
The arrangement unravelled in December 2020, when Tshisekedi moved to break Kabila's parliamentary dominance and build his own majority. The former allies became rivals, and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in South Africa.
From exile, Kabila's criticism of Tshisekedi grew louder.
He returned to DR Congo in 2025 and appeared in rebel-held Goma. In September that year, a military court sentenced him to death in absentia on charges including treason and financing violence in eastern Congo.
At the time, he rejected the accusations.
Yet another intriguing sub-plot to the announcement is Kabila's relationship with Rwanda's President Paul Kagame.
In the early years of his presidency, ties were strained between DR Congo and Rwanda, which accused its giant neighbour of not doing enough to remove ethnic Hutu militias involved in the 1994 Rwandan genocide from its territory. Their presence in what is now DR Congo has been used to justify Rwanda's repeated military involvement in its giant neighbour, going back to its backing of Laurent Kabila's rebellion.
The M23 was formed in 2012, vowing to stand up for the rights of ethnic Tutsis and to protect them against these militias, but also battling the Congolese army, under the control of Joseph Kabila.
From the start Rwanda was accused of backing them. It has always denied these allegations, as it still does despite overwhelming evidence.
However, relations later improved and Kabila's government worked with Rwanda against the Hutu militias.
Alex Adams, Africa programme director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Kabila's appointment as rebel leader could bring his interests into alignment with those of Rwanda's president, even though their objectives differ.
"Kabila wants to recover political influence nationally, while Kagame is primarily concerned with Rwanda's security and strategic position in eastern Congo. This is an alignment of convenience rather than a partnership built on deep trust," he said.
Policy analyst Mayala said Kabila's involvement could help Rwanda counter accusations that it was interfering in Congo's internal affairs.
"This is a former president. It's finally a Congolese rebellion," he said.
Even before the announcement of Kabila as the rebellion's leader, fighting was continuing despite a peace accord overseen by Donald Trump last year.
Part of that deal saw the US sign an agreement to extract DR Congo's mineral wealth and the US has since seemed to side with Tshisekedi by imposing sanctions on various Rwandan officials and bodies, accusing them of prolonging the violence.
Elections are scheduled for 2028, but Tshisekedi has warned that fighting in the east could delay voting.
Against this backdrop, Kabila has questioned whether elections alone can resolve the country's political crisis.
"Does Congo need elections or a revolution?" he asked, arguing that lasting peace required a fundamental overhaul of the country's executive and legislature.
International security analyst Ovigwe Eguegu argues that Kabila is banking on military force to regain political influence, while Tshisekedi seems to be trying to extend his time in office beyond what the constitution allows.
"It looks like the Congolese people are going to lose either way, because neither of these two sides present a credible economic transformation plan for both the eastern Congo and the entirety of the country," Eguegu said.

'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
- Published
A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.
The Odyssey, which was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, was placed under arrest on Sunday morning, Singapore's court records show. Local authorities say the vessel is currently anchored in Singapore port waters.
Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".
The crew onboard are reported to be well, says Singapore's port authority.
"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," AFP news agency reported the authority saying.
There were no passengers on board, it added.
Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.
The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024, was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.
Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.
"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.
However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.
While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.
CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.
It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.
Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.
As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.
It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.
