Chris Harrison, who spent nearly 20 years working on The Bachelor, is back in the dating pool with new reality series The Vow.
But Harrison, who left the ABC franchise in somewhat unceremonious fashion five years ago, has vowed to do things differently with the Fox Nation show, which was first revealed by Deadline earlier this year.
Firstly, he’s done with eliminations, but he’s also found faith and is now working with his wife, Lauren Zima, a former senior producer and host of Entertainment Tonight, who covered The Bachelor for years through the Roses and Rosé recap show.
After he left The Bachelor franchise, Harrison was regularly pitched other dating formats, but he felt they were “gimmicky”.
Watch on Deadline
“Right when I left, we were being pitched ideas that felt gimmicky that didn’t have the depth, and I [wanted] to wait until we found something that had soul, that we could really lean into and that’s what The Vow became. It was hopefully the most authentic, intentional dating show ever. Anything short of that was didn’t seem like was worthy of our time and effort,” Harrison told Deadline. “If it never felt right again, then we never would have done a show. But all of a sudden, I think more than ever, there is a need and a want for love, and a need and a want for a great love story to be told, so the timing was perfect to create The Vow.”
Zima added that Harrison had made people feel connected to him throughout his career and they wanted to replicate that. “If he was going to come back with anything, it needed to be something that was deeply authentic and that was about the pursuit of a real soulmate type of love, which means a lot to both of us. I think we both think of each other as our soulmates, and we wanted to work on something that felt meaningful. Our business is hard, and you give it your all, and so it really helps when it feels like it’s coming from a deep, true place,” she told Deadline.
The pair worked with Lionsgate Alternative Television on the project before selling it to Fox Nation.
One of the main format points of The Vow, which stars 30-year-old Jace Cates as its first bachelor alongside ten single women, was the fact that there were no eliminations.
Harrison said that elimination ceremonies and dates to Bora Bora didn’t feel “real” or “authentic”.
“It was the removal of a lot of things that was scary as a producer because you lean on those things to create moments, create drama, to get you in and out of ad breaks, get you in and out of episodes, to create cliffhangers etc. To pull away from that is actually a very scary process, and you really have to trust what you’re doing is going to deliver, and when you do something for the first time, there is a bit of unknown. There’s a bit of hope, and you trust your instincts. You got to trust what you’re doing, but you hope it’s there at the end of the day,” he added.
Zima said that they didn’t have a “roadmap” for such a process, but wanted to be more agile in filming those real-life moments.
“Audiences today are really smart. We live in a world where so much of that fourth wall has been broken and the curtain has been pulled back, and so we certainly wanted it to be as authentic as possible, and that means they’ve seen these contrived ceremonies for many years. I think it’s meaningful to see it’s all stripped away now,” she added.
The pair weren’t even sure if Cates would eliminate any of the women in the first episode, which premiered today (November 11).
“We kind of assumed he wouldn’t send anybody home. We would have been fine with that. We’re just getting to know everybody, and right away he just wasn’t feeling it with one woman, and he wanted to set the tone, that was 100% on him,” said Harrison. “All of us in the control room, that’s kind of the moment we were like, okay, this is the ride we’re on. This is going to be wild. The unpredictability, and not knowing what’s coming next, is going to be the drama.”
Having worked on The Bachelor franchise for so long, Harrison also had to unlearn some of the tropes that made that show work. He was also surrounded by people who had also worked on The Bachelor. These included Louis Caric and Elan Gale who both worked on the Warner Bros. TV-produced ABC franchise for around ten years, as well as director Michael Shea and casting director Lindsay Liles.
Talking of The Bachelor, Harrison and the team received a cease-and-desist notice from Warner Bros., which produces the ABC show through its Warner Horizon arm, that claimed images of red rose petals, a mansion and the use of the words ‘The Bachelor’ followed by a man in a tux in the trailer impinged its IP. Fox’s counsel hit back and said that WB attorneys “wrongly assume that Warner Bros. holds any intellectual property rights whatsoever in a falling roses motif or in the words ‘The Bachelor’ when used colloquially to describe a single man.”
Harrison believes that his former employers were making it “personal”.
“You can’t put a cease and desist on love,” he said. “I’ve been away for five years. There have been dozens of other dating shows. They’ve come after one very publicly. Is it a coincidence? I don’t think so. On the flip side, there are many friends of ours on that show still, people I care about and this business is hard. I don’t wish anybody to lose their jobs. There’s enough room for everybody to be successful.”
Harrison admitted that he always watches the ratings of The Bachelor, which is gearing up for season 30 in March 2027, having been off the air since January 2025.
What followed that was The Bachelorette initially skipping a cycle, followed by the departure of its showrunners Claire Freeland and Bennett Graebner, who had been promoted in the wake of the departure of creator Mike Fleiss following a misconduct investigation, before season 22 of The Bachelorette was pulled after The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Taylor Frankie Paul became embroiled in a domestic assault investigation.
Harrison has joked that you don’t mind if you ex gains weight, but what you don’t want to see is the “revenge bod”.
“I wish them well. I hope they clean up their mess and get back on track. I think it does all of us good. I think a rising tide lifts all boats, and so there was the side of me that felt, yeah, you guys are making it personal, but no ill will here. I take it as flattery. I mean, I think they see something coming down the tracks, and it’s a train,” he added.
The Vow was also the first show that Zima has exec produced. “I’m grateful for my journalism background and how much storytelling matters in that field and how it applies here,” she said. “I was honored to be on that set all day, every day. I wanted to soak up and learn as much as I could to know what I didn’t know.”
Harrison added, “Having an experienced, brilliant journalist in the room, she’s so adept at pulling on a thread and extrapolating what that thread is going to lead to, and telling that story, and seeing that journalism brain go into reality TV was brilliant.”
The pair were buoyed by the casting process and believe there are plenty more fish in the sea if the show is successful and renewed.
“I think we have kicked over the proverbial ant hill, and we are hearing from so many women,” Harrison said. “These aren’t Instagram famous people. They don’t have a million followers. They’re just diamonds in the rough. These are people who truly want this life. In the blessing of seasons two through ten, I think we can find many more. By the way, if we can’t, we won’t do a season.”
Harrison called the whole process “refreshing”. “I just think you’re going to see and hear conversations you’ve never seen on reality TV before,” he said. “I think people are really going to like this and feel like this is oddly something new.”

- The claim that Democrats won the 2026 U.S. midterm elections in all the states that don't require people to show ID to vote is true.
- According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, 14 states and Washington, D.C., do not require voters to show ID at the polls.
- Election results from The Associated Press showed that Democrats won a Senate seat, more than half of a state's U.S. House seats — or both — in those 14 states.
- However, there was no evidence that Democrats won races only in states that had no voter ID requirements. Democrats won Senate seats or the majority of a state's House races in several states with ID requirements. Conversely, Republicans won some individual races in states that do not require ID on polling day.
- Snopes based our assessment of this claim on midterm election projections from the AP. Though many news outlets "call" races on election night, results are not official until a state's elections officials have certified them.
Following the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, a claim circulated that Democrats won all the U.S. states that do not require people to show ID to vote.
For example, one X user wrote (archived):
Fun Midterms fact:
- Dems won all of the states that do not require voter ID at the polls. 100%.
- States that GOP won such as Florida, Alabama, Wyoming etc., require voter ID
- GOP won none of the no-ID states such as California, New York, Illinois, etc. Zero.
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived). Days before the election, the Australian TV journalist James Morrow made a similar claim, saying, "So, are people going to start to put two and two together and say, gosh, why do all these Democrats keep running in cities where you don't need ID?"
It's unclear what the social media posts mean by "winning a state." For the purposes of this fact check, we've defined "winning a state" as winning a Senate seat, more than half of a state's U.S. House seats, or both.
The claim that Democrats won all the U.S. states that don't require voters to show ID at the polls is true, though election results from The Associated Press showed that Democrats also won a Senate seat or more than half of a state's House seats in several states that do require voters to show ID. Conversely, Republicans won individual races in states that do not require ID on polling day.
According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, which collates legislation from all the states on various topics, 14 states and Washington, D.C., do not impose any ID requirements on voters at the polls. Democrats won Senate seats or made up more than half of the state's representatives (or both) in all 14 of those states. (Washington, D.C., does not elect a senator and has a non-voting representative in the House.)
However, Democrats also won Senate seats or made up more than half of the state's representatives in several states that do require voters to show ID at the polls. Democrats won a majority in the Senate and House in three states that require voters to show ID, meaning there was no evidence to suggest that Democrats could win only in states with no voter ID requirements at the polls.
It's worth noting that we based our assessment of this claim on midterm election projections from the AP. Though many news outlets "call" races on election night, results are not official until a state's elections officials have certified them.
The breakdown
According to the NCSL, these 14 states don't ask voters to show any ID at the polls: California, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Vermont.
The remaining 36 states have laws that request or require voters to show some form of ID at the polls. Some of these states specifically require photo ID.
While it's true Democrats won Senate seats or made up more than half of the state's representatives in all 14 states without voter ID requirements, that's only half the story.
Democrats also won a Senate seat or made up more than half of the state's representatives in several that do require voter ID: Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Texas, Virginia and Washington.
In Iowa, for example, Democrat Josh Turek flipped Republican Sen. Joni Ernst's seat. Democrats also won three of the state's four races for the House.
According to Iowa's secretary of state, voters must show "an Iowa driver's license or non-operator ID, U.S. passport, U.S. military ID or veteran's ID, tribal ID/document, or Iowa voter ID" at the polls. Iowa elections officials also require photo ID if someone is registering to vote on Election Day.
Michigan, New Hampshire and Rhode Island all require voters to show photo ID at the polls. Democrats won a majority of the seats in the House and a Senate seat in these three states.
Because the claim that Democrats "won" all the states that don't require voter ID is true, the claim that Republicans only won states that did require voter ID is also true.
Republican candidates didn't win any Senate seats in states with no voter ID requirements. However, they did win a minority of the available House seats in nine of the 14 states with no voter ID at the requirements.
For example, Republicans won six out of 17 House seats in Pennsylvania and six out of 26 in New York, which are both states that don't require any form of voter ID at the polls.
Democratic wins in 'no ID' states not a sign of fraud
There is no evidence tying Democrat wins in states that don't require voter ID at the polls to election fraud theories such as noncitizen voting. Snopes reported in advance of the midterm elections that noncitizens rarely vote in U.S. elections.
Based on accounts from elections officials, we found that existing protections throughout the registration process would make it extremely difficult for bad actors to register enough ineligible voters to sway elections. We also found that existing protections already work to ensure that only eligible voters can register and cast a ballot.
According to the Fair Elections Center, a nonpartisan voting rights and election reform organization, all the 14 states that do not require voter ID at the polls require voters to submit either a state driver's license number, state ID number or part of their Social Security number when registering to vote.
There was also no evidence to suggest that Democrats could win only in states that did not have voter ID requirements at the polls.
For further reading, follow Snopes' coverage of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.

As Kolkata choked on toxic air following Diwali and Kali Puja celebrations, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari accused those raising concerns over firecracker pollution of being communists opposed to Hindu traditions. His remarks were consistent with the concerted push by a section of the Right wing to portray criticism of firecrackers as an attack on Hindu religious practices. However, among those complaining about noise levels and pollution in Kolkata were members of Adhikari’s own party and cabinet.
The Bengal CM made the remarks while addressing the media during a visit to the coastal town of Digha on Monday, where he had gone to attend an administrative meeting and visit the Kali Puja organised by the Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Traders Association.
Speaking to reporters, Adhikari said, “There has been an awakening of Sanatan in this state, and some people have a problem with that. The people making these allegations (about firecrackers) had turned Hindu religious festivals into cultural fests… These people do not apply ‘tika’ or religious markings on their foreheads, they do not wear ‘dors’ or religious threads on their wrists, nor do they wear tulsi beads around their necks.”
Adhikari further said, “The communists are raising this issue of firecrackers. We have controlled it in accordance with the Supreme Court’s directives. Firecrackers were burst in some places even after 10 pm, and the police took necessary action. We have stopped DJs, and we do not want environmental pollution. But people will have fun during Diwali. They will celebrate with lights and burst firecrackers. Where is the problem with that?”
While acknowledging that firecrackers had been burst beyond the time limit prescribed by the Supreme Court, Adhikari sought to deflect criticism by pointing to action taken by the administration.
“Those complaining that sound crackers were burst for a few hours longer than the time stipulated by the Supreme Court should know that the Pollution Control Board and the police are taking action against such violations. I would request those complaining about firecrackers to also congratulate the state government for stopping DJs. I will not say that DJ incidents did not happen in remote corners, but I did not hear them blaring, at least near the roads,” he said.
Firecrackers can Cure Diseases, Says Bengal Minister, then Apologises
According to the Supreme Court’s directives, only green firecrackers were allowed to be burst between 8 pm and 10 pm on Diwali. However, statements by ministers, the West Bengal Police’s deletion of a post urging responsible Diwali celebrations, and the general perception that a BJP government would not impose restrictions on Hindu festivals had collectively sent out a clear message: When it came to celebrating a majoritarian festival, the rules could be bent, if not ignored altogether.
BJP leader and Tollygunge MLA Papia Adhikary said on Monday, “Our honourable chief minister has said that people will definitely burst firecrackers. How can we celebrate Kali Puja without firecrackers? But we will burst them in accordance with the instructions of the local police station. Also, many diseases can be prevented simply by lighting firecrackers.”
Although Adhikary later apologised and backtracked on her statement, claiming that the media had misinterpreted her remarks, the message had already got across.
A section of social media users also began targeting dissenting voices who tried to reason with their fellow citizens. A user named Partha Pratim Kundu, who describes himself as a wildlife photographer, asked in a post how elderlies, children and birds and animals survived in earlier times when there was no curb on firecrackers.
Another Facebook user, Chayan Mukherjee, who hailed the chief minister’s indulgence on firecrackers, claimed in a post that “most of the Indian environmentalists and human rights activists, as well as professors at various institutions, receive funding from outside to oppose the country’s development.”
Domkal’s CPI(M) MLA Mostafijur Rahaman Rana had urged people to celebrate Diwali as a festival of lights, without noise and loud firecrackers. BJP MLA Tarunjyoti Tiwari gave the issue a communal twist by asking whether the legislator would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’.
State BJP leader Keya Ghosh also criticised Mostafijur Rahaman for advocating a noise-free and smoke-free Diwali.
The lone CPIM MLA of West Bengal had wished smokeless, soundless Diwali.
Would he wish a bl0odless Eid too?
#JustAsking https://t.co/SELbzbuJNF
— Keya Ghosh (@keyakahe) November 9, 2026
AQI in 500-600 Range
The political messaging was accompanied by widespread violations on the ground. A large section of the public openly flouted firecracker regulations. Almost all media outlets reported that loud firecrackers were burst throughout the night severely inconveniencing elderlies, children and also pets, birds and stray animals.
Kolkata’s AQI reached 623 around 11 pm on Sunday night, reported The telegraph. At 12.51 am on Monday, IQAir classified the city’s air quality as hazardous, recording an AQI of 532, with PM2.5 at 342 and PM10 at 405. Both particulate matter concentrations were several times higher than the WHO’s recommended limits.
Left with no other option, residents in several localities took matters into their own hands, protesting against the rampant bursting of firecrackers and intervening to stop it. Facebook user Anitesh Chakraborty narrated his experience in a post.
Chakraborty went up to a neighbouring apartment’s rooftop around 1.45 am to ask people bursting firecrackers to stop. While some residents supported his objection, others on nearby rooftops mocked him with gestures and taunts. Nevertheless, the intervention succeeded in stopping the firecrackers. He observed that the rooftops of apartment buildings had become spaces where people felt free to flout restrictions, and argued people to raise their voices against such violations.
According to a report by the Times of India, by 1 am, the West Bengal Pollution Control Board had received 84 noise-related complaints, while Kolkata Police had recorded 434 complaints.
Police rounded up 371 people for bursting illegal firecrackers, arresting 205 of them. Another 387 people were arrested for disorderly conduct. Several commentators pointed out that the most effective way to curb the use of illegal firecrackers was to stop their manufacture and sale. This year, only 238.6 kg of such products were seized, compared to 853 kg last year.
Kolkata’s high-rise buildings were particular hotspots for violations of firecracker and noise restrictions. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari himself acknowledged that the rules could not be enforced in every high-rise apartment building, as the state did not have enough police personnel.
Even hospitals located in silence zones were not spared. According to a report by The Telegraph, areas near hospitals such as B C Roy, R G Kar, M R Bangur and Sishumangal also faced onslaught of loud firecrackers.
To Celebrate Responsibly or Not? Bengal Police in a Fix
Signs of this situation had emerged earlier, when the West Bengal Police deleted a firecracker awareness post within hours of publishing it, as previously reported by Alt News.
Published on the morning of November 5 with the caption, “Please celebrate responsibly. It’s our Diwali too!”, the AI-generated poster featured two stray cats and a dog shivering due to the loud noise of firecrackers. However, it was deleted within three hours.
The post’s comment section was flooded with threatening messages directed at police and familiar Right-wing arguments, including questions about whether the police would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’ and why the police and administration interfered only in Hindu festivals.
Similarly, Delhi Police, too, deleted a firecracker awareness post, while the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) removed a video featuring actor Dia Mirza advocating for a pollution-free Diwali from its social media accounts. Both decisions followed social media outrage from BJP-RSS supporters who claimed that the posts hurt Hindu religious sentiments.
A similar message by AISA leader Neha Bora also faced backlash from the far-right social media ecosystem.
It is that time of the year where our conversations will be accompanied by sore throats and respiratory problems.
But who is responsible for this?
Clean air and a pollution free city is a right and must be demanded from the government. https://t.co/SZHAC7l1fl
— Neha (@neha_aisa) November 4, 2026
BJP MLAs Complain about Noise Levels
Although a section of the Right wing encouraged unrestrained celebrations during Diwali and Kali Puja in the name of upholding Hindu traditions, some voices within the BJP struck a different note.
BJP leader and Sonarpur Dakshin MLA Roopa Ganguly tagged Kolkata Police in a post on Facebook stating she was unable to sleep because of the noise of firecrackers. However, the post is no longer available now.
State urban development minister Agnimitra Paul was seen roaming around the city in a police vehicle, attempting to curb the firecracker menace.
Paul said, “Please think about other people. Consider the condition of the elderly and the sick. The firecrackers are bursting so loudly that my heart is trembling.”
However, these interventions came too little, too late. The ruling dispensation had, through its rhetoric and its reluctance to enforce restrictions, effectively given people a free hand to flout the law, with the environment and public health bearing the consequences.

This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026
Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.

Nintendo sold 5.2 million copies of its “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” remake in just four days, invigorating the Switch 2 platform that had been waiting for a blockbuster hit.
Released on Nov. 5 for $59.99, the 2026 edition is a complete recreation of the 1998 classic action-adventure game for the Nintendo 64 console, replete with new graphics, level and character designs. It ranks among the best-reviewed video games of recent times, earning a score of 96 out of 100 from both players and professional reviewers on aggregator Metacritic.
The Switch 2 console has had an uneven first year on the market, challenged by the rising cost of memory pushing hardware prices up. The fast start by the new “Ocarina of Time” takes the Zelda game past the cumulative sales of “Donkey Kong Bananza,” another popular title from 2025. Only “Mario Kart World,” which was part of a launch bundle with the Switch 2 console, has sold more units so far.
The first Switch, released in 2017, got a huge boost from having “The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild” as a launch-day title that helped draw in gamers from outside the Nintendo ecosystem. Though a remake, the new “Ocarina of Time” may have a similar effect as Nintendo heads into the crucial holiday season.

Does Pickford finally face serious competition for his England place?
- Published
When England head coach Thomas Tuchel decided to pick Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford to face World Cup holders Spain at Wembley in the last international break, it sparked the first stirrings about preparations for life without long-time first choice Jordan Pickford.
Tuchel made it clear Pickford was still England's number one pick, but the simple fact he decided to alternate keepers - playing Trafford in the 3-2 loss to Spain then victory against Czech Republic, before Everton's 32-year-old returned for the Wembley win against the Czechs and the 7-0 rout in Croatia - created intrigue and debate.
England meet Croatia at Wembley on Thursday before facing the biggest test of their Uefa Nations League campaign when the play Spain in Madrid on Sunday.
Tuchel maintains strong faith in Pickford, an outstanding performer for England, but Trafford has at least had the chance to stake his claim.
Tuchel has suggested he may use a rotation system for the pair once more in the upcoming internationals, which will only increase scrutiny on England's goalkeeping position.
'Pickford has to be at the top of his game'
Pickford's record is outstanding since he made his debut in a 0-0 draw against Germany at Wembley in 2017.
In his time as first choice, England have once more emerged as major players on global stage, reaching the World Cup semi-finals in 2018 and 2026, as well as successive Euros finals at the delayed 2020 tournament and Euro 2024.
Measured by Opta stats, Pickford has made only two errors leading to goals in 93 appearances, with 46 clean sheets and a 74% save ratio.
Trafford's international career is in its infancy and, while former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson says Pickford remains Tuchel's undisputed first choice, he believes the head coach's recent strategy is a sensible one.
Robinson told BBC Sport: "It obviously remains to be seen what Thomas Tuchel does in these two England games, but I could see exactly what he was doing by giving James Trafford game time in the last round of matches.
"We are so guilty as a nation of taking one goalkeeper to a tournament who has 70, 80, 90 caps, then the two of three below him could have less than double figures combined."
Robinson's point is proved by the statistic that 80 of Pickford's appearances have been competitive games, with 33 at major tournaments, made up of 19 at the World Cup and 14 at European Championships.
"Competitive and tournament caps give you the type of experience you can't get as a number two or three keeper," said Robinson.
"James Trafford is only 24 and has four caps - two of them competitive - so you can see exactly what Tuchel is doing, looking ahead to a situation where England's recognised number one is not available to him, or there is a drop off in form.
"We saw the last selections and all thought Jordan Pickford's place is under threat and James Trafford is going to be the next number one. I don't think Thomas Tuchel saw it as starkly or simply as that.
"It's a conversation that will definitely take place down the road, but not now. Jordan is England's first choice, in my opinion, rightfully so given his consistency and performances over such a long period.
"This is a debate and conversation for the future definitely because Father Time catches up with everyone eventually and the manager needs to have a contingency plan, but Jordan Pickford very much remains number one and Thomas Tuchel has said as much.
"I don't think Jordan Pickford is under threat for his jersey on a permanent basis any time soon, irrespective of the next selection, but what Tuchel is doing reinforces the impression that he has to be at the top of his game and maintain high standards, which he certainly has been doing when I've watched him this season.
"The biggest compliment I can pay Jordan Pickford is that when you have got that England goalkeeper's shirt, everybody thinks somebody else should be doing it. I know that from personal experience.
"You're there to be shot at, but there has been no noise around Jordan Pickford for a very long time now.
"It has worked both ways for Jordan, James and Thomas Tuchel, and worked very well. Jordan knows he can't rest on his laurels and he will just play regardless. He has to be playing well.
"Is James Trafford challenging Jordan Pickford right now? Yes he is - if Jordan Pickford isn't playing very well and Jordan Pickford is making errors.
"None of the above are true right now because he's playing well for Everton and has done nothing wrong for England."
Robinson also drew on club form to support Pickford's case. Since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford at Everton.
Raya has 39 clean sheets in that time, while Pickford has 27, with Robinson saying: "That's a superb record and all logic tells you Pickford will have to work a lot harder for his clean sheets than David Raya."
Who are Pickford's main competitors?
Trafford staked his claim in those Nations League games against Spain and the Czech Republic, putting him at the forefront of Tuchel's thoughts as the main understudy to Pickford.
Crystal Palace's Dean Henderson is now back in contention after injury and hoping to add to his six caps, although he has not been included in Tuchel's latest squad.
Trafford moved to Leeds United from Manchester City in the summer in a British record deal for a goalkeeper that could be worth up to £45m.
It came after a £23m move to City from Burnley the previous summer, when his hopes of becoming Pep Guardiola's first choice were unexpectedly ended by the decision to sign Gianluigi Donnarumma from Paris St-Germain.
Robinson said: "James Trafford needed that move to Leeds United and Leeds United needed a keeper of his level. This is a match made in heaven.
"And don't forget, in a Premier League career with Burnley, Manchester City and Leeds United, Trafford has only played 42 Premier League games – just a little more than a full season – and one Champions League game. He needs this experience.
"He's got a huge amount of potential, with his quality, all-round goalkeeping and mental approach. He has the potential be England's future number one, which Tuchel clearly sees him to be.
"He has the mentality to reach the very top, which is very difficult because not all goalkeepers have that. It's a tough place to be, a very lonely place to be, but he has the ability to cope with that situation.
"I was at Bournemouth when he made an error in the Leeds United defeat there, but, knowing the type of character he, is it won't faze him. It won't bother him. Because of his personality and his character traits, he has got the ability to go right to the top.
"You'd think Dean Henderson will be back in the squad in due course once he has played more games.
"Jason Steele is in there again, but he's a mentor figure behind the scenes, not someone who will ever start or threaten the established goalkeepers.
"If you rewind back 18 or 24 months, you had Nick Pope, Sam Johnstone, James Trafford, Dean Henderson, Aaron Ramsdale and Jordan Pickford - a real plethora of England goalkeepers.
"Now Nick Pope is not playing at Newcastle United, Sam Johnstone's not in the equation and Aaron Ramsdale is nowhere near."
Ramsdale's decline has been dramatic after leaving Arsenal for Southampton in August 2024, with a loan spell at Newcastle United proving to be unsuccessful. He has effectively been fourth choice at Saints this season, failing to make matchday squads.
Robinson said: "I find Aaron Ramsdale's situation very sad because I believe he's a goalkeeper able to play at the top level.
"He should be in this conversation because he's a goalkeeper I really like, but he's been very unfortunate with selection of clubs and the way their season have gone. I still think there is time for him to come back into the reckoning.
"For now, though, if there is a conversation to be had about England's goalkeepers, then Jordan Pickford and James Trafford is that conversation, with Jordan still very much the number one right now as far as I'm concerned."

Quick Answer
If your Android phone’s battery drains too quickly, try enabling auto-brightness, using dark mode, limiting background apps, reducing screen timeout, and turning off unused features. These 15 practical tips can improve battery life and help maintain battery health.
I cannot function without my phone. It makes my experience better during my walks, jogs, and all other activities throughout the day. Unfortunately, I have to charge my phone multiple times a day or keep a power bank as a backup, just in case. The ease created by my Android phone is instantly undone by the quickly draining battery. Along with the phone, I should carry a cable, an adapter, and a power bank.
In that frustration, I started looking into why my Android phone battery was draining fast. I checked the battery usage data, identified what was causing the drain, and fixed those issues. Now, my battery lasts longer. These are the tips that helped me improve the battery life on my Android phone.
Table of Contents
Android Phone Battery Draining Fast? Try These 10 Tips
I used these tips to improve my Android phone’s battery life on a single charge. You can use the tips that work for you without sacrificing the functionality you need.
Enable Auto Brightness
Brightness affects how visible the display is, irrespective of the light in our surroundings. When we keep the brightness too high, it affects our eyes in the dark. In addition to that, the battery drains too quickly when powering the high brightness for your phone’s display.
If we keep the brightness low, it affects the visibility of our phone’s display during daytime when we are out in the open under the sun. To not affect the visibility and save the battery from draining quickly, we can enable Auto Brightness on our phone.
The auto-brightness feature on our phones adjusts the brightness of our display based on the light in our surroundings. For example, when you are outside where there is abundant sunlight, the auto-brightness feature increases the brightness to make visibility better for you. Similarly, it decreases the brightness when you are in a dark or dimmed environment.
To enable auto-brightness on your phone, open the Settings app and go to Display or Display & brightness settings. The jargon for options varies by manufacturer.
Find Brightness options and toggle the button beside Auto brightness to enable it. You will see the brightness of your screen increase or decrease as per your environment in real time.
Enable Dark Mode
Android phones with OLED or AMOLED displays consume more power for display. If it is set to light mode, a major chunk of battery life goes to power. Setting the screen to dark mode makes it easier on the battery. The battery does not need to power the entire display by switching off the black pixels.
You can enable dark mode in the display settings of your phone. Open the Settings app and find the display settings. Set the display mode to Dark mode.
Dark mode, at first, may look odd. Once you get accustomed to it, there is no going back.
Disable Always-On Display
Always-On Display consumes a significant amount of power from the battery. The display always shows time or notifications even when you are not using the phone actively.
You must disable the Always-On Display feature if you do not have any use for it. Open the Settings app on your Android phone and search for Always-On Display. It will show the option. Tap on it. Toggle the button beside Always-On Display to turn it off.
It may not reduce battery drain noticeably, but small things like these can help optimize battery life.
Set Screen Refresh Rate to Auto
The screen refresh rate feature on Android gives us a smoother display experience. Manufacturers flaunt the screen refresh rate while launching and advertising new smartphones. The higher the refresh rate of a screen is, the more battery it consumes. If you are not a gamer or do not use your phone for experiences that demand a higher refresh rate, you may set the Screen refresh rate to Auto.
Open the Settings app on your phone, search for refresh rate, and open the refresh rate options. Then, set the refresh rate to Auto or Auto-select. Instead of using a higher refresh rate that consumes more battery, your phone now optimizes the screen refresh rate based on the app or activity for a smoother experience. You may also set it to Standard or anything that offers a 60 Hz refresh rate to extend battery life.
If you are a gamer, Auto refresh rate would be the best option.
Decrease Screen Off Time
Screen off time is something we mostly overlook when looking to optimize battery on our phones. If the screen off time is set to a longer time, it consumes battery and aids in draining faster. Small things like these add up and drain the battery.
Open the Settings app on your phone and search for screen off. You can find the Screen off feature in Display settings. Tap on the Screen off or Auto Screen off options (based on your manufacturer) and select a shorter time.
Now, when you do not use the phone, the screen will be turned off as per the time you have selected. The shorter the time, the more you optimize the battery.
Disable Unnecessary Sounds and Vibrations
Sound and vibration for ringtones and notifications are okay. But touch vibrations, keyboard sounds, dial pad tones, lock sounds, and other such sounds or vibrations when we do something on our phone are not necessary. They stress the battery and make it drain faster.
Disabling those unnecessary sounds and vibrations enhances the battery life and saves you from charging the phone frequently.
Open the Settings app on your phone and go to Sound & vibration settings. Go to More sounds (on OxygenOS) or similar settings where you can enable or disable additional sounds, based on your manufacturer.
Then, disable the sounds that you feel are unnecessary by toggling the buttons beside them.
This can optimize battery life, and you can notice the difference within a few hours. Additionally, you can tweak the vibration intensity to optimize your battery further regarding sound and vibration settings.
Check for Apps That Use a Lot of Battery
Android provides detailed battery data where we can see which app is consuming more battery, how long each charge lasts, etc. Using the battery data, we can optimize the apps that consume a lot of battery or install alternatives that consume less battery.
We can access the battery data through the Battery settings. Open Settings and go to Battery settings on your device. Scroll down to the Battery usage by app section in the Battery settings and see which app is using more battery. Tap on the app that is consuming a lot of battery.
It opens the detailed view of battery consumption in the last 24 hours. You can also see options to control battery consumption for the particular app by restricting background activity, etc. Select Restrict background activity if you want to optimize battery and extend its life.
If you want the app to run in the background, you can set it to Smart mode if your manufacturer provides such an option. Repeat the process until you restrict all the power-hungry apps on your device. This significantly improves the life of your battery in each charge.
Turn On the Option to Enter Power Saving Mode Automatically
In the Battery settings, you will find Power saving settings or options. Go to Power saving settings and toggle the button beside Automatically enter Power saving mode. Then, set the battery percentage that should trigger the power saving mode on your device.
Your device will enter Power saving mode when it triggers the battery percentage you set, and it will last longer.
Disable WiFi, Mobile Data, Location, and Bluetooth When Not in Use
You might have noticed your phone battery drains quicker than normal when you pair Bluetooth devices or use location actively. It is better to turn them off when you do not use them.
Keeping WiFi, mobile data, location, and Bluetooth on, even without any usage, consumes a good amount of battery. When you are not actively using any of them, turning them off saves you some battery.
Turn Off Additional Features
There are many features that we rarely use, but consume a good amount of battery. They are live wallpapers, widgets that we do not use, opening web pages and leaving them running in the background, manufacturer apps that run automatically, etc.
Disabling or turning them off saves us a lot of battery. In addition to them, when we install a new app, it asks for notification permissions, location permissions, etc. Disabling notifications for unimportant apps also saves our battery from draining quickly.
These tips, when used together, will optimize your Android device’s battery and extend its life in each charge cycle. Even after doing all this, the battery may drain quickly due to deteriorated battery health. Let’s see how to check and optimize battery health on Android.
How to Optimize Battery Health on Android
The battery on our Android phone degrades with use, and the health drops from 100% to lower levels. The lower the health of your battery, the less power it stores. The capacity keeps on degrading. This is not limited to iPhones. Android phones also started showing battery health. It depends on your manufacturer.
To check the battery health on your Android, you can use third-party apps like Battery Guru or AccuBattery. You may use the app of your choice too, if your manufacturer does not provide an option to look at your battery’s health.
To expand the life and usability of our Android phone, we need to preserve the health of the battery. If not, we may have to replace the battery or the phone altogether. You can preserve the battery health on Android by following these simple tips.
Set a Custom Charging Limit
Android phones let us set a custom charging limit to preserve battery health and protect it from fast degradation of capacity. Manufacturers recommend setting the charging limit to 80- 90% and not beyond that. Charging our phone up to 100% every time is actually not recommended by manufacturers.
We always need to make sure our phone battery never falls below 10% or charges beyond 90%. You can set a custom charging limit in the Battery settings of your phone.
Open the Settings app on your phone and search for Battery health. Open the Battery health options. Toggle the button beside Custom charging limit. Then, set the limit as per the recommendations of the manufacturer.
These options may vary based on your phone manufacturer. The options remain the same, but the wording may change. Follow accordingly to set a custom charging limit.
After setting the custom charging limit, your phone will never charge beyond that percentage. If your manufacturer offers Smart Charging, Adaptive Charging, or Smart Charge options, you may even enable them to let them implement charging patterns based on your charging habits.
Use Chargers or Cables From Device Manufacturers
Charging phones with the available charger is bad for our device’s battery. We must get an adapter and cable made by the manufacturer to save the battery. If they are not available, we must ensure we get charging accessories that are compatible with our device from trusted brands.
Before getting a new charger for your phone, look at the specifications of your device and get the adapter and cable that support the power specified for your device.
Never Let Your Phone Overheat
Batteries degrade faster when they overheat or are exposed to heat. Do not expose your phone to direct sunlight or hot areas. Do not use your phone for heavy activities like gaming while it is charging.
Use Recommended Battery Settings
Phone manufacturers recommend certain settings to preserve battery health and extend its life. They can be found under the options provided in the Battery settings or the Battery optimization app provided by the manufacturer.
Follow those recommendations strictly to save your battery from degradation and faster draining.
Install Updates Regularly
It is not a wise choice to ignore installing pending updates. Android phones get monthly security updates and software updates regularly. We need to make sure they are installed automatically.
Fix a Fast-Draining Battery on Android
If you notice the battery of your Android phone is draining fast, you need to make sure there are no apps running in the background. Limit app activity in the background, update apps, turn off features that you do not use, install updates, and fix all the issues that are contributing to fast battery drain.

Nvidia said on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The Republican-led foreign affairs and intelligence committees of the US Congress asked Huang to testify next week at a closed-door briefing on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” in response to a New York Times report in October alleging he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang said in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping, China’s president, and seated at the top table with Donald Trump and Xi.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.
Robert Mackey, Nick Robins-Early and Blake Montgomery contributed reporting

Hajra Begum rolls a potato in her hands, checking its skin for cuts, soft spots and signs of rot. After a day harvesting in her family’s field in Chorwan, a remote mountain village in Gurez, Indian-administered Kashmir, she is sorting the crop for winter storage. Some of the potatoes will feed her family through the cold months; others will be saved for planting in spring.
“It should be perfect for planting,” she says. “If you keep a bad potato, you will waste the whole next year.”
Begum, 40, is preparing to lower the potatoes into a khraw, a traditional underground storage pit lined with straw and sealed against the cold. For generations, khraws have kept potatoes, turnips and cabbages through Himalayan winters, when heavy snowfall cuts villages off from the Kashmir valley and temperatures fall below -20C (-4F) – cold enough to crack pipes and freeze diesel.
But the practice is slowly dying out. As roads have improved and young people have left for work and education, fewer families maintain the pits. Their decline threatens not only a traditional way of storing food but also the local potato varieties themselves and the knowledge of which ones store well, resist rot and produce reliable harvests.
“When I was young, almost every family had three or four pits,” Begum says. “Now, down in the main valley, they have abandoned the practice altogether. Only a handful of families still use them. The rest buy from the market or subsidised ones from the government.”
Begum learned from her mother how to tell potatoes that store well from those that rot or sprout too quickly. She is passing this on to her daughter, but is unsure whether the skill will survive into another generation.
Gurez is a high-altitude Himalayan valley perched near the Line of Control, the heavily militarised boundary separating Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. About 80 miles (125km) from Srinagar, the valley remains cut off each winter when snow closes Razdan pass, its main road link, which sits at roughly 3,600 metres.
It is home to the Dard-Shin people, an Indigenous community who speak Shina and have a culture that is distinct from Kashmiri, with community links across the border in Gilgit-Baltistan, administered by Pakistan.
Potatoes account for about 45% of Gurez’s cultivated area, according to a 2019 study by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research’s National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (ICAR-NBPGR), a government body that studies and conserves India’s crop diversity. Yet the genetic diversity of the valley’s potatoes has not been systematically documented.
Dr Sheikh M Sultan, a senior scientist based at ICAR-NBPGR’s Srinagar station, surveyed the valley and later struggled to find some of the varieties he had once encountered. “When I first visited, I saw many varieties,” he says. “Later, I could hardly locate even one sample of some. The loss of genetic diversity is tremendous.”
Sultan says migration, improved roads and changing lifestyles have contributed to the decline. As traditional farming disappears, so does knowledge about selecting, cultivating and preserving local varieties.
“When people stop producing their own seeds and start relying entirely on commercial varieties, the loss can be irreparable,” he says.
He warns that research institutions often prioritise introduced varieties over indigenous crops whose characteristics remain poorly understood. “Our indigenous varieties may possess valuable characteristics, including tolerance to cold and resistance to certain pests and diseases,” he says.
“These are resources we should be studying and improving, rather than neglecting.”
Climate breakdown is adding to the pressures on farmers across the Himalayas. People in Gurez report drier springs, reduced snowfall and water shortages, which they say have affected potato production.
Abdul Jabbar Mapnoo, 70, a farmer in Chorwan, remembers winters when deep snow covered the valley. “Every house used to have two or three khraw, each holding about five quintals – 500kg – of potatoes,” he says. “The springs are drying up, and there is less snow in winter. Potato production has fallen. I remember winters when six feet of snow would cover the valley in January or February.”
As farming becomes more difficult and markets easier to access, households have less incentive to grow their own potatoes. Varieties adapted to local conditions over generations could disappear from cultivation before researchers establish what makes them distinctive.
Dr Parveen Kumar, a scientist at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir, says locally adapted varieties should not be overlooked. “Climate change is a reality, and farmers need to be aware of adaptation strategies,” he says.
Pressure on farmland poses another risk. In Gurez, where cultivable land is scarce, the Kishanganga hydroelectric project has affected land in the valley through acquisition and submergence. Among the areas affected is Badwan, a village known for its potatoes.
One potential route for preserving the varieties could be through using geographical indications – a designation granted by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, and is similar to the French appellation d’origine contrôlée. It can be used on goods that have a specific origin and possess qualities or a reputation linked to this – which can help increase the market value and give them greater recognition. This, and the globally important agricultural heritage systems programme have helped areas such as the saffron-growing landscape of Pampore in Kashmir.
However, recognition alone will not preserve the varieties. They must be identified and documented before they disappear from cultivation, along with farmers’ knowledge of how to select, store and replant them.
In Chorwan, Begum unloads the last sack of potatoes into the pit and covers it, ready for another winter. Some will feed her family; the rest will be replanted in spring. Knowing which potatoes to eat and which to save as seed relies on knowledge passed down through generations.
If these varieties are not documented while they are still being cultivated, Kashmir may lose a living agricultural treasure trove before scientists can fully understand what it contains.

A purported video of former Western Command chief Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.) is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows him expressing concerns over India’s military preparedness and alleging that China has advanced 25 km into Arunachal Pradesh, an advance that Indian forces have been unable to contain. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.) expressing concern over China’s 25 km advance into Arunachal Pradesh.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. The original footage is from Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd. )’s media interaction at Chandimandir, Panchkula, on 30 March 2026, ahead of his retirement. He discusses Operation Sindoor, Operation Rahat and Western Command initiatives, but makes no remarks about China advancing 25 km into Arunachal Pradesh. The Indian Army’s fact-checking wing also confirmed the manipulation, while AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya, indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.) made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating it.
We noticed that the viral video carries a watermark from the news agency ANI. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 30 March 2026, featuring the same footage of Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.), in the same attire and speaking against an identical background. However, his remarks in the original video are entirely different. He was speaking ahead of his retirement and discussed the successful thwarting of Pakistan’s objectives during Operation Sindoor, the procurement of new equipment, including drones and counter-drone systems, and various welfare initiatives undertaken by the Western Command for its personnel. He also highlighted the Command’s role in Operation Rahat during the floods that struck the region the previous year. The original footage contains no remarks about China advancing 25 km into Arunachal Pradesh or concerns over Indian aircraft losses, as claimed in the viral video.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, suggesting that fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear that Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.) was expressing concern over China’s alleged 25 km advance into Arunachal Pradesh.
The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also debunked the claim in an X post, stating that the video was digitally manipulated and falsely attributed remarks to former Western Command chief Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.). It clarified that the original footage was from his media interaction at Chandimandir, Panchkula, on 30 March 2026, on the eve of his retirement. The Army confirmed that he discussed Operation Sindoor, Operation Rahat, operational preparedness, and other Western Command initiatives, but made no statement about Arunachal Pradesh becoming India’s next major military flashpoint.
To sum up, this viral video of Lt. Gen. Manoj Kumar Katiyar (Retd.) expressing concern over China’s advance into Arunachal Pradesh is AI-manipulated.

New York is forcing T-Mobile to stop putting data caps on low-income home internet plans
The company was throttling speeds for plans offered under the Affordable Broadband Act.
New York's attorney general found that T-Mobile was not following the state's Affordable Broadband Act, which sets requirements for offering service to low-income residents. Under the ABA, eligible households must be able to purchase broadband at speeds of at least 25 Mbps for $15 a month or 200 Mbps for $20 a month without additional taxes or equipment fees. Providers are also required to make "reasonable efforts" to promote these low-cost options.
The Office of the Attorney General discovered that T-Mobile had placed monthly data caps on its ABA plans. According to the press release, T-Mobile would throttle speeds to as low as 650 kilobits per second after a customer had used 50GB of data, which could happen in about four days of typical broadband use. The company was also only offering its ABA plans in areas where it had 5G wireless deployed and was preventing information about those plans on its website from being seen by search engines.
Following the investigation, T-Mobile will remove those data caps, make its ABA plans available in all places in the state where it offers home internet service, and will ensure that search engines can access details about ABA plans.
"Reliable and affordable internet service is a basic need for all New Yorkers, but T-Mobile flouted the law designed to help vulnerable New Yorkers access it," Attorney General Letitia James said. "My office is committed to seeing the Affordable Broadband Act realize its goal of ensuring that New Yorkers in need are not denied access to affordable home internet. I encourage all eligible New Yorkers to enroll in a low-cost home internet plan through the ABA."
In a statement shared with Engadget, T-Mobile the company said "We have a long history of helping customers in New York stay connected through low-cost broadband, and we're updating our plan to meet the state's requirements while maintaining the same low price. We've reached an agreement with the New York Attorney General that builds on that commitment, provides greater clarity around our offering and makes the plan available to more eligible customers."
