There’s a degree of second-hand embarrassment that comes from watching David Leitch’s Amazon-backed, influencer-age heist movie “How to Rob a Bank.” It’s a film that bids so desperately for cultural relevance, stylistic cool and progressive brownie points that it trips on its own painstaking efforts to astoundingly lame results. What if Deadpool (Leitch directed one of those films, plus “Bullet Train” and “The Fall Guy”) broke the fourth wall to quack at us about his anti-capitalist revolt? Not that popular uprisings are evil, but this aggressively annoying, tonally berserk actioner serves mostly as a reminder that the revolution will not only be televised but digitally packaged and disseminated via the lousiest algorithm.
As the title promises, YouTube-esque explainer videos featuring four gunmen in wolf masks bring the tips and tricks of bank robbing to a legion of online followers. Headed by the Marx-reading Ryan (Nicholas Hoult), the anonymous crew posts videos of their real-life exploits, with pop-up graphics flashing over blown-out Go-Pro-esque footage of their stick-em-ups and getaways. The erratic opener is one such movie-within-the-movie, passing through the stages of a heist as designed by the crafty group — two minutes at the bank, an anonymous 9/11 call about a mysterious package to divert police attention, and a speedy escape with motorbikes. All of the crew’s robberies throughout the film play out in this twitchy meta-mode, which makes for a bewildering, sloppily overloaded delivery of thrills.
But the reason for this rather ugly framing device is that the team strives to educate the masses in the art of bankrobbing at the expense of being caught. Their Youtube channel includes direct-to-camera rants delivered by their lupine avatars that preach their screw-the-man gospel, entreating their massive following to take back what’s been denied them by the real fat cats and crooks. Most convincing is their claim that the government is too broken and incompetent to do anything about it, giving a Trump-era rationale to their ambitions. But the idea of sympathetic bank robbers flouting a system that only protects the rich and powerful isn’t particularly novel — it’s what underpins many a fine heist film. (There’s even a shoutout to “Point Break” in one scene.) Here, that messaging is spelled out in garish Jokerman typeface.
As Ryan and his collaborators — wig-wearing decoy Emi (Anna Sawai), backup muscle Vince (Pete Davidson) and hacker Hugo (Rhenzy Feliz) — continue robbing banks and making content, amassing hundreds of millions of dollars along the way, FBI agent John West (a weirdly humorless John C. Reilly) recruits deadpan tech-wiz Raegan (a quirked-up Zoë Kravitz) as his sidekick. Raegan is on house arrest after creating an illegal software that can triangulate someone’s location by culling through online images, and but when John shows up at her Pittsburgh apartment — trying to ignore the Cheetos in her hair and the smell of weed — he promises to clear her charges in exchange for using her invention to track down the wolf-pack.
Their rapport gives the investigation a buddy-cop vibe that’s meant to be cute and breezy, but Mark Bianculli’s script relies on clunky wisecracks and labored eccentricities that flatten whatever low-bubbling chemistry the actors share. In any case, the intentionally odd pairing of pragmatic cop and stoner chick allows for thematically appropriate banter about the meaning of justice and peacekeeping in a chaotic and corrupt society.
According to the film’s press notes, the four bankrobbers are meant to be thinly drawn, so that the audience can more easily project themselves onto their respective plights: Vince is a war veteran with a young daughter; Hugo, the son of undocumented immigrants; Ryan and Emi, college sweethearts whose baby boy lost his life when a white-collar insurance scam bankrupted the couple, leaving them unable to pay for his treatment.
In other words, they’re vessels for sadly familiar American grievances, though that doesn’t excuse the perfunctory nature in which their stories are mapped out — or the late-breaking revelations that drop like campy soap-operatic twists. Or the drearily drawn-out emotional reckonings that feel almost offensively unearned (and wildly undeserving of not just one but two plaintive Billie Eillish needle-drops). In fact, at two hours, the whole thing plods along interminably — and in the end, it’s even silly (or shameless) enough to make a case for its own self-importance.

The White House has claimed that a woman's laughter heard at the start of President Donald Trump’s phone call to C-SPAN was "leftover audio from a previous caller who had not disconnected yet."

Social media users quickly began guessing who the voice belonged to, with several observers pointing toward the president's personal aide.

Rather than addressing the mystery voice, Trump turned his focus to media coverage surrounding the logistics of the appearance. After The New York Times reported that his call to the network was unannounced, the president pushed back in a post on Truth Social around 1 a.m.
“The New York Times incorrectly reported that ‘Mr. Trump called into the premier of a C-Span show, APPARENTLY WITHOUT NOTICE.’ This is WRONG,” Trump wrote. “It was a fully scheduled call, as a favor to C-Span, set up through White House Communications. A security researcher has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene.
The UK government has defaulted to openly publishing code it produces with public money for around a decade because it’s transparent, and making it easier for code to be reused is cost-efficient. This includes within the Department of Health and Social Care, and the Home Office, as well as local authorities.
But funding squeezes have left departments neglecting maintenance and improvement of their technology estate. While ControlPlane security researcher Chris Nesbitt-Smith found the vulnerabilities using Claude’s Opus and Sonnet AI models, he says that he used consumer-grade models on a laptop and that many of the issues could have been caught by a routine IT health check. “None of this is the level of sophistication that general media is worried about in terms of cyber attacks,” he tells WIRED. “It’s all daft stuff.”
In the most serious case he identified, the Planning Inspectorate, which handles land-use matters across England, had failed to fully remove a login after it accidentally committed them to public repository GitHub. The fact the credentials gave such wide access—and seemingly didn’t expire—compounded with the agency’s accidental publication of them, “made it particularly dangerous for them.”
The complete Microsoft Entra ID would have given “god-tier” read and write access to all SharePoint sites and private employee OneDrive accounts, according to Nesbitt-Smith, including HR records. It also would have given access to sensitive libraries which safeguard evidence under legal hold for statutory planning inquiries and appeals, according to the security researcher who found it. “The option for ransomwaring them, for encrypting all the data, or just stealing all the data, was abundantly there,” Nesbitt-Smith says.
A spokesperson for the Planning Inspectorate told WIRED its cyber monitoring tools immediately detected Nesbitt-Smith’s activity in August and that it had already been handling this as a cyber incident when ControlPlane made contact. The agency identified and fixed this vulnerability within 20 minutes of the report and verified that no data breach occurred. “We have reviewed and strengthened our systems and processes to prevent this type of issue recurring and we are grateful for the researcher’s work and for alerting us to it,” they told WIRED.
The Planning Inspectorate issue “isn’t about open source but internal housekeeping when using public tools,” Amanda Brock, chief executive officer of nonprofit industry group OpenUK. “That data was exposed because of a failure not to follow good process,” she adds. “That’s not an open source security issue.”
In around two-thirds of the 349 public sector codebases across 33 organizations Nesbitt-Smith scanned, he said he found vulnerabilities. Several of these were found in the Department of Education’s code, including in a procurement service used by schools, in a teacher application service containing personal details, qualifications, employment history and identity documents, and England’s main register of government-funded training providers and apprenticeships. He also found a vulnerability in a Scottish Government open data portal which would have allowed any visitor to read administrative account information and to change site configuration. The organizations have since dealt with the issues.
Recently, there have been arguments for public sector departments to stop publishing source code in the open, now that AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery. The NHS reportedly ordered technology teams to transition away from open source code in May amid security concerns about the impact of AI models.
Doing this without immediately fixing the underlying issues would be the “worst case scenario,” according to Nesbitt-Smith, as it prevents researchers like him from finding them, and it’s likely that an adversary has already mirrored these repositories and so will maintain access to them. “Unless you’re going to go and fix all of the problems, if anything, you’re probably drawing more attention to it by closing it,” says Nesbitt-Smith, “because you’re like, ‘Here be dragons over this space. Don’t look here though, please.’”

Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.
The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.
Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.
The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.
“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.
The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.
“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.
Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.
During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.
“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.
It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.
Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.
Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.
The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.
Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.
“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

Scott Colom defeats Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by a razor-thin margin in a major midterm flip
Democratic challenger Scott Colom defeated incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi election for the US Senate, media projected on Wednesday, making him the Southern state’s first black senator since the Reconstruction era that followed the US Civil War.
The result was a stunning upset in the heavily Republican state and expanded on the national drubbing the Democrats delivered to President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.
The Mississippi Senate race was one of the final races to be called after the elections. The contest was so tight that Colom at times led the vote count by only a few dozen votes.

I Tried 20 of the Most Popular Indoor Gardening Systems
Featured in this article
Did you cut down on lettuce consumption due to cyclosporiasis outbreaks over the summer? I didn't. Not because I threw caution to the wind and bought the produce anyway, but because I grow multiple types of organic lettuce myself, in my own house, in less than a few square feet. And you can too.
For the past two years, I've been testing various indoor smart garden systems in my home, which have given me year-round access to fresh tomatoes, peppers, strawberries, and even mushrooms. Most of them are easy for anyone to set up and use, with minimal space and maintenance requirements.
There's an indoor gardening setup for just about any household. The Gardyn Home 4.0 ($899), for example, offers total success with no green thumb required if you pay for a subscription, while the Auk Mini 2 ($239) is the perfect attractive yet low-maintenance solution for those who just want fresh herbs. Are these gardens worth it? How much can you really grow? How can you be sure which option is best for your specific lifestyle? Below, learn which gardens stood out in testing, why, and which option might be ideal for your home and needs.
Check out our other sustainable home-tech buying guides, including the Best LED Grow Lights, Best Mushroom Growing Methods, Best Smart Bird Feeders, and Best Kitchen Composters.
Updated November 2026: I’ve added the Lykyn Smart Mushroom Grow Box as a pick, moved a couple of gardens to Others Tested and another to Not Recommended, and ensured up-to-date links and prices.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Others Tested
Click and Grow Smart Garden for $102: Click & Grow Smart Garden's seed pods come in a Nespresso-evoking plastic three-pack with a tear-off cover. (A three-pack of pods starts at around $15.) Put a nutrient-packed “smart soil” seed pod in one of the Click & Grow’s cups with the wicking bottom, fill the reservoir, and that’s it. It was one of the simplest watering systems I tried: a wick at the bottom of the cup brings water up to the pods, and the roots stay in the cups. A little bobber on one end tells you when the water level is low and needs a top-off, simply by floating lower than the growing surface. It's also small, so you can plop it on a shelf or countertop. (Note that the 9, pictured above, is currently out of stock, but you can sign up to be notified when it's available.) At the same time, this was also one of the slowest-growing gardens I tested—it took weeks to get even one lettuce leaf. One of my lettuce pods didn’t even sprout at all. Still, this isn't a terrible option for busy people who are interested in growing something like flowers, where yields aren't a concern.
North Spore Automated Monotub Kit for $165: If you already know how to DIY your own mushroom-cultivating monotub setup, this is not for you. Nor is it for those who want something fully plug-and-play. It's a bare-bones kit—a tub with a lid, filters, a hygrometer, a humidifier, and a fan to maintain airflow—for growing either fruiting blocks or substrate-based mushroom species. My kit came with no paper instructions, so I had to figure out how to use it completely via YouTube and trial and error. That said, when you figure it out, it works. I've run it through multiple harvests now, producing more oyster and lion's mane mushrooms than I knew what to do with. However, note that you will need to replace the filters after a couple of runs; mine got blocked and grew mold.
Rise Garden 3 for $1,499: The three-level Rise has far and away the biggest capacity of any non-DIY indoor garden I’ve seen, along with a pretty traditional form factor. In fact, I'm pretty sure I saw one of these in the corner of my college biology class. Since it's so large, assembly was a bit tricky, and vague instructions weren't helpful. I also didn't find out until after I had already set it up that the peat pods need to germinate first in plastic-lidded “nurseries.” My test unit didn't come with enough nurseries, so I had to improvise with shallow plastic containers, with the pods weighted to keep them upright in water. After a few days, I noticed the containers—all of them, including the provided nurseries—had begun to grow algae, and the black-plastic surface of the Rise trays was noticeably warm. I brought out my infrared temperature gun to test the temperature and found that the 195-watt LEDs paired with the black plastic had brought the surface up to 95 degrees Fahrenheit. For reference, all of the other indoor gardening systems were room temperature, in the mid-70s. Over time, I noticed herbs and lettuce bolted faster in the Rise 3 than in other gardens, likely due to this heat, which also puts plants at risk for cases of root rot. I'm still a big fan of the Rise's form factor and its capacity, though, and I think it would be a first choice for heat-tolerant crops, like tomatoes and peppers.
Modern Sprout Garden Jars for $20: These cute Mason jars are as simple as it gets: Rinse the included gravel, then add seeds and water. They're guaranteed to sprout in five to 10 days and make a fun hostess gift with a tea towel and/or a bottle of olive oil. However, they are definitely more for looks than harvests—I have had the basil, cilantro, and rosemary versions on my windowsill for a little over a year, and I’ve only seen a few usable leaves.
Lettuce Grow Counterstand Set for $149: New from the makers of the flashy Lettuce Grow Farmstand (8/10 WIRED Recommends), this simple, no-pump setup consists of three amber beakers that look straight out of a high school chemistry lab, plus an 18-inch-tall LED lamp that runs on a 16- or 18-hour timer. It relies on the Kratky method of hydroponics, invented by horticulturist Dr. Bernard Kratky, where the plant sits in a cup above a nutrient-enriched water source. In the Counterstand's case, a wick draws water up to the seedling until its roots can grow into the water. Included with your order are three credits for live seedlings of your choice—I picked parsley, basil, and butter lettuce. This setup is stylish, but consider the counter space it requires, the yields are tiny—maybe a small handful of leaves a week.
Vego EZ Microgreens Planter (2-pack) for $60: This system for growing nutrient-packed microgreens for salads, smoothies, and sandwiches isn't smart, but it is nifty enough to warrant a mention. Just fill each half-gallon reservoir (made of food-safe plastic) with water, and then cover it with the optional humidity dome. From there, bamboo-fiber capillary grow mats on top will absorb water to germinate your microgreen seeds (not included). Set it near a sunny window, use a grow light, or add Vego's 10 x 20 dome with a built-in grow light ($80), which fits over both planters. I placed my planters on a Ferry-Morse pop-up plant stand with a grow light from LetPot and had consistent success across multiple grows.
Not Recommended
Plantaform Smart Indoor Garden for $800: Plantaform is “the world's first smart indoor garden that uses fog to grow plants,” according to the company's press release, and it has definitely garnered attention, winning an Innovation Award at the 2025 Consumer Electronics Show (CES). The “fogponics" technology, ostensibly building on NASA-developed aeroponics, delivers water and nutrients to plants' roots via an ultrafine mist. The futuristic look of the egg-shaped planter certainly captivated us at WIRED, but when contributor Lisa Wood Shapiro tested it to grow lettuce, she found that you can't combine different types of plants (i.e., you can only grow lettuce at one time, or tomatoes, or herbs). The machine also degraded her indoor air quality, as tested with an air quality monitor. Users must add an included fertilizer mix to the water, with the resulting concoction being what's aerosolized in the container; Wood Shapiro found this was not airtight. She suggests limiting the Plantaform's use to a basement or another space where air quality isn't as much of a concern, but it's probably best to hold off on this one until Plantaform can work out some more kinks.
LetPot Smart Seed Starter for $84: There are many grow-light–enabled seed starters on the market, but LetPot's Smart Seed Starter has more features than most, including a sensor for soil temperature and EC and a 24-watt heating pad underneath. A plastic lid with adjustable vents on either end sits on top. I love the concept, but sadly, quality control is lacking. On my test unit, the power adapter makes a high-pitched sound when the lights are on, the EC sensor only works intermittently, and auto-mode erases whenever it's unplugged. After about six months of regular use, the light stopped staying on, and to get the unit to cooperate, I had to unplug and replug it repeatedly.
AeroGarden Harvest Lite for $93: Formerly my top pick for Most Giftable, I loved the simplicity of this system, which requires no app—push or hold a single embossed AeroGarden logo on the top to run through all of the controls and settings. However, it doesn't include sponges, baskets, or pods, which is a bit of a miss at this price point, and the pump failed after only a year of use. AeroGarden offers no replacement parts to fix this issue, which online reviews suggest isn't uncommon, so faulty units end up in the landfill.
FAQs
What Is Hydroponics?
In the simplest terms, hydroponic gardening means growing plants without roots in soil. Sometimes plants are suspended in water, like in the Rise or Gardyn; sometimes they're in pods attached to a wick, like in the Click & Grow; and sometimes water is sprayed or misted onto their roots, like in the Lettuce Grow. Usually, this process works alongside an artificial light source, either indoors or in an outdoor enclosure.
What Are the Benefits of Hydroponics?
In addition to the obvious plus of cleaner produce without mud, dirt, or synthetic pesticides, hydroponic systems use much less water than conventional growing methods, since all the water used is either recirculated or taken up by the plants. Some farmers also say they get higher yields from hydroponic systems, as the variables of weather, light, and nutrients are far easier to control. And, because of these variables, farmers are also able to grow varieties of plants in just about any season or region. And there are no weeds!
What Kinds of Things Can I Grow in a Hydroponic Garden?
Just about anything you can think of! I asked FX Rouxel, creator of Gardyn, if there was anything you couldn't grow in these systems, other than ground-dwelling plants like peanuts or potatoes. “All the things that have big roots,” he said—like carrots, parsnips, and so on. “Otherwise, mostly things that are too big, like apples or lemons.” So, there you have it: No long roots, no trees. But anything else is fair game to try.
What Are the Downsides of Hydroponic Systems?
First of all, it's no secret hydroponic systems cost more than just planting some seeds outside in the dirt. Then you've got to worry about power outages, pump maintenance, algae, and just general maintenance. And if you're not careful, water can harbor some nasty stuff, even if that's just fertilizer, as WIRED contributor Lisa Wood Shapiro found when she reviewed the Plantaform. Some also claim that hydroponically grown herbs, greens, and vegetables have less flavor than their soil-grown counterparts, but I personally have not noticed a difference; I've grown perfectly flavorful snap peas, cauliflower, shell beans, salad greens, and even strawberries in nutrient-infused water. In fact, one of the best cucumbers I've ever had in my life came from my Gardyn Studio, of all places.
Will I Save Money by Growing My Own Vegetables?
In short, no. The ready-made systems simply remove a great deal of hassle and guesswork from the process, and they usually look pretty cool in the process. It's also nice to have warranty and tech support in the event something goes wrong. As is often the case with anything filled with water, when something does go wrong, it goes really wrong. (Speaking of, be sure to check out our guide to the Best Water Leak Detectors.)
How Much Can I Really Grow in These Things?
It largely depends on what you're growing and how many individual plants can fit in your system. My yields have ranged from a handful of lettuce leaves in the Click & Grow to huge bagfuls of salad greens per day in the Rise—more than my family could possibly eat. As a rule, lettuces and other greens tend to grow faster, while fruiting plants like tomatoes and peppers grow slower and sometimes need pollination to produce. (For instance, with strawberries I have to use a small paintbrush to brush the flowers each morning.)
Where Can I Put Them in My House?
Most of these systems take up only a square foot or two, so space isn't as much of a consideration as lights and pump noise. Lights for these gardens typically need to be on around 16 hours a day, and they are bright, so if this schedule would be disruptive, you may want to place them away from a bedroom or any other room where darkness is necessary. On a related note, many of these gardens, like the Lettuce Grow and Gardyn, have loud pump cycles, while Rise's pump runs continuously. I wouldn't recommend placing a garden with a noisy pump cycle near a TV or office, where the noise could be a disturbance during certain times of the day. If any amount of noise is a concern (perhaps you live on the top floor of an apartment), you may want to consider a totally silent garden like the Auk or Click & Grow.
How Much Do They Cost to Keep Going?
Gardens with subscriptions and/or proprietary pods, like Gardyn and Click & Grow, are obviously going to be more expensive over the long run than a truly DIY system like the LetPot. On the one hand, with proprietary pods, you won't have to source seeds or sponges; you can be assured the seeds are appropriate for that system and hydroponics in general, and if something doesn't germinate, you will be able to get a replacement or a refund. But on the other hand, this is a recurring cost that will reduce any savings you gain from growing your own food or flowers. As for power, systems with a continuously running pump, like Rise, are going to cost more than ones with no pump, like the Auk. However, I haven't noticed a significant bump in my electricity bill while testing these gardens, except for one period where I had seven (yes, seven) going at one time.
How I Tested
I unboxed, assembled, and set up each garden exactly as described in the provided instructions, using the seeds, pods, or seedlings that came with the garden. I paid attention to ease of setup, ease of use, maintenance needs, how much space each system required, and how well (or not well) the plants did and why. I noted what was or was not included with each system, and allowed all of the plants to grow to the harvest stage, paying attention to bolting, yields, and general health. I'm a full-time working parent, so I also paid attention to maintenance needs, light schedules, and any general hassles that came up and annoyed me.
How I Chose Which Gardens to Test
I am genuinely passionate about indoor gardening and have an eye on what’s going on in the landscape: what’s new, what’s hot, what’s working for people, what’s not working. I’m always on the lookout for interesting new devices that I find cool and that I believe WIRED readers would like to know about. Affiliate status does not factor into my decision about what to test and write about. If you have a unique, tech-forward indoor garden you like that I haven’t featured, please let me know in the comments.
How Do I Acquire Gardens to Review?
Most of the gardens I receive to test are samples provided by the companies, with no guarantee of coverage or expectation of what that coverage will look like. Some of the gardens are kept by WIRED in order to perform extended testing, while others are donated locally.

On Election Day last week, white nationalist Nick Fuentes urged his supporters on X to “get out and vote Democrat today.” The post racked up over 12 million views. Hours later, in the wake of the Democratic sweep, Fuentes took credit for the victory. “We did it again” he wrote on Telegram, later calling the phenomenon “the Groyper Effect,” a reference to the nickname given to his followers.
In recent days, Fuentes has claimed the election results are an opportunity for him and his allies on the far-right.
“Let the Democrats rule, see how that goes,” Fuentes said during a livestream last week. “There will come a time when the far left will terrorize people, and they're going to push all of them into the arms of the right. Who's going to fight the far left? Only the far-right. This is why we have to take over the right wing now.”
In another livestream last week, Fuentes added a warning to the GOP leadership: “It’s our party now … You need to cooperate with us… Groypers are open for business. It has [to] be America First—and if it's not, we'll do it again for the enemy.”
A WIRED review of comments from white supremacist, Christian nationalist, and other far-right groups in the wake of the midterm results shows much of the same. While the groups are uniformly attacking Trump’s failure to prioritize white, Christian American values, they also believe that this sudden shift to the left will result in a backlash that will see more people embrace far-right groups and ideologies.
“Many prominent figures in racist extremist movements have taken to declaring the MAGA movement dead since midterm elections, claiming that the results validate their previous criticisms of the Trump administration and opens new opportunities for their movements to push disaffected voters toward their ideological beliefs,” Jared Holt, senior researcher at Open Measures, tells WIRED.
While some of the Republican party’s extremist candidates were rejected during the elections last week, many did win their elections.
The Institute for Research and Education on Human Rights tracked 535 candidates running in statewide races who were members of at least one far-right Facebook group. The researchers found that of the 476 races that had been called by last Friday, 338 of those candidates were victorious, representing a 71 percent win rate (the vast majority of these races saw GOP incumbents retain their seats). In Florida, for example, 34-year-old citrus farmer Marshall Rawson, who attended the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville in 2017, easily defeated his Democrat opponent in the state’s 10th District State House race.
Many states also passed ballot measures that could further far-right agendas, including anti-transgender rules, onerous voter ID laws, and anti-immigrant measures.
“Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska, and Washington approved bans on trans athletes in female sports, so girls in Washington State, for instance, will now have to go through a genital exam or pass a DNA test before they can participate in youth sports,” Devin Burghart, executive director with IREHR, said on Friday during a briefing with reporters.
The success of these ballot measures were celebrated by extremists groups as evidence that Americans wanted that the current GOP could not deliver.
The Proud Boys, the street-fighting group that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency operations made largely redundant in recent years, were optimistic following the losses. “The ultimate rebuke of the current Republican establishment was citizens voting them out of office then doing their job for them by passing ballot measures on issues the Republicans should have already handled,” the Cape Fear Proud Boys wrote in their Telegram channel.
“What this signals to me is even in those places where they lost, they're getting 41-47 percent of the vote [so] there's still a mass base to try to be mobilized,” Chuck Tanner, research director at IREHR, said during the briefing. “That's the lesson that some of these groups are taking out of it, is that there's still that mass base.”
And it is the existence of this base, extremist groups claim, leaves the Republican Party vulnerable to takeover from the inside.
“Now is the time, if you're a nationalist, to start looking at moving on the Republican Party where you live,” Warren Balogh, a white supremacist from Pittsburgh who attended the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville in 2017, wrote on his Telegram channel. “And by that I mean, organizing your guys and going in to do a hostile takeover.”
“This may be the best thing that has happened to the Republican party in a half-century,” the Cape Fear Proud Boys declared in a post on Telegram days after the election. “Now you will learn to placate us, or you will continue to fail. Understand this: You’re going to run people we like and you’re going to do what we say.”
But other extremists appear less inclined to wait until the next general election in 2028, preferring a more direct takeover.
"I'm not saying that we will win through democracy, I'm just saying we'll win,” Joel Webbon, a Christian nationalist pastor said last week in a video posted online after the election. Webbon and fellow far-right pastors, as well as guest speaker and noted conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, are set to meet at a conference in Texas this week where attendees will discuss, in at least one talk, “battle plans” for “Christian nationalists on the right to be able to seize power.”
Experts WIRED spoke to said they have not yet seen any explicit calls for violence from the far-right groups they are tracking, but some figures are already looking ahead of January 3, when Congress is set to certify the midterm election results.
Far-right activist and pardoned January 6 rioter Jake Lang, however, is planning an event in DC on January 3. It is unclear how many people are planning to attend, but one of the Christian nationalist pastors listed by Lang as an official speaker has already said he won’t be speaking.
Lang, who spent last weekend disrupting a cat convention that he thought was a furry convention, did not respond to a request for comment.

Pair discussed China-US relations and final preparations for when the two heads of state sit down at the Apec summit in Shenzhen
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held a phone call with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Wednesday to finalise preparations for next week’s meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China.

“The stable momentum of China-US relations has not come easily and is the two major countries’ rational choice based on their respective and common interests.”

- Kai Cenat completed all five mainline GTA games in just over 130 hours ahead of GTA 6.
- Cenat praised GTA 4 for its cinematic presentation and darker atmosphere during the marathon.
- Kai Cenat plans to stream GTA 6 until he achieves 100% completion after its November 19 launch.
The Kai Cenat GTA marathon is officially complete, with the streamer finishing all five mainline Grand Theft Auto games, GTA III, GTA: Vice City, GTA: San Andreas, GTA 4, and GTA 5, in just over 130 hours. The streamer began the challenge on November 5, playing through the main GTA game storylines in release order ahead of the GTA 6 launch on November 19.
Cenat reached the final game after completing the first four titles in under 100 hours. He has now wrapped up the entire challenge, revisiting five major entries in the GTA games franchise before Rockstar’s next release.
Highlights from Kai Cenat GTA Marathon Before GTA 6
During the marathon, Cenat spoke about how the series changed with each entry. He had particular praise for GTA 4, describing it as a cinematic experience with darker visuals and a grittier atmosphere.
“GTA 4 feels like a movie. It feels like they took a whole different approach with the coloring and everything,” he said during the marathon before GTA 6.
“It feels darker, it feels more gritty. It feels like a movie. I feel like I’m watching an entire movie as I’m playing it.”
His GTA 5 playthrough also produced a funny moment when he struggled with the aiming controls during the opening story mission. Cenat eventually switched to Full Assisted Aim, giving viewers another memorable clip from the marathon.
Kai Cenat Is Preparing for His GTA 6 Marathon
Cenat has also asked fans to avoid posting GTA 6 spoilers when the game launches. He warned viewers that anyone planning to experience the story themselves should avoid watching his stream unless they are comfortable having his gameplay in the background.
With GTA 6 preloads hampering internet speed, it is obvious that one of the biggest streamers on Twitch will not avoid a large viewer base. So, it is fair that he wants the gamers who want to explore Leonida to explore it without getting spoiled.
Cenat has already shared plans to stream GTA 6 until he reaches 100% completion. That means his next marathon could last considerably longer, especially if he takes time to explore Leonida and complete activities beyond the main story.
GTA 6 pre-orders are still live for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S until the release date. With all five previous games now complete, Cenat has finished his warm-up just in time for Rockstar’s next chapter.

Telangana to introduce 10+2 system in all state-run schools from 2027-28 to prevent dropouts, says CM Revanth Reddy
Under the proposed new structure, education will be divided into three stages: primary, secondary and senior secondary.
The Telangana government will introduce a 10 plus 2 education system in all the state-run schools from the next 2027-28 academic year, extending school education up to Class 12 on the lines of Kendriya Vidyalayas, chief minister A Revanth Reddy announced on Wednesday.
Currently, school education till Class 10 is overseen by the School Education Department, with the 10th-grade Secondary School Certificate (SSC) public examinations conducted by the Telangana Board of Secondary Education. The next two years are called Intermediate Education and are governed separately by the Board of Intermediate Education (BIE).
Under the proposed new structure, education will be divided into three stages: primary education from nursery to Class 4, secondary education from Classes 5 to 8, and senior secondary education from Classes 9 to 12, all governed in a single system.
What CM Reddy said
At a review meeting held with education department officials at the Marri Channa Reddy Human Resources Development Institute, the chief minister said the decision was aimed at reducing student dropouts after Class 10 and ensuring continuity in education, particularly among girls and students from disadvantaged communities.
Revanth Reddy directed the department officials to make all necessary arrangements for implementing the new system from next year as part of a broader initiative to overhaul the state's education sector.
He said the government's objective was to provide quality education from the nursery level to university and equip students with the knowledge and skills required to compete in the modern world.
Revanth Reddy emphasised that students should develop proficiency in languages and communication skills by the time they complete Class 12.
“They should also be given opportunities to pursue subjects of their choice after the senior secondary stage and develop expertise in their respective fields,” he said.
The chief minister expressed concern over the increasing number of students dropping out after Class 10, particularly girls and children belonging to Dalit, tribal and minority communities.
“Extending schooling up to Class 12 within the same education system would help address the problem by ensuring uninterrupted access to education,” he said.
He pointed out that institutions such as Kendriya Vidyalayas, Navodaya Vidyalayas and Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas, which provide education up to Class 12, record comparatively lower dropout rates.
Officials briefed the chief minister on progress in preparing the proposed education structure, which covers the entire learning cycle from nursery to intermediate education.
The meeting also discussed the implementation of the 10+2 system in 18 other states nationwide. The Telangana government has decided to introduce the system with the stated objective of improving access to quality education, reducing dropouts and providing students with better academic and career opportunities.

NVIDIA shareholders are suing the company and CEO Jensen Huang
The company’s shares have plummeted in response to the exec’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The unfolding drama around NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman now accused of being a spy for the Chinese government may be getting its first courtroom chapter. A shareholder in the computing giant has sued accusing NVIDIA and Huang of misleading investors about the nature of the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Taiwanese company Megaspeed who is now suspected of being an espionage asset for China. Huang is a common surname; The pair are not related.
Mark Kistenmacher filed the complaint and is seeking class action status for anyone who purchased NVIDIA shares between October 9 and November 8. The first date is when The New York Times published a story on NVIDIA and Megaspeed detailing a connection between the pair, which was rebuffed by NVIDIA as a routine business relationship; the second date is when the NVIDIA founder admitted to an affair and the company publicly disclosed that it was launching its own investigation into whether its top exec had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.
In the interim, The New York Times published an in-depth feature on October 29 claiming that the NVIDIA CEO had become the subject of a suspected Chinese intelligence action. The piece cites NVIDIA representative John Rizzo, who said, "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." This statement, the lawsuit alleges, was not true.
The company's shares have dropped in the fallout of the allegations, with NVIDIA on track to lose more than $470 billion in market value over the past two days. "As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages," the complaint states.

The young politicians with African roots making history in the US midterms
- Published
"JD [Vance], habibi (my love)".
It was an unlikely greeting to hear at a Democratic Party victory rally after the US midterm elections.
Abdul El-Sayed, 42, born to Egyptian immigrant parents, playfully addressed Vice-President JD Vance, who had campaigned against him but will now swear him into office in January as Michigan's new Senator.
The US-born Democrat spent much of his campaign fending off attacks from conservative media and President Donald Trump, who accused him of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejected the allegations.
"My name is Abdul Rahman Mohammed El-Sayed," he said in an Egyptian Arabic accent to the cheering crowd at his victory rally. His Arabic Muslim name was a target for many of his opponents. He is set to become the first Muslim senator.
El-Sayed ran a social media-first campaign, with TikTok edits showing him speaking directly to young voters, tapping into Gen Z humour, and sporting friendship bracelets.
The former public health administrator's campaign centred on a progressive agenda, including Medicare for All, affordable housing and curbing corporate influence in politics. He has also been a vocal critic of US military aid to Israel.
But El-Sayed was not alone. From an Ethiopian-born Gen Z congresswoman to candidates with Nigerian heritage, several other politicians with African roots won in this year's midterms.
The elections, held halfway through a president's four-year term, decide who represents Americans in Congress, as well as in thousands of state and local offices.
At 29, Melat Kiros became the first Gen Z woman elected to the US Congress.
Born in Ethiopia, she arrived in the US as a baby and grew up in Denver. She had never held elected office before defeating a 15-term incumbent in Colorado's 1st District in the Democrat primary before winning a landslide in Tuesday's election.
Kiros, like El-Sayed, campaigned on issues that have become central to young progressive voters: the cost of living, universal childcare and Medicare for All.
Endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, she has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement and ending US military aid to Israel.
Her outspoken criticism of Israel's war in Gaza has attracted controversy. Kiros has said her criticism is directed at the Israeli state, not Jewish people.
She was fired from a top New York law firm in 2023 after she refused to take down an open letter to dozens of law firms who had urged law school deans to crack down on antisemitism on campuses as students engaged in pro-Palestinian protests.
Kiros condemned antisemitism, but warned the law firms, including the one she worked for, against conflating "such bigotry with the geo-political question of Israel's legitimacy".
She said she started thinking more seriously about politics in general after being fired.
Adrian Boafo, meanwhile, a second-generation Ghanaian-American, will represent Maryland's 5th Congressional District after succeeding veteran Congressman Steny Hoyer, who retired after a political career spanning more than four decades.
The 32-year-old was born in Virginia and raised in Prince George's County, Maryland. His parents immigrated to the US from Ghana.
Boafo's route to Congress began in local politics. He served on the Bowie City Council before becoming a Maryland state delegate in 2023. He also worked for Hoyer before eventually winning the race to replace him.
His campaign focused on the cost of living, childcare and protecting federal workers, a major issue in a district close to Washington DC and home to thousands of government employees.
In his victory statement, Boafo said representing his constituents had "never felt more urgent", pointing to federal job cuts, rising costs and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
Among those returning to Congress is Somali-born Ilhan Omar, 44, who won a fifth term despite an ongoing federal investigation.
Federal agents searched her Washington home in October as part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork. Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.
First elected to Congress in 2018, Omar became the first Somali-American and one of the first Muslim women to serve in the chamber. She has also been a frequent target of President Trump, who has repeatedly criticised her and other Somali immigrants.
Trump has previously used derogatory language to describe some African countries, including Somalia. In October, his Yemeni-born adviser Amer Ghalib said the president would refrain from using such language.
Others made their breakthroughs in state and local politics.
Junior Ezeonu was born in Nigeria and moved to the US as a young child. By 27, he had already become Grand Prairie's youngest city council member before winning a seat in the Texas State House.
Then there is Carol Kazeem, 34, a Pennsylvania state legislator of Nigerian heritage who has retained her seat at District 159. At least four candidates with Nigerian heritage won in the 3 November midterms.
For some young Africans watching from across the Atlantic, these victories have offered a glimpse of what a new generation of voters could achieve at home.
On social media, users have shared the election results as a source of inspiration, particularly in Nigeria and Kenya, where major elections are due in 2027.

United says it won’t let personal AI assistants book tickets on the airline, citing both privacy and regulatory concerns.
United won’t let your AI agent book your flight
AI agents can’t attest that you don’t have explosives in your bags.
The company says it hasn’t yet seen many people try to use AI agents to book their flights, The Wall Street Journal reports, in line with observations from other businesses like Doordash. But United is concerned that agents could expose customers’ information or make purchases they didn’t intend, and potentially skirt federal rules about the kind of information airlines need to share with customers — like having them attest that their bags don’t have explosives.
While agents can still show users United flights, they won’t be able to actually complete the transaction on their behalf. The decision, and others like it, could limit the potential usefulness of newer personal AI assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. “To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman,” United CEO Scott Kirby said at an event on Tuesday, according to the Journal.
Across sectors, businesses are grappling with whether to let AI agents transact on their sites, and United is not alone in blocking access for unauthorized agents. eBay appeared to block agents from browsing the site, and several major banks have also placed restrictions on them. United suggests it could reconsider its decision based on future advancements. “As third-party AI agents advance, we see the opportunities they present. However, at the same time, allowing them to interact directly with a United account or booking could involve sensitive actions, and we want to make sure we have established protections for travelers first.”

While Khamenei did post to X that "the process of the US's collapse has accelerated," that remark was part of a larger statement about the Iran war and America's role in global politics.
In the days following the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats gained comfortable majorities in both the House and Senate, some people on social media highlighted what they claimed were comments made by Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei about the Democrats' victories.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claimed, "Iran's leader celebrates Democrats' win." The post included a picture of Khamenei with the quote, "The process of the US's collapse has accelerated."
Other posts claiming Khamenei said "the process of the US's collapse has accelerated" in reference to the midterm elections spread on X (archived) and elsewhere on Facebook (archived). Some Snopes readers searched the site to see whether the claim was true.
Khamenei posted the remark to X (archived) on Nov. 4, the day following the midterm elections, as part of a larger statement focused on the Iran war. Aside from the date of the post, there was no context that supported the claim that the quote was about the midterm elections. Therefore, we've rated this claim false.
The supreme leader of Iran uses an X account to make statements in English. On Nov. 4, Khamenei made an statement about Iran's "National Day of Fighting Global Arrogance" (archived) through a series of X posts.
According to news agencies supported by Iran's government, Mehr News Agency and Tasnim News Agency, this holiday commemorates several events from Iran's history that occurred on Nov. 4. Most notably, the day commemorates the student takeover of the U.S. embassy on Nov. 4, 1979.
Near the beginning of his statement, Khamenei wrote (archived): "Nov. 4 this year, Iranians understand their stance toward the criminal US more clearly and unequivocally than ever before. Nevertheless, reviewing the reasons of US's hostility – and the Iranian nation's firm resistance to them – serves as a guiding light for the path ahead."
Later, Khamenei wrote (archived) that "The situation in the Persian Gulf, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz, has shattered the myth of the US invincibility."
Those posts, plus several others praising the military successes of Iran and its allies in the Middle East, led to a post in which Khamenei said (archived), "Today, the declining power and hegemony of the United States has suffered an irreversible fall in both dimensions of its power: its hard military power and its international soft power."
That post was the one immediately preceding the post in which Khamenei said "The process of the US's collapse has accelerated."
Khamenei's statement was translated differently on the website for Iran's supreme leader. The quotes about the collapse of the U.S. and its declining power are in the same paragraph, and the collapse's acceleration is framed as something that has actively been happening: "Today, because of the arrogant powers' self-inflicted disgrace, America's power and domination have suffered an irreversible decline. This applies to both its hard military power and its international soft power, and this collapse has been accelerating."
The very next X post (archived) after the one about the collapse of the U.S. can be reasonably construed as referencing the midterm elections. However, the post was a warning to Iranians that the U.S. would be hostile to Iran no matter which party is in power:
If there are still those who entertain the slightest hope that the hegemonic system may change behavior or shifts in its political parties may bring about change, or that by making concessions to the US, they can persuade it to abandon its hostility, they're gravely mistaken.
No other posts in Khamenei's series of Nov. 4 posts appeared be related to the U.S. midterm elections, though Iran's chief negotiator and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf did directly refer to the results of the midterms. According to The Associated Press, he wrote on social media, "Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message."
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei also reacted to the U.S. midterm election results, saying, "The American people have now sent you a clear message. But if you continue to ignore reality, disregard the lessons of history and persist in this dangerous course, the consequences of this grave miscalculation will go far beyond anything you have witnessed so far."
For further reading, Snopes previously confirmed that a Time magazine depicted Trump with an "I Voted" stick covering his mouth after the Republicans' midterm losses.

Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race
Democrat Scott Colom has won election to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi, according to a race call by the Associated Press, narrowly defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
After more than a week of counting outstanding, absentee ballots and affidavit — or provisional — ballots, Colom won the closest Senate race in the country by just a few thousand votes. His victory expands the majority Democrats will have in the new Congress to 55 seats, with the race in Alaska still undecided.
Loading...
In a midterm full of stunning upsets for Democrats, Colom's victory underscores a dramatic shift in the political landscape across the South driven by a surge of Black voter turnout.
Mississippi has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40%, but President Trump won the state by 23 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than 40 years and hasn't sent a Black senator to Washington since Reconstruction.
The state's rural, agriculture-heavy economy was disproportionately impacted by rising prices, and saw millions in investment from both parties, particularly in the final weeks of the race. Colom, a district attorney, made cost of living a centerpiece of his campaign message, decrying "Cindy High-Prices" as bad for Mississippi.
Hyde-Smith conceded the race in a video posted to social media shortly after the AP's race call on Wednesday.
"While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."
Unlike most other contested Senate races that flipped, Mississippi did not see much national money or attention until the closing days of the election. That included a rally in the final week by President Trump and high-profile visits from former Vice President Kamala Harris, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and other Democrats. The Cook Political Report had the race rated as Likely Republican going into election night.
Colom told NPR earlier this month that a lack of investment from national Democrats until the last minute was a mistake.
"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he said. "The Democratic Party has not been trying to win Mississippi. Let's stop kidding ourselves, right? They spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states. They spent almost nothing in Mississippi."
Colom's campaign was a contrast in style from Hyde-Smith, who rarely spoke to reporters in Washington and had minimal presence in the state.
When asked about high beef prices earlier this year, Hyde-Smith — a cattle rancher and onetime state agriculture commissioner — said that "you have so many other proteins to choose from."
That led to a viral campaign ad from Colom, which featured several people expressing disbelief at the senator's suggestion to "pick another protein." Instead, the ad said, it was time to "pick another senator."

The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) seized drugs and cosmetics worth ₹34.51 lakh, cancelled 122 licences and suspended 422 others following enforcement action across the State in October 2026, according to a press note issued by the department on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The FDA conducted 1,986 inspections of drug manufacturing, sales and other regulated establishments during the month and issued 674 notices. Of these, 1,694 inspections were conducted at drug sales establishments and 292 at manufacturing and other regulated establishments. The department cancelled 105 licences and suspended 367 licences of sales establishments, while 17 licences were cancelled and 55 suspended in the manufacturing and other categories.
The department also carried out 11 search and seizure operations involving alleged violations related to the manufacture, storage and sale of drugs and cosmetics. Two FIRs were registered, and four persons were arrested under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act in connection with the illegal sale of narcotic drugs.
Among the major seizures, FDA officials recovered allopathic drugs worth ₹22.03 lakh from the premises of Phoenix Medicorp in Nagpur on October 7. According to the department, the establishment had stored drugs at unlicensed premises despite surrendering its licences.
In Mumbai, FDA officials seized spurious drugs identified as Empirime tablets and Cardiurex 2 ml, worth ₹1.01 lakh, from INHS Asvini in Colaba on October 29, according to the department.
In separate operations in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar on October 14 and 25, officials seized 199 Nitrosun 10 tablets containing Nitrazepam. Four persons were arrested in connection with their alleged illegal sale.
The FDA also seized cosmetic soaps worth ₹4.05 lakh from Vedas Herbals Mahila Gruh Udyog in Baramati, Pune district, on October 14, for alleged manufacturing without a licence. In Vasai East, officials seized raw materials, packaging materials and machinery worth ₹1.83 lakh from G.B. Cosmetics on October 10 in connection with alleged unlicensed manufacture and sale of nail polish.
The Konkan division recorded the highest number of inspections in October at 556, followed by Pune with 375 and Greater Mumbai with 322. Konkan also accounted for the highest number of regulatory actions at 156, followed by Greater Mumbai with 105 and Pune with 77.
Between April 1 and October 31, the FDA conducted 7,950 inspections across Maharashtra, issued 2,888 notices, cancelled 555 licences and suspended 2,074 licences. The department recorded 2,629 regulatory actions, comprising licence cancellations and suspensions, during the seven-month period.
The FDA urged citizens to report instances of illegal drug manufacturing or sales, as well as suspected substandard drugs, medical devices and cosmetics, to its commissioner’s office or the nearest district office.

Andreeva wins 11 games in a row to thrash Sabalenka at WTA Finals
- Published
Mirra Andreeva won 11 games in a row as she thrashed world number two Aryna Sabalenka to reach the last four at the WTA Finals.
French Open champion Andreeva was 4-1 down in the opening set before producing some superb tennis and taking advantage of an increasingly erratic Sabalenka performance.
The 19-year-old Russian went on to deliver a statement 6-4 6-0 victory over four-time major singles winner Sabalenka.
"I will be honest, I feel like Aryna did not have the best day," Andreeva told Sky Sports.
"I feel like I cannot really take all the credit today - I feel like that is not very fair in some ways.
"I'm just happy. I had a goal in front of me to commit no matter what and control the things I can control."
As poor as Sabalenka was, Andreeva produced a mature, intelligent performance to shut her out of the match.
She used loopy high balls to initially wrong-foot Sabalenka and then showcased her easy power, hitting 16 winners to only six unforced errors and creating brilliant angles from the baseline.
The only blip came when she found herself 15-30 down as she served for the first set. However, Andreeva calmly hit three aces in a row to take the lead and she never looked back.
Just as in the French Open quarter-finals, where she lost the third set 6-0, Sabalenka could not find her rhythm or range.
The Belarusian hit 23 unforced errors and failed to produce a single ace at Indian Wells, where she won the WTA Tour title earlier this year.
The second seed had taping on her knee but it did not seem to hinder her - this, rather, was a performance similar to some of the collapses she has had this year.
From having a double-break lead, Sabalenka only won a further 10 points in the match as Andreeva dominated.
The result means the winner of the final group match on Friday between Sabalenka and Elina Svitolina will advance to the semi-finals, while Andreeva goes through as the group winner.
Svitolina channels 'anger' to inspire comeback win
Svitolina said she "got a bit angry at myself" to inspire a comeback victory over Karolina Muchova and keep her title hopes alive.
Ukraine's Svitolina lost 6-4 6-0 in her first group match against Andreeva on Monday and made an equally poor start against Muchova.
It looked as though things were getting worse for Svitolina when she took a medical timeout for a right hip injury after losing the first set, before finding herself an early break point down.
However, the sixth seed saved it and then gradually wore down Wimbledon runner-up Muchova to win 3-6 6-2 6-2.
Muchova hit 39 unforced errors throughout the match - the majority of which came from her forehand - as Svitolina ground her down.
Svitolina made no mistake, with the 32-year-old tipping her head back and roaring in celebration after securing the win.
"I was really angry at myself after the first match and the first set," Svitolina told Sky Sports.
"Sometimes it [channelling frustration] happens in a good way and sometimes in a bad way.
"I tried to direct my anger towards the ball and I found my game in the end."

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to the prime minister, Narendra Modi, and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, step down over the voter list revision that critics say favours the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5km march on Sunday from central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi traffic police said a “large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally ... we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party – allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.
