- The claim that the U.S. Air Force had held Maj. Jason Watson, an active-duty airman who publicly called for the impeachment of President Donald Trump, in solitary confinement for more than 80 days by November while he awaited court-martial is still under investigation.
- CNN reported that the Air Force took Watson into pretrial confinement on Aug. 18, under conditions his lawyer Christopher Mutimer later described as "basically in solitary confinement." Mutimer said in early October that Watson was "still in solitary confinement."
- Speaking to Snopes on Nov. 10, Mutimer confirmed Watson had been held in Calvert County Detention Center, Maryland, since Aug. 18, for a total of 85 days and counting. Mutimer explained that because Watson was a military officer, he could not be held with civilian prisoners, meaning he was "in a room by himself 22 to 23 hours a day." Watson had sought pretrial release and a military court was set to consider this motion on Nov. 17, Mutimer said.
- At the time of this writing, the Air Force District of Washington, which the Air Force Press Office said covered questions about Watson, had not commented on Watson's confinement conditions. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
In November, a claim (archived) circulated online that the U.S. Air Force had held Maj. Jason Watson, an active-duty airman who publicly called for the impeachment of President Donald Trump, in solitary confinement for more than 80 days while he awaited court-martial.
CNN reported that the Air Force ordered Watson into "pre-trial confinement" on Aug. 18. Two days later, on Aug. 20, Watson's lawyer Christopher Mutimer told CNN that Watson was "basically in solitary confinement." He repeated this claim in early October, telling CNN (at 1:46, archived) that Watson was "still in solitary confinement."
One X user who claimed Watson remained in solitary confinement in early November — 84 days after the Air Force first ordered him into pretrial confinement — wrote:
Maj. Jason Watson has been in 24-hour solitary confinement for 80+ days & has reportedly lost 20 pounds, all before any trial. UN experts consider solitary beyond 15 days to be torture. He offered to resign, give up all his benefits, & the Air Force said no. Because he protested.
The claim also circulated on Facebook and Threads (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
Speaking to Snopes on Nov. 10, Mutimer confirmed Watson had been detained at Maryland's Calvert County Detention Center since Aug. 18 and described conditions that he said met generally understood definitions for solitary confinement.
Mutimer said Watson "is in a room by himself 22 to 23 hours a day. No one stays in there with him, he is not allowed to have any interaction. When he's let out it's to shower, make a phone call, get some time in the yard by himself." He described Watson's cell as a "pen" where "the light is on all the time."
The Air Force District of Washington, which the Air Force Press Office said handled questions about Watson, had not replied to a question from Snopes about whether it held Watson in solitary confinement at the time of this writing. Military.com reported that an Air Force spokesperson said on Oct. 14 that Watson had access to "exercise, the library, and personal hygiene items" in his pretrial confinement and that an agreement between the Air Force and Calvert County Detention Center required Watson to be held "separately" from convicted prisoners.
Mutimer corroborated the Air Force's October statement, saying in November, "Because he's an officer, he is in the military, that contract says he is not allowed to be with anybody who is not in the military."
Pending comment from the Air Force District of Washington on the conditions of Watson's confinement, we leave this claim unrated.
By November, the docket of the Air Force's military justice branch showed Watson was due for general court-martial in February. Mutimer said he would argue a petition for Watson's pretrial release on Nov. 17.
Mutimer also confirmed the claim some social media users made that Watson had attempted to resign after his July 1 arrest but said officials had denied his resignation and instead pressed ahead with the court-martial, a move that Mutimer described as "absolutely unheard of."
Tracking Watson's case
Capitol Police arrested Watson on July 1 on after he publicly called for Trump's impeachment while wearing his Air Force uniform. A live stream (at 50:56) of the arrest showed Watson standing on the Capitol steps in uniform while holding a sign that read "Impeach Convict Remove."
Watson said at a news conference earlier that day that he was calling for Trump to be impeached because he thought the president and Vice President JD Vance had governed in an unconstitutional way throughout their administration.
Watson highlighted the war in Iran, Elon Musk's sweeping cuts to federal government and the Department of Homeland Security's immigration crackdown and killings of protesters as "high crimes and misdemeanors" (at 28:28) for which "the president and vice president must be impeached, convicted, and removed."
The Air Force major repeated his call for Trump and Vance's removal while speaking to CNN's Erin Burnett (at 1:52) on Aug. 17. Burnett said (at 2:41) during the interview that the military had placed a "gag order" on Watson after his July 1 protest and that he was "under investigation."
According to a later CNN report, the Air Force took Watson into pretrial confinement days after he spoke to the network.
CNN reported that the Air Force charged Watson with 10 violations of three articles of the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the military's legal framework, on Aug. 20. Mutimer reportedly spoke to Watson on that date and reported that he was "basically in solitary confinement."
On Sept. 29, The New York Times reported that an Air Force investigating officer had recommended Watson's case for general court-martial, the military's highest level of trial court.
According to the Judge Advocate General's Corps Department of the Air Force, which investigated and charged Watson, the major faced charges of four violations of articles 88, 92 and 133 of the UCMJ.
Article 88 (Page 34) of the UCMJ states that any commissioned officer who uses "contemptuous words" against certain public officials, which includes the president and vice president, should face a court-martial. Article 92 (Page 35) states that a person subject to the code that fails to obey an order or regulation can be subject to court-martial. Article 133 (Page 48) states that "Any commissioned officer, cadet, or midshipman who is convicted of conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman shall be punished as a court-martial may direct."
The code does not explicitly define what "conduct unbecoming an officer" means.
An Air Force spokesperson reportedly told Military.com in October that the Air Force had acted in accordance with the Rule for Court-Martial 305 when it took Watson into pretrial confinement in August. That rule says someone can be placed in pretrial confinement if there is probable cause they committed "an offense triable by court-martial."
That rule also says that someone taken into pretrial confinement can ask a military judge to review the "propriety" of the confinement, meaning whether it is appropriate. Mutimer said such a review for Watson would happen on Nov. 17.
According to the UCMJ's Article 13 (Page 5), it is prohibited to punish a service member awaiting trial. Any confinement before trial must not "be any more rigorous than the circumstances require to insure his presence, but he may be subjected to minor punishment during that period for infractions of discipline."
At the time of this writing, Watson had not been convicted or sentenced. Punishments for service members convicted by court-martial range from reprimands and salary reductions to dismissal or discharge.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated whether an active-duty soldier took part in an anti-immigration-enforcement protest.

The European Commission announced a sweeping set of updates to consumer law on Wednesday to protect European Union citizens from “harmful digital practices”—whether while online shopping, browsing social media, or doing their Duolingo lesson.
Within the package, the Commission unveiled its Digital Fairness Act to address harmful practices online. Proposed rules include banning dark patterns—practices which manipulate consumers into making decisions they would not otherwise make, such as falsely claiming a product is running low. They will also curb dynamic pricing by ticket retailers, like Ticketmaster; force influencers to disclose when they are being paid to promote a product; outrule personalized advertising and pricing targeting minors or taking advantage of sensitive data; make digital subscriptions easier to cancel; and give consumers a right to interact with human customer service.
The package “represents the most significant reform of EU consumer protection rules in more than 20 years” according to Michael McGrath, the EC Consumer Protection Commissioner, noting that existing consumer rules were developed before ecommerce, the attention economy, and use of personal data for marketing took off. “The digital fairness act will make sure the digital economy works for consumers and not against them,” he said at a press conference.
The bill will also enable all consumers to turn off addictive design features on digital services, such as autoplay of videos and streaks—including on apps like Strava and Duolingo.
Some of these patterns the EU has already restricted for children through its Kids Act, which in addition to banning under-13s from accessing social media and chatbots, targets addictive designs in those services. Some European rights groups have called for those protections to be extended to all consumers and, teasing the Digital Fairness Act in September’s State of the Union address, President Ursula von der Leyen said: “But it is not only minors who are at risk. Addictive design, for example, is harming everyone. That is why we need a wider framework.”
Some of the risks are also already regulated by the EU Digital Services Act. On Friday, the European Commission said ByteDance’s TikTok had breached those rules with the “rabbit hole effect” of its “For You” feed algorithm which personalizes content recommended to users. The tech regulator had previously found TikTok’s “addictive design” broke the rules by including features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, and push notifications, in addition to the algorithm. In July, it found Meta to be in breach of the act due to similar features on Instagram and Facebook. If confirmed, both companies may now face fines of up to 6 percent of worldwide annual turnover.
The new regulation is designed to fill the gaps between this, the Digital Markets Act, and August’s AI Act, says executive vice president Henna Virkkunen, “not duplicate this.” The package should simplify consumer protection rules across the bloc’s 27 members and be a “strong safety net in the digital world,” she adds.
The Commission aims to accelerate cross-border cooperation through strengthened enforcement rules. These would also give the regulator direct powers to investigate large-scale impact and fine firms up to 6 percent of their worldwide annual turnover. Non-EU companies would be required to appoint a local legal representative to cooperate with authorities.

In the Israeli legislative elections held in late October 2026, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, falling short of the 61-seat majority required to govern. The Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, alongside other opposition factions, won 48 seats. Notably, Arab-led parties made historic gains, winning 19 seats and becoming potential “kingmakers”. Following the vote, President Isaac Herzog formally accepted the results. He opened a two-day consultation window with party leaders to determine who is best positioned to assemble a stable coalition.
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament building.
Fact: The video does not show the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament. It shows a pro-Palestine activist replacing the German national flag with a Palestinian flag on a flagpole outside the Reichstag building, which houses the German Parliament (Bundestag), in Berlin on 08 November 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring visuals similar to those seen in the viral video. According to these reports, the incident took place outside the Reichstag building, which houses the German Parliament (Bundestag), in Berlin on Sunday, 08 November 2026.
The reports (here, here) state that a 22-year-old pro-Palestine activist climbed a 30-metre-high flagpole in front of the Reichstag building at around 11:30 am, removed the German national flag, and replaced it with a Palestinian flag.
The group ‘Peacefully Against Genocide‘ claimed responsibility for the incident, stating that the action was a protest against the German government’s pro-Israel policy and its silence on alleged human rights violations in Gaza.
According to a press release issued by Berlin Police on 08 November 2026, two people who allegedly assisted the 22-year-old activist were detained and later released after their identities were established. The Palestinian flag was subsequently removed with the assistance of the Berlin Fire Brigade. Police also launched an investigation into suspected offences, including insulting state symbols, damaging government property, trespassing, and violating Berlin’s assembly law.
To sum up, the viral video shows the Palestinian flag hoisted outside the German Parliament, not the Israeli Parliament.

Dismissing the BJP’s criticism of his plans to visit Ayodhya next month, Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday (November 11, 2026) emphasised that “God belongs to everyone” and slammed his critics for their alleged loot and destruction in Ayodhya.
Mr. Yadav is scheduled to visit the Ram Temple in Ayodhya on December 12, with his family. BJP leaders triggered a political war of words by terming his visit politically motivated.
“God belongs to everyone. So why should we not visit these places? We will visit Kedareshwar, Mathura and Vrindavan as well. We have been visiting these places before, and we will continue to do so. Those who looted and destroyed the livelihood of common people should answer,” Mr. Yadav told journalists in Lucknow.
‘BJP’s end is near’
The SP president claimed that Uttar Pradesh voters have determined to bring his party back into power in the State.
“The farmers, youth, labourers, and traders of Uttar Pradesh want change. The public has made up its mind to form the government of the Samajwadi Party in 2027. The people of the State are ready; the end of the BJP is near. Under the BJP government, injustice, oppression, inflation, and unemployment are at their peak. The Chief Minister is unaware of the employment rate and unemployment rate,” Mr. Yadav said, urging party workers to win booths and be vigilant.
“The BJP wins elections through dishonesty and fraud. The BJP wanted to commit dishonesty through the [special intensive revision] SIR process, but the workers of the Samajwadi Party and the PDA guards saved their votes. It is the responsibility of all leaders and workers to keep their votes safe and strengthen the booths,” he added.
‘Aadhaar should be linked to voter list’
The SP chief demanded that the voter list be linked with Aadhaar cards and said that these cards should be made of metal so that fakes cannot be created. “If everyone’s Aadhaar card is biometric, then why is the voter list not being linked to the Aadhaar card? When discussions are being held about Digital India and becoming equal to the world, why is the voter list not being linked to the Aadhaar card?” he asked.
Mr. Yadav claimed that the BJP was scared of the PDA, his acronym for an alliance of minorities, Dalits, and backward class voters. “Now the fight is not 80 versus 20, but 95 versus 5. This time in the Assembly elections, the BJP will not be visible on the ground. Seeing the BJP’s defeat, the Chief Minister’s language and behaviour have changed,” he said.
Ten years of demonetisation
Celebrating the birthday of Khajanchi, a 10-year-old boy born during demonetisation in 2016, Mr. Yadav described ‘note bandi’ as the most corrupt decision in the world’s history.
“The Samajwadi Party celebrates the birthday of Khajanchi every year. Khajanchi was born during the demonetisation. His birthday should be celebrated by the BJP. The BJP should adopt it, but not in the way that BJP leaders adopted the village and then left it orphaned,” he said.
“The BJP should remember a decade of demonetisation. This is ten years of the BJP’s failure. Demonetisation proved to be an ocean of corruption for the BJP government. There has been a 70% increase in the circulation of cash. No other wrong decision of such magnitude has occurred in the entire world. None of the superficial targets during demonetisation were achieved. Demonetisation was like slow poison,” he added.

ByteDance plans the release of a Muse-like AI assistant in the coming weeks to augment its lead in AI video, a milestone event the company hopes will help close the gap with top U.S. labs in as soon as three years.
Speaking to its AI team in an all-hands meeting recently, co-founder Zhang Yiming told researchers, engineers and supporting staff about the plan and set out key priorities, according to people familiar with the matter. He sees ByteDance able to compete with leading industry names like Anthropic and OpenAI at the cutting edge, though he cautioned it would take until at least 2029 or 2030, the people said, asking not to be named as the meeting was private.
The planned new artificial intelligence agent will serve a similar role to Muse, introduced by Meta Platforms this September. Muse has proven a big hit for its U.S. creator, consolidating Meta’s extensive AI research into a voice-based agent with an animated avatar that helps users with various tasks. Meta is distributing Muse across its hardware portfolio that includes various models of smart glasses and an upcoming Muse Charm gadget just for the agent. After Michigan voters elected Democrat Abdul El-Sayed as senator in November 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that he had failed the background check required for classified Senate briefings.
One X user named Jonathan Gregory who shared the claim wrote that El-Sayed's alleged failure would exclude him from some meetings as a senator. The user wrote:
Abdul El Sayed has failed the background check required for classified Senate briefings. The denial blocks him from any session that involves sensitive national security information. Officials who conduct the clearances reported that the review did not meet the standards necessary for access to restricted materials. The failure leaves open the question of what specific issues prevented approval.
Senators who receive classified briefings must clear the same process before they can attend. El Sayed's rejection means he cannot participate in those meetings. The decision places him outside the normal flow of information that other members receive. Americans who expect every senator to qualify for the same briefings now see one individual excluded by the clearance system.
(@TrumpNews_Baby, accessed via X)
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to verify whether it was true.
The claim was false. El-Sayed could not have "failed" a background check "required for classified Senate briefings" because no such background check exists.
Congress members, including senators, are not required to pass a background check to gain security clearance and access classified material, according to a Congressional Research Service "Frequently Asked Questions" report about security clearances from 2023.
The U.S. Constitution, which lays out the requirements for senators, does not include a requirement for them to pass a background check to access classified information. According to Constitution Annotated, the Library of Congress' legal analysis and interpretation of the Constitution, the document has never allowed for changes to the requirements for a senator because that would undermine the legislative branch's investigative powers.
Additionally, federal law exempts members of Congress, including senators, from legislation that governs background checks and security clearances.
The false rumor may have originated as satire. Snopes previously linked another false claim about election fraud to Jonathan Gregory, who shared the first instance of the rumor about El-Sayed that we identified on X. Gregory labels himself as a comedian on his Facebook page, though his Instagram and X accounts don't display such a label. None of Gregory's profiles specifically mention the word "satire," though he has previously used the term near the very end of some of his posts — potentially as a way of hinting at the truth about his content.
We've published fact checks about other matters originating from Gregory's social media accounts, all of which involved false claims.
We contacted El-Sayed's campaign to ask if he had ever applied for, been granted or denied government security clearance before becoming a senator-elect. We also asked the national intelligence director's office whether it had ever granted or denied security clearance to El-Sayed in the past. We await replies to our questions.
Congress investigative powers allow members access to classified information
Members of Congress are implicitly allowed to access classified information because the U.S. Constitution gives the legislative branch investigative powers to inform laws and ensure they are being carried out. In practice, carrying out these investigations can mean that members of Congress need to access classified material, and the Information Security Oversight Office, which is responsible for the policy and oversight of the U.S. government's security classification system, wrote in 2001 that this is generally allowed (PDF Page 66).
It is important to note, however, that though El-Sayed and any other member of Congress bypass the normal procedure for getting security clearance, that does not give them unlimited access to classified information.
For example, the ISOO wrote in 2001 that though members of Congress were exempt from background checks and filling out the government's classified information nondisclosure agreement, they were not exempt from the "'need-to-know' requirement" (PDF Page 66).
For example, the office wrote (PDF Page 66) that members of Congress, "are not inherently authorized to receive all classified information, but agencies provide access as is necessary for Congress to perform its legislative functions."
Subject to election certification by state officials, the 120th Congress, which will include El-Sayed as one of two senators from Michigan, will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027.
For further reading, Snopes frequently investigates rumors relating to El-Sayed.

A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen, a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Researchers have been searching for a drug to lower Lp(a)
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence.
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
What went wrong?
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz, a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal, a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron, a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson, a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

NASA has unveiled a new experimental vehicle, the X-70 Fractal, although many of its features remain a mystery. The agency describes it as a research platform designed to conduct advanced aeronautical tests, but so far it has released only computer-generated images and some technical specifications regarding its capabilities.
Despite the secrecy, it is possible to get some idea of what the new vehicle is like. First of all, it’s not a spacecraft, meaning it is not designed to reach Earth’s orbit or operate outside the atmosphere. However, this crewed, subsonic aircraft is capable of flying far above commercial jets, reaching altitudes over 45,000 feet, well into the stratosphere. Other specs released include the plane’s max speed of Mach 0.75—about 575 miles per hour—and that it can travel nearly 1,700 miles in a single flight.
According to NASA, the X-70 Fractal will enable research into maneuver capabilities never before demonstrated in crewed aircraft, although the agency has not specified what types of maneuvers it intends to perform. The plane will also be capable of carrying up to one ton of experimental equipment and is expected to make its first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years.
One of the key features of the craft will be its modular design, allowing for the rapid installation and replacement of experimental equipment both inside and outside the aircraft. This is largely why it is referred to as an “experimental platform.” It will also feature reconfigurable flight control systems so that NASA can study different ways of steering an aircraft without having to develop a separate platform for each research project.
Although NASA is best known for its space missions, it’s long been dedicated to aeronautical research. That’s what the first A stands for. The agency also traces its origins to the creation of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, which was founded in 1915 and was folded into the newly formed NASA in 1958.
Since then, the space agency has developed numerous experimental aircraft to test technologies that range from supersonic flight and propulsion systems to new aerodynamic configurations. Not all of these prototypes go on to become operational aircraft, but the knowledge gained contributes to the development of future commercial and military aircraft as well as space vehicles.
Among its most recent projects is the X-59, developed in collaboration with aerospace and defense company Lockheed Martin to investigate ways to reduce the noise produced by supersonic aircraft. The X-70 Fractal will join this tradition of pioneers in the sky.
The development of these technologies also has a strategic dimension. In its budget documents for 2027, NASA identifies aeronautical research as a tool for maintaining US technological leadership in the face of growing international competition. The agency also plans to collaborate with the Department of Defense to advance new flight capabilities, although it has not yet announced any military applications for the X-70 Fractal.
During the unveiling of the new aircraft, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman noted that the project represents only one part of a new era for federal aeronautical research and hinted that more announcements are coming. For now, the agency has not provided details on what those initiatives might be, nor has it specified when it will release more information about the X-70 Fractal.

Why is gasoline suddenly under $4 a gallon?
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Drivers are starting to see some relief from high fuel prices. For the first time in months, the average price of a gallon of gasoline has dipped below $4, according to AAA.
The price crossed below the $4 threshold on Tuesday, and is currently down to a national average of $3.94 for a gallon of regular. Prices have dipped about 40 cents over the past month, with much of that decline happening in the past two weeks.
"Many will assume the election had something to do with it, but that's a myth," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote in his industry newsletter.
Instead, he continued, gasoline prices are dropping for a more banal reason: "For now, it's the seasonal shift, not politics, driving the relief at the pump."
Gas prices often ease in the fall.
One reason: It's no longer summer, which is the peak season for gas. (Fewer people drive in colder weather, AAA points out.) With less demand, there's a touch more gas on the market.
Refineries also finish their annual maintenance by late fall. So that adds a bit more gas to go around.
And the blend of gasoline that's on the market gets cheaper.
Refineries make two types of gasoline every year: summer and winter blends. The summer blend produces less smog, because it evaporates less quickly in the heat; the winter blend helps engines start up in freezing weather, and uses a bit more butane, which helps lower its cost.
(Normally, the switch happens around September 15. This year, the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of Energy said the switch would happen on September 1, citing gasoline prices that have been driven up by the war in Iran.)
But none of those are the biggest reason why gas prices are falling, says Jorge León, head of geopolitics at the research group Rystad Energy. The main driver is the falling price of Brent crude oil, which is now down to about $90 a barrel, and which is what refineries need to make gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
That price is falling because there's a bit more oil coming out of the Middle East via pipelines, and because market traders have rejoiced at the intensifying diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran.
That progress could easily be reversed if the war escalates, León wrote in an email to NPR. "President Trump may see further military action as a way to regain negotiating leverage before Democrats take control of Congress in January. If we see renewed escalation, much of last week's oil price decline could quickly reverse," he wrote. The same would be true for gas prices.
Congressional Democrats have expressed their support for ending the war in Iran. While they have limited power to do that, they do control the power of the purse, and can withhold additional war funding or hold back confirmations of key officials.
For now, if the price of Brent crude keeps falling, so could prices at the pump. "However, this does not mean a complete 'normalization,' a return to the price levels we had before this conflict started," Jaime Brito, executive director of refining and oil markets for Dow Jones Energy, wrote in an email to NPR.
To get back to pre-Iran war gas prices, the whole oil supply chain would have to recover. Ships that have been running long alternative routes to avoid the Strait of Hormuz would have to return to their points of origin, then resume their normal routes, taking crude oil to refineries. Those refineries would have to pump out enough fuel to alleviate global demand — and depleted stockpiles. The whole process could take months after a lasting peace deal.
"Coming back to those levels will require a return to normal crude production, shipping and refining of the entire global supply chain," Brito continued.
And while $4 a gallon may seem like a bargain these days, in an update on its website, AAA said that gasoline prices are still the highest they've ever been at this time of year.

Mammography uses low-dose X-rays to examine breast tissue and can help identify abnormalities that may not be detectable through physical examination. AI-based positioning support is designed to assist in accurate positioning and consistent image acquisition.
The equipment takes approximately five seconds for standard image acquisition and 12 seconds for high-resolution imaging. It also has features such as flexible positioning, intelligent breast compression and automatic decompression to help reduce discomfort during the examination.
Speaking at the launch, S. Subramanian, Chairman and Managing Director of V.S. Hospitals, said early detection was important in breast cancer care and that mammography played a key role in identifying breast abnormalities.
The hospital will offer free mammography screening to underprivileged people throughout November 2026. Those seeking to avail themselves of the screening can contact the hospital at 7448850500.

Kiara Advani and Sidharth Malhotra brought plenty of humour to the latest episode of Koffee With Karan 9, offering viewers a glimpse into their everyday relationship dynamics. Koffee With Karan 9: Kiara Advani reveals she checks Sidharth Malhotra’s phone; actor complains about Kiara’s photography skills
The segment began with Johar asking the couple to drink if they had ever gone through their partner’s phone. While Sidharth did not immediately respond, Kiara took a sip of her lemon juice and turned towards him, asking, “You have never gone through my phone? Yeah.. you have never gone through my phone.”
When Johar asked what she usually looked for, Kiara admitted, “I like to read sometimes. A former Eli Lilly sales rep filed a lawsuit alleging that she was fired after complaining the company was promoting its Mounjaro diabetes drug to combat weight loss before receiving regulatory approval to do so.
Jennifer Mansion, who was hired as a senior territory manager in Dallas four years ago, claimed that she observed other Lilly sales reps promoting the diabetes drug as a salve for obesity. Mansion also contended that a physician touted Mounjaro as a weight loss option during a luncheon sponsored by the drugmaker, according to the suit filed in federal court in Texas.
Such promotions are known as off-label marketing in the pharmaceutical industry. The phrase refers to promoting a medicine for a usage that was not approved by the Food and Drug Administration. A physician may prescribe a medicine for an unapproved use, but a drugmaker is not permitted to market its drug for that purpose.

It’s definitely an upgrade to the typical indoor basketball experience. Plenty of play modes (perhaps too many), plus lots of streaming options.
TIRED
The hard included ball makes for a very noisy experience. Battery drains quickly, even when not in use. Some app modes didn’t work at all. Buggy remote. Weak speakers. No Netflix. Eventually it all gets a bit stale.
If your mom was one of those who always said, “Don’t play ball in the house,” well, she’s going to absolutely hate the Huupe Mini 2.
Huupe manufactures smart basketball hoops and add-on kits for existing setups that track shots, light up the board when a point is registered, and include social features like global challenges and leaderboards. The Huupe Mini 2 is the pint-sized, indoor version of that idea, clipping over the top of a door so you can shoot hoops without ever having to leave the room.
I’ve been testing one out for weeks, and while it’s a fun diversion, some of its features overreach beyond its core functionality, resulting in an experience that bricks as much as it dunks.
Season Tickets
The Huupe Mini 2 is, effectively, a smart television with a basketball hoop mounted to it. Or rather, a smart TV that comes with a basketball hoop that you have to mount yourself, courtesy of four screws and a little elbow grease. The LCD screen measures 19 inches diagonally, plus a hefty border that includes stereo speakers and a camera used to track you and your b-ball prowess. (Total size of the backboard is 25 inches diagonally, which fits comfortably within a door frame.)
A 5-inch inflatable rubber basketball is included, along with a small hand pump and needle. Also in the box are a small but otherwise traditional remote control—required to do anything with the Huupe—and a USB-C charger and lengthy cable so you can top up the battery without removing it from the door.
After a quick charge, the unit is ready to set up. I was surprised to discover there’s no app for the device; while larger Huupe hardware works with one, the Mini 2 is completely self-contained and web-based. Just connect the backboard to your Wi-Fi network through a process that you step through with the remote, just like you would on any modern television.
What’s new vs. the original Huupe Mini? According to the company, most of the upgrades are behind the scenes: a faster CPU, a larger battery (rated lifespan is now four hours), better display quality, and “significantly” better shot tracking. New games are also included, which I’ll cover in the sections to come.
Dunkin’
Once connected to the web, the Huupe Mini 2 opens up a world of entertainment to you, and, to my great surprise, not all of it is basketball-related. At first blush, the options available are actually quite daunting. It’s all arranged into traditional tiles on the home screen, which you scroll through with the remote.
Just Huupe is the board’s most basic scoring system, tracking shots and recording your shooting percentage in an untimed session. If you want to get competitive, Huupe Live and the Daily Prize Challenge are social games where you challenge players worldwide to score the most points in a given time frame. The winner gets a nominal prize—10 bucks for the daily challenge, a “cozy sweatsuit” for a monthlong challenge. Other games are fairly self-explanatory, like Most 3 Pointers in 90 Seconds and Family Mode (basically Horse).
Many of the games require online friends to play against; if you don’t have pals with their own Huupe Minis, you’ll probably be locked out of these modes—not that they add much beyond their multiplayer features.
Things get a little kookier—and buggier—from there. For example, Huupe Flyers is designed to be played without a ball. It’s a gesture-based version of Flappy Bird, wherein you literally flap your arms around to keep a basketball in the air, tracking your movements via the camera much like an Xbox Kinect. Unfortunately, unlike the ball-based games, I was never able to play it, as it failed the calibration process every time I tried to fire it up.
The system also works as a fairly straightforward streaming platform. Included are apps for YouTube, HBO Max, ESPN, Disney+, Prime Video, Hulu, Spotify, and more. There’s one glaring omission in that list, of course, and I’m not talking about Paramount+ but rather Netflix. Without Netflix support, can you even call yourself a streaming device? It’s also worth noting that the built-in speakers are surprisingly weak. On some apps the audio is OK; on others it’s nearly inaudible.
The Fade Away
The Huupe Mini 2 includes not just a sensor that can detect when a basket is successfully made; it also includes a camera to track how far the shooter is from the backboard. This is used to assign point values to various shots (depending on the specific game you’re playing), with more points earned the farther away you are from the hoop.
The good news is that in weeks of playing on the Huupe Mini 2, I never noticed a time when a successful basket was recorded as a miss or vice versa. The distance calculation, however, is another thing. I’ve shot from across the room and had it count as 1 point, while some shots from just a few feet away ring up as 3 points. I could never figure out much rhyme or reason for this variability, except that shots straight-on to the backboard generally registered as lower point values, even if they were distant, while shots from the wings earned more. Of course, navigating all of this is highly dependent on the geometry of your room. Unless you have the Huupe Mini 2 set up in an empty garage, you are probably, like me, going to have plenty of obstacles that get in the way of a lot of your shots—and plenty of crawling under furniture to retrieve wayward balls.
Out of Bounds
I can say with authority that it is harder to make a basket on the Huupe Mini 2 than on a regulation basketball goal, even at a very close distance. The hoop is small, and the ball tends to rebound wildly off the springy backboard. It’s quite unforgiving, and it didn’t really make me want to spend a lot of time playing, chasing balls that bounced into the corner or rolled under the bed.
The other big problem: When the included inflatable ball hits the Huupe Mini 2, the impact is extremely loud, to the point where I was promptly informed by my wife that it was not appropriate for use when anyone else was in the house. While Huupe says the device is intended solely for use with the included ball, I found a workaround by purchasing a 5-inch foam basketball from Amazon, which makes a bit less noise on impact and also softens the rebound a bit. It has had zero trouble registering baskets.
Battery life is another issue. While four hours is plenty of playing time, the battery continues to drain when the Huupe is in standby mode, which meant I would play a few games in the morning, ostensibly shut the Huupe off, then come back in the afternoon to a completely dead device. The Huupe can run with the power cord attached, but only once the battery has charged to at least about 5 percent.
Unfortunately, even turning the power off is puzzlingly difficult. The power button on my remote control did nothing; I ultimately had to turn the system on and off with the physical button on the bottom of the backboard.
At $429 (on deep discount from a hefty list price of $799), the Huupe Mini 2 sits perhaps just over the edge of what might pass for a quirky holiday gift—and I think it’s safe to say no one is buying this device for themselves. You’d have to be a huge basketball nut to get enough mileage out of the device to make it worthwhile. I expect you would also have to loathe leaving your room. With today’s kids, who knows.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

The TV landscape has changed dramatically this past year. New art televisions now look like matte-finish paintings on the wall. RGB televisions use red, green, and blue lights for accurate color. But OLED televisions still reign supreme for deep and rich blacks. They can control individual pixels or turn them off completely for an inky, cinematic look.
Fortunately, probably because of this intense competition, many OLED televisions are more affordable than ever. After testing many of the best models this year, I narrowed down my favorites to the ones that truly deserve a place on your TV stand.
For more home theater and audio recommendations, check out related guides to the Best RGB TVs, Best Home Theater Projectors, and Best Soundbars. Or, if you don't know where to start, read our guide on How to Buy the Right TV in 2026.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Why Choose an OLED in the First Place?
An OLED television is different from LCD displays like LED and micro-RGB TVs. OLED (organic light-emitting diode) uses special organic material that lights up when fed electricity. That means each individual pixel can be turned completely on and off independently.
For movies and shows, that means dark scenes look more realistic and show extra shadow detail. In practice, when Star-Lord flops onto the screen in the intro of Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2, you can see more details in his dark gray suit—folds, ripples, and belts.
What Size TV Should I Get?
A good rule of thumb? Choose your OLED size based on the size of the room and how far away you will sit from the screen.
Larger sizes are more expensive—doubly so for OLED models. While an 85-inch OLED screen will look spectacular, it will cost you, and will be really hard to move around and install.
For most larger living rooms or group viewing areas, 65 inches is the standard. Anytime we quote a price or link to a retailer below, assume we are linking to the 65-inch version of the TV (unless we specifically call out another size).
Are RGB TVs Better Than OLED?
I've tested a lot of RGB TVs in 2026, and put them through the wringer against OLED models, often in the same room. In my results, OLED TVs still generally have the upper hand because individual pixels can be dimmed dark gray or turned off completely. Dark scenes in movies like The Batman look more realistic on an OLED than an RGB TV. However, I expect RGB TV tech to improve quickly. By next year, it might finally trump OLED.
Best Overall OLED TV
Samsung S95H Specs
| Display type | QD-OLED | 
| Refresh rate | 165 Hz | 
| Operating system | Tizen OS | 
| Connectivity | HDMI 2.1 (x4), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Amazon Alexa, Samsung Bixby | 
| Speaker layout | 4.2.2 channel | 
What sets the Samsung S95H apart from other OLED models is a brighter, clearer, and more colorful picture. It's simply the best OLED display I’ve tested this year.
Picture quality is outstanding. Extra features like the AI picture optimizer actually make a big difference in eking out even more detail. For example, Game of Thrones looked a bit dark at first watch—that is, until the AI optimizer kicked in and made everything more visible, no diving into settings necessary.
The S95H also has a new, sleek design this year. The main display sits just in front of a silver bezel, giving it a more modern, picture-frame look. (The previous Samsung S95F was all black with no silver bezel.) Another win for the S95H is that it no longer requires the Samsung One Connect breakout box to use. You can use one if you want (purchased separately), but the HDMI ports are now on the TV itself, which I find far more convenient for keeping my gear in one place near my TV. The remote is still logical and intuitive, though I can't say the same for the Tizen operating system (you get used to it).
Best Budget OLED TV
LG B6 Specs
| Display type | OLED | 
| Refresh rate | 120 Hz | 
| Operating system | WebOS 26 | 
| Connectivity | HDMI 2.1 (x4), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Amazon Alexa, LG voice recognition | 
| Speaker layout | 2.0 channel | 
Using the word “budget” to describe any OLED television might seem misplaced. However, the LG B6 bucks the trend at $1,300, and performed commendably in most of my tests.
I love how easy it is to set up using the LG ThinQ app, which does most of the heavy lifting, like choosing which apps to install by default. The all-black, unassuming design (no silver accents here), won't turn heads, but at this price, that's expected.
Picture quality is great for the price, but obviously outclassed by pricier models like the midrange LG C6 and flagship LG G6. Still, some of my test movies, like The Creator, looked surprisingly cinematic and colorful for a budget TV. For more challenging scenes (dark scenes in Game of Thrones and The Batman), be ready to tweak the settings dial in the picture. The 120-Hz refresh rate makes this TV no slouch for gaming, either—Resident Evil: Requiem running on a high-end gaming PC looks photorealistic.
Best Gaming OLED TV
Sony Bravia 8 II Specs
| Display type | QD-OLED | 
| Refresh rate | 120 Hz | 
| Operating system | Google TV | 
| Connectivity | HDMI 2.1 (x2), HDMI 2.0 (x2), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Google Gemini | 
| Speaker layout | 2.2 channel | 
A Sony OLED only makes sense for gaming, especially on a Sony Playstation 5. The Sony Bravia 8 II runs at a common 120-Hz refresh rate, but works seamlessly with the PS5 in ways other TVs don't. It can automatically enable features like HDR tone mapping (for a more colorful picture) and low-latency gaming mode (for a slight advantage in quick controller nudges).
Of course, the Bravia 8 II is excellent outside of gaming too. For movie night, we found that 4K and even older 1080p HD movies and shows looked crisp and colorful, with deep blacks. Off-angle viewing is also exceptional, helping those sitting off to the side in your entertainment room to still enjoy the experience without any weird dimming or glare. It also runs Google TV OS, one of the easiest operating systems to use. Google Gemini in particular is great at searching for content—prompts like “Show me the best psychological thrillers from the '90s” actually worked.
One downside is ports—this TV only has two HDMI 2.1 ports. Most premium models these days have four. Viewing in especially bright rooms can be challenging, but that is a common problem with many OLED TVs.
Best Premium OLED TV
LG G5 Specs
| Display type | OLED | 
| Refresh rate | 165 Hz | 
| Operating system | WebOS 25 | 
| Connectivity | HDMI 2.1 (x4), Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, Optical, Ethernet | 
| Voice assistant | Amazon Alexa, LG voice recognition | 
| Speaker layout | 4.2 channel | 
Yes, this model was replaced by the LG G6 (which we are still testing), but honestly, the 2025 LG G5 is a crown jewel of OLED televisions, and on sale for much less than the G6. With deep and rich blacks, a speedy operating system, and exceptional gaming features like a 165-Hz refresh rate, it’s one of my favorite premium OLED TVs.
I tested the movie Tron: Ares on this television and was blown away by the picture quality. The OLED tech made the blacks look so rich and inky, even the helmet on the main character looked realistic, with clearly visible crevices and shadows on his uniform.
Sound is also premium—the G5 supports Dolby Atmos surround sound on the television itself, making movies sound more like they do in the theater straight out of the box (though I would still recommend a soundbar).
Sure, the Samsung S95H is the better overall pick, but the G5 surprised and delighted me with things like its lightning-fast processor, operating system, and size options (it goes all the way up to a 97-inch model that costs $25,000).
Honorable Mentions
Roku Pro Series OLED for $1,200: If you're OLED-curious, on a budget, and a big fan of the Roku operating system, consider the Roku Pro Series OLED. It's incredibly easy to set up, runs on Roku's simple operating system, and has a great remote-finding button on the side of the TV itself. It's even cheaper than the LG B6, though it isn't as bright or as colorful.
Sony Bravia 6 OLED for $2,000: This entry-level OLED launched in 2025 and has been on sale at up to 40 percent off, putting it on the same price tier as the LG B6. One reason to pick the Bravia 6 over the LG B6 is operating system—the Bravia 6 runs on Google TV, which I strongly prefer for quick voice searches using Google Gemini compared to webOS on the LG models. The B6 has a superior picture and deeper blacks, though.
OLED Alternatives
For picture quality, OLED TVs still reign supreme because they can control individual pixels and turn them off completely. However, over the last year, art TVs and RGB TVs have started to take more and more real estate on store shelves. Some brands, like Hisense and TCL, have a totally OLED-free TV lineup for 2026, switching focus to RGB and mini-LED. If you're curious about the competition, I’ve listed a few other TV types to consider.
An art TV: Samsung The Frame Pro (2026)
I absolutely loved this premium art television. I mounted it on the wall in my office for a couple of months, showcasing shipwrecks and masterpiece paintings daily. The matte finish and anti-glare tech make this television able to display more like a piece of wall art in a museum than a shiny, reflective black box. The Pro version in particular offers far better picture quality for TV shows and movies than other art TVs on the market.
An RGB TV: LG Micro RGB Evo 75-inch
My top pick for an RGB television, the LG Micro RGB Evo is highly customizable in terms of picture quality. You can tweak just about every color and brightness setting to make sure dark scenes look textured and clear and colors look realistic, not oversaturated. It's unfortunately only available in larger sizes: 75, 86, and 100-inches.

I love my old iPhone 14, but I’m starting to face the facts: It’s going to die. The battery is about to go; apps take longer to load than they used to. Some of it I can fix. I can go to the Genius Bar and swap the battery. Maybe I could even do it myself; that’d buy me some time. But eventually, Apple won’t support this wildly expensive device at all, and there’s not much I can do about it.
Apple did start offering self-repair services a few years ago, but it involves renting nearly 80 pounds of equipment and requires you to use official parts. When all is said and done, it doesn’t save you that much money versus just going to the Apple Store. But if I buy a screen or a camera component from a third party, there's a chance my iPhone is gonna lock me out of certain features because it doesn't recognize it.
This problem goes far beyond iPhones. Manufacturers have put similar locks on all kinds of gadgets, from video game consoles to cars to smart home devices, making them hard to modify and even harder to restore after some firmware update renders a certain feature unusable.
Not surprisingly, a lot of people think this isn't fair, that there should be a better way to do it. I think at this point it's safe to say it qualifies as a movement, one that unites under the banner of “right to repair.” Built around the radical idea that when you buy something you should be able to truly own it, right-to-repair advocates believe consumers have the right to maintain, fix, or modify any piece of hardware they’ve purchased. The movement has gained even more traction now that AI makes it even easier to hack the software powering consumers’ devices.
To find out what’s next for the right-to-repair movement, I went straight to the source: Louis Rossmann, a YouTuber and consumer rights advocate who recently organized the Own Your Shit tour, which went around the US earlier this year to call for the death of Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, which prohibits users from bypassing digital restrictions put on devices by manufacturers.
Rossmann and I talked about more than just Section 1201. We also discussed the US midterm elections, putting out bounties to find product fixes, and what will happen as the right-to-repair movement collides with the rise of AI.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Got it.

When I started doing this, I was just talking about right to repair for Apple devices, which is what my small shop worked on. I saw it from my small lens. I focused on the items where I knew exactly what was going on, and I really thought, “This is a problem that only affects me.”
It wasn’t until about 2017 when I went to Nebraska for this legislative hearing that I realized that it really is not just something that affects my small field. As time went on, my channel stopped just discussing right to repair, and it started discussing how right to repair is a small element under this umbrella of ownership. And ownership being taken away is, in my opinion, the real problem. Your inability to fix what you own is one thing, but also the fact that everything is turning into a subscription, that the things that you buy must connect to the manufacturer’s server in order to work, which means that they can disable your product at any time.

When I speak to farmers, it’s very much the same version of what I deal with in my business, where you’ll see a headline where a company says they’re supporting repair, and then you actually look into the details of it, and it’s really very surface level.
One of the examples I have of this is with Samsung. They had released this independent repair program, and they made screens and batteries available, so you could buy a battery. I remember the producer came to me and said they wanted to do a piece on how Apple is bad with upgrades. Have faith.”
They took it to Apple. They said, “We gotta do the motherboard,” all this other stuff. So I take a tweezer, bend it back, and it works. It was featured on national news.
There’s some other inflection points, like in 2016 when Apple had asked if I would take down one of my videos showing where a fuse was. So I showed how to replace this thing. At 55 seconds in the video, I’m showing where the fuse is in the motherboard, and they asked me to take the video down, and I’m like, “I don’t want to. File a DMCA claim.” That got some attention. I started a nonprofit to try and do this more professionally and push this forward in a more organized manner.
I think a lot of people might say, “That sounds good, and I’m behind it,” but the idea of a fuse, a motherboard, those are things people aren’t always comfortable messing with. It sounds intimidating to someone who’s not steeped in tech. Is that so in practice? Has it become easier to fix stuff even as companies make it harder?
The right to repair doesn’t mean that you have to fix something, nor does it mean that you have to go incredibly deep to fix the issue. If you’re the type of person that wants to pay somebody else to fix it, I respect that. If you wanna replace the entire display assembly, meaning the entire lid on the laptop because that’s easier for you, and you’re willing to pay an extra $100 or $200 to buy the screen preassembled, go for it.
If you wanna replace the LCD cell, which is just the front layer that makes the picture, which is absolutely miserably difficult to do—but you can buy that part sometimes for 30 to 50 bucks—do that too. I am not telling people that they should have to fix anything, and I’ll never shame somebody because they decide to buy something new or have somebody else fix it.
Right to repair simply means that you have the right to fix it if you want, or send it to the manufacturer, send it to a third party, or buy something new if you don’t want to fix it. Ironically, most of the devices in my house that don't work, I don't wind up fixing them. I wind up buying something new, because after 12 or 15 hours a day of fixing other people’s stuff, I just don’t have it in me to fix my own.
The wall of laptops I see behind you are a testament to that.
So recently, for instance, my air conditioner broke, and I was willing to pay somebody to fix it, and he ghosted me three times. And the company said, “We don't fix them. We can give you a new one for $10,000.” And I look at the cost of the unit that I have and it’s $2,500, and I’m just like, “What?” So I opened it up and I realized the contactor, which is a relay, it’s the thing that every time your thermostat says “turn on the AC” it sends 24 volts to this thing, and then that turns on the 240 volts going to the AC. It was filled, absolutely filled, with fire ants. I don’t know why fire ants love 240 volts. They really love it even though it’s not good for them. And that was kind of fun for me. So at that moment, I wanted to fix it because I was boiling hot, and it was taking forever for somebody else to.
Now in this case, there was not a lot that was stopping me. My unit is so old that I was actually able to find the schematics for it online, so if I wanted to buy parts for it, I could. And that's really all most people are asking for. I'm not saying that you have to do a motherboard repair yourself, but it would be nice if somebody who's qualified to do so is not blocked from being able to do so.
Now, it’s not Apple’s job to make it easy for me. It’s not their job to design their product in a way where I have a more luxurious experience while I’m doing the job. My job is gonna be difficult, and that's part of the game. Technology is consistently evolving.
Where right to repair comes in is when I try to talk to the electronics distributor that sells all these chips, and I say, “I wanna buy this,” and they say, “You’re not on the list. We can’t sell to you.” That’s where right to repair comes in and says that’s not OK.
Companies will say—and I know this because they say it to us all the time when we go to them with stories about this—that, fundamentally, a lot of this is about quality control. If we let you use an unauthorized part, we’re not gonna guarantee that the device is gonna perform up to our standards. If we let you tinker around with this, you might break it. We want to guarantee a certain level of quality with the experience of our devices. How does that reasoning sit with you?
If the issue is quality control, then why does my store have a better rating on Google Maps than every single Apple Store in the country?
What is right to repair asking for? Right to repair very often asks for the ability to buy the same part that they are using. I want to be able to buy the parts that go into the device.
We’ve seen stories in recent weeks where now that people have Claude Code they can use it to check their smart TVs and get rid of all the bloatware and all the adware and have a more streamlined smart TV experience. I think those tools also give them access to guides to figure out how to replace all kinds of things, how to fix software in all kinds of ways. Is part of the future of owning our things also making it easier to not just tinker with the hardware aspect of it, but to get into the software and make it more in line with what we want out of our experiences and give companies less control over the advertising, the spyware, whatever it is?
I love it. I love seeing people being able to use AI in that way. I love the idea of it being used to break digital locks, that you could just get access to what the company has taken away from you. I think that that is a great use of AI. The only issue there is when you’re talking about ownership, when people are using these frontier models, when they’re using Claude Code or Codex you’re using a model that runs on somebody else’s computer, and if you type the wrong thing, it’s easy to get around some of Claude Code’s guardrails, and sometimes I’ve done some experiments to have fun with it. But there are a lot of guardrails on it, and I wouldn’t be surprised if at some point in the future, enough of these companies started saying, “Hey, people are using Claude Code to actually free themselves from our bullshit.
