This is where it’s nice to see that it’s not just the US leading in this. Many other countries are creating their own AI models that can run on your system. I’m very excited to see what happens, as time goes on, when models that can run on a standard laptop like this have the ability to actually do this.
You know, when people are remaking Adobe Suite with Claude Code, I wouldn’t be surprised if one or two years from now they can’t do that at all because it’s able to detect, “Hey, you’re actually trying to free yourself from Adobe.”
But what I’m hoping to see happen is that there are enough local models that run on your system that you don’t have to worry about some company that gets to tell you what you can do, being able to help people get around all these types of digital locks and bullshit. I don’t think that that’s gonna happen in the next year or two, but I think it’s coming, and I’m excited to see it.
This does lead us to the fact those digital locks and bullshit are in legally murky territory sometimes, right? Or at least companies can claim legal defenses. I’m talking specifically about Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, something that you do not like, and I think it’s fair to say you want to see it gone for good.
Do you mind telling us a little bit about what Section 1201 of the DMCA is and how it ties into this conversation and makes it a little bit more fraught to do that unlocking?
Section 1201 of the DMCA makes it illegal to bypass a technical protection measure, otherwise known as a digital lock, to gain access to a protected work, even if it’s for the purpose of repair. It was put in place to try and stop piracy, and it was put together in one of the most corrupt ways possible.
Congress repeatedly said no to this law. No, this is way too restrictive. So the architect of it, Bruce Lehman, decided to try and get it negotiated into an international treaty. Then he came back to the United States and said, “Look, we signed this treaty, so now you have to pass this law. We’re going to be out of step with our obligations to the international community.” So he’s potentially sidestepped Congress in order to get this law passed that says that you cannot bypass a digital lock, even if it’s on something that you own.
Now, I can’t go to your house and break into your home. That’s illegal. I should not be allowed to do that. But if I spend $600,000 on a house, and I notice that there’s a locked closet in the house, once I’ve paid $600,000 for the house, I should be able to break that lock to get into that closet, because I own the house.
The problem with this law is that it allows companies to lock you out of things that you have already paid for. And the way that you see this being abused now is when you see companies taking away features from you or sending out firmware updates that stop features from working on the device after the company has gone bankrupt and they figure out, “Oh, wait, we need more money.”
I’ve had companies that failed before, and I really wish I had the ability to say, “You know what? I realize that I sold it at a price that’s a little too low. I’m gonna need to take $5 from every customer I had in the past year.” I’m not allowed to do that. I can’t stop my customers’ products from working.
But because I was selling a physical good that did not have any sort of firmware on it that connects to the internet, I’m not able to do that. Section 1201 of the DMCA is a law that came out in the late 1990s. This was before most normal people even had the internet, much less had their washing machine, their television, their dryer attached to the internet like they are now.
That law was, in my opinion, horribly put together for the world of the mid- to late-1990s, and it is way worse built for today. The architect of the law also said that the purpose of it was to try and fight piracy, and he admitted in 2007 and 2013 when he was looking back on it that it didn’t do that at all.
It’s very easy right now. I was able to show my 79-year-old father how to pirate television, movies, music, and it took me less than 10 minutes to show him how to use something like SoulSeek or Usenet to be able to get whatever he wants. These laws fundamentally have not worked, but what they’ve done a very good job of is making it much more difficult for people who wanna follow the law to be able to use their media.
Right.
If I want to rip my legally purchased Blu-ray and be able to play it on my legally purchased phone, I have to break the digital lock inside the Blu-ray disc to do that, which is illegal. What I’m actually supposed to do is I’m supposed to buy another version of it that’s only gonna work on here, and it makes it much more difficult for people who actually want to obey the law.
I think people are now waking up to this, but software is copyrightable. So when you buy a book on Amazon Kindle, say, and you have a Kindle book, what you’re actually doing is you’re signing an end-user licensing agreement that gives you the right to access that book.
You don’t own that book in a technical way, even though it feels like you should and feels like you do. So we’ve had cases where Amazon has actually removed books from Kindles after you bought them, and there’s no recourse for that. I think the idea of ownership in the digital age is informed by so much of Section 1201 and the way that we approach copyright and software.
Do you see any progress towards changing that?
Instead of every single year going back and asking for an exemption, what we’d really like to do is we’d like to pass durable legislation that doesn’t require that we ask for an exemption. We’re starting with the area that is the most reasonable, which is repair. If you want to be able to fix what you bought and paid for, that should not be a crime.
You should be able to repair what you own, and you should be able to show other people how to repair what they own without that being considered a copyright crime. We’re not even saying, “Can I please rip my legally purchased Blu-ray so that I could watch it on my legally purchased portable media player?” Right now, we’re simply saying, “I would like to fix what I bought and paid for.”
The problem that I’ve experienced throughout this process is there’s always an issue that people find more exciting, that’s more accessible, because you can only focus on so many things at once. If people are concerned about the economy, culture-war issues, if somebody’s concerned about immigration or Covid or policing—there’re so many issues that resonate far more with the voting public than this. The right to repair is this really abstract issue, and when you start talking about digital locks—my job, as I see it, is to get ordinary people to understand why this acronym and set of numbers directly ties into your thermostat saying it’s not gonna work anymore unless you give them $10 a month.
I don’t think that I’ve done a good enough job of that over the past 12 years to get it on par with all these other issues that people face every day. Admittedly, if you’re paying like $5, $6 a gallon for gas, you’re probably gonna care about that before you care about this.
So we’re talking not long after the midterms, and Democrats have won control over the Senate and the House. You do have a couple of politicians who actually have been speaking out about the right to repair who are in office now: Josh Turek in Iowa; Jake Johnson in Minnesota looks like he’s gonna get a seat. Is it encouraging that it’s even an issue people are talking about, or is that still not enough?
It’s encouraging to see that they’re talking about it, but I also realize that, especially going into this next Congress, there is going to be so much work and so many things that they’re going to want to do. I remember somebody asking me, “Like, no offense Louis, but I’d rather see them spend time on, I don't know, getting rid of Pete Hegseth.” I never tell people my issue is more important than your issue, and everybody votes according to what is important to them.
But there’s so many things that I imagine this Congress is going to want to do when they get elected that my job is gonna be making sure that there’s enough of a base of support and showing that there’s enough people that care about this, that if you spend the 20 minutes to do something about this, that it will actually work in your favor.
And that’s part of what we’ve been trying to do with the FULU [Freedom from Unethical Limitations on Users] Own Your Shit tour over the past few months. We’ve traveled around the country to 13 different cities, and in every one of these cities, we are trying to bring people together.
We had one of the ex-FTC commissioners show up, which was really cool. He gave an inspiring speech in San Jose. We’re also inviting their congresspeople to say, “Yeah, this is an issue that I will actually be more likely to vote for. This is as important to me as the other issues.” And our job is showing the people that are elected that we care about this. Because what’s their job? Their job is to represent us. If people are not talking about this issue or it's only being talked about on a couple of subreddits or on the fringes of the internet, I almost don't blame the representative for not prioritizing it. But our job is to show them that if they prioritize it, they'll be rewarded for it.
So I am happy to see that there are people talking about it. I remember when right to repair was put into an executive order by Biden in summer of 2021. I was excited, but there wasn’t a lot that came from it. I’m hoping for something different here.
So FULU is your organization that supports right to repair. You also have bounties that you pay out for people who can disable these digital locks. How is that going? Have you successfully paid out bounties yet? Can you talk about that program a little bit and why you're sort of taking matters into your own hands here?
That program came out about 2:00 or 3:00 in the morning. I was doing a video on Futurehome after somebody who works there, or used to work there, sent me information on what they were doing. He was talking about this thermostat that when it got a firmware update after the company went bankrupt, it stopped you from being able to use some of the features you could use before.
I did the video going over it, and I’m just sitting there at, like, 2 am editing this and thinking, “This is not enough.” And I said, “I'll give $5,000 or $10,000 to whoever makes this thing work again.” I was thinking back to what I was doing when I was doing all these repair videos showing the schematics.
Now you have hundreds of people doing repair videos that are way better than mine every single day on YouTube, and I love it. But back in 2013 and 2014, I didn’t see anything like that, and that’s because at the bottom right corner of the screen, it has this little message on the schematic. It says, “Proprietary property of Apple Inc. Keep confidential. Do not share.” Most people don’t like getting sued or having their livelihoods destroyed. For me, that’s like a Tuesday. I find it fun. I enjoy going to court. I encourage my employees to go to court.
Got it.
So I was thinking, “How do I get more people to start poking at these things? How do I get more people to start saying, ‘No, this is not enough. You can’t do that.’” So we came up with this bounty, and you could see in that video that most of it was done during the day, and the part with the bounty was done at 3:00 in the morning in some corner of my house when I’m dead tired.
I said, “5,000 bucks to whoever makes this work again.” And there was an employee that emailed me with a solution shortly thereafter, and he said, “Louis, I appreciate this. I would’ve done this for free, but here I made a Home Assistant integration,” and people were able to use the thermostat again.
So what we’re trying to do with the bounty program is we’re trying to show people that, A, this is a problem, and B, we’re trying to incentivize people to start making things work again so that we can point to how bad this law is. We can also point to things that tangibly work again. The reason that the right-to-repair stuff with Apple that I was doing was successful is because I wasn’t just saying, “Here’s why you should care about this.”
Millions of people probably have working MacBooks again because of those videos that I was doing back in the day. So when somebody personally saves $1,000, when they personally get their data back, they are now invested in my cause in a way that no Twitter hashtag and no bumper sticker is ever gonna make happen.
What’s a gateway drug into right to repair? If you want to get into repairing your own stuff, what is an easy thing? Is it an iPhone battery replacement or a trackpad upgrade? What do you point people to and say, “This is something that you can actually do. This is something you can manage. It’s gonna make your life better. It’s gonna make your experience better”?
I don't have a very well-packaged answer for that. For me, it it has to be something fun. It has to be, It's 103 degrees in Texas this week, and my asshole air conditioning technician has stiffed me three times. Let me open it up and, oh, I just used compressed air on the contactor and I blew out the fire ants, so now it works again. That’s what’s gonna get people excited about this. I get excited about repair not because of the repair that’s being done, and admittedly not even the money, it’s the story that’s involved in it.
So anytime you’re fixing something because I need this to work right now, or I don't have the money to make this work again, anytime there’s some sort of story attached to it, it’s going to be something that gets you excited.
Some people may feel incredibly excited about replacing the battery in their phone. Some people are really just gonna hate it. But I think there has to be some sort of story behind it that makes it worth it. I actually don’t find repair fun. I don't think that putting 96 solder balls back onto a chip that's the size of my pinky fingernail is fun.
I don’t do it for that. I do it for the hug that the customer gives you when you get back all their baby pictures, or when you do this for the police and they're able to catch the murderer because of it. I don’t find taking a battery out of a phone, using a heat gun, and using a little spudger to get all this off, but not breaking the screen—that’s not fun.
It’s fun if you can’t afford a new one. That makes it a lot of fun. It’s fun if you’re doing it to get something back. But there has to be a story. There has to be a reason that makes that particular repair exciting to you, and that's gonna be different for everybody, and it’s usually gonna be based on whatever your circumstances are at the time.

Speculation over what Nvidia's future could look like without its high-profile chief executive ramped up on Wednesday.
The chipmaker's stock fell 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that its board was preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang.
The New York Times also reported Wednesday that Huang had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him, citing five people who worked at the company.
The report came days after Huang said in a memo to employees that he had an extramarital affair, and after Nvidia's board launched an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The New York Times previously reported US officials believed Huang had grown close to a tech executive, Alice Huang, who had been recruited to gather information for the Chinese government.
As the chip giant's succession plans remain unknown, here is what smart people in business and tech are saying about Huang's potential exit from Nvidia.
Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management
Ross Gerber said Huang's departure would be a disappointment for Nvidia shareholders but said the company could move forward without him.
"Looks like Jensen is done. What a disappointment. Sad day for Nvidia shareholders and looks like another tough day for the stock. Never would have guessed he'd go down this way," Gerber wrote in one of several posts on X on Wednesday.
"Jensen will be replaced and Nvidia is still Nvidia. That's business. He must go and Nvidia needs to focus on selling chips!" Gerber added.
Eric Wallerstein, chief macro strategist at Clocktower Group
Eric Wallerstein wrote on X on Wednesday that Huang's likely ousting could shake investor confidence in the broader AI trade, given Nvidia's role in financing the industry.
"Jensen has helped foster a complex web of circular financing relationships, and ultimately backstopped the AI trade, with Nvidia's balance sheet," Wallerstein said.
"Removing that Put, or even placing uncertainty on its availability, will cause investors to increase the risk premium on AI-related assets," Wallerstein added.
Ed Zitron, CEO of EZ Primary Research
Ed Zitron said in a post on X that he questions what else Nvidia might be withholding from investors, pointing to the company's past regulatory troubles.
"Oh so NVIDIA knew about this affair already, huh? What else is this company not telling us?" Zitron wrote on Wednesday.
Zitron also cited two previous SEC cases involving Nvidia, one in 2002 over accounting practices and one in 2022 over disclosures related to cryptocurrency mining and gaming revenue.
Jason Calacanis, co-host and executive producer of the All-In Podcast
Jason Calacanis said the company shouldn't be so quick to remove Huang.
"A much better solution for NVIDIA's board, shareholders, customers and employees (and America) would be to (a) finish their investigation and (b) make @JensenHuang the chairman if it comes to that," Calacanis wrote on X on Wednesday.
"China doesn't need NVIDIA's chips. America needs NVIDIA to win. Act accordingly," Calacanis added, alongside a screenshot of his new Nvidia share purchases.
Keith Urbahn, president of Javelin
Keith Urbahn, president of Javelin, a literary and creative agency that has repped prominent figures like James Comey and Tucker Carlson, said Wednesday in an X post that the situation was "a generational case study in how not to manage a crisis."
He outlined several lessons to take away from the ordeal, including: "Never let a CEO's personal crisis take precedence over the interests of the company and its shareholders."
"The board must speak with its own voice. It cannot outsource its institutional credibility to the CEO," he added.
Byrne Hobart, venture capitalist and founder of The Diff
Byrne Hobart, general partner at Anomaly Fund and founder of The Diff, a finance and tech newsletter, suggested ousting Huang could lead to new competition for Nvidia.
"On one hand, boards have to do what they have to do. On the other hand, he's a guy who's worth $150bn, knows everyone in hardware, named his company after the Latin word for "spite," and he lives in a state where you can't enforce noncompetes," he wrote in a post on X.
Anthony Pompliano, crypto investor and entrepreneur
Anthony Pompliano, a crypto investor and entrepreneur, wrote on X: "Jensen's yet-to-be-launched Nvidia competitor is going to do numbers in the seed round."
Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management
Gene Munster, a tech analyst and managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, said in an X post that Nvidia will go on, with or without its famous CEO.
"Remember: AI infrastructure customers will act in their best interest," he said. "That means they'll keep buying just as many $NVDA chips with or without Jensen."
He also said he guesses the stock will open on Thursday at $150, or about 20% lower than the close at the end of last week, but that he expects it to "quickly rally back."
Jim Cramer, host of CNBC's Mad Money
Jim Cramer, who has interviewed Huang on several occasions, questioned how investors should value Nvidia if Huang were suddenly gone.
"As I said this morning, there is a bench. As Mike from Coreweave said, there is a company," Cramer said on X on Wednesday. "What is it worth when a key man is just erased?"
"Let me think about how sickening this is and then i will come back to you," Cramer added. "I want to throw up."

Delhi Water Minister Parvesh Verma on Tuesday rode a jet ski on the Yamuna at the launch of the city's first cruise service, Namo Yamuna River Safari.
Verma, who could be seen steering the jet ski from left to right while riding with a guide, said the BJP government has taken significant steps toward rejuvenation work along the Yamuna's 52-km stretch through Delhi over the past 18 months.
“Our priority from day one has been to clean Maa Yamuna and develop a beautiful riverfront for Delhi, just like the Sabarmati riverfront (in Ahmedabad). I believe that a riverfront can become a reality only when the river is clean,” Verma said.
"In the next phase, we will focus on the stretch from Wazirabad to Kalindi Kunj, which will take another two to two-and-a-half years," he added.
The Namo Yamuna River Safari operates along an approximately 4-km stretch between Sonia Vihar and Jagatpur.
Delhi government has developed a riverfront terminal at Sonia Vihar, complete with two floating jetties to facilitate passenger boarding and disembarkation.
The broader project identifies an approximately 6-km stretch between Wazirabad Barrage and Jagatpur as suitable for water transport. A minimum navigational depth of 1.5 metres has been prescribed for operating small passenger vessels along the stretch.
The Delhi government plans to introduce a second electric cruise with similar capacity by February-March 2027.
Entry Fee: ₹50 for access to the riverfront premises.
Cruise Fare: ₹500 for a complete journey.
Duration: The electric vessel accommodates 30 passengers and takes about 35 to 45 minutes to travel the designated route and return to the starting point.
Monsoon Schedule: The service will remain closed from July 1 to September 30 each year due to changing river conditions.
The riverfront terminal, developed at Sonia Vihar, has two floating jetties to facilitate passenger boarding and disembarkation. The terminal also has ticket counters, a guard room, paid vehicle parking, a waiting area, a food court and commercial shops.
The premises feature a children's play zone, gaming activities, and ecological trails and walking paths, allowing visitors to explore the riverfront beyond the cruise.
A theme-based musical fountain has also been developed, through which the story of Lord Krishna and the significance and glory of Yamuna will be presented through music.
Other facilities include a charging station for electric cruises, separate toilet facilities for men, women and persons with disabilities, a sewage treatment plant, a borewell for drinking water and kitchen and storage areas.
The project also includes lighting arrangements and a concrete-block access road. Electric-powered vessels are intended to promote environment-friendly transport and sustainable river tourism.
The nearest transit hub is the Sonia Vihar Metro Station on the Delhi Metro's Pink Line. E-rickshaws and auto-rickshaws are readily available from the station to cover the short distance to the riverfront terminal.
Visitors opting for public transit can take DTC bus routes, such as the 258 (which runs from Mori Gate and passes through Sonia Vihar's Pusta roads), to reach the terminal area.
If you are driving, the Sonia Vihar riverfront is easily accessible via the Wazirabad Road and the Signature Bridge. The terminal features a dedicated paid vehicle parking area, making it highly convenient for those travelling in personal vehicles.

On Nov. 3, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. In the days that followed, a claim circulated that El-Sayed had said that "Michigan is the capital of Arab America," sparking vitriol from opponents.
The alleged quote played into a trope — commonly used against Muslims, immigrants and other communities — that institutions such as the U.S. government are being "infiltrated" by foreigners. For example, the caption of one Facebook post sharing a purported clip of El-Sayed saying the quote began: "WE'VE BEEN INVADED" (archived).
Other social media users, including Turning Point USA CEO Erika Kirk, shared the clip (archived). "There is no 'Arab America.' There is only the United States of America," she wrote. Readers also wrote in to Snopes, looking for answers.
The quote was correctly attributed to El-Sayed, and the clip of him saying it was authentic. He made the comment during a speech at the CONNECT Empowerment Summit, also known as the Arab American Leadership and Empowerment Summit, in the Washington, D.C., suburb of Chantilly, Virginia, on Nov. 6.
The video clip is available on multiple platforms, including C-SPAN.
"Ahlan wa sahlan," he opened his comments — "welcome" in Arabic. He then introduced himself as "Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed," his full name, before saying:
I'm honored to be the next United States senator from the great state of Michigan. Which of course — I know we're here in D.C., which of course is the capital of the United States of America, but Michigan is the capital of Arab America.
His remarks were met with cheers.
Michigan has a rich Arab American history, with the highest-concentrated Arab population in the country, according to World Population Review. In cities such as Dearborn, Arab Americans make up more than half the population.
For further reading on El-Sayed, we've previously covered a claim that he would force Michigan students to learn Arabic numerals (they already do) and a false rumor that he said it was acceptable for young girls to see male genitals in their locker rooms because "they are going to see them on the internet anyway."

Suspected IED blast on NH-2 in Nagaland; no casualties reported
Director general of police (DGP) Nagaland, Rupin Sharma told HT that explosives were speculated to have been planted behind a retaining wall along the highway
An explosion occurred on Wednesday morning on the National Highway-2 near Khuzama village in Kohima district, officers suspect it was an improvised explosive device (IED) blast.
Director general of police (DGP) Nagaland, Rupin Sharma told HT that explosives were speculated to have been planted behind a retaining wall along the highway, with a wire triggering the explosion and damaging about two and a half meters of the wall. No casualties were reported, an officer said. An investigation is underway to ascertain the nature and intent of the blast, he added.
Chief minister Neiphiu Rio condemned the incident, saying in a post on X, “I strongly condemn the reported blast at Khuzama, Kohima. Such acts have no place in a civilised society. It creates fear among our people & threatens peace & harmony. The Govt. is seized of the situation. All steps are being taken to ensure the safety & security of our people.”
The Southern Angami Public Organisation (SAPO), a tribal body under whose jurisdiction the blast took place, said in a statement, “SAPO views this dastardly act not merely as an explosion, but as a direct and deliberate assault on the peace, security and dignity of the peace-loving citizens of Southern Angami in particular, and the people of Nagaland in general.”
Condemning the act, the organisation said it is a brazen challenge to values of peace, unity and brotherhood in the region, and SAPO would not allow those values to be held hostage by a handful of misguided miscreants.
“To plant a lethal explosive on a public highway, a lifeline traversed daily by students, farmers, commuters, patients, tourists and security personnel, is an act of utter cruelty and moral bankruptcy,” the body said.
It called for citizens to be vigilant, and pledged its cooperation to the investigating agencies to unearth the facts behind the act.
The NH-2 connects Nagaland with Manipur and Khuzama is the last village on Nagaland’s side of the inter-state boundary.

Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.
Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. You can save up to 14 percent on plans for the first three months, whether you're signing up as an individual or as a business. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.
Save up to 14% Off These Google Workspace Promo Codes 2026
There are some notable differences between each Workspace plan – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.
What Is the Best Google Workspace Plan?
Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.
Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.
Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.
Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.
Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.
At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.
Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.
Why Teams Love Using Google Workspace Flows with Google Workspace
Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e., update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.
You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.
Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.
Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.
Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow-up message. No apps or links are needed.
Does Google Workspace Offer a Free Trial?
Even with a discount, Google offers a free trial for all new Workspace subscribers. Your first 14 days are free, regardless of which plan you choose. You can also use our links at the top of this article to get promotional pricing. Just make sure to cancel if you don’t want to continue. After 14 days, you’ll be billed, and that will start your new billing cycle.

Healthcare AI startup Froncort.AI has secured $2.3 Mn (₹21.5 Cr) in fresh capital from Google’s philanthropic arm, Google.org, to scale its AI-powered disease surveillance and detection platform. The support also includes $200K in Google Cloud credits and pro bono technical expertise from Google's AI specialists. The funding will help Froncort.AI develop mAI-NETRA, a mobile version of its public health platform AI-NETRA, which uses AI, satellite imagery and government health data to identify higher risk areas for catching infectious diseases. It also guides frontline health workers towards targeted screenings. The startup is among 15 organisations selected globally for Google.org's Impact Challenge: AI for Government Innovation. Founded in 2024 by physician-scientist Dr Ujjwal Rao, Froncort.AI aims to improve early disease detection by helping frontline health workers enhance their vigil over disease prone areas. In a validation study conducted with Maharashtra's state TB programme,Froncort.AI claims that teams using its AI-NETRA identified a similar number of confirmed pulmonary TB cases while screening two-thirds fewer people than conventional methods. The cost per confirmed case also declined from around $29K to $10K, while 92% of participating frontline workers reported a lower workload. The platform combines government health programme data with Google's Earth AI models and local risk indicators, including settlement density, land use, rainfall and flooding, to identify high-risk geographical clusters. It then converts these insights into ranked work paths, mapping household clusters and builds routes for health workers to follow during field visits. With the latest funding, Froncort.AI bids to enhance its platform to extend its capabilities across 6 infectious diseases — TB, Leprosy, Malaria, Dengue, Cholera and Leptospirosis. Froncort.AI also plans to release mAI-NETRA as an open-source blueprint, allowing governments to adopt and adapt the technology for their public health programmes. Apart from its public health platform, the startup also operates RegDoc, a regulatory technology platform that prepares compliant submissions for clinical research organisations, pharmaceutical companies and medical device manufacturers. The capital raise comes at a time when AI’s deployment in strengthening India's public healthcare infrastructure, particularly in areas such as disease surveillance and early diagnosis, is picking up. In a statement issued in February, the government said that India is fundamentally restructuring its public health delivery by integrating AI into a unified strategy. "By deploying AI-enabled tools within the National TB Elimination Programme, the National Diabetic Retinopathy Screening Programme, and the Media Disease Surveillance System, the government has empowered non-specialists to perform high-level screenings, resulting in a 27% decline in adverse TB outcomes and over 4,500 outbreak alerts," the statement read. It is pertinent to note that AI is attracting a growing share of investor capital even as funding across the wider startup ecosystem remains under pressure. The IndiaAI Mission is expanding access to compute, supporting indigenous foundation models and providing assistance for AI startups. Based on Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI funding in India grew 235% YoY, while the number of deals rose 35% to 35 from 26 in Q3 2025.

Seagate doesn’t think hybrid drives are done just yet. On Tuesday, the company announced the launch of the new FireCuda Forge line of storage drives. The new drives combine the high capacity of a traditional plattered HDD with the speed and responsiveness of a user-supplied solid-state drive (SSD). The new hybrid storage solution is Seagate’s first to be powered and managed by the new Alkemi intelligent storage platform.
The FireCuda Forge is available right now through Seagate’s web store, and comes in 8TB ($699) or 20TB ($899) HDD configurations—neither of which includes the required SSD. Users will have to bring their own SSD, with some specific restrictions. The FireCuda Forge is compatible with M.2 2280 NVMe drives that are PCIe Gen3 or higher. The maximum supported NVMe capacity is 1TB, which means that’s as much data as you’ll be able to dedicate to storage on the “fast side” of the hybrid setup. The NVMe will require minimum speeds of 2,400MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write, and a unit with DRAM cache is recommended. Seagate claims 2,500MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write speeds for the combined system, along with USB4 and support for Windows 11 and macOS 26+.
After dipping to historical lows earlier in the decade, storage pricing per TB has exploded amid the AI boom. According to data collected by Tom’s Hardware, some solid-state drives now cost two to three times their historic lows, and it’s not just SSDs. Mechanical drives haven’t been immune either. A San Francisco court has sentenced Nima Momeni to 16 years to life in prison for the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee. The tech consultant learned his fate on Tuesday, more than a year and a half after a jury convicted him of second-degree murder. That jury, which delivered its verdict in December 2024, rejected Momeni's claim that he had acted in self-defense.
He has been in custody since his arrest, which came nine days after the killing on April 4, 2023. Before passing sentence, San Francisco Superior Court Judge Alexandra Gordon turned down Momeni's request for a new trial. His attorneys have said they plan to appeal.
Lee was 43 when he died, having been found staggering on a deserted downtown street, dripping a trail of blood and calling for help. He later died at a hospital. Prosecutors said Momeni planned the attack, driving Lee to an isolated spot under the Bay Bridge and stabbing him three times, including once to the heart, with a knife he took from his sister's kitchen.
They said Momeni was angry with Lee for introducing his younger sister to a drug dealer, who, she says, gave her GHB and other drugs and then sexually assaulted her. Momeni gave a different account when he testified on the stand, saying Lee was the one who attacked him with a knife, angry after the tech consultant chided him about spending more time with his family instead of searching for a strip club that night.
Momeni, who studies martial arts, said he didn't realize he had fatally wounded Lee or that Lee was even hurt. In court on Tuesday, Momeni, wearing an orange jail jumpsuit, maintained that he acted in self-defense. He told Lee's family that he understood their loss. “Unfortunately, we have completely different understandings of what transpired,” Momeni said.
Members of Lee's family addressed the court, including his 18-year-old daughter, Scout Lee, who spoke directly to Momeni. “You did not just end his life, you ended an entire future built around a man,” she told Momeni, according to media reports. The jurors rejected a charge of murder in the first degree, which required prosecutors to prove that Momeni acted deliberately, willfully, and with premeditation.
Murder in the second degree does not require premeditation. Lee, a renowned tech mogul, had created the mobile payment service Cash App and was the chief product officer of the cryptocurrency MobileCoin when he died.

A US judge has ruled that Thomas Markle should be detained “separate, to the extent practicable”, from the general prison population on his return to jail.
Markle, who is the father of the Duchess of Sussex, was taken back into custody after cutting off his electronic tag within days of his arrest for allegedly possessing child sex abuse material, including images of himself with naked young girls.
Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin found he had breached the conditions of his pre-trial release, and also noted his housing situation had “become untenable”, court documents show.
Markle had been living in a dementia care home in Florida before his arrest.
FBI agents took him into custody last Friday after seizing a haul of material from two Los Angeles storage units he rented for nearly two decades. The items included slides, film negatives, and books that contained suspected child sex abuse material. Two of the images allegedly depict an adult man – whom a witness “positively identified” as Markle – with a nude young girl.
In one of them, according to court documents, the man “appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s”, which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades, given Markle is now 82.
A third image is said to show a nude young girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Other photographs allegedly show Markle with children in various stages of undress.
He is charged with one count of possession of child pornography. If convicted, he would face at least 20 years in federal prison.
Following his recent arrest, the court had released him on bail on condition he was subject to home detention and wore an electronic tag.
He was also ordered to undergo a psychiatric examination, amid concerns he may not be unable to understand the proceedings or properly assist his lawyer.
Prosecutors requested his recall to jail and detention pending trial after he removed the location monitoring bracelet in the early hours of Monday morning.
First assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said: “Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions.”
Approving his return to custody following a hearing in Tampa, Florida, Judge Griffin said in her written ruling: “I found that the defendant violated the conditions of his pretrial release and that, based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant’s appearance in court.
“Accordingly, for the reasons stated at the hearing, the defendant’s pretrial release is revoked, and he is detained pending the resolution of this case.”
She added: “The defendant is committed to the custody of the attorney general or his designated representative for confinement in a corrections facility separate, to the extent practicable, from persons awaiting or serving sentences or being held in custody pending appeal.”
Court documents also show Markle has surrendered his US passport and tourist visa for the Philippines.
He came under investigation after he was reported to police in the Philippines and the FBI last month by his son, Thomas Markle Jr, who allegedly found illegal images in his father’s belongings in Cebu City.
Mr Markle Jr told The Sun newspaper he had tipped off the authorities about the LA storage facilities.
Meghan Markle, who moved back to the UK with the Duke of Sussex in August, said she was “deeply distressed” at the accusations against her father. She has been estranged from him since the run-up to her 2018 wedding.
She revealed she was sent a letter via the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection in 2019 which made “troubling and disturbing allegations” about her father, but she was given assurances these were being investigated.
The Met has admitted it never shared the details with other law enforcement agencies.
The police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct, is now investigating the force’s conduct.
The duchess had wanted to “speak out” immediately after reading the letter but police advised her against this, sources said.
When former TV lighting director Markle Sr had his leg amputated in the Philippines last year, he made pleas for the duchess to contact him.
Meghan is said to have written him a final letter in which she said she knew he was an abuser and that he would never see his grandchildren, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.
Harry told the European Parliament in Brussels on Monday that children “deserve to feel safe wherever they are” as the duchess made her first public appearance since her father’s arrest.
Meghan pulled out of speaking alongside the duke because she was not “strong enough emotionally”.

India on Wednesday signed a pact with Sri Lanka to supply 100 additional ambulances to the island nation's emergency service with grant assistance of USD 5.28 million, the Indian mission here said.

The India-assisted ambulance services were initially launched in July 2016 in Sri Lanka's Western and Southern Provinces under a grant assistance of USD 7.5 million. In July 2018, it was expanded country-wide by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then Sri Lankan Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe, with an additional grant of USD 15.02 million, covering 209 ambulances, their operational expenses and training costs.
The latest expansion will add 100 ambulances to the existing fleet of 322 vehicles operated by the country's free emergency ambulance service, known as 1990 Suwa Seriya.

It is estimated to respond to 1,000 to 1,200 patient-transfer calls daily, providing free emergency medical transport across the country.

Health Minister Nadda is in Sri Lanka to attend the first BIMSTEC Health Ministers' Meeting in Colombo on Wednesday.

In Maine, a new approach to practicing medicine in the sky
Clipboard in hand, pilot Will Bradbury stands near a helicopter at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. He's running down emergency landing tips with his crew.
"If we need to get out quickly because of smoke or fire, just watch the terrain so that you're not walking uphill into the rotors," he reminds flight nurse Denise Saucier and paramedic Brian Merklin.
The team is getting ready to take off on a medical transport flight. Saucier folds herself into the compact helicopter. She's worked for the air ambulance service for seven years and still calls it a dream job.
Dream job or not, the life of a flight clinician is hard and, given the headwinds slamming rural healthcare, getting harder.
Since 2015, demand for medical flights in Maine has doubled. In 2025, LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights, more than one every three hours. This year, demand is up another 10%.
Nationwide, air medical services are filling the gaps left behind as rural hospitals close, convert to outpatient-only rural emergency hospitals, or stop offering unprofitable services like labor and delivery.
And, as Medicaid cuts estimated by the Congressional Budget Office at $911 billion over ten years take effect, it's going to get worse. Hundreds more rural hospitals or maternity departments are at immediate risk of closing. With every closure, medical care gets further away.
And, increasingly, ground ambulance stations, many of which are also struggling to keep their doors open, can't meet the need. That leaves flight clinicians like Saucier and Merklin seeing more patients every day.
"We're seeing this across the board. The need for air medical services is increasing year over year," says Nicholas George. He runs the ETHOS Database, a national tracking system for air medical programs.
When the rural health care system breaks, EMS — on the ground and, increasingly, in the air — is the backstop.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Healthcare of last resort
Every week or two, Saucier finds herself on a flight to one of Maine's thousands of islands. Occasionally, crews even land in the state's vast forests and mountains, then take snowmobiles to reach patients.
But "scene calls" to roadside — or trailside — accidents are less than 10% of LifeFlight's transports. (They're a higher percentage in urban areas.)
Most are interfacility transports, like today's. They'll stabilize a patient at a small, local hospital and fly them to a larger, better resourced one.
Saucier glances out the window for hazards. The view still reminds her of the role the organization plays in Maine, one of the country's most rural states.
"You go so long of a distance without seeing any houses, any roads," Saucier says. "It really hits home how rural Maine is and how necessary EMS is in the state."
And the pressure is on air ambulances as ground services in Maine are increasingly strained. The system is so fragmented that patients can fall through the cracks. Last year, a woman in a small northern Maine town died while the county dispatch center called 10 ambulance services. None responded.
Air ambulance services, though, come with unique challenges, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. It's been difficult to retain staff with the medical expertise to treat everything from heart attacks to injuries to fragile newborns, and who can stick with the demanding job without burning out.
Almost a quarter of ground-based EMS workers leaves the field every year. While there's no comprehensive staffing data for air medical services, flight clinicians face a slew of unique stresses, including dangerous conditions; long shifts and unpredictable hours; ever-increasing training and certification requirements; and significant mental health burdens. And then there's the pay, which is low throughout emergency medical services.
For years, LifeFlight retained only 60% to 70% of its workers, says CEO Joe Kellner.
"This is a really hard job," Kellner says. "By their job description, they are seeing people on their worst day, over and over again."
Training elite clinicians
This year, for the first time in nine years, LifeFlight is nearly fully staffed. One of the nation's handful of independent nonprofit air medical companies, LifeFlight has taken an innovative approach to the problems that plague the industry, including a combination of better training, higher pay and in-house mental health support.
Mike Abernethy, an EMS expert and retired emergency medicine professor at the University of Wisconsin, considers the company one of a handful of model programs for the industry. LifeFlight of Maine is a nonprofit, unlike much of the industry, which is dominated by for-profit businesses with reputations for charging exorbitant prices.
"There's just absolutely no comparison in the aviation and medical quality of these programs" versus an average for-profit air medical business, Abernethy argues.
When Kellner, a paramedic himself, became CEO in 2023, he began addressing the recruitment and retention problems. What LifeFlight calls the "Critical Care Academy," a six- to eight-month orientation program, is intended to address both issues.
Emergency critical care advances quickly. So most clinicians need regular education, both to remain successful on the job and to get hired in the first place.
On another day at headquarters, four instructors sit in a claustrophobic control room. Through a window looking into what appears to be a hospital room, paramedics Daniel Horne and Brad Alleger are undergoing an annual skills assessment, a simulation of a real-life medical crisis.
Dr. Dave Saquet turns on a mic and coughs. "It's hard to breathe," he whispers urgently. "It hurts everywhere."
His voice seems to be coming from the patient — a breathing, bleeding mannequin lying on a hospital bed.
"What happened to you?" Horne asks.
"My house was on fire," Saquet chokes out.
A wall monitor displays the patient's vital signs — which Saquet is manipulating on his laptop.
Medics and nurses here do simulations often, both to pass the Critical Care Academy, and also to stay up to date on occasional but critical events, like emergency births, newborn resuscitation, and burns. Before the assessment ends, the paramedics will have tried and failed to intubate the patient. After that "failure," they performed an emergency procedure to enable breathing, switching from the mannequin to a pig trachea.
Because it's hard to find recruits qualified enough for the rigorous training, the company also started a mentorship program for people considering applying. Some even attend the academy, gaining skills even if they'll never work for LifeFlight.
Success comes slowly: Recently, LifeFlight hired one of last year's mentees.
Experiments
Kellner instituted an unusual change that he says even nurses endorse: LifeFlight raised paramedics' pay to match flight nurses' compensation. Industrywide, paramedics make less. That keeps costs down, which is why pay equity is rare. Kellner believes the change has helped with recruitment.
Another experiment: LifeFlight hired a full-time mental-health counselor.
EMS workers' rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety and depression are more thanfive times higher than the average American's.
"That has led people to leave this profession," Kellner says.
That was true for paramedic Brian Merklin, who was working for a different service in Nevada during the pandemic.
"We got hit really hard," he says. "The crews were just flying nonstop. We did four-day shifts, so for 96 hours we were just going, going, going."
About a third of the staff quit, he says. "They were getting air medical service plus COVID, right in the teeth."
Eventually, Merklin too needed a break. He left the profession for a few years. Then, when he felt the urge to fly again, he found LifeFlight.
Today's trip
The helicopter, which took off from Bangor, lands on a community hospital's rooftop helipad. Merklin and Saucier hurry to the patient's side. Most LifeFlight patients are unconscious or too ill to consent to share their stories, so the details are private. The injuries are shocking. If this patient doesn't get to a trauma center quickly, they might die.
Merklin and Saucier are unfazed.
But it's this kind of incessant trauma exposure that makes mental health support for first responders so invaluable.
Merklin serves on a peer support team.
"There's a lot of lip service paid … to the cost to your mental health in this profession. But this is the only place I have ever worked that actually provided support," he says. "I would love to see it take hold in other areas."
If counseling keeps two or three people from leaving, it's a wise investment, Kellner argues: "The cost of training somebody new into our organization is about $100,000."
As both air and ground EMS become even more essential, the task is to recruit and keep more people like Merklin and Saucier.
Because, if hundreds more hospitals do close, highly trained EMS workers may be the only people standing between patients dying and getting the care they need.
Elaine Appleton Grant's reporting was supported by the National Institute for Health Care Management.

Police in Bangladesh have fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse supporters of the deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who are demanding her return to the country.
A police vehicle was set on fire in Gopalganj district, where the banned student wing of Hasina's Awami League party clashed with security forces.
Nationwide protests by pro-Hasina activists started a day after the former leader said she had requested a passport to return to Bangladesh from exile in India.

A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.
Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.
Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.
"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.

Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.

How good is Hamilton and how long can he stay in F1? - Q&A
- Published
McLaren's Lando Norris converted pole position into a race win at a wet-dry-wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday.
Max Verstappen came through the field to take second after starting at the back of the grid because of an engine penalty, while his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar was on the podium in third.
Mercedes sealed the constructors' championship for the first time since 2021 at Interlagos following a fourth-place finish for George Russell and fifth for new world champion Kimi Antonelli.
Here BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
Lewis Hamilton has just completed his 400th F1 grand prix, with more than 100 of these races having him on pole position. There are drivers with a better pole percentage than this, so just how good is he and for how much longer can he stay at the top? - Clive
Lewis Hamilton is unquestionably one of the greatest Formula 1 drivers in history.
He's statistically the most successful - with the most race wins and pole positions.
He's tied with Michael Schumacher for the most championships with seven, and many would - and do - argue he should have eight, given the controversy of the mishandled final race of the 2021 season.
Greatness as an F1 driver is about more than raw statistics, but even so Hamilton has consistently proved to be at the very highest level, with a series of outstanding drives in races that will go down in history as some of the greatest ever.
Examples of those would be the 2008 British Grand Prix and the 2021 Brazilian Grand Prix, along with many others.
All of this should go without saying.
He's also won races in nearly all his seasons - the only exceptions being 2022, 2023 and 2025.
There is no question that, within the context of his remarkable career, Hamilton struggled relatively in the era of 'ground-effect' cars from 2022-25.
He was beaten by Mercedes team-mate George Russell in two of their three seasons together, and looked a shadow of his usual self against Charles Leclerc in 2025.
Those performances led some to question why a driver formerly famed and lauded for his adaptability did not seem as able to adapt to the driving style required of those cars.
And that, in turn, led to questions as to whether the fact he apparently could not was related to his age - he is now 41.
But with this year's cars, Hamilton is back in much more familiar territory, is performing extremely well again and is neck-and-neck with Leclerc.
Those questions about the four years from 2022-25 will remain just that, but there is no doubt Hamilton is sensitive to them. He has referenced them a number of times this year, including last weekend in Brazil, when the topic of his 400th race came up.
"I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that," he said. "It's crazy because I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week, I still have the pace, I still have the speed and I still have the dedication, which is most important and the focus. For me, that number is kind of irrelevant."
Longevity in sport depends on many factors, and each athlete is different.
On the face of it, however, there is no obvious reason why, on an age front, Hamilton cannot continue for a good few more years - Fernando Alonso is 45 and is still performing at an extremely high level, as he proved yet again in Brazil at the weekend.
Hamilton has said he wants to race at least until F1 returns to Africa, which will not be until 2030 at the earliest, when he, too, will be 45.
For that, he will need at least one new contract, as his current one with Ferrari is believed to end next year.
- Norris sparkles in Sao Paulo despite firework mishap 
  - Published1 day ago
We heard, and saw, a lot of 'yo-yo racing' in the first half of the season. This seems to have reduced. What has changed? - Ali
'Yo-yo racing' was a term coined at the start of this year for a new character of on-track battle in which cars swapped positions multiple times over a series of laps.
This was caused by the new power-units introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power and are fundamentally energy starved.
The operations of these engines included 'overtake' and 'boost' modes.
'Boost' is a facility for a driver to demand extra electrical energy whenever he wants, as long as the battery has charge.
'Overtake' mode gives a driver following within one second of a car in front an extra 0.5MJ of energy recovery and deployment capability per lap.
At the start of the season, this - combined with the teams' and drivers' relative unfamiliarity with the new technology - led to a number of examples of yo-yo racing in the early grands prix.
This is where one driver has more electrical energy available, uses it to overtake, whereupon the driver behind now has more and overtakes back, and so on.
This has been less prevalent recently and there are two reasons for that.
Primarily, the tracks in recent weeks have been less 'energy-starved'. And the more energy-starved a car is at a track, the more likelihood there is for yo-yo racing.
The overtaking comes from the variation in energy levels, and being at tracks where drivers can't use all the energy they want all the time.
On top of that, drivers and teams have now been using the engines for a season and are much more on top of how to use them, and therefore how not to leave themselves vulnerable.
At the same time, rule changes have been introduced since the start of the season to reduce the impact of energy starvation, such as imposing energy limits on tracks where it is a major issue. This flattens out the peaks and troughs in energy availability.
And into next year and beyond further steps are being taken to make the engines more "normal" in operation - by changing the energy split to 60-40 in two steps by 2028.
This is almost certainly going to lead to the frequency of overtaking reducing, while the drivers become happier with how the cars feel to drive.
Whether the audience perceives that as better or worse racing remains to be seen.
What is the reason a driver like Esteban Ocon would want to stay in F1 as a reserve driver rather than commit to race elsewhere in a different series? All F1 drivers are very, very good, and presumably would be in demand, so why not compete elsewhere, win some races, be a hero? - Stephen
When it became clear that Ocon was not going to be retained by Haas next year, and that his options for a race seat seemed to have evaporated, the Frenchman was insistent that his F1 career was not over.
Staying involved in the sport as a reserve driver - if he can find a spot - is the best way to keep current in the sport.
It means a driver is available should either of the race drivers at whatever team he can land with be incapacitated.
It keeps him familiar with current F1 machinery through simulator sessions, and perhaps driving recent cars.
And it simply keeps his face around and in people's minds.
Go and race elsewhere, whether it's Indycar, Formula E or endurance racing, for example, and it's much easer to be forgotten, or for people to assume your time has come and gone.
Why hasn't Liam Lawson been confirmed for 2027 despite his brilliant driving this year? - Pete
The decision as to which two of the three drivers in contention to drive for Racing Bulls next year is in the hands of the Red Bull shareholders Chalerm Yoovidhya and Mark Mateschitz, and Red Bull's ultimate F1 boss Oliver Mintzlaff.
Lawson is in contention along with his current team-mate Arvid Lindblad and F2 front-runner Nikola Tsolov.
The old Red Bull way - under Helmut Marko and Christian Horner - would have been to jettison Lawson now on the basis he has had his chance in the lead team and is unlikely to be considered for another, and put in Tsolov as the next cab off the rank, so to speak.
The counter-argument is that leaves two unproven talents going against each other next year, which would leave Red Bull not knowing what they are looking at.
Better, this argument goes, to keep Lawson and Lindblad together next year for a fuller reading on Lindblad, with Lawson as a known-quantity benchmark, then drop whoever performs least well at the end of 2027 in favour of Tsolov.
In not so many words, Racing Bulls team boss Alan Permane made this second argument in Brazil at the weekend.
"Red Bull's had a very successful young driver programme," he said, "and I don't want to be critical of it, but I think if you guys are critical of it, maybe sometimes the drivers haven't been able to have enough time to settle, or maybe some snap decisions have been made.
"We're trying to apply a little bit of science, and that takes some time.
"So we are looking at everything and studying, analysing, and time is on our side. We're not in a rush to do anything, and I'm very confident the right decision will be made.
"I realise it's frustrating for our drivers. I realise it's frustrating for everyone else, but we want to get it right, and we will get it right."
Interlagos consistently produces thrilling races. Should F1 be doing more to preserve racing at 'classic' circuits? - Nathan
F1 faces a difficult balancing act with the calendar.
It wants a truly global world championship. It wants exciting racing that engages audiences. It wants a good mix of circuit types for variation and interest. And it wants to make money.
When it comes to 'classic' race tracks, that's not always an easy equation to solve.
The main reason is that the classic tracks are often in countries that are not able or willing to pay the big-money fees.
The same model and restrictions do not apply in autocracies that want to use races for national self-promotion, hence they can and do tend to pay bigger fees.
But F1 is well aware of the importance of classic circuits, and it wants to ensure it keeps the best of them.
As a consequence, F1 does make compromises that ensure the likes of Monaco, Silverstone, Spa and Suzuka stay on the calendar, even if not every year any more in the case of Spa.
At the same time, the sport makes a considerable effort to make new tracks as interesting as possible. Some are more successful than others, but that's always going to be the case.
Take Las Vegas, for example. It is far from the greatest track in terms of driving challenge, and was hardly likely to be given it is made up of streets in an American city, but it makes up for that with spectacle and kudos.
As for forthcoming permanent circuits, former F1 driver Alex Wurz - the designer of the new tracks in Qiddiyah, Saudi Arabia, and Rwanda, which are both due to come on to the calendar in the next few years - has done his level best to ensure they are fulfilling and challenging for drivers and promote good racing.

One child succumbed to burn injuries, and 269 people were treated for firecracker-related burns across Tamil Nadu during the Deepavali festivities, according to official data tracking emergencies over a 24-hour window.
As per the official bulletin, the state 108 emergency ambulance network received 16,079 calls between 7 a.m. on November 7 and 7 a.m. on November 8.
Of the total distress calls, 2,475 were related to accidents, 396 for minor injuries, and 98 specifically for burn injuries.
To manage the festive emergency load, 1,283 ambulances were deployed on active duty across the State.
Statewide government hospitals recorded a total of 1,387 inpatient admissions during this period. The admissions included 956 for accidents, 321 for minor injuries or assaults, and 110 for burn injuries. One burn-related fatality was recorded, involving a child under the age of 15.
No adult deaths due to burns were reported during this timeframe.
Demographic data for burn injuries shows that men formed the largest group of victims, with 92 treated as outpatients and 76 admitted as inpatients.
Children under 15 were the second most affected demographic, with 48 outpatients and 17 inpatient admissions. Adult women accounted for 19 outpatients and 17 inpatients. In total, hospitals saw 159 outpatients and 110 inpatients for burn cases.
The Thanjavur Government Medical College Hospital recorded the highest patient volume for burns, accidents, and minor injuries, treating 36 outpatients and admitting 87 inpatients.
Other major medical centres handling the bulk of the emergency caseload included the Madurai Government Medical College Hospital with six outpatients and 84 inpatients, and the Chengalpattu Government Medical College Hospital with 85 inpatients.
The Periyar Nagar Government Hospital recorded one outpatient and 64 inpatients, while the Thoothukudi Government Medical College Hospital treated 46 outpatients and 13 inpatients.

Have you heard of the names Kadambini Ganguly and Anandibai Joshi? Considered India’s first female doctors, these names have often been looked past in the pages of history and even medical textbooks. Today, let’s talk about the story of Kadambini Ganguly — India’s first practising lady doctor.
It was in 1861 that Brahmo reformer and headmaster Braja Kishore Basu had a daughter. She was named Kadambini Basu. Young Kadambini, despite hailing from a community that did not necessarily support women’s education like many others at the time did, received an education at the Brahmo Eden Female School and later at the Hindu Mahila Vidyalaya.
As the daughter of someone who organised and fought for women’s emancipation, Kadambini went on to study in college and became the first woman to pass the University of Calcutta entrance examination. In 1882, she passed the examination for the Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree along with Chandramukhi Basu from the University of Calcutta, making her and Chandramukhi the first female graduates in the country.
Entry into medicine
Wanting to study medicine, Kadambini decided to enrol at the Calcutta Medical College after graduation. She was, however, believed to have been unable to receive the BMC certificate due to a shortage of a couple of marks. She did receive the GBMC (Graduate of Bengal Medical College) degree, though, in 1886. Thus, she became the first Indian woman to be allowed to practice Western medicine.
Around 1888, Kadambini started working at the Lady Dufferin Hospital for a monthly salary of 300 rupees. She had even gone to Nepal to treat British royalty. Along with pursuing medicine, she was also politically quite vocal and active. Around 1899, Kadambini was one of the first women delegates elected to the Fifth Session of the Congress in Bombay and the next year, she won to become the first women speaker at the Congress.
She also served as the president of the Transvaal Indian Association, founded by Gandhiji’s colleague Henry Pollock. She was a member of the Women’s Conference held in Calcutta and even presided over the General Brahmo Samaj session in Calcutta.
A doctor, wife and mother
Around 1883, Kadambini married Dwarakanath Ganguly (thus the change in name from Kadambini Bose to Kadambini Ganguly in many documents). Dwarakanath Ganguly was a Bengali Brahmo reformer, educator, journalist, and pioneer of women’s rights in British India.
She was a mother to eight children and is often said to have been deft in needlework. She became a practising doctor while equally devoting herself to family and household affairs, an action which was deemed impossible by many in the era.
Despite having being burdened with domestic chores, like most women of that time, Kadambini still managed to smash the glass ceilings and societal stereotypes in both her professional and personal life.
A name which should not be forgotten in the course of time, Dr Kadambini is a reason many of us are able to pursue our passion — in medicine and in life.
