A video circulating on X, bearing the logo of M World, purports to show Russian foreign minister Sergey Viktorovich Lavrov saying that India is merely an oil-trading partner to Russia and that the two countries share only a commercial relationship. In the video, Lavrov is also heard claiming that India has no right to interfere in Russia’s foreign policy or advise Moscow on matters concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States or any other country.
Supreme Court advocate and activist Prashant Bhushan shared the video on his X account (@pbhushan1), which he later deleted. In his post, he criticized the Indian government and questioned what kind of advice external affairs minister S Jaishankar gave to Russia.
Another X account, Diya Kapoor, also shared the video with the similar claim of Sergey Lavrov drawing clear boundaries about the relationship with India.
🚨🇷🇺🇮🇳 RUSSIA DRAWS A CLEAR LINE!
“India is a trading partner, nothing more. We supply oil, and India pays for it. This commercial relationship does not give New Delhi the right to dictate or interfere in Russia’s foreign policy.”
Sergey Viktorovich ⚠️🌍 https://t.co/uX1x0adl0G
— Diya kapoor (@DiyaKapoor113) November 2, 2026
Some X accounts also shared this video with the claim of Sergey Lavrov dismissing India.
Fact Check
After a closer examination of the video, the movements of Sergey Lavrov while speaking appear unnatural and seem out of sync with the audio. This suggests that the clip may have been edited or manipulated. Using this as a lead, we performed a Google reverse image search on several keyframes from the video and found a video with the same background and clothing uploaded by M WORLD on October 31.
A comparison of the two videos shows that Sergey Lavrov’s clothing, background, head movements, and hand gestures are the same, with only the audio being different. Even the ‘M World’ YouTube channel logo appeared in both videos, confirming that the original video had been digitally manipulated. Both videos also feature the exact same glitch at the same moment.
In the original video, Sergey Lavrov is seen refusing the reports from Ukrainian officials claiming that Russian President Vladimir Putin refused to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and stating if Zelenskyy wants a direct meeting, he must travel to Moscow, where Russia will guarantee his safety and security.
Media outlet DW News posted the original video on October 31 showing the conversation about President Putin and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy meeting.
Furthermore, the official X account of the Russian Embassy in India, Russia in India (@RusEmbIndia) has also debunked the video. “Please stop copying silly AI fakes,” it said in a comment to the X post by Diya Kapoor.
@DiyaKapoor113 Please stop copying silly AI fakes
— Russia in India 🇷🇺 (@RusEmbIndia) November 3, 2026
Union government’s official MEA fact check account, too, flagged the post as fake.
Fake Alert!!! 🚨🚨🚨
The video of the Russian Foreign Minister being used in this post is fake! https://t.co/jpEX6qu19p
— MEA FactCheck (@MEAFactCheck) November 3, 2026
To sum up, the viral video claiming that Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov publicly dismissed India’s diplomatic standing is completely false and an AI-generated deepfake. The original footage contains a briefing regarding Russia-Ukraine relations, and there is no mention of India.
Twinkle Shrivastav is an intern at Alt News.

The parents of a 13-year-old girl have sued Google claiming she planned a potential suicide and funeral using its AI technology on a school-issued computer.
Filed Monday in a California court, the complaint is the first known case accusing Google of negligence related to AI integrations on Chromebooks, the tech giant's low-cost laptops used by millions of students in the United States and around the world.
The teenager was not able to access Google's Gemini app, nor OpenAI's ChatGPT, because they were blocked by her school. She was nonetheless still able to use Google's search engine, which contains AI-powered tools.
Those features were notably not among the tools that Google announced this week will be disabled by default for students.
"Schools should turn search off and keep it off until Google removes AI mode from search or ensures that every single student is always safe when they're interacting with AI," Andrew Liddell, one of the family's attorneys, told AFP on Thursday.
The complaint alleges that the child had been a "happy 13-year-old girl" in North Carolina who received great grades, played music and participated in Girl Scouts.
Despite "no history" of mental illness, within months of using Google's AI-powered search on her school laptop, she began a "quiet spiral into a severe psychological crisis" according to the complaint.
On March 17, the school's monitoring software flagged a document titled "Funeral," and the school notified her parents.
Her mother then saw the child writing a farewell letter in real-time after logging into her daughter's account, and her father intervened.
"We are reviewing the claims in the lawsuit and we take this very seriously," Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda told AFP.
Google argues that AI mode includes safeguards against self-harm and attempts to bypass them.
But the child "was able to keep going back over and over and over again," Liddle said. "Whatever safeguards they think they put in place were obviously insufficient."
Developers of fast-evolving AI technology are facing a litany of similar lawsuits in the US.
OpenAI faces several wrongful death suits, including from the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, a teenager who committed suicide allegedly using methods advised by ChatGPT.
Google and the startup Character.AI agreed in January to settle several lawsuits filed by families of teenagers out of court.
On Wednesday, Google, TikTok and Meta each separately sued California to block a law that prohibits social media companies from providing addictive features to users under 16.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law in September, and it goes into effect on January 1, 2027.

The earliest example of the footage appeared on a Dearborn news agency’s social media account on June 28, 2026, months before the midterm elections. The video shows Shiite Muslims observing the holy day of Ashura.
On Nov. 3, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, resulting in numerous claims focusing on his religious identity. Footage spread online claiming to show Muslims in Dearborn, Michigan, demanding the implementation of Sharia, or Islamic law, in the United States.
The footage appeared on Facebook and X with captions calling it "an invasion" by Muslims. One post stated: "Thousands of Shia Muslims marched in Dearborn demanding Sharia in Michigan and rejecting American law. Now that they have a Muslim senator, they will become more emboldened than ever."
The footage in question was not taken after the Nov. 3 elections. A local Dearborn news agency shared it on Instagram on June 28 with a caption saying that it showed Shiite Muslims observing the holy day of Ashura, which has nothing to do with implementing Sharia. As such, we rate this claim miscaptioned.
Details indicated that the footage was not shot in November, including the facts that all the people marching are wearing T-shirts and the leaves on the trees are green. In November, Dearborn is cold and leaves have changed color and fallen.
Using Google's reverse image search tool, we found what appeared to be the original source of the footage. On June 28, the Instagram and TikTok account for local news organization dearborn.org, which focuses on immigrant Arab and Muslim news, posted the same footage in a reel (archived) with the caption, "From the Annual Ashura march in Dearborn."
A local newspaper, the Detroit Free Press, also covered the same march, posting photographs of the same men in black shirts, green vests and black-and-red vests.
As we have previously reported, Ashura is a holy day for Shiite Muslims. The reel shows a group of men participating in a religious ritual during Muharram, the first month of the Muslim calendar. The month is an important mourning period for Shiite Muslims in particular as it marks the anniversary of the seventh-century Battle of Karbala (in present-day Iraq) and the martyrdom of the Prophet Muhammad's grandson Imam Hussein.
It is common practice for Shiite Muslims to observe the period by wearing black, crying and beating their chests, particularly on Ashura, the 10th day of Muharram.
Similar footage of another procession went viral after Zohran Mamdani, who is a Shiite Muslim, became the Democratic nominee for New York City mayor in 2025. The footage spread with miscaptioned text claiming that the procession was taking place in New York City because of Mamdani, when it was actually from Azerbaijan.
For more reporting on El-Sayed, we have previously covered the claim that he would force Michigan students to learn Arabic numerals (they already do), the true claim that he called Michigan "the capital of Arab America" and a false rumor that he said it was acceptable for young girls to see male genitals in their locker rooms because "they are going to see them on the internet anyway."

China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.
Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.
Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.
“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”
For autocratic states without free and fair elections, seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added.
“They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”
He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”
China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.
Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way: “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”
China as a ‘doer and go-getter’
The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows.
Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.
The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue.
“Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”
Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed.
Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.
The need for trust
China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.
Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”
If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.
Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.
They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.
For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … so no major drama.”

Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
- Published
When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee.
"That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat.
In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil.
Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission.
Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".
Hosted in Senegal, Saturday's opening ceremony will launch the first ever Olympic sporting event on African soil.
Africa is home to nearly 45 million displaced people, out of almost 120 million globally, representing the world's biggest displacement crisis.
Biel says for the refugee team, the Youth Olympics is "a chance for them to tell the world and also to represent the population, especially the refugee population, in Africa".
"It's about representing the hope of young people who are living in a refugee camp, who have lost their motivation or their talent."
Biel was a child when he was forced to flee his home in South Sudan after his village was attacked.
He ended up in Kenya, telling BBC Newsbeat: "It traumatised me, starting a new life, being alone in Kakuma," referring to the major refugee settlement close to the border between Kenya and South Sudan.
"But I started a new life, I believe that school helped me a lot. It helped me to interact with young people who faced the same challenges."
The rest of his childhood was spent on the refugee camp where he took an interest in football.
After realising it wasn't the sport for him, he gave running a go during trials set up by the International Olympic Committee - where he raced without shoes.
It made him "believe that if I can work harder by myself, I can achieve", he says.
One of the athletes on the refugee team, Arno Yafunga Botay, also lived at Kakuma after fleeing his home in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2017, when he was six.
Now 15, he will be competing in judo and told BBC Sport Africa he's promised to bring back a gold medal which he'd like to take to the refugee camp.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo," he said.
As for Biel, he says it's an honour to be chosen as the team's Chef de Mission.
"This is so important for them, to learn from my experience as an athlete and also as a refugee who is coming from a refugee camp," he says.
"So this role means a lot to me and also means a lot to those young athletes who are going to compete."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins later, with the opening ceremony on Saturday.

Lawmakers question police chief about wiretaps alleged to target President Prabowo
Indonesia’s police chief is set to appear before a parliamentary panel as lawmakers investigate allegations that President Prabowo Subianto was targeted in an illegal wiretapping operation
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesia's police chief is set to appear before a parliamentary panel Thursday as lawmakers investigate allegations that President Prabowo Subianto was targeted in an illegal wiretapping operation by several high-ranking officials, including his own chief of staff.
The wiretap allegations, which have rattled the country’s political and security establishment, came to light after three senior police generals were detained including Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who was named chief of staff to Prabowo in October and has close ties to former President Joko Widodo. Since then, a fourth top police official has been implicated.
Prabowo's office said the operation was being investigated as a case of possible treason. The government ordered 20,000 troops to Jakarta as a precaution, though there has not yet been any sign of a major military presence on the streets of the capital, with most kept on standby in barracks.
Part of the investigation is determining the origin of the order to wiretap the president.
Widodo, known popularly in Indonesia as Jokowi, has ties to the main suspects, which already has deepened a rift between the former president and Prabowo, said Evan Laksmana, a Singapore-based analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
“The majority of Prabowo's political decision making in the past two years always have some Jokowi overshadowing,” Laksmana said. “So this is kind of Prabowo finally potentially stepping out of Jokowi's shadow and maybe even going into open political confrontation.”
National Police Chief Gen. Suyudi Ario Seto was expected to field questions from parliament's Commission III, which oversees law enforcement and security affairs and is trying to determine the motive behind the wiretapping operation and uncover whether others were involved. Seto, whose office oversees the current investigation, took over from Listyo Sigit Prabowo as national police chief after the latter was named Prabowo's chief of staff.
“We will see this case through until the facts are fully and clearly revealed,” said Commission III Chairman Habiburokhman, who like many Indonesians uses a single name. “Anyone found to be involved must be held legally accountable.”
Beyond Prabowo, who has not commented on the case, there are allegations that Cabinet officials, politicians, journalists, civil society leaders and business executives also were subjected to unauthorized surveillance. Amnesty International has called for a complete investigation, saying the wiretap operation could have been used to intimidate critics and weaken civil liberties.
Anti-government protests recently have been held in several of Indonesia's major cities. Demonstrators called for accountability in the wiretap case while criticizing former President Widodo's continued political influence and demanding the resignation of Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who is Widodo's son. On Tuesday, 154 people were detained in the city of Yogyakarta following clashes after a protest by about 2,000 students and activists.
In addition to Listyo Sigit Prabowo, authorities also have detained National Police Legal Division head Ahrie Sonta Nasution and Eko Hadi Santoso, a senior instructor at the National Police Education and Training Institute, who are both two-star police generals.
Slamet Uliandi, a two-star police general who heads the Criminal Investigation Agency's Information and Communications Technology Division, has been implicated but is not in custody due to health reasons.
Nasution was dishonorably discharged from the police Tuesday following an internal ethics hearing that was prompted by the wiretap case. Similar proceedings against the three others were to be held soon, police spokesperson Johnny Eddizon Isir said.
None of the suspects have made any public statements about the case.
Listyo Sigit Prabowo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, though the former president has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation. Widodo has said little about the case other than to comment that the legal process should be respected as the investigation continues.
Prabowo, a former military general, lost two presidential races to Widodo but ended up serving as the popular leader's defense minister. He then campaigned as a successor to Widodo, who was term limited, and chose Widodo's son as his running mate and received Widodo's backing for his campaign.
But Raka on Tuesday offered to resign in response to an investigation into his academic credentials unrelated to the wiretap case, which has added to the political turmoil and the split between the current and former presidents.
“I think this will be a long, and most likely painful, breakup between Jokowi and Prabowo, and I don't think you can go back to normal after this,” Laksmana said. “And this is going to be a long painful breakup with many political and security ramifications across the country at a time when the country isn't doing well.”
Police alleged the unauthorized wiretapping took place between 2025 and 2026, after Prabowo took office and while Listyo Sigit Prabowo was still national police chief.
Little has been released so far about the investigation, but last week police said they had uncovered evidence that Nasution, who at one point was an aide-de-camp from the police forces to President Prabowo, requested Uliandi's permission in October to delete recordings made of Prabowo's telephone conversations. They said Uliandi approved the request and the files were deleted.
Nasution’s lawyer, Krisna Murti, did not directly address the allegations but said his client would cooperate fully.
“Our client will be open to clarifying this case,” Murti said in a video statement.

In a major regulatory shift for India's EV supply chain ecosystem, the Centre has issued directions to prohibit export of ‘black mass’, a mineral-rich product of recycled EV batteries. The directorate general of foreign trade (DGFT), under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, notified the amendment yesterday. It is immediately applicable to all outbound shipments of the battery waste material. “The export policy of waste and scrap of primary cells, primary batteries and electric accumulators; spent primary cells, spent primary batteries and spent electric accumulators - Unsorted and not containing lead, cadmium or mercury (Lithium-lon Battery Black Mass) under ITC (HS) Code 85491400 is amended from ‘Free’ to ‘Prohibited’ with immediate effect, until further orders,” the directorate said in a circular. For context, black mass is a powder obtained from shredding end-of-life lithium ion batteries that is rich in valuable metals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel. These metals can be recovered from the black mass and reused in new batteries, which saves costs compared to mining fresh reserves. As India is dependent on imports for these raw materials, black mass has strategic value by enabling these metals to be sourced locally. The new export policy ties into the centre’s strategic push to reduce India’s dependence on imports of critical minerals. In September 2025, the government approved incentives worth ₹1,500 Cr to develop domestic capacity for recycling critical minerals. It followed up on the move earlier this week with the Capex Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing, which committed an outlay of ₹2,814 Cr to set up two plants each for lithium and nickel processing. According to the Observer Research Foundation, India can recycle over 60,000 tonnes of batteries per year, which can generate around 30,000 tonnes of black mass. However, due to limited processing capacity, the black mass typically gets exported to foreign markets. Hence, this new restriction could retain critical raw materials within domestic borders. That said, India’s black mass extraction and refining capabilities still need to be built up in order to ensure that the full economic value can be captured. India’s battery recycling market reached $603.9 Mn in 2025 and is projected to reach $1.3 Bn by 2034, growing at a CAGR of 8.65%. As the battery manufacturing ecosystem scales, ensuring that strategic materials can be processed within domestic borders will be critical to building a more resilient supply chain.

Danielle Thumann Severs, Federal Communications Commission nominee, waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce, Science, & Transportation Committee on Tuesday, November 10, 2026.

Getty Images | CQ Roll Call
Danielle Thumann Severs, Federal Communications Commission nominee, waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce, Science, & Transportation Committee on Tuesday, November 10, 2026.
Credit:
Getty Images | CQ Roll Call
Senate Democrats today opposed President Trump’s nominee for an open Federal Communications Commission seat, and criticized Republicans for moving to confirm a new commissioner during the period before Democrats take control of Congress in January 2027. Democrats also plan to use their majority next year to launch probes of FCC Chairman Brendan Carr.
“After the American people last week overwhelmingly rejected the MAGA agenda, there is no justification for this committee to advance partisan nominees during the lame-duck period,” Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) said today at the Commerce Committee’s nomination hearing for Danielle Thumann Severs, Trump’s pick to fill an empty commissioner’s seat.
Thumann Severs, an attorney and senior counsel to Carr, faced questions from Democrats about whether she supports Carr’s attacks on TV broadcasters.
“Do you support Chairman Carr’s illegal campaign to remove Jimmy Kimmel from the nation’s airwaves?” Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) asked the nominee.
Thumann Severs responded that she has not advised Carr on media-related topics and declined Luján’s request to identify any specific policy issues on which she disagrees with Carr.
“I don’t think Chairman Carr is going to be around more than another three or four months”
Luján predicted trouble for Carr when Democrats take the majority in both chambers of Congress. He seemed to suggest that Carr will quickly grow tired of having to testify in Congress multiple times a month under the Democratic majorities.
“I don’t think Chairman Carr is going to be around more than another three or four months because when we have the gavels in here, he will be here once a month,” Luján said. “And Mr. Carr, if you’re listening now, know you’re going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions, and you don’t have the protection of the gavel any longer.” Luján said Democrats will use “subpoena authorities that you have to respond to so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place.”
Markey accused Thumann Severs of evading questions about Carr threatening and taking actions against broadcasters on behalf of Trump. “Anyone seeking a seat on the Federal Communications Commission must be willing to stand up to such threats and to defend the First Amendment, and you’re not willing to do so here in your confirmation hearing,” Markey said.
Democrats similarly criticized Thumann Severs for not giving a clear answer on whether the FCC has authority to eliminate E-Rate, a $2 billion-a-year program that was created by Congress to connect students and library visitors to the Internet. Carr has proposed eliminating or scaling back the program. Thumann Severs said she helped Carr work on the E-Rate Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, which seeks public comment about the program and the FCC’s authority to change or eliminate it.
“I can’t prejudge the open proceeding [on E-Rate] at the FCC right now,” she said today.
“I am not comfortable with your answers today”
Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) criticized Thumann Severs’ answers. “If you’re confirmed, you’re going to be one of the votes that decides whether the FCC stays an independent regulator, or becomes an arm of the White House press office. We deserve to know where you stand, and I am not comfortable with your answers today,” Duckworth said.
Duckworth told Thumann Severs that the FCC cannot eliminate E-Rate without Congressional approval. “We never directed the FCC to eliminate the program and frankly, at a time when the price of gas, groceries, and utilities is skyrocketing, the last thing the FCC should be doing is making it harder for schools to stay connected,” Duckworth said.
The Senate Commerce, Science & Transportation Committee held today’s hearing for Thumann Severs and three other nominees for federal positions. Senators have until Thursday to submit additional questions for the record, and nominees will have until November 16 to respond.
Thumann Severs needs approval from the committee and then the full Senate to be confirmed to the FCC. Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is trying to get her approved before Republicans have to give up their Senate majority.
Thumann Severs would give Republicans an unusual 3-1 advantage on the FCC, which usually operates with a 3-2 split. Democrats criticized Republicans for not pairing her nomination with a Democratic one. The commission has only one Democrat, Anna Gomez, and she would have to leave at the end of 2027 if she is not given another term.
“For many decades, the Senate has paired commission nominees: A Republican and a Democrat moving together,” Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) said. “Congress established the FCC as an independent, bipartisan agency… a bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation, and I think also more fundamentally to protect a free and diverse press.”
Carr’s threat to ABC “were his words… not my words”
Because US law requires the FCC to have three commissioners for a quorum, Gomez’s “presence in the current 2-1 Republican majority is necessary for the FCC to conduct business,” Hickenlooper said. The Communications Act prohibits a single party from holding more FCC seats than is necessary to form a majority, but Hickenlooper predicted that Trump will fire Gomez to give Republicans a 3-0 stranglehold.
“If today’s nominee is confirmed, President Trump could then fire Commissioner Gomez and have an FCC with no Democratic voice at all,” Hickenlooper said.
Hickenlooper questioned whether Thumann Severs is sufficiently independent from Carr. “Ms. Thumann Severs, your career has largely been spent serving Brendan Carr,” Hickenlooper said. “[You are] currently Chairman Carr’s senior counsel; previously, you were legal advisor to Commissioner Carr. Your official duties include near-daily meetings with Chairman Carr and working to advance his agenda, amplify his messaging.”
Markey asked Thumann Severs if it was appropriate for Carr to use the FCC’s regulatory authority to pressure broadcasters into taking a comedian off the air. Markey was referring to an incident last year in which Carr threatened to revoke ABC broadcast TV licenses over remarks made by Kimmel, who was then suspended by ABC owner Disney.
“We can do this the easy way or the hard way,” Carr said at the time, adding that Disney must “take action” on Kimmel “or there’s going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.”
When asked about Carr’s comments today, Thumann Severs said, “Those were his words. They were not my words, and I have not advised him or worked with the chairman on these particular issues. I can say that if I were to be confirmed as commissioner, I would make all of my decisions [based on] the facts and the law and the record.”
FCC review of ABC station licenses
Senate Democrats tried to get Thumann Severs to discuss Carr’s decision to order an early review of ABC station licenses. “Do you think the FCC should revoke broadcasters’ licenses because the president does not like their coverage?” Duckworth asked.
Thumann Severs answered that the FCC “has a responsibility to fully investigate any complaint… and to evaluate that complaint on the merits. I don’t think a decision should be made purely based on someone’s discontent with the content being aired.”
Although the ABC license review is widely seen as retaliation against the network for its news coverage and other programming, Carr’s proceeding is ostensibly based on an allegation that Disney’s diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices are discriminatory.
“Based on publicly available material, which is all I have seen on that particular matter, the licenses were called for early renewal as part of an investigation into potential rule violations,” Thumann Severs said today.
Ted Cruz satisfied by nominee’s answers
Cruz mentioned the Carr FCC’s review of ABC licenses and noted that “ABC argues [the review] is actually in retaliation for the network’s programming.” Cruz also alleged that in Democratic administrations, “the FCC has previously used its public interest standard as a weapon against conservatives.”
“If you are confirmed, will you commit to basing licensing decisions on the law and the record and to not using the FCC’s authority to pressure or punish a broadcaster for protected speech?” Cruz asked the nominee. She answered, “Yes.”
Cruz then asked Thumann Severs if she supports the JAWBONE Act, a bill that Cruz introduced with Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) to enable lawsuits against federal officials who try to coerce broadcasters or tech platforms into restricting speech.
Thumann Severs answered that she supports the bill. “I think it’s incredibly important that federal officials not use their position… to coerce against protected speech,” she said.
Cruz seemed satisfied with her answers. While Democrats recognized that Republicans have the votes to advance the nomination, they spent much of the hearing criticizing Thumann Severs’ answers and the Republican plan to confirm her without a paired Democratic nominee.
“We should not be confirming a Republican nominee without also renominating and confirming Anna Gomez, the Democrat, and filling the other vacant Democratic seat,” Markey said. “There is a potential next year where there will be three Republicans and no Democrats on the Federal Communications Commission… that is wrong, and that is why I do not believe we should proceed with this nomination at this time.”
Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India, a country he visited many times on extended trips.
His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company.
Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.
Roy’s other books included A Brief History of Tea (2003), an authoritative account of the complex political and horticultural history of tea, and Outlaw (2010), which looked at the life of India’s “bandit queen” and politician Phoolan Devi, drawing on Roy’s friendship with her before her assassination in 2001. His last book, The Theft of India (2015), documented the rivalry between European colonial powers and the impact this had on Indians themselves.
Roy was born in Evesham, Worcestershire, to Marie (known as Min, nee Bland) and Wilson Moxham. Wilson, a baker, died when Roy was 11, after which Min, a shop worker, raised her three sons under straitened circumstances, often taking in lodgers to make ends meet.
After leaving Prince Henry’s grammar school in Evesham in the early 1960s, Roy put an advert in the Times newspaper that read: “Young man, good A-levels, seeks opportunity in Africa in tobacco or tea.” He received a reply offering him a job on a tea plantation in the British colony of Nyasaland (now Malawi), where, despite his youth, he became a supervisor in charge of 1,000 female tea pickers. Later he switched to selling agricultural machinery across east Africa, particularly in Kenya. In the mid-70s, after 13 years in Africa he returned to the UK, where he opened a gallery in Covent Garden, London, selling African art.
Following a period of squatting in Covent Garden, Roy became an early and longstanding member of the Seven Dials Housing Co-operative, living in one of their properties in that area for most of the rest of his life.
In 1978 he changed direction by studying book and paper conservation at Camberwell College of Arts, after which he worked as a conservator at the Canterbury Cathedral Archive, then at Senate House Library, University of London, where he remained until 2005.
While working, Roy had begun travelling regularly to India from 1992 onwards, and it was on those journeys that he began his three-year search for the Great Hedge. The book was hugely successful, often referenced by historians, writers and artists, and even inspired a Horrible Histories sketch.
After retiring in 2005, Roy lived in India for a number of months each year. His book about Devi, a champion of the Indian poor, came about after he wrote to her when she was in prison. When she was released they arranged a meeting, and became great friends.
Roy is survived by his two brothers, John and Jim, a nephew, three nieces and me.

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.
It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.
See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.
Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.
While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.
Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.
“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.
“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”
Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.
As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.
Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.
“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.
“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”
See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

Samsung Gallery now syncs with Google to back up your photos
The company ended Gallery's Microsoft OneDrive integration back in September.
If you've ever owned a Samsung phone, you've most likely seen your device prompt you to back up your media to OneDrive at least once in the past. Back in September, however, Samsung removed its Gallery app's ability to sync with Microsoft OneDrive. Well, the phonemaker was likely cooking up another partnership behind the scenes, because it has just announced that its Gallery app can now sync with your Google account.
In the past, if you wanted to back up your photos and videos to your Google storage on a Samsung phone, you've had to use Google Photos instead of (or in addition to) your device's native Gallery app. With this update, you can stick to Samsung's Gallery app if you want to.The feature is currently only available on select Galaxy devices running One UI 9, Samsung's latest custom Android interface, but the company says it will roll out to more devices in phases. To enable the feature, tap the Cloud icon in Gallery or go to Gallery Settings and switch on Sync photos and videos.
Since the feature syncs media files to your Google account, you'll be able to access them in the Gallery app of another Samsung Galaxy device. Simply log into the same account on your other device and enable sync on it, as well. You'll then be able to see previews of your synced photos and videos on that device. If you want to access the original files, just select and download them. In case you want to do the opposite and remove files from your phone or tablet after they've been synced to Google storage, you can use Samsung's other new feature. It offers a Free up space option in the Sync photos and videos settings, which deletes original files from your device while keeping thumbnails visible in the Gallery app.
It's worth noting that Gallery sync will take up storage space on your Google account. Each Google account comes with 5GB of free storage by default, which you can expand to 15GB if you verify a valid phone number. If you want or need more than that, since that storage is shared across Google's services, you'll have to purchase a Google One subscription that will set you back $2 per month for 100GB of storage or $3 for 200GB.

The State government’s decision to construct a railway tunnel to Vizhinjam International Seaport costing over ₹1,500 crore through a densely populated region, despite the availability of an alternative land alignment, has raised eyebrows among many, with experts and members of the public questioning its environmental and social costs against the backdrop of the State government’s stated commitment to sustainable development.
The proposed tunnel between Balaramapuram and Vizhinjam to provide rail connectivity to Vizhinjam International Seaport has triggered serious environmental and land stability concerns in the region. The project, which is set to become the State’s second major tunnel project and the country’s third-longest railway tunnel, has been disputed by experts regarding its feasibility beneath the Vizhinjam-Balaramapuram road, who termed it potentially unviable given the region’s fragile geology, soil types and high population density.
Dr. V. Nandakumar, former head of the Natural Hazards Research Group and former director (In charge) of the National Centre for Earth Science Studies, said no comprehensive study involving competent national institutions appeared to have been conducted on the geological formations along the proposed 10.7-km alignment, variations in soil types or the east-to-west groundwater flow before the project was taken up.
Drawing on more than three decades of field experience, Mr. Nandakumar said most stretches of the proposed alignment are likely to pass through geologically weak terrain. Beneath the top layer of laterite, the subsurface is expected to comprise of decomposed lithomargic clay interspersed with hard rock in some locations. Other sections consist of inconsistent red soil underlain by layers of clay and sand. Such formations, according to him, are unsuitable for a tunnel carrying container trains weighing several tonnes.
The proposed alignment also passes through some of the most densely populated areas of Thiruvananthapuram district, where a large section of the population depends on open wells for drinking water. He warned that the impervious concrete tunnel structure, laid at a depth of around 30 metres, could act as an underground barrier, disrupting the natural movement of groundwater. This could eventually cause wells to dry up in an area already facing water scarcity.
He also flagged the risk of vibrations generated by heavy container trains passing through tunnels bored into weak soil. Such vibrations could damage existing structures, ranging from large buildings to smaller houses, causing cracks and, in extreme cases, structural collapse. Land subsidence and building damage could pose long-term risks along the entire stretch, he cautioned.
He also opined whether authorities had adequately explored an alternative alignment through lower-lying areas, including the fringes of the Pallichal-Mudavoorpara paddy fields, which is elevation-wise 10 m lower than the proposed tunnel alignment, which is 30 m below the road surface and almost having a parallel elevation with the port and the Trivandrum- Nagercoil rail link. Such a route, according to him, could avoid potential hazards to densely populated areas and minimise risks to existing structures, groundwater resources, environmental stability and local livelihoods.
It could also reduce construction and maintenance costs. A surface-level alignment would also offer greater scope for future track doubling and expansion, which would be difficult to achieve with the proposed tunnel, he said. The project in its present form could destabilise the region and may disrupt the livelihoods of millions of people living along the Balaramapuram-Vizhinjam corridor. The land above the tunnel, including the buffer zone, could remain locked subject to restrictions on development, building permits and other uses. This also may even affect property ownership and transfer rights. The disposal of excavated rock and soil generated during tunnelling could pose another major environmental challenge.
He urged the government to reconsider the tunnel proposal and instead opt for an overland railway alignment after establishing its economic viability. Senior government officials said they selected the alignment as the shortest route from the existing railway lines to the port, although an overland alignment with relatively lower cost is available through a paddy field in the region.

Employee stock options (ESOPs) have become a major talking point in India’s startup ecosystem this year, with questions around liquidity, employee wealth creation and the ability to monetise years of accumulated stock options taking centre stage. While Flipkart’s ESOP-related employee woes have been in the news all through this summer, digital commerce startup GoKwik has brought another dimension to the ESOP debate. GoKwik, which is backed by the likes of Z47 Partners, Peak XV Partners, RTP Global and Think Investments, has amended its existing ESOP Plan 2021, through the insertion of a new non-compete clause, naming nine companies that employees are barred from joining or associating with, if they want to retain their ESOP rights. The provision gives the startup the authority to revoke unvested and vested-but-unexercised employee stock options if employees (even those who have quit GoKwik) are found to have breached the restriction. Inc42 has seen a copy of the internal document in question which has caused consternation among current and former employees. The mail was also sent to former GoKwik employees who continue to hold options. The insertion of the clause has raised questions around employee mobility and the rights of existing ESOP holders, particularly as the new provision applies to options granted in the past as well as future stock options. The clause was communicated to employees in the month of August, amid a spate of senior-level exits. The exits include vice president Sneha Rao, Sharad Gupta, the senior director of product management for the Checkout business, and Siddhartha Bahl, head of product, among others. The policy lists Razorpay, Shiprocket, CRED, Cashfree Payments, BiteSpeed, Snapmint, WebEngage, Shopflo (acquired by Pine Labs), and Pine Labs as competing businesses. Under the provision, employees cannot accept employment with, render services to, advise, invest in or otherwise associate with these companies. If the company determines that an employee has breached the restriction, it can forfeit their unvested options as well as vested options that have not yet been exercised. The GoKwik ESOP Plan 2021 (“Plan”) allows GoKwik to cancel or forfeit both unvested and vested-but-unexercised options if the Board or Nomination and Remuneration Committee determines that an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach”. While unvested options are stock options that employees are not yet entitled to exercise, vested-but-unexercised options are those that employees are entitled to exercise but have not yet converted into shares. The provision does not affect ESOPs that have already been exercised. In effect, an employee joining a competing business could lose options that are yet to vest, as well as those that have already vested by have not been exercised. This means that even employees who completed the vesting period and earned the right to buy shares coils lose those options if the company determines that they have breached the competition restriction. However, options already exercised and converted into shares are not covered by this forfeiture provision. Importantly, the restriction applies to all grants, whether issued before or after its effective date, and continues to bind former employees holding vested options even after their employment ends. The restriction, however, is not indefinite. A special resolution passed by GoKwik shareholders at the company’s September, 2025 AGM provides that the competition related restriction will remain in force from the grant date until two years after an employee;s last date of employment or engagement with the company or its affiliates. In other words, the restriction applies throughout an employee’s tenure at GoKwik and continues for two years after their departure. During this period, joining or associating with a competing business could put their outstanding ESOPs at risk. The policy appears to carve out passive investments in publicly traded securities. It also allows the GoKwik Board to approve exceptions in writing, with employees required to write to the company for such deviations. The inclusion is significant because it directly links an employee’s association with named competitors to the potential loss of their stock options, including options that have already vested but remain unexercised. Questions sent to GoKwik didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story even after Inc42 extended the deadline for responses upon the company’s request. Instead, GoKwik issued a press release claiming former employees might get 9X average returns on their ESOPs and the startup has turned EBITDA positive in October 2026. But this press release does not mention any of the concerns that employees have brought up. Employees In Limbo “The sudden change in the ESOP policy was a shock. People who have quite a significant ESOP holding are all of a sudden in fear that they will lose it if they leave the company and try to join a better company. Now the names that they have mentioned are much superior companies that they would want to join as part of having a better career trajectory,” a former GoKwik employee told Inc42. Employees with significant ESOP holdings, particularly those who may consider moving to other companies in the same sector, are stuck in limbo. Sources in the company say they are weighing potential job opportunities against the potential loss from forfeiting their outstanding stock options. This is especially relevant for employees whose options have vested but have not been exercised, since the new clause explicitly includes vested-but-unexercised options within the scope of potential forfeiture. The forfeiture, however, is not automatic. The Board or the Nomination and Remuneration Committee has the discretion to determine whether an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach” and decide whether to cancel or forfeit their unvested and/or vested-but-unexercised options. Worryingly for employees, the provision is ambiguous about what kind of relationships are covered. For instance, it says that ESOPs may be revoked for employees who may “otherwise associate” with a competing business. This could cover relationships beyond direct employment, and the policy does not make the scope of this phrase immediately clear. The timing of the amendment is also notable against the backdrop of GoKwik’s growth ambitions and recent senior-level departures as well as layoffs. Founded in 2020 by Chirag Taneja, Vivek Bajpai, and Ankush Talwar, GoKwik is an ecommerce enablement startup that offers software tools to help online brands improve checkout, reduce order returns, automate customer engagement and increase sales. Earlier this year, Inc42 exclusively reported that GoKwik had laid off around 120 employees. The startup has to date raised $68 Mn in funding and counts investors including Peak XV Partners, Z47 Partners, RTP Global, and Think Investments, among others. In an interview with BW Disrupt, published in July 2025, cofounder and CEO Taneja said the company generated around ₹250 Cr in revenue in FY25. However, GoKwik Commerce Solutions Pvt Ltd’s financial disclosures show consolidated operating revenue of ₹146.2 Cr for FY25, and total consolidated revenue of approximately ₹163 Cr. GoKwik did not respond to questions about this discrepancy. Among the nine companies named in the policy, GoKwik directly competes with the likes of Shiprocket’s Fastrr, Razorpay’s Magic Checkout, Shopflo, and Cashfree’s One Click Checkout, while the remaining companies operate in adjacent or overlapping segments of ecommerce enablement, fintech, and merchant services ecosystem. Making Sense Of Non-Compete For ESOPs Non-compete restrictions are commonly included in employment agreements in India, although their enforceability is difficult to establish. However, explicitly naming competitors in an ESOP policy and linking an employee’s association with them to the cancellation of vested-but-unexercised options is unusual, according to Siddharth Manchanda, Partner at JSA Advocates & Solicitors. Manchanda further clarified that his comments reflected a general understanding of the law and should not be construed as an opinion on GoKwik. He also said that a restriction on an ESOP policy is unusual but its substance is not entirely new. Most ESOP policies, in his view, contain provisions that allow options to lapse if an employee breaches their employment agreement. Since employment agreements commonly include non-compete restrictions, companies may already have an indirect route to link an employee joining a competitor with the loss of ESOPs. However, companies do not typically go after employees solely for joining a competitor, unless the situation also involves allegations of confidentiality breaches, data theft or misuse of proprietary information. Under Rule 12(8)(f) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, unvested options ordinarily expire upon resignation or termination, while vested options can be exercised within the period specified by the ESOP scheme. The more consequential question, according to Manchanda, is whether a company can introduce additional grounds for forfeiture after employees have already received their options. While employers have discretion to set the grounds for cancellation when drafting an ESOP policy, changing those terms later to employees’ disadvantage could be legally questionable. In GoKwik’s case, the amendment applies to options that were already outstanding. As per another lawyer Inc42 spoke to, this change could be challenged from a legal standpoint, as amendments that adversely affect employees’ existing ESOP rights raise questions around their validity. He added that the enforceability of non-compete restrictions and the cancellation of ESOPs on that basis remains an unsettled issue that could be tested in legal dispute. ESOPs Turn Into A Governance Question The clause also raises a governance question that goes beyond enforceability. Plus, some clauses in the changed policy are ambiguous at best. Under the plan, it is the Board or its Nomination and Remuneration Committee that decides whether an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach”, a decision in which employees, and the former employees the clause continues to bind, have no part. ESOPs are a critical lever when it comes to attracting employees to early stage startups. They stand in for salary. An early stage startup can’t match what IT services giants, multinationals or global capability centres (GCCs) pay. Stock options fill the gap. The employee takes a lower monthly salary in exchange for a share of the upside in the future. At that stage the ESOP is part of the offer, not a perk. ESOPs are also seen as a retention tactic. Options vest over time and it ties in employees to the success of the business in the long run. Leaving early means giving up the options that haven’t vested or even leaving money on the table. And finally, ESOPs are one wealth creation instrument in the hands of employers. A total of 12 startups executed ESOP buybacks in 2025, paying ₹1,409 Cr ($158 Mn) to more than 9,200 employees. In 2024, 23 startups paid out ₹1,448 Cr to employees through buybacks. Even a minor change in the ESOP policy can lead to employees having to sacrifice an amount that can be equivalent to years of salary. GoKwik would not be the first startup to change ESOP terms after the options were granted. In December 2025, Unacademy cut the window its former employees had to exercise their vested options from 10 years to 30 days, while it was in M&A talks. Unacademy put the change on hold a month later, after a backlash from former employees. GoKwik’s claim of 9X average returns for former employees tells us what the options may be worth, but do employees get to keep them? GoKwik’s handling of the issue will be tested the first time an employee with vested options joins one of the nine companies it names, unless, like Unacademy, the ecommerce company decides to revisit this provision before then. Until that happens, every employee holding ESOPs, current or former, is left with the question: does a vested option actually belong to them even if it has been allocated on paper, or is it only theirs for as long as they stay away from the companies that GoKwik bars? A video is going viral on social media, where a young man is heard saying in Bangla, “We won’t allow any Hindutva aggression or Indian aggression in Jagannath University.”
The video wad shared by X handle Voice of BD Hindus (@HinduUnityBD) on November 7 with the claim that Muslim students of Jagannath University in Bangladesh had declared Diwali as a form of Hindutva aggression. (Archive)
🚨 BREAKING : Jamaat Student leaders at Jagannath University have declared Diwali a form of “Hindutva aggression” and “Indian aggression,”
announcing that they will not allow Diwali celebrations to take place on campus. But they can celebrate EID. A Hindu Zamindar Built Jagannath University.
— Voice Of BD Hindus 🇧🇩 (@HinduUnityBD) November 7, 2026
In the 25-second-long clip, the man states, “We won’t allow any Hindutva aggression or Indian aggression in Jagannath University. This university is situated in a country of 92% Muslims, and the university claims that it runs by nurturing the culture, ethics and heritage of the Muslims. If anyone wants to make things work differently, the people of Bangladesh will give a befitting reply. Inshallah”.
The video was also shared by X user Monica Verma with the claim that “Muslim Students in Bangladesh are calling Deepawali celebrations as “Hindu aggression” warning the Hindu students of consequences if they celebrate it.”
Muslim Students in Bangladesh are calling Deepawali celebrations as “Hindu aggression” warning the Hindu students of consequences if they celebrate it.
Indian as well as the global Media will never show you this side of the F*cked Up Bangladeshi Gen Z. https://t.co/wij366yQtp
— Monica Verma (@TrulyMonica) November 7, 2026
Several other prominent Indian social media users shared the same video with similar claims.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the claim, we conducted a reverse image search using key frames from the video in question.
This led us to a video published by Bangladesh-based media outlet ‘Desh Somoy News’. The video is identical to the one currently going viral and was published on October 16 in connection with the beef festival controversy at Jagannath University in Dhaka.
The controversy at Dhaka’s Jagannath University began on October 12, when students of the department of Islamic history and culture organised a beef feast near the university’s central temple. Hindu students objected to the proximity of the cooking arrangements to the temple and the alleged use of temple bricks to build a makeshift stove. Protests followed, triggering a wider dispute on campus.
On October 14, the university administration issued a notice prohibiting animal slaughter on campus, prompting further student protests.
Protesting against the administrative decision, students led by the Jagannath University Central Student’s Union organized a rally in the campus on October 14 itself, and held an impromptu press conference after the protest rally. The video in question is from that press conference.
Bangladesh-based online news portal Bd24report covered the press conference on its Facebook page on October 14. The live video is 17 minutes long, and from 5:13 minute mark, the press conference can be seen. At the 8:39-minute mark, the social work secretary of the Student’s Union, Mustafizur Rahaman, addresses the press. Rahaman is the same person seen speaking in the viral video.
Rahaman spoke from 8:50 till 10:56 minute mark, and the viral snippet is from 10:22 till 10:47. There was no mention of Diwali in the entire programme. The students spoke in protest against the University administration’s decision to ban animal slaughter within the campus.
Although the administration subsequently softened its position, students led by the Jagannath University Central Student’s Union slaughtered a cow on October 16 and organised a beef feast. The student’s union is run by Jamaat-e-Islami Bangladesh’s student wing Islami Chatra Shibir backed candidates.
On October 17, Bangladesh Khelafat Chatra Majlish held a similar feast, slaughtering a second cow and organising a Qawwali programme.
It is also important to note that Diwali celebrations and Kali Puja were organized on the Jagannath University campus this year. A pandal was set up for Kali Puja and students were seen creating ‘alpona’, a traditional Bengali art form drawn on floors, which is considered auspicious.
To sum up, a video related to the controversial beef festival on Dhaka’s Jagannath University campus in October is viral with the false claim that Jamaat student leaders objected to Diwali celebrations at the university. The statements made in the clip have got nothing to do with Diwali. Besides, Kali Puja was held on the campus like previous years.
