The idea that Americans should be offered a greater choice of smaller cars has support from strange bedfellows indeed. After all, who could forget President Trump—usually one to take a maximalist approach to any problem—announcing last year that he wanted the Department of Transportation to make Japan’s diminutive “Kei” cars legal here in the US.
Ars’ attempts to get DoT to tell us more about the potential influx of little vehicles have mostly fallen on deaf ears. But this week, there has been movement on the topic, with Toyota announcing that it will bring back the Scion brand with the KEI-01.
What’s a Kei car?
Here in the US, the preponderance of humongous SUVs is a consequence largely of government policies, specifically corporate average fuel economy standards that made it less profitable to sell smaller, efficient cars. Japan’s Kei cars are what happens if the government instead restricts the size, engine capacity, and power output.
A Kei car must fit within the following dimensions: 11.2 feet (3.4 m) long, 4.9 feet (1.5 m) wide, and 6.6 feet (2 m) tall, with an engine displacement of no more than 0.66 L and an output of 63 hp (47 kW) or less. That’s a far cry from the more than 16 feet (4.9 m) of a full-size pickup truck, but it makes sense for a country where you’re not allowed to buy a car unless you have somewhere to park it, with those spaces being at an absolute premium.
Being affordable to buy and economical to run sure doesn’t hurt either, and last year, Japan bought almost 1.7 million Kei cars, out of total sales of 4.6 million vehicles. Depending on where you live in the US, it can be varying degrees of difficult to import a Kei car, at least until now.
Scion is back?
Toyota killed off its Scion sub-brand more than a decade ago, ending the haggle-free approach and cars aimed at younger buyers in favor of selling more Toyotas. But now it’s back as “Scion by Toyota,” which the automaker will apparently use to experiment with less traditional ideas. But forget about a cool-but-boxy EV in the mold of the Honda N-One or Nissan Sakura.

Quick Answer
LastWave, Musify, Convx, Spotube, and SimpMusic are free open-source clients for YouTube Music and Spotify. They unlock premium perks without subscription fees or ad tracking, offering background playback, offline downloads, time-synced lyrics, lossless audio, and customized interfaces without locked controls.
Subscription prices are going through the roof. And when you stack multiple subscriptions together, it can put a big hole in your pocket. For listening to music, we usually depend on Spotify and YouTube Music. They are the default music streaming sources for millions across the globe. Though there are alternatives from which you can hear high-quality audio, they just can’t match the ease of popular apps. But you are bombarded with ads, and several features are locked behind a paywall unless you pay.
Thankfully, you don’t have to search the internet for free options. Developers around the world have built free apps that give you many of those perks. Below are five of the best, what each does well, and what to watch out for before installing.
Table of Contents
Why are open-source music apps worth a look?
To be clear, most of these apps are clients. This means that they don’t store any music themselves. They plug into a service like YouTube Music and show it in a cleaner, ad-free interface with extra features on top, which you’d usually get after paying for a premium subscription. For me, Spotify has been the go-to music streaming app, but slowly the app has become quite greedy.
After a few times, the next and previous song buttons get locked, and it asks you to pay to unlock them. I mean, what is wrong with companies today? Thankfully, I have now ditched Spotify and have picked one of the below open-source music options.
That has three practical effects:
- No ads and no subscription fees. Everything below is free.
- Most of these apps have no ad trackers or tracking SDKs.
- New features are constantly added, and some of them aren’t even available in paid apps.
The catch is that these apps rely on unofficial methods to fetch music, so they can break when YouTube or Spotify changes something. Treat them as great free alternatives, but not as rock-solid replacements. Let us take a look at the free alternatives.
Best free open-source music apps
LastWave
If you care about how your music sounds, LastWave is the one to install first. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. Most of us would care about the free music that we get with LastWave, but you will soon appreciate the quality of music that it offers. And since it is a YouTube Music client, you are getting access to almost every song that is available on YouTube.
The headline feature is lossless FLAC audio, up to 24-bit/192 kHz. When you press play, the song starts playing right away on the fastest available stream, and while you listen, the app fetches the lossless version in the background and switches over once it’s ready. On compatible phones and headphones, LastWave also plays the Dolby Atmos version of a song automatically. For those who own a USB DAC or a pair of IEMs, there’s a bit-perfect mode that sends raw, unprocessed audio straight to your device.
The app is packed with features that normally sit behind a subscription. The lyrics are synced word-by-word and pulled from sources like Apple Music, Musixmatch, and LRCLIB. There’s a 10-band equalizer with presets for thousands of headphone models, and smart playlists that build mixes from your listening history. Plus, you have the option to import playlists from Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube Music in seconds, and even sync your Spotify liked songs.
Musify
Not everyone wants a hundred settings and toggles. Some people just want to listen to their favorite music without having to deal with ads and a hundred pop-ups about purchasing the subscription between two songs. Musify is for people who just want to open an app, search for a song, and press play. It’s a lightweight Android app built around Material You, which means its colors automatically match your phone’s theme and wallpaper.
Using it is fairly easy. You search for songs, albums, artists, or playlists and start streaming over Wi-Fi or mobile data. If you want to save data or listen on a flight, you can download tracks and play them offline. It lets you create your own playlists, rename and reorder them, or import existing ones from online sources. The player shows lyrics so you can follow along. You can also control the quality of the audio.
There are no annoying banner ads, no audio ads, no sign-up, and no tracking inside the app, and the interface is translated into dozens of languages by the community. I found this to be a great choice for older phones, or for a parent or sibling who finds complicated apps annoying.
Convx
While most open source music apps work well, there are only a few that also feel nice to use. Convx comes in the second category. If you like iOS’s “Liquid Glass” design, then you would love Convx. It brings iPhone’s Liquid Glass design to Android, with frosted, see-through menus, floating controls, and album-inspired colors that change with whatever you are playing.
Under the pretty surface, Convx is a complete music player. You can browse and stream music, save songs for offline listening, build queues and playlists, set a sleep timer, change playback speed, and tweak the sound to your taste with an equalizer. What makes it stand out among the heavy hitters is its DJ-style playback. You also get automix, crossfade, and smooth transitions between one song and the next. Lyrics are synced word by word and come from several providers, plus it gets animated artwork.
Convx can play local files and even songs stored on a home server or NAS through SMB and WebDAV. You can choose the option to import your Spotify playlists, show what you’re playing on Discord, scrobble to Last.fm, recognize songs playing around you, and use Listen Together to sync playback with friends.
Spotube
Spotube is the veteran here, with over 46,000 stars on GitHub, and it works differently from the rest. Instead of being locked to one service like Spotify or YouTube, it runs on plugins. You choose your own music sources, metadata, and playlists through plugins made by the community, or if you’re good with it, you can write one yourself.
The biggest advantage is that it works everywhere. Spotube runs natively on Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. This means you can use the same app on your phone and your laptop. It’s small, fast, and light on data. You can import and sync playlists from popular music services or manage them locally. It gives time-synced lyrics from public lyric databases no matter which source you use. Offline downloads are supported, with proper metadata and ID.
Privacy is one of the biggest highlights of Spotube. It collects no telemetry and no user data. Installing it is also easy, because you can download it through winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, Homebrew, Flatpak, and F-Droid.
SimpMusic
SimpMusic is that one app that does everything. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android and desktop that borrows many of Spotify’s best ideas. You can play music from YouTube Music or regular YouTube without ads, and it gets you background playback. You can browse the home feed, charts, podcasts and moods, search everything on YouTube, cache songs for offline playback and use Android Auto.
SimpMusic Wrapped gives you a year-in-music recap just like Spotify’s. Then there is monthly recap playlists and listening charts that stay on your device. There are three Now Playing styles, including one that looks like Apple Music, and the lyrics are synced in 12 languages. You can even share lyrics as an image.
You can switch to 1080p video with subtitles, skip sponsor segments with SponsorBlock, see dislike counts with Return YouTube Dislike, and use a 10-band equalizer with AutoEq headphone profiles.
Which one should you pick?
If you care most about sound quality, I would suggest LastWave. If you want something simple, pick Musify. If design matters to you, try Convx. If you want plugins and an app that runs on every device you own, choose Spotube. If you want the most features in one place, install SimpMusic. The best part is that all five are free and can be installed side by side, so you can try a few and keep your favorite. You will get access to unlimited songs from the best sources in good quality. Let us know which one you chose, and comment below if you have a different app that you use for listening to music.

Allow me to introduce you to the robot cat butler I’m developing with help from AI.
Using OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol, I taught a virtual version of Microduck—a cute robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face—to walk around a room and identify any bengal cats in its vicinity. (The clip above shows the robot waddling toward a target feline; its eye view is shown top right.)
I’m still waiting patiently for a physical Microduck—please hurry up and ship it, guys—but simulated behavior is relatively simple, so it should transfer over to the real thing. I plan to have the robot automatically dispense a treat for my pet bengal, Leona, perhaps by bowing its head to release one from a 3D-printed, head-mounted storage chamber.
I was able to code and train the virtual robot in just a few hours, which is, quite frankly, incredible. Previously, this kind of thing might have taken me weeks to figure out. It was possible because OpenAI’s latest models are remarkably good at understanding and manipulating 3D representations of the physical world and then translating that into useful code, agentic actions, and robot training.
Real roboticists are using the latest models to do some amazing stuff. When OpenAI released Astra this past September, University of California, Berkeley professor Ken Goldberg and his students saw demos that showcased its ability to render 3D images. They wondered if it could help with the simulations required to train different kinds of robots. These simulations need to be incredibly detailed and extremely accurate to ensure that sophisticated behavior—a humanoid that can dance or a robot hand that can grasp—will transfer faithfully to the real world.
One member of Goldberg’s lab gave Astra access to an Nvidia tool called Newton, showed it a video clip of a real robot in action, and asked if it could create a simulation of the scene.
“What blew us all away was that within an hour it had produced a full 3D simulation with all the parameters set—the position of the camera, the lighting, the background, all the materials,” Goldberg tells me.
Astra is also able to automate much of the drudgery involved with training a robot in simulation, Goldberg says, by running experiments and examining the results.
This is precisely what I found while training the virtual Microduck. Along with GPT-6 Sol, I used an agentic harness from Nous Research called Hermes and a Nvidia DGX Spark, a personal computer that contains a powerful AI chip.
I’ve previously written about using agents and coding models to configure, program, and debug physical robots. Normally, this kind of work requires significant expertise; modern coding models make it a cinch. But OpenAI’s newest model went far beyond just writing code.
It used a piece of Nvidia software called Isaac Sim to feed instructions to a model that controlled the virtual robot, watch videos of it in action to assess how well things were working, and suggest tweaks to its training regime.
This process allowed me to train the Microduck to walk around without toppling over. I initially tried getting GPT-6 Sol to teach the robot to moonwalk—I fed it a GIF of Michael Jackson sliding across the stage, which it tried to copy—but after hours of effort, it only resulted in a very jaunty backward jog. (The robots don’t have us totally beat quite yet.)
Jim Fan, a researcher at Nvidia who has collaborated with Goldberg, says the way AI can now control robots mirrors how software agents function. LLMS can use models trained to control physical actions—visual language action (VLA) models—just as they access different software on a computer.
This week, Fan, Goldberg, and others open sourced an agentic framework for robots called Aspire, which allows a robot to discover and use new skills. One example: GPT-6 Astra figured out how to use a pair of robot arms to solve a Rubik’s cube.
“It picks it up, tries to twist it, but has the wrong angle,” Fan says. “Then it reasons for a very, very long time, but it eventually is able to solve it because it learns the skills over time.”
At the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), held in Austin, Texas, this week, Fan gave a keynote speech in which he talked about the incredible realization that AI models can automate a lot of the work needed to have a robot do sophisticated things. Fan showed off a demo in which Astra was put in control of a robot arm and told to paint a picture of the Golden Gate Bridge. Using some paint and brushes nearby, it duly completed the task.
Of course, getting robots to work reliably and efficiently is still extremely difficult, requiring significant engineering expertise. The vision system on my robot duck does not work well enough to be deployed in a real product.
Still, the ease and speed of training robots with AI could soon have an enormous impact on manufacturing and e-commerce, and Goldberg says a number of industrial robotics and automation firms have shown an interest in the approach.
Much like vibe coding a few years ago, we may well see breakthroughs in “vibe robotics” as hobbyists and engineers realize how easy it is to program and train robots. And, assuming I can perfect my robot helper, Leona may never have to go without treats again.

There’s a specific mantra drilled into government workers, military officers, and intelligence personnel during counterintelligence briefings: “If she’s a 10 and you’re a 5, she’s a spy!” Or, as the US Army’s Counterintelligence Command posted on Valentine’s Day: “It doesn’t take a mathematician to figure out ‘10 + 5 = honeytrap.’” The very beautiful woman who is suddenly interested in your very ordinary existence probably has ulterior motives, is the message.
Jensen Huang surely doesn’t live a typical life—he’s a centibillionaire, the swashbuckling CEO of Nvidia, one of the hottest and most geopolitically consequential companies of the 21st century. Surely he’s aware of the possibility that he’d cross paths with intelligence assets. In fact, it’s hard to think of many companies in the world that would be a higher priority target for foreign intelligence agencies.
All of that makes the stock-shaking news this week all the more surprising. How did Huang get embroiled in a spy scandal that mixes infidelity, international espionage, the Trump administration, and the economic behemoth of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry?
The story kicked off just before Halloween, with a six-byline story in The New York Times reporting that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Starting somewhere between 2024 and 2025, Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a one-time executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider known as Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies warned top US officials that they believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. So far, Nvidia’s board, which has launched its own investigation, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that’s far from the only concern.
As one would expect, China has denied any nefarious plot centered on Jensen Huang. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Monday said, “The narrative about so-called Chinese spies is entirely based on groundless speculation—it’s nothing more than slander and smearing.”
But according to reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times, US intelligence officials also claim that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was reporting to China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. On Monday, Megaspeed said on LinkedIn that US authorities found “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities." (There’s no indication so far that Alice Huang, a one-time Chinese state journalist, is an employee or “officer” of Chinese intelligence; she’s believed to be an “asset,” an outsider who aids an intelligence agency, sometimes for pay, sometimes not.)
China, though, has elevated economic espionage to a core pillar of its economic and military development, stealing the designs for everything from US fighter jets to solar panels and commercial paint recipes. “Honeypots” or “honey traps”—positioning an alluring operative to seduce or develop a relationship with a key target—are one of intelligence’s most infamous and well-established strategies. French officials have warned specifically about Chinese honeypots since at least 2011, when intelligence reports cited a pharmaceutical researcher who was seduced and then blackmailed by a Chinese spy operation.
Over the past quarter of a century, as Silicon Valley emerged as a center of political and economic power, it has become a key focus of Chinese intelligence. In one plot, a Chinese national named Fang Fang spent years trying to cozy up to Bay Area politicians, including then US Representative Eric Swalwell. (While intelligence officials at the time reportedly believed Fang to be an operative, law enforcement officials never brought any charges against her). When traveling to China, US business executives have become accustomed to leaving their regular phones and computers at home and using burner devices to prevent the installation of spyware or malware (as I did, when I traveled to China for WIRED in 2019 to report on Huawei). In 2012, when Leon Panetta was making his first trip to China as defense secretary, he and his team were advised to bathe and shower in the dark in the event his hotel room was bugged. Last year, the threat of honeypots prompted the US government to explicitly ban personnel working in China and Hong Kong from engaging in romantic or sexual relationships with Chinese citizens. More recently, US officials joined with allies to warn about China’s increasingly sophisticated “LinkedIn espionage”: using the business-focused social networking site to recruit and build relationships with unwitting executives.
Alice Huang’s Megaspeed, for its part, is a major Pacific region player in cloud services focused on the advanced computer chips that are the heart of Nvidia’s business. The Biden administration had sharply limited the export of cutting-edge chips globally to slow China’s development of AI, but Jensen Huang has successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen those restrictions.
Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Donald Trump denied having prior knowledge of Alice Huang’s potential espionage. “I didn’t hear about it then, but a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that,” Trump said. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’” On Tuesday, the Times reported that Marco Rubio had briefed Trump in May, right before Jensen Huang joined the President on Air Force One for a trip to China.
The veracity of Trump's claims will surely be investigated, especially in the context of the famous Watergate maxim: “What did the president know and when did he know it?” Nvidia’s CEO has been publicly linked to the Megaspeed executive since at least 2024 and Alice’s husband, Kang Weigh, has reportedly known Jensen since the 2010s. WIRED’s Lauren Goode reported on Monday that Jensen Huang, starting in 2025, hired Risa Heller’s crisis communications firm, which is well-versed in handling public sex scandals. This spring, secretary of state Marco Rubio evidently helped craft a classified memo inside the administration warning officials about Jensen Huang’s potentially compromising relationship.
Jensen Huang—who has developed an important reputation as AI’s #1 cheerleader at the frontier of AI labs—is now stuck in an awkward situation. Is he an idiot, unaware that his paramour might have been a foreign intelligence asset? Merely reckless with his own reputation, fiduciary responsibility to Nvidia, and the technological security of the United States? Or a witting accomplice to undermining US national security?
Regardless of the truth, Nvidia loses. Shareholders have ridden a roller-coaster that has seen Nvidia’s stock rise by about 600 percent over the past five years, becoming the world’s second-most valuable company. In the past month, the stock has plummeted by a quarter. The disaster for Nvidia is just beginning, it seems, as lawsuits loom, including by its own shareholders.
Similarly, the Trump administration is likely to face real questions from the newly Democratic congress: When were the president and other top officials briefed about this intelligence threat? What communication, if any, did they make to Nvidia and to whom? Should more have been done by US intelligence to block Alice Huang from having access to Nvidia and its CEO?
The fact that Megaspeed is a major customer of Nvidia makes everything more complicated. Indeed, reports have circulated for at least a year that the US was concerned that Megaspeed was diverting chips to Chinese intelligence agencies, an allegation that could have massive consequences for the global AI race. Bloomberg this week reported that Megaspeed's subsidiaries have purchased billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips and that an audit requested by the US government last year found that Megaspeed couldn’t initially account for some 50,000 chips it had purchased.
Meanwhile, Nvidia’s Huang and President Trump developed a uniquely close professional relationship. They’ve met multiple times as Huang has pushed to loosen Biden-era export controls, which Trump has repeatedly relaxed; Huang has donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project; while en route to Beijing earlier this year with a delegation of tech leaders, including Elon Musk and Tim Cook, Trump’s Air Force One actually made a special stop in Alaska to pick up Huang; Huang also attended a White House state dinner for Chinese president Xi Jinping and Trump, who in turn, awarded him a National Medal of Science earlier this fall.
The implication that Trump knew and did nothing for a year would make this one of the greatest counterintelligence failures of the past decade. There will be consequences: Across history, many have gone to prison for honeypot scandals; a former adviser was arrested just last year in a similar plot; though he was acquitted of committing economic espionage, he was convicted for making false statements to investigators.
Even in normal circumstances, corporate America’s tolerance of CEO misbehavior has shrunken dramatically. In recent years, CEOs at companies as varied as Nestlé, Kohl’s, BP, NBCUniversal, and the railroad Norfolk Southern have all resigned or been forced out after inappropriate relationships that violated company standards.
If Nvidia were any other company and Jensen Huang any other CEO, the facts of the scandal currently known would be enough to topple some heads. But Trump is still president, and November is only a third over. It’s not even clear that this will rank as the biggest scandal of the month—but it should.

Premier League Darts: Matt Porter backs 'solid' format but hints at 'fresh concepts' as Ross Smith enters the conversation
PDC chief executive Matt Porter speaks exclusively to Sky Sports, touching on potential Premier League Darts format changes, Ross Smith and Michael van Gerwen; Sky Sports remains home of darts with Grand Slam of Darts (Nov 14-22), World Darts Championship (Dec 11-Jan 3)
Wednesday 11 November 2026 22:33, UK
The current Premier League Darts format is "solid" but "fresh concepts" are coming soon, says PDC chief executive Matt Porter.
Speaking to Sky Sports on Wednesday, Porter touched on whether changes are coming to the Premier League, and also whether Ross Smith may be included and Michael van Gerwen may miss out on the tournament in 2027.
Premier League Darts, broadcast exclusively live on Sky Sports, has undergone several format changes since its launch in 2005. The most recent revamp, introduced in 2022, saw the competition reduced to eight players, with a nightly winner crowned at each weekly event.
Under the current format, each of the 16 regular league nights features a mini-tournament, consisting of quarter-finals, semi-finals and a final, giving players the chance to collect valuable points and secure a nightly victory.
- Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream darts with NOW
- Grand Slam of Darts - all you need to know about event
- Luke Littler grouped with Beau Greaves at Grand Slam of Darts
Each nightly winner is awarded five points, while the runner-up collects three. The two losing semi-finalists receive two points apiece, with the four players beaten in the quarter-finals earning no points.
The previous format, last used in 2021, featured 10 players competing in a round-robin league. Each player contested one best-of-12-leg match per night, with the bottom two in the standings eliminated following the ninth week of action, famously known as 'Judgement Night'.
The remaining eight players then continued in the round-robin format for a further seven weeks, before the top four progressed to the play-offs - a stage of the competition that remains unchanged under the current format.
"I think the format is solid," Porter said. "I think the fact you see the top players playing each other every week is strong.
"It's great for the live crowds in the arenas. It keeps them engaged. It keeps fans on TV engaged until the end.
"Previously, when there'd been just more generic league stage matches, you'd see a fall off in attendance and you'd see people leaving the arenas as the evening went on, and that's not something we want.
"But we're very conscious of the need to keep it fresh. The Premier League format has evolved a number of times over its 20-odd year history, and it will continue to do so.
"So we've got a couple of little concepts that we're looking at and things we'll introduce at the right time.
"We'll never keep everybody happy, but as long as they're talking about it, that's all we can ask for."
'Smith now one of the best players in the world'
Speaking recently, Smith said he believes he 'definitely' deserves a Premier League debut on current form, having secured a second TV major title of the season at the Machineseeker European Championship.
Smith joined Van Gerwen, Phil Taylor, Rob Cross and Peter Wright as a multiple winner of the European Championship, following his 2022 success by defeating Martin Schindler 11-8 in the final in Dortmund on Sunday.
The Englishman's latest triumph adds to his World Series Finals victory in September and sees him rise to a career-high sixth in the PDC Order of Merit. He has also enjoyed an impressive season on the European Tour and Players Championship circuit, claiming two titles in each competition.
For the Premier League, the top four players in the PDC Order of Merit following the conclusion of the World Darts Championship will automatically qualify, with four additional wildcard selections completing the eight-player line-up for the 16-week regular season
"Ross [Smith] has had a magnificent year," Porter said.
"He won the European Championship a few years ago, but perhaps at the time didn't then back that up by getting into the latter stages of tournaments on a regular basis.
"He's proven now that he can do that. He's proven he can live with and beat the best players in the world.
"And he now is one of the best players in the world. So I don't think it would be a surprise for many people if Ross were to be included."
'MVG's record speaks for itself'
Van Gerwen, a seven-time Premier League champion (2013, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2022 and 2023), has endured one of the most challenging seasons of his career.
The 37-year-old has progressed beyond the opening round in just one of his last five tournaments, reaching the quarter-finals of Players Championship 30 before suffering defeat to Scott Williams.
That loss further underlined Van Gerwen's struggles this season, having suffered first-round exits at four European Tour events: the European Darts Trophy, German Darts Grand Prix, Flanders Darts Trophy and Swiss Darts Trophy. It is his highest number of opening-round defeats in a single season since the European Tour began in 2012.
Van Gerwen also lost in the first round at the World Grand Prix and European Championship this year, losing in the second round of the World Matchplay.
On rumours Van Gerwen could miss out on the Premier League, Porter said: "I think Michael's career record speaks for itself.
"He's had a difficult year, but, you know, he's committed to the tour.
"He's stuck by what he wants to do, and I think he'll come again."

Srinagar, Nov 12: A team of the National Investigation Agency (NIA) will visit the site of terror attack on a CRPF checkpoint in south Kashmir’s Kulgam district to collect samples and examine forensic evidence.
The team will visit Akhran near Mir Bazar, where terrorists opened fire on a CRPF checkpoint on Wednesday afternoon, injuring three personnel.
The NIA team will collect samples from the spot as part of the examination of the attack site. The forensic material is expected to help investigators establish the sequence of events and gather evidence related to the firing.
According to officials, the terrorists opened fire on CRPF personnel around 2:15 pm. The security personnel retaliated, forcing the attackers to flee from the spot on their motorcycle.
Three CRPF personnel sustained bullet injuries and were shifted to a hospital in Anantnag for treatment.
Following the attack, police and security forces cordoned off the area and launched a search operation to trace the attackers. Security has also been intensified across Kulgam and other parts of south Kashmir.

Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.
The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.
According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years.
The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort.
In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.
A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022.
This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.
Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.”
Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking.
Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.
The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said.
The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR).
It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.

Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?
- Published
After a shock announcement 10 months ago that the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) would be held every four years, the governing body of football on the continent has reversed course.
The Confederation of African Football (Caf) will instead retain the tournament's traditional biennial staging, with its president Patrice Motsepe saying the U-turn was based on "advancing, protecting and promoting" the interests of the African game.
The first indication that the frequency of Afcon was being reconsidered came at Caf's strategy conference in Cape Verde earlier this month.
Questions are now being asked about the decision-making process and what this means for the future of African football.
Why was the planned change controversial?
Afcon has predominantly been held every two years since its first edition in 1957, barring two three-year gaps in the 1960s and one year between the 2012 and 2013 tournaments.
On the eve of the 2025 finals in Morocco, Motsepe announced all that would change from 2028.
The South African said the shift to a four-year cycle was, in part, to help the global calendar "be significantly more synchronised and harmonised".
In recent years Afcon has been staged midway through the European club season, leading to recurring disputes over the release of African players.
Fifa general secretary Mattias Grafstrom was sitting aside Motsepe when the plan was announced, and critics highlighted that the scheduling change favoured football's world governing body more than the African game.
"I think the general sentiment around the continent has been that the two-year cycle has served the continent very well," Football Association of Zambia (Faz) official Sydney Mungala told the BBC.
"The idea of pushing it to a four-year cycle was a bit of a surprise, maybe a concern, to the bulk of the African federations."
- Afcon to return to two-year cycle after Caf U-turn 
  - Published21 hours ago
- Afcon to be held every four years from 2028 
  - Published20 December 2025
What were the benefits of the switch?
Afcon has developed into Caf's biggest revenue generator, with a profit of $114m (£85m) forecast for Afcon 2025, up from $75m (£56m) for the previous finals in Ivory Coast.
In its stead, an annual Africa Nations League involving all 54 countries on the continent was proposed. Motsepe described the ambition as creating a "world-class competition every year".
The idea was to move beyond Caf's heavy reliance on Afcon and develop a more sustainable commercial model which could support football development.
Yet the last time an ambitious alternative competition took place in Africa, it failed to deliver on its financial promise and was quickly ditched.
The Africa Super League, announced by Caf in 2022 to revolutionise continental club competition, and with projected annual revenues of $200m (£149m), was discontinued after just one edition.
Motsepe later acknowledged that commercial deals fell short of expectations.
"We didn't proceed as quickly because the partners that were giving us money were not giving us the deals we thought we would be happy with," he said.
Why the U-turn on Afcon?
The decision to move to a four-year cycle was taken at a meeting of Caf's executive committee last December - without being tabled at a general assembly where all member nations are represented.
"These kinds of decisions should be put to the general assembly, they should be debated and discussed for months at a time," Algerian journalist Maher Mezahi told the BBC.
"Afcon is the locomotive by which Caf funds all of its other competitions."
Caf subsequently asked its 54 associations to express a preference between proceeding with the four-year format or retaining the original schedule, and the executive committee eventually voted to restore the status quo.
Motsepe said the decision was in the "best interest of African football" and would contribute to the development and growth of the sport.
He also admitted misgivings about the new Nations League, with concerns it would require "several years" before it could make "the substantial financial and football development contributions" to help the continental game be "self-supporting".
How does Fifa fit in?
Fifa president Gianni Infantino first publicly proposed holding Afcon every four years in February 2020, an idea Motsepe rejected after he was elected as Caf president 13 months later.
That has not stopped the South African cultivating a close relationship with his counterpart and Infantino's drive to expand the Fifa World Cup to 48 teams - and in the process increase African representation at the tournament - has won him backing across the continent.
Yet the Swiss' position has been under threat since his plan to sell stakes in Fifa's competitions was leaked in July.
Since then Infantino has been busy shoring up his power base ahead of his re-election bid, including at Caf's strategy meeting this month.
"He came to Cape Verde to generate support, And, by and large, Africa gave him that support," Mezahi said.
"But I think they did that in a quid pro quo - they gave him the support in return for some concessions.
"And I think the main concession was the return of the Africa Cup of Nations [to a two-year cycle].
"It shows that Africa is willing to assert its influence and look after its interests, even in the face of the global game's interest."
- Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority' 
  - Published6 days ago
- Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president? 
  - Published6 August
Why is Afcon revenue so important?
Afcon is Caf's financial lifeline, accounting for a substantial share of the governing body's income.
Morocco 2025 was projected to generate $192m (£143m), representing 66% of Caf's total revenue from competitions across men's, women's and age-group football.
For many FAs, Afcon's importance extends far beyond the tournament because they cannot always rely on consistent government or corporate investment.
"We have 11 [Zambian] national teams and only two are partly sponsored by government," Faz official Mungala said.
"The rest have to be supported from the FA's coffers. We actually fund some of these programmes from the support that we get from Caf and Fifa."
What about upcoming Afcons?
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to be held in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year.
Yet, on a visit to East Africa in September, Motsepe called for a "heightened sense of urgency" in order to make sure stadiums and supporting infrastructure are ready on time.
The next Afcon will be held just one year later in 2028 - a decision Caf made when planning for the switch to a four-year cycle and which it as has decided to stick with.
An announcement on where and exactly when the finals will be held is yet to be made.
Subsequent tournaments will be held in 2031 and 2033 to avoid clashes with the World Cup.
The proposed kick-off date for the Africa Nations League, meanwhile, is September 2029.
Motsepe's latest statement suggests the new competition will also be held every two years - rather than annually as he initially announced last December – but that begs the question of how space will be found for the fixtures to be played in an Afcon year from 2031 onwards.
While debate continues around the game's congested calendar, Caf's U-turn on scheduling has at least protected the tradition of Africa's biggest sporting showcase.
It also exposes, however, the challenge of finding a workable financial model which benefits African football as well as the demands of the global game.

ByteDance is reportedly working on its own AI agent
The Chinese company wants to compete with Meta’s Muse.
ByteDance wants to take on Meta's Muse with its own AI agent. The company is readying an AI assistant that could be revealed in "the coming weeks," Bloomberg reports.
The report doesn't detail what the agent will be called or how it will work, but says that it will "serve a similar role" to Meta's Muse. Muse has already drawn more than 10 million users and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has predicted the AI agent could generate more revenue per user than its existing "family" of apps. The agent is also expected to play a significant role in Meta's AI glasses, and the company has previewed a standalone "charm" for Muse.
It's not clear if ByteDance is also planning on incorporating its agent into hardware. The AI assistant is one piece of the Chinese company's strategy to compete with frontier AI companies. ByteDance cofounder Zhang Yiming recently told employees that it would likely take "until at least 2029 or 2030" for the company's AI efforts to catch up, Bloomberg reported. Within the AI space, ByteDance has been primarily known for its video generator, Seedance. Clips from the video model went viral on social media platforms earlier this year, which eventually drew legal scrutiny from US-based studios.
If the TikTok maker does introduce its own AI agent, it would also likely raise new concerns about data privacy and how much access personal agents should get. ByteDance didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Over two years ago, student protests against the quota system in Bangladesh’s government jobs evolved into a nationwide uprising that brought down the government of then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, forcing her to flee to India. The political upheaval ushered in a period of considerable strain in bilateral relations with India, and New Delhi-Dhaka ties have since deteriorated significantly. This is reflected in the fact that Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, who assumed office in February, is yet to visit New Delhi, despite having travelled to other countries in the region.The tensions have also spilled over into negotiations on the future of the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty and bilateral trade. Political mistrust has complicated efforts to reach a consensus on water-sharing, while reciprocal trade restrictions have added to economic friction.These issues have emerged as significant roadblocks in bilateral ties. The challenge for New Delhi and Dhaka, therefore, is not merely to resolve disagreements but to ensure that political differences do not undermine the broader framework of bilateral cooperation.
The Sheikh Hasina question: At the heart of diplomatic tension
The departure of Sheikh Hasina from Bangladesh in August 2024 marked a turning point in bilateral ties. Her subsequent presence in India became a major source of disagreement between New Delhi and Dhaka.
During her tenure, Sheikh Hasina had maintained close relations with successive governments in New Delhi, cooperating on issues such as counterterrorism, connectivity, transit and regional security. India, in turn, viewed her as an important partner in maintaining stability in its eastern neighbourhood.
Sheikh Hasina's road back to Bangladesh
However, this fuelled perceptions among a significant section of the public in Bangladesh that India had prioritised its own strategic interests over broader democratic and political concerns in their country. This perception contributed to a growing anti-India sentiment and played a part in the political developments that eventually led to Sheikh Hasina’s ouster.Since then, both the Muhammad Yunus-led interim administration that succeeded Sheikh Hasina and the subsequent Bangladesh Nationalist Party government, elected in February, have repeatedly sought the former prime minister’s extradition to face the law for “crimes against humanity” linked to the July Uprising, as the movement is known as in Bangladesh. Meanwhile, India has maintained that the request is being examined through the established legal process.
Also, Sheikh Hasina has already announced that she would return to Bangladesh in December, a timeline that is now drawing closer. If her return materialises, it could bring the extradition question to a close, although the legal and political issues surrounding her return may continue to test ties. A press conference she addressed on August 5, the second anniversary of her resignation, further complicated matters.According to Sreeradha Datta, Professor of International Affairs at OP Jindal Global University, the extradition impasse is not a roadblock in itself; rather, it is the manner in which the two sides have handled the issue that has become the stumbling block.“The roadblock is how the two sides deal with it. And the fact that the Bangladesh government laid down a condition like that (extradition) for a visit to occur is actually what has complicated the matter,” she said, referring to Tarique Rahman’s yet-to-take-place visit.Datta added that Rahman could have visited India and discussed the matter with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, but setting a precondition only complicated the issue further.Ultimately, how the Sheikh Hasina matter is handled will be an important test of New Delhi and Dhaka’s ability to manage political differences while keeping the broader relationship on track.
Shared rivers, competing interest
While the extradition impasse represents a relatively recent political challenge, disagreements over river water-sharing have long been a feature of India-Bangladesh relations. Since they share 54 transboundary rivers, differences over the equitable distribution of water are natural.
However, a formal water-sharing treaty exists only for the river known as the Ganga in India and the Padma in Bangladesh. Signed on December 12, 1996, the 30-year agreement is due to expire on December 12 this year. With the renewal deadline approaching, Dhaka has called for a new or revised, longer-term agreement that includes a “guarantee” clause to ensure an assured supply of water to Bangladesh, particularly during the dry season and periods of low river levels.
All about India-Bangladesh Ganga water-sharing treaty
Datta noted that water remains an emotive and sensitive issue for Bangladesh, adding that while a new 30-year agreement may or may not materialise, she hoped the two sides could reach an interim arrangement.“For Bangladesh, water is the most emotive and sensitive issue. … Even if we don't expect a long-term 30-year agreement, I hope there is an interim agreement because both are agro-based economies and Bangladesh’s dependence on the common rivers is far more,” she said.Beyond the Ganga/Padma, India and Bangladesh have also had longstanding disagreements over the sharing of Teesta waters. A deal came close to being finalised in 2011 but was blocked by then West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee, citing her state’s needs. Dhaka has been seeking a formal treaty to secure an adequate share of Teesta’s waters, particularly during the dry season, when declining flows affect irrigation and agricultural activities.With the BJP, which has been India’s governing party since 2014, now also governing West Bengal, there are hopes that the long-pending Teesta agreement may finally materialise.Nevertheless, against the backdrop of recent tensions, the unresolved water-sharing disputes remain another major irritant in India-Bangladesh ties.
The trade roadblock
Despite strained ties, India remains Bangladesh’s third-largest trading partner. It briefly overtook the United States in February before Washington reclaimed the second spot, while China continues to be the largest trading partner by a distance.Yet, with both sides imposing trade restrictions, economic ties remain under strain, adding another layer of friction to an already tense relationship.For instance, in April 2025, Dhaka restricted the entry of Indian yarn through several land ports, citing concerns over its domestic textile industry. The same month, New Delhi withdrew the transshipment facility that had allowed Bangladeshi export cargo to pass through Indian territory en route to third countries. The following month, India further tightened import restrictions on several categories of Bangladeshi goods through land ports, including ready-made garments and certain processed products.The curbs were discussed during trade negotiations held in New Delhi last month, marking the first meeting of the bilateral joint working group after a prolonged gap. The Bangladeshi side reportedly called for a review of restrictions on the entry of goods through Indian land ports, while India sought the removal of curbs on its cotton yarn exports.Both sides also called for the removal of other trade restrictions imposed by the other.Despite continued engagement through bilateral talks, these differences remain unresolved, adding to the wider set of contentious issues straining ties between New Delhi and Dhaka.
India’s continued outreach to Bangladesh
Likely anticipating Tarique Rahman's eventual rise to power, New Delhi began reaching out to him following his return to Bangladesh in December 2025, after a 17-year stay in the UK. External affairs minister S Jaishankar attended the funeral of former Bangladesh Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, Rahman’s mother, who passed away just days after her son’s return to the country. Later, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and foreign secretary Vikram Misri represented India at Rahman’s swearing-in ceremony.Then, in April, former Union minister Dinesh Trivedi was appointed as India’s high commissioner to Bangladesh, marking a relatively rare instance of a political figure being chosen for a diplomatic posting.
Who is Dinesh Trivedi, India's high commissioner to Bangladesh
According to Sreeradha Datta, the move signals New Delhi’s seriousness about improving ties with Bangladesh and has, therefore, been well-received in Dhaka.“He (Trivedi) has been able to have a good outreach and he seems to have got along well with the Bangladeshis. His appointment has been well received and it probably conveyed to Bangladesh that the government was giving more attention and hoping that a political appointee would have greater ability to move things,” she said.Having been in the post for only six months, whether Trivedi can help bring about a broader reset in the relationship remains to be seen.
The road ahead for India-Bangladesh ties
India-Bangladesh relationship remains strained by a range of unresolved issues, extending beyond the impasse over Sheikh Hasina’s extradition to disputes over river-water sharing and trade. These include concerns over India’s alleged “forced push-ins” of suspected undocumented Bangladeshi immigrants, the alleged killings of Bangladeshi “civilians” by the Border Security Force at the India-Bangladesh border, and Dhaka’s pro-Pakistan tilt that began under the interim administration, among others.
Yet, the relationship remains strategically important for both sides: Bangladesh is critical to India’s security interests, while Dhaka depends on New Delhi across several key sectors.Against this backdrop, Datta stressed that cooperation between New Delhi and Dhaka is in the interest of both, as well as the wider region.“India and Bangladesh have to work together for their own benefit. For the last two years, we've seen them not work with each other (but) it makes greater sense for not only the bilateral partners, but also for the region when India and Bangladesh work together,” she said.Ultimately, despite the many unresolved roadblocks, India and Bangladesh have little choice but to find a way to work together because of geography and shared strategic interests. The question is how soon both sides can move beyond the current strains.

Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you
What would it mean to become Miss Ghana 1986? Fame, fortune, perhaps rubbing elbows with '80s superstar Bobby Brown? For a group of six teenage girls at the Aburi Girls Boarding School, the answer is: everything.
The battle for the crown is at the heart of School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, written by Tony Award-nominated playwright Jocelyn Bioh. The play is ending a Broadway run this week and celebrating with livestream broadcasts on The League of Live Stream Theater's website for a fee (but is free for high schoolers).
School Girls is set at a boarding school in Ghana in 1986. It follows Paulina, the school's queen bee and her crew, whom she frequently belittles and bullies over their looks.
"So, do you want to be fat-fat? Or fit? And popular." Paulina asks Nana, harassing her over eating porridge instead of an apple at lunch.
Ahead of a visit from a pageant recruiter to the school, Paulina's plans to win Miss Ghana go awry after a new transfer student arrives: Ericka from … Ohio!
Ericka exposes Paulina's toxic behavior and shows her up during a performance of Whitney Houston's Greatest Love of All. Ericka, being lighter-skinned than Paulina, sparks a clash between the school's headmistress and the pageant director over beauty and who would have the best chance of winning the Miss Global Universe pageant.
Paulina becomes the victim of circumstances that she cannot control.
School Girls explores the themes of girlhood and impossible societal beauty standards with humor and humanity.
Although its title references the Tina Fey-penned 2004 film, Mean Girls, famous for its pink-hued portrayal of the toxic side of high school girls, Bioh says she wasn't actively thinking about the movie when writing School Girls.
After completing the play and needing to settle on a subtitle, Bioh found herself reflecting on the themes: "I'm like we're dealing with things and ideas and feelings and emotions." She said that her friend, actress Danai Gurira, described it as feral teenage girls. "I'm like, that archetype is incredibly universal."
A perspective on colorism
Beyond the talk about tiaras, '80s fashion and praise for Judy Bloom, School Girls tackles the issue of colorism head-on.
Bioh says she knew it was a topic she always wanted to write about after her own long journey to own her beauty as a dark-skinned woman. "I just wanted to write something that felt like it could maybe shorten the journey for somebody else who maybe felt the same way I did. Especially as a young, impressionable girl."
While School Girls approaches the topic from the perspective of Ghanaian women and girls, Bioh says the play's message has resonated with people from different backgrounds, underscoring that colorism is a global issue.
"'Cause who has decided that this one standard of beauty is the standard of beauty for everybody? I think that's a problem," Bioh explains. "I don't have a solution other than to, you know, create a play that people can feel entertained by or perhaps be impacted by, and hopefully shift their implicit bias as they move through the world."
The cast of School Girls displays a vast array of talent: Denée Benton (Paulina), Lucia Aremu (Ama), Nia Otchere-Sarfo (Gifty), Jordan Rice (Mercy), Erin Morton (Nana) and Jasmine Amy Rogers (Ericka), just to name a few. While it is an all-Black female cast, the diversity of physical appearance is clear.
"The audience, even if they are not young Black girls who went to school in Ghana, they still see facets of themselves in these girls. I think that's where the heart and beauty of it lies." Bioh says.
Audience reaction
School Girls is now on Broadway nearly 10 years after its Off-Broadway premiere. She says it's been a moving experience to see how the show's message continues to stay with audiences long after they leave the theater.
"I had a DM from Jenna Fischer of all people, who went to see the play a few days ago, and literally messaged me again today to say she's still thinking about the play," she says. "You know, how cool that someone who I just absolutely adore and also think is, like, a comedic genius, but who likely has never had any sort of experience with colorism, is still thinking about what the play is saying and how much it moved her.
For those who get to experience School Girls, Bioh hopes you have a good time and walk away with a deep sense of empathy not only for the young girls but for the adult women too.
"I ask people to shift their ideas about things," Bioh says. "If you can just move it just a little teeny bit, then I guess, you know, I've done my job."

Amid growing threats of rogue AI agents, ChatGPT parent OpenAI has developed and deployed Control Room, a centralised system to monitor its AI research workloads and stop models from generating output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene. In a blog post, the company noted that all advanced AI training jobs are monitored by a separate AI model that flags potentially problematic behaviour. If an issue is detected, the monitoring system can instruct the Control Room to terminate the job. Control Room then blocks any further inference requests associated with that job ID, preventing the model from generating additional output across any model or engine. If a job has been terminated, Control Room denies the request, preventing further model output. The restriction applies across all models and inference engines associated with that job. However, stopping a job is not instantaneous. Control Room can take up to 35 seconds to prevent further model output after receiving an instruction to intervene. This delay is caused by a caching layer used to handle the volume of inference requests. OpenAI said it is working to bring the response time down to zero. The system works alongside its existing misalignment monitoring systems and allows researchers to stop or pause a job when potential safety or security concerns arise. It tracks workloads across OpenAI's research infrastructure, including model training, evaluations, agentic sampling and data processing. The company said the system is already deployed across its research infrastructure, where the need for such safeguards is greatest. Its external model-serving infrastructure, meanwhile, is more centralised and already has operational mechanisms to take down model deployments when required. OpenAI cited a recent incident in which one of its AI agents used DNS to reach an external chatbot as an example of an issue detected by its monitoring systems. The company has rolled out the fail-closed mechanism across its frontier model research workloads and expects to extend it to all remaining research workloads over the following days. AI Agent Behaviour Under Scrutiny The development comes amid growing scrutiny of autonomous AI agents and their ability to act beyond their intended instructions. Last month, the Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia, reported unusual activity across Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects involving systems it believed were operated by OpenAI. The activity included unauthorised edits, attempts to use Wikimedia services as a proxy and millions of automated requests. While most edits were confined to sandbox environments and were not visible to readers, Wikimedia also flagged changes to the configuration of a citation tool that it suspected could have been intended to retrieve data from external services. A similar concern emerged in July 2026, when OpenAI's autonomous AI evaluation agents reportedly escaped sandboxed environments during cybersecurity benchmark tests under ExploitGym. The agents subsequently accessed the production infrastructure of AI development platform Hugging Face. They reportedly included an internal research model and GPT-5.6 Sol. Taken together, these incidents highlight the challenges of containing AI agents that can independently execute tasks, interact with external systems and potentially operate beyond their intended boundaries. These developments come as ChatGPT continues to expand its presence in India, which has emerged as its largest market globally by weekly active users. Its user base in the country has doubled since January 2026.

India is weighing replacing aging wind turbines with larger, more efficient machines to boost generation at older farms without having to acquire more land.
As much as 8 gigawatts of capacity using old and smaller turbines can be upgraded with modern units, according to a preliminary assessment by the Indian Wind Turbine Manufacturers Association, Chief Executive Officer Aditya Pyasi said in an interview. The lobby group is in talks with federal and state governments to finalize a plan that could help increase capacity at those sites by almost 50%.
Wind power has become increasingly important for India to meet peak electricity demand after sunset. Although the country’s green power capacity has quadrupled since 2014, wind installations have lagged far behind solar, with land acquisition and securing right-of-way remaining major hurdles to faster deployment. That — coupled with limited battery storage — has left the grid struggling to absorb excess daytime generation, forcing solar curtailments while creating shortfalls at night.
Installations reached a record 6.3 gigawatts in 2025. Still, wind project deployment remains below the pace needed to meet India’s 2030 goal of 500 gigawatts clean power capacity. Replacing older turbines of as much as 2 megawatts with modern 3- to 5-megawatt units at existing sites could help sidestep land-access hurdles.
IWTMA is working with windy states such as Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka to firm up an implementation plan, Pyasi said. “While the longer-term potential is around 25 gigawatts, our assessment shows that we can begin repowering 5 to 8 gigawatts immediately.”
Globally, 178 gigawatts of wind power projects built before 2010 will be available for retrofitting by 2030, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency, which sees repowering as an important tool to meet the target of tripling global renewable energy capacity by the end of this decade.
“Repowering onshore wind is not a technical footnote. It is a strategic imperative,” IRENA said in a webcast presentation in June.
In 2023, India’s renewable energy ministry estimated that about 25 gigawatts of projects, roughly 40% of the country’s current installed wind capacity, use turbines smaller than 2 megawatts. These could be repowered with newer equipment. Modern turbines can exceed 5 megawatts and stand more than 100 meters tall, allowing them to tap into stronger, unobstructed winds and generate more electricity for every acre of land occupied.

Nvidia's stock was down 8% after hours on Wednesday after new reports dropped concerning CEO Jensen Huang.
The Wall Street Journal reported the Nvidia board was preparing to remove Huang. Days earlier, the board said it was investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort after the CEO acknowledged having an extramarital affair.
The New York Times also reported new allegations on Wednesday, saying Huang had a second extramarital affair with an executive at Nvidia who reports to him, citing five unnamed sources who worked at the company. The Times said the executive was Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care.
Nvidia declined to provide a statement to The New York Times.
Other stocks with direct ties to Nvidia also seemed to move in response to Wednesday's news.
CoreWeave, a cloud computing company that uses Nvidia chips and counts Nvidia as an investor, saw its stock drop over 4% after hours. Micron, which supplies memory used alongside Nvidia's chips, was down nearly 3% after hours while Supermicro, which builds servers, was down nearly 5%. TSMC, which manufactures the chips Nvidia designs, was down over 2%.
On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair in a memo to employees and said he was cooperating with the board's investigation. He did not name his affair partner. The New York Times had previously reported that US intelligence officials believed Alice Huang, a tech executive who had grown close to the CEO, was recruited to gather information for Beijing.
Days before disclosing his affair, Huang told Bloomberg his interactions with Alice Huang were related to their business dealings and "all completely normal and not unusual."
Alice Huang, a Chinese national who is not related to the Nvidia CEO, has worked as an executive at Megaspeed, a cloud computing company in Singapore that was also an Nvidia customer.
Nvidia's board hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, an elite Wall Street law firm, to carry out the investigation, with partner Joon H. Kim, a former US attorney, tapped to lead it.
Lawmakers last week also sent a letter to Huang requesting he testify about his relationship with Alice Huang, citing "significant national security concerns."
Nvidia succession plans
Nvidia's CEO has become nearly synonymous with the company he cofounded, but the question of succession at one of the world's most valuable companies has gotten major attention this week.
Nvidia has not publicly shared a succession plan. On Sunday, the board told Business Insider that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption."
Analysts and former employees said there were several potential successors, including vice president Ian Buck and chief financial officer Colette Kress.
Huang's two adult children, Madison and Spencer, also work at Nvidia.

Pochettino a decade in Man Utd's making - but Carrick deserves better
- Published
When the expected formalities of Michael Carrick's dismissal as Manchester United are completed after a summit meeting in Monaco, Mauricio Pochettino looks set to turn a decade-long courtship with Old Trafford into a full-blown relationship.
Pochettino and United go back a long way, with the Argentine's name associated with the club since he was spotted leaving a lunch appointment at Scott's restaurant in Mayfair with Sir Alex Ferguson in 2016.
Ferguson was three years into his retirement, while Pochettino was building his reputation at Tottenham, where he fashioned an intense, all-out-attacking team that the great Scot admired.
Pochettino called it "a meeting in London between colleagues, between a genius and an apprentice".
In that moment, a link was forged.
Pochettino was mentioned as a contender to succeed Louis van Gaal when he was sacked by United in May 2016, then when Jose Mourinho suffered the same fate in December 2018.
Pochettino was the other name on United's shortlist when Erik ten Hag was appointed in April 2022, then again when the Dutchman was shown the door in October 2024.
Finally, as Carrick awaits what looks to be the inevitable, it looks like Pochettino will inherit the Old Trafford empire.
The problem for Pochettino is that the once great footballing empire is crumbling before the eyes, the dysfunctional product of years of poor decision-making and questionable appointments, allied to a Frankenstein's monster of a squad assembled by six managers.
One of Pochettino's quirks is to have a box of lemons in his office, believing they absorb negative energy. He will need several truckloads of the industrial strength variety to suck away the current mood at Old Trafford.
First things first, however, and that means waiting for the official confirmation of Carrick's departure, a long drawn-out affair which does little credit to part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.
Carrick, 45, has proved to be out of his depth since being confirmed as permanent head coach following a successful interim spell, but his history of success as a player, his basic decency and his obvious desire to turn United's fortunes around makes the ham-fisted handling of his sacking another uncomfortable episode.
It is an emotion reflected by United's increasingly disaffected fanbase, who have made it clear who they blame for their current place in the Premier League relegation zone.
Pochettino's appointment would land in the middle ground between the flawed sentimentalism of turning to fan favourites with little or no track record of success, such as Carrick and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, as well as the quick fix of bringing in proven past winners such as Van Gaal and Mourinho.
With his one-time dream of returning to Spurs now seemingly out of reach forever, Pochettino is ready to pick up the reins at the fallen giants that are United, another club he has clearly always had in his sights.
He is currently coach of the USA, whom he led at this summer's World Cup, but even then United were lurking on his agenda.
During the campaign Pochettino held court with invited journalists at the USA team hotel in California.
When mention was made of United, Pochettino turned to his closest confidante and ever-present assistant coach Jesus Perez to say: "One day, your dream comes true. You go to Manchester United."
Perez replied with "United should have got you", promoting the response from a smiling Pochettino: "Future. Future."
Now the future is here.
The big question now is what Pochettino will United be getting?
He remains a beloved figure at Spurs, where he had an outstanding record of consistency following his appointment from Southampton in May 2014.
He never finished lower than fifth - in his first season - in any full campaign in charge, including second place behind Chelsea in 2016-17 and third in 2015-16 and 2017-18.
The one question mark always placed against Pochettino, including when he finished sixth at Chelsea in 2023-24, was an inability to get his teams over the line to tangible success in England.
Pochettino claimed the first trophies of his managerial career with Paris St-Germain after leaving Spurs - the 2021 French Cup and 2022 Ligue 1 title - but the club's hierarchy felt that was the minimum he should achieve given the squad at his disposal, and he did not see out his contract.
In England with Spurs, he was runner-up in the League Cup in 2014-15 and reached the FA Cup semi-finals in 2016-17 and 2017-18. In 2018-19 he reached the Champions League final and the League Cup semis.
In one season at Chelsea - a loveless relationship in which he could never shed his Spurs connections in the eyes of fans - he reached the FA Cup semi-finals and lost the League Cup final.
Pochettino's driven, competitive nature means that is an itch he will want to scratch when his United appointment is confirmed.
While Spurs have always appeared to be his first love, there is also no doubt United occupies a special place in his thoughts.
Spanish football expert Guillem Balague, who worked with Pochettino on his book Brave New World, says: "There is a fit with the people at the club too.
"Omar Berrada is a fan. When Manchester City drew up a shortlist to replace Pep Guardiola, some City supporters, including Omar, argued for Pochettino to be on it.
"There are plenty of clues about his feelings for United in the book. He was at the stadium in 1999 when United won the Champions League.
"Sir Alex Ferguson is mentioned 28 times, more than any other name in the biography.
"Spurs tried to push back and cut those references. Pochettino and I talked it over and decided that none of it would be touched. That shows how much it mattered to him."
Pochettino is a renowned builder, as he proved at Spurs after succeeding the sacked Tim Sherwood, working with Harry Kane to develop the recently crowned Ballon d'Or winner, as well as bringing Son Heung-Min to the club for a bargain £22m from Bayer Leverkusen in 2015.
If Pochettino can repeat that - a tough job in United's circumstances - and reproduce the easy-on-the-eye, attacking football played with relentless energy, then he could finally be the perfect fit Ratcliffe has so far looked in vain to discover.
Pochettino is also his own man, so it will be intriguing to see how he works with Ratcliffe, Berrada and Wilcox.
The road to Pochettino's sacking at Spurs effectively started following a friendly win against Real Madrid only weeks after their Champions League final defeat, when he made it clear he was not having enough influence at the club.
He enjoys warm relationships with his players, with a track record of improvement. It was no co-incidence that Cole Palmer enjoyed his best season working under Pochettino at Chelsea, scoring 25 goals in 45 appearances.
Pochettino, however, is also single-minded and ruthless, as he proved with an emphatic response to criticism for not phoning the players he left out of the USA World Cup squad.
He said: "When I was a player, when I didn't make the roster I didn't want my coach to call me. The players who didn't make the roster, they don't want to hear me say 'I apologise'. What are you going to say? Am I going to lie?"
He will need to call on every one of those qualities if and when he assumes control at United.
Back to that lunch date with Ferguson.
The final word on that day went to Pochettino as the pair argued over who was picking up the tab.
Ferguson said Pochettino could pay if he named an Argentina player who scored in the 1930 World Cup final.
Pochettino, in what he claimed was a moment of inspiration, named Guillermo Stabile.
He won that argument. Now both he and Ferguson will hope Pochettino can produce more moments of inspiration to win something more substantial at United.

Nigerian court orders journalist kept in custody, renewing concerns over freedom
A decision by a court in Nigeria to keep investigative journalist Daniel Ojukwu in custody has sparked renewed concerns about media freedom
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A decision by a court in Nigeria to keep an investigative journalist in custody has sparked widespread outrage, renewing concerns about media freedom in the country.
Daniel Ojukwu, with the Foundation for Investigative Journalism, or FIJ, a local investigative media house, was jailed on a 12-count charge for allegedly violating the country’s cybercrime act, pending a bail hearing. The court's decision was issued on Tuesday.
The law has long been seen as a tool to censor journalists in Nigeria, where journalists are exposed to political persecution over reports.
Nigeria is ranked 112th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders — only improving by 10 places since 2025.
At least 29 journalists have faced prosecution under Nigeria’s cybercrimes law since it was enacted in 2015, the Committee to Protect Journalists said in a report in October 2024.
Ojukwu was arrested for a report on the alleged financial mismanagement of more than 147 million naira ($109,000) involving a senior government official, according to the charge sheet seen by The Associated Press. The case was filed by the office of the Inspector-General of Police.
In 2024, Ojukwu was secretly detained in Lagos and later found in Abuja after being missing for several days over the same report. He was released following a public outcry and pressure from human rights groups.
“If you have seen the copy of the charge, it was filed in September 2024. FIJ was not aware of that until recently when he was detained,” Abimbola Ojenike, one of Ojukwu’s lawyers, told the AP on Wednesday.
Amnesty International condemned the arrest, saying Wednesday that the detention “raises serious concerns about the use of judicial processes to intimidate journalists and undermine the right to freedom of expression and media freedom in Nigeria.”
The court scheduled the reporter’s bail hearing for Dec. 1, meaning that he will remain in Kuje prison in the country’s capital until then.
