No one's home tonight, but the sensor on your home office window upstairs alerts your phone: “motion detected.” Maybe it's just your cat or a flicker of a passing car’s headlights. Instead of shrugging it off, you ask Alexa to send your Ring Drone Cam to check it out.
The tiny, 165-gram drone lifts out of its charging dock, buzzing loudly, and autonomously flies upstairs, giving you a first-person view on your phone’s screen as it scans the room. Since it's dark in the house, the Drone's spotlights kick in, making it look like someone's physically in the home and moving around—a potential deterrent to would-be thieves. All clear? It heads back to its base to recharge.
That's the peace of mind Ring wants to offer with its latest home security solution, which it announced today for $250, alongside the Ring Rover Cam, a $1,000 roving security robot designed to help businesses monitor warehouses and factories. Both fall under the company's new Ring Robotics brand. The Rover Cam launches first on December 16, followed by the Drone Cam on January 27.
This isn't the company's first at-home drone camera. CEO and founder Jamie Siminoff says he had the idea for a flying sentry in 2016 before Amazon bought Ring. The company previously announced an indoor security drone in 2020—the Ring Always Home Cam—and nearly launched it last year. But Siminoff says the team kept running into edge cases that forced them to add more sensors. Those additions required more computing resources and made the drone more power- and battery-hungry, which made it harder to fly. The solution? Move the intelligence off the vehicle and into the cloud.
The Drone Cam has enough smarts to land if it loses internet connectivity, but the rest of its intelligence now sits entirely in the cloud; the drone sends video straight to Ring’s servers, where a custom AI Pilot agent tells it where to go. That lets the drone be lightweight and nimble.
It will avoid people and objects, and if you accidentally stick a finger into the propellers, Siminoff says, you will feel it, but “you'll be fine.” If your cat manages to swat it out of the air, however, that's a different story. A Ring spokesperson tells WIRED customers shouldn't “fly it” if it's damaged and should contact support for help (no word on repairability). The Drone Cam runs a motor health check before take-off every time and won't fly if it detects a problem.
Users can't manually control the drone but can also set up custom flight routes and patrol schedules. It can automatically respond to alerts from security sensors you may have set up in the home, like motion, door, or window sensors. It will not leave your home, as it needs a Wi-Fi network to operate and uses the Alexa Home Map you may have created with existing Echo devices to help it navigate. It can fly five to eight minutes per charge. (The final production model will be black, not white like in the photos.)
“There are times when you do want to just be able to see everywhere around the home, but you don't necessarily want a [fixed] camera," Siminoff says. “That's why we invented Ring Robotics.”
Because it doesn't work outdoors and since it's well below the 250-gram threshold, the Drone Cam doesn't need to be registered with the Federal Aviation Administration. Drones have also struggled in the US after the Federal Communications Commission banned DJI from importing foreign-made drones without certification. But Siminoff says the Drone Cam complies with all US regulations and is assembled in Texas.
But what if a bad actor gets access to the Drone Cam? Siminoff points to the company's TAKE technology, or Throw Away the Key Encryption. It encrypts video in transit and rotates keys every few minutes, but Ring temporarily holds the key to run cloud-based AI features before deleting its copy. That brief server-side access window makes it less foolproof than true end-to-end encryption. (Every Ring account requires two-factor authentication to log in.)
Hackers have also invaded smart home devices and peeked through robot vacuum cameras, baby monitors, and other gadgets, so it's not hard to imagine a similar situation with the Drone Cam. To counter the threat of surreptitious surveillance, Siminoff says, the Drone Cam is loud by design—the extremely loud buzz of its propellers means a bad actor couldn't remotely snoop without tipping off people in the home.
Concerns don't just stem from third parties trying to access your devices, though. Amazon's Ring has been accused of normalizing suburban surveillance, partly stemming from the company's cozy relationship with law enforcement, and it has even handed Ring videos to cops without warrants.
Thorin Klosowski, a senior security and privacy activist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, says a device like the Drone Cam is a personal choice and that people should “think through” how it will make others in the home—or visitors—feel.
“I think the companies who make these sorts of surveillance products are invested in us feeling less safe at home,” Klosowski says. “If there is a way to sell a product that helps alleviate the problem they are creating, I think they will do it.”
Ring Robotics' second robot is designed for businesses, not consumers. The Ring Rover Cam might look familiar—it shares many of the same hardware guts as Amazon's Astro, the short-lived home robot that didn't do much. Amazon had even pivoted it as a $2,350 security robot for businesses before eventually bricking them 10 months after launch.
Siminoff says the robot was great, but the software needed polishing, and people largely wanted to use Astro for security—that's why the Rover Cam ditches the cute face seen on the previous bot. It has the same AI Pilot as the Drone Cam, which helps it navigate through spaces and avoid obstacles. A telescoping 4K camera pops up to monitor its surroundings, and the Rover beams a light circle to the ceiling so you can always glance up to see where the short bot is on the factory floor.
It responds to sensor alerts, can automatically check an area, features two-way talk, and has a built-in siren. It covers up to 5,000 square feet and returns to its charging dock after its patrol ends. (It can do about 30 minutes). It's significantly cheaper than Astro was, but buyers still face the lingering risk that Amazon could pull the plug if Ring Robotics doesn't pan out.

French Open champion Mirra Andreeva stormed past Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 6-0 to reach the last four of the WTA Finals on Wednesday as Elina Svitolina kept her bid on track with a three-set win over Karolina Muchova.
Russian 19-year-old Andreeva held her nerve after falling behind 4-1 in the opening set -- winning the last 11 games to seal the round-robin victory in just 62 minutes.
“Oh my God, I’m even happier than I was after my first match,” Andreeva said. “I feel like I can play another two matches, I’m so full of energy. I’m so pumped up. I’m so happy.”
Andreeva, whose three titles this year include her maiden major at Roland Garros, is making her singles debut in the elite season-ending event.
The world number three seemed to be feeling the nerves in the early going against second-ranked Sabalenka.
Irked that she had given up a break with a double fault, she was able to flip the switch, dealing handily with Sabalenka’s big serves and pushing the Belarusian star back with her own big groundstrokes.
Andreeva crucially kept momentum on her side with a break for a 3-0 lead in the second set.
Sabalenka, trailing 0-40, saved three break points, but Andreeva gave herself another with a swinging volley winner and grabbed another break when a Sabalenka forehand flew just long.
The increasingly demoralised Sabalenka had no answer. After the Belarusian smacked a backhand into the net to give her opponent match point Andreeva polished things off with a service winner.
It was another disappointing performance for the 28-year-old Sabalenka, whose three wins this season include prestigious back-to-back victories at Indian Wells and Miami but no Grand Slams.
“She definitely played great tennis,” Sabalenka told reporters. “The good thing is that I still have a chance to qualify. The bad thing, that I’ll need some time to recover after I don’t even know how many games in a row I lost.”
Making her sixth straight Finals appearance, Sabalenka can still advance if she beats Svitolina in their final round-robin match on Friday.
Svitolina roared back from a set down to beat Muchova 3-6, 6-2, 6-2.
Ukrainian veteran Svitolina lifted the WTA Finals trophy in 2018 but hadn’t been back to the elite season-ending event since 2019.
She got off to a rocky start against Muchova, who broke Svitolina three times in the opening set.
Trailing 2-1 on serve in the second Svitolina found her range, winning five straight games to force a third set.
“I was not happy with the first set,” Svitolina said. “I didn’t play as well. I just made some adjustments, tactical adjustments.
“I think it helped me also to be more aggressive, because I was too passive in the first set,” Svitolina said.
Muchova’s second round-robin defeat coupled with Andreeva’s victory means the Czech was eliminated from semifinal contention.

China and ASEAN make progress on South China Sea pact but can't finish talks this year
Regional diplomats say China and Southeast Asian countries have made progress on a South China Sea pact but won’t be able to conclude negotiations this year as agreed
MANILA, Philippines -- China and Southeast Asian countries have made progress on a South China Sea pact but won't be able to conclude decades of negotiations this year as agreed, three regional diplomats said Wednesday.
China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations began negotiating the so-called “code of conduct” in 2005 to prevent occasional confrontations in the disputed waters from turning into a major conflict that could threaten Asia’s economies. The accord mainly calls for self-restraint and discourages aggressive acts that could spark clashes in the waterway that is a key global trade route.
After years of closed-door negotiations, which at times were delayed due to tense clashes in the contested waters, China and ASEAN agreed in 2023 to speed up the negotiations and conclude the talks by this year.
Three senior Southeast Asian diplomats with direct knowledge of the negotiations told The Associated Press that after the final round of this year's talks last month, China and the ASEAN have provisionally agreed on about 80% of all the paragraphs that will be included in the agreement.
The last major sticking points are the geographic scope to be covered by the agreement, the definition of sensitive terms and whether the accord should be legally binding or not, according to the three diplomats. They spoke on condition of anonymity and without elaborating because they were not authorized to discuss the issues in public.
Negotiations will have to continue next year, when ASEAN's leadership rotates to Singapore. The Philippines, which led the bloc this year, initiated more meetings, at least once a month, which effectively provided more time for negotiators to try to resolve issues, the diplomats said.
China and Malaysia, which currently oversees ASEAN's overall relations with Beijing, jointly led at least 10 major rounds of negotiations this year.
The status of the negotiations on the proposed agreement, as well as continuing incidents in the South China Sea, will be high in the agenda when ASEAN leaders hold an annual summit in Manila starting this weekend. They will engage with leaders of Asian and Western nations, including the United States and China, after their meeting.
China and four of ASEAN’s member states — Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam — along with Taiwan have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which is also believed to be sitting atop undersea deposits of oil and gas.
Confrontations have escalated particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals in recent years. A 1988 clash with Chinese forces over a disputed reef killed dozens of Vietnamese military personnel in some of the deadliest fighting known so far in the South China Sea.
Julio Amador III, a Manila-based geopolitical analyst, said the proposed code of conduct may not be able to totally deter aggression in the disputed waters, but if it’s combined with other actions, including foreign diplomacy and a strengthened military capability, it can make would-be aggressors think twice.
“Restraining great powers takes a lot of effort,” Amador said in reference to China. “We cannot be a one-trick pony as a country. You need to have all the tools, whether it’s a code of conduct, whether you bring a case against China or whether you increase your military spending.”
The contested territory has long been feared as an Asian flashpoint and has become a sensitive front in the U.S.-China rivalry in the region.
Washington has repeatedly warned that it’s obligated to defend the Philippines, its oldest treaty ally in Asia, if Filipino forces come under an armed attack, including in the South China Sea. China, however, has warned the U.S. to stay away from what it calls a purely Asian dispute.

El Salvador's Bukele makes a political gamble with a Haiti gang offensive ahead of an election
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele has sought to present himself as the savior to Haiti’s gang crisis
MEXICO CITY -- Salvadoran troops bombard a gangster’s home from helicopters over the Haitian countryside. Civilians cheer on marching camouflage-clad soldiers. Armored cars drive through the Caribbean nation’s gang-ravaged streets.
The videos flood the social media of Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, Salvadoran officials and an army of pro-government influencers with a simple message in a mix of Haitian Creole, English and Spanish: “We will help you take back your country ... Finally, Haiti will be free.”
It's part of Bukele's push to present himself as the savior to Haiti’s gang crisis.
By doing so, experts say the communications specialist-turned-president seeks to defuse mounting international scrutiny over his troops' deployment and drum up political support in his own country ahead of February elections.
But they say the offensive in Haiti is a high-stakes gamble that could both isolate allies like the Trump administration and dent popular support in his own country.
“It’s an electoral campaign to promote Nayib Bukele and portray him as if he’s a superhero. They're selling an Avengers movie,” said Salvadoran political communications strategist Roberto Dubon. “He's using Haiti as a testing ground to implement his policies on an international level.”
El Salvador ’s military offensive in Haiti began in mid-October, when four Salvadoran aviation technicians working with a U.N.-backed mission went missing in a gang attack. Since then, the government has sent 2,500 soldiers to the Caribbean country with little transparency or oversight.
The disappearances posed a challenge for Bukele, who gained international fame with a political narrative centered on beating back El Salvador’s gangs with a heavy hand.
As international scrutiny has mounted over the operation and a gang leader said that the four technicians are dead, the president’s narrative has shifted from rescuing the Salvadorans to eradicating Haiti’s gangs.
“We kept our promise,” Bukele posted on Tuesday, sharing a video of Salvadoran forces bombing a gang leader’s house after previously asking for the coordinates on X. “Most of them ran away without even trying to fight. What cowards!”
The tongue-in-cheek tone and images of soldiers mirror cinematic videos the government produces in its own country to craft a careful narrative around Bukele's gang crackdown, which has fueled accusations of mass human rights abuses.
In Haiti, just like in El Salvador, throngs of pro-government influencers quickly latched onto and magnified that message, said Dubon.
Meanwhile, Bukele gears up for February presidential elections, which he is all but guaranteed to win with fierce support for his crackdown on gangs. Polling puts approval for the president well over 90%.
Democratic concerns hang over the vote after the legislature controlled by Bukele’s party moved up elections from 2029 to 2027 and eliminated presidential term limits in the constitution — paving the way for the populist to stay in power indefinitely.
In the face of democratic criticisms, a lagging economy and Salvadorans normalizing newfound freedoms after years of not living in constant fear of the gangs, the Haiti offensive offers Bukele a tool to remind Salvadorans of his security wins ahead of the vote, said Luis Enrique Amaya, a Salvadoran security consultant.
“He has to construct this narrative of success (in Haiti) to strengthen his image as president,” Amaya said. “Bukele won’t allow even a centimeter of his popularity and legitimacy to be lost. Not even a millimeter, not a single vote.”
Bukele has toyed with the idea of taking his contentious anti-crime campaign abroad for years, but his current offensive is increasingly seen as a risky bet.
On Monday, the rights group Amnesty International called on El Salvador and Haiti's governments to publicly disclose the agreement allowing forces into Haiti, and to “comply with international human rights law." It warned of operations potentially exacerbating violence and affecting civilians.
The same day, Bukele ally U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio distanced himself from the Salvadoran offensive when speaking to press, saying the U.S. was “not actively involved.” He threw his support behind the U.N.-backed gang suppression force, of which El Salvador doesn't form part.
“There is no plan B,” Rubio said.
Security experts like Diego Da Rin, Haiti analyst for International Crisis Group, have cast doubt on Bukele's ability to replicate his model to vanquish Haiti's gangs.
Bukele debilitated El Salvador's two powerful gangs by suspending key constitutional rights and detaining more than 1% of the small Central American nation's population. The Salvadoran investigative news organization El Faro, whose staff has since been exiled from the country, also reported that Bukele had negotiated with those gangs.
Haiti's gang warfare is far more convoluted. Roughly two dozen well-known gangs operate in Port-au-Prince and dozens more have launched deadly attacks outside the capital. They have spent years leeching off political turmoil and overwhelmed police forces to make power grabs and sow terror.
They wield weapons smuggled mainly from the U.S. and are far more well-armed than Salvadoran gangs once were. They are deeply entwined with some of the country’s political elite, making it nearly impossible for Bukele to replicate his war on gangs.
That will either push Salvadoran troops into an extended conflict or, more likely, push Bukele to make quick shows of force to project victory before retiring troops, said Tiziano Breda, an analyst with Armed Conflict Location & Event Data.
Breda warned that costs incurred by the foreign offensive — Bukele's government has said it's footing the bill — could fester resentment in El Salvador, where one in four people still live in poverty.
Da Rin said that Salvadoran troops could pressure Haitian police and international forces to better organize and more effectively push back the gangs, something they have failed to do for years. But he warned it could also push rival gangs to unite and form coalitions, as has happened in the past.
Similar to El Salvador's own war on gangs, that could have a human toll, he warned, especially if Salvadoran troops don't operate under strict rules like the U.N.-backed force.
“The Salvadoran troops' eagerness to secure quick, symbolic victories entails huge risks for civilians who can be caught in the crossfire,” Da Rin said.

Missing 11-month-old baby rescued after being buried alive in a crate in South Carolina
- Published
An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.
Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.
The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.
The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.
Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.
The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.
Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah.
Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said.
He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.
Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard".
"The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.
He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot.
"The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained.
Of the parents' relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show.
Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems.
"Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

A US-based robotics startup has invited job applicants for an unusual night shift: staying awake throughout the night to supervise humanoid robots. The California-headquartered Figure AI is paying a whopping ₹4,217 per hour (up to $45) for the role, according to a Business Insider report. The job role requires candidates to manage operations, check for technical issues, and ensure workplace safety. According to the company's job advertisement, the position of night-shift coordinator in Santa Clara is being offered on a contract-to-hire basis. The working hours are 10:30 pm to 7 am, and the selected candidate will work five days a week, including one weekend shift. Responsibilities include coordinating robot operators, assigning duties to humanoid robots, monitoring the performance of these machines, and rectifying any technical problems they encounter. This position requires quite a bit of physical effort from the incumbent. The prospective employee must be capable of standing for more than eight hours while handling equipment or robotic hardware weighing about 50 pounds (or about 23 kg). Candidates must have prior leadership experience, some basic knowledge of robotics/mechanics, and the ability to make sound judgements in cases where engineering support is lacking. Highlighting the level of accountability attached to the position, the company's job advertisement states: “You'll be the one making the calls.” The recruitment drive comes amid growing investor interest in humanoid robots and physical artificial intelligence (AI). According to Business Insider, citing PitchBook data, companies operating in robotics and physical AI attracted $33.4 billion in global investments during the first six months of 2026. The figure is already higher than the $28.7 billion raised by the sector throughout 2025. Meanwhile, Figure AI's competitor Agility Robotics began trading on the Nasdaq on November 5 after completing a merger with a special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC). Figure AI was founded in 2022. In September 2025, Figure AI reached a valuation of $39 billion after raising over $1 billion in a Series C funding round led by Parkway Venture Capital. Figure AI is working to introduce robots into several industries, such as manufacturing, logistics, warehousing and retail. Its technology is especially aimed at sectors that struggle with workforce shortages. Figure AI's long-term ambition goes beyond robots that help workers. According to the company's website, Figure AI sees a future in which humanoid machines can work with very little human involvement. "Over time, humans could leave the loop altogether as robots become capable of building other robots," the company states. Until that vision becomes reality, however, human workers will continue to play an important role in ensuring that these machines remain functional, even during the night. England make massive step up in Australia victory
- Published
In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on an impressive 45-22 win for Steve Borthwick's side against Australia in the Nations Championship on Sunday.
Beating Australia with their record points tally against the Wallabies was a very positive way for England to start the autumn series, given the break they have had and how the beginning of the year went.
England were very accurate, very disciplined, creative and genuinely did not give Australia a sniff.
Before the game, I was expecting Australia to provide much more of a stern test. Some people might be a bit too critical of Australia, saying they did not turn up, but I think it edges more towards how well England played than how average Australia were.
I am not saying by any stretch that it was the perfect performance but, all in all, it was a massive step up from the Six Nations and even from the Nations Championship games in the summer.
Intensity, accuracy and discipline in abundance
A couple of days before the Australia game, Jamie George said the England team had been galvanised by a newspaper article which claimed the end of their summer tour had been marked by player unrest over head coach Borthwick's leadership.
When you are inside those international camps, you are very deliberate in staying tight and not letting anybody in in whatever way, shape or form, therefore you become very sensitive to any kind of criticism.
There is a reason for doing that - it draws you together and allows you to create a bit more determination and drive to be successful.
You could see England's intensity, their accuracy and their discipline. All the things that have maybe been highlighted over the past nine months as things England have been lacking, there was an abundance of all of it.
As much as it is easy to try to pick holes in England because it is England, sometimes you have got to pat people on the back and say they got it right.
The opposition was dangerous with good individual players, but from the off England's tactics were spot on. Their decision-making was controlled and they looked like a very well-drilled side.
- England swat aside Wallabies to back up Borthwick 
  - Published14 hours ago
- Feyi-Waboso burns bright as England energy endorses Borthwick 
  - Published11 hours ago
How England might unlock the best of Slade
England's back three of George Furbank, Tommy Freeman and Immanuel Feyi-Waboso caused plenty of problems for Australia, but I think you have to include Fin Smith and Henry Slade in that as well.
Potentially, there is something in that backline that may allow us to see the Slade we see for Exeter that we have not seen as much for England.
Having the likes of Feyi-Waboso, Freeman and Furbank around Slade and them understanding the sorts of positions he can get them into - there might be some long-term benefits to that.
Feyi-Waboso is X-factor, there is no question about that. For his early disallowed try, he shifted his weight and beat someone with that pace - I do not think there are many people in the world who could do that.
When you have got players like him who can do that regularly, all of a sudden you are getting momentum.
There was a massive difference in ruck speed and in momentum; England were getting lined up defensively and pushing Australia back, whereas when you have got players like Feyi-Waboso and Ben Earl, and then when Henry Pollock comes on as well, you have got plenty of players who can break the line in traffic and it makes attacking that much easier.
Fin Smith is leading the team, he looks like he is a general and in control of the game.
He has got a safe pair of hands and communication from Seb Atkinson, he has got vision from Slade and then a back three that if you give them half a chance, they are going to bust the line, create opportunities and probably finish.
There were bits of Sunday's game where if New Zealand were doing it, everybody would be ranting and raving about how complete some of those tries were.
Pollock's flexibility a fantastic weapon
Feyi-Waboso's injury meant Pollock came off the bench to play in an unfamiliar position on the wing and he ended up scoring two of England's seven tries.
He did very well considering he was on for a whole half. Going forward, what is the difference having Pollock there? He has got a winger's speed, the step, great hands, the power and the bulk that other wingers do not have and he is going to be a handful for the opposition.
Defensively, he was tested a couple of times and that is inevitable, but to have that flexibility on the bench allows England to have that six-two split because you have got a player who can now pretty much cover so many positions.
As great as it was, and I am sure he absolutely loved it, unfortunately he is probably inking himself in to be quite a significant bench player moving forward, which is not really what I think he would like to be labelled as.
Selfishly, from an England point of view, it is a fantastic weapon to have.
The whole bench did really well and made a difference. It goes all the way back to selection, something Borthwick has previously come under fire for a little bit.
It does not mean that just because he has got one right, the autumn is going to go swimmingly well, but from the off the selection has been right, the gameplan was a bit more expansive than I thought it was going to be and they absolutely nailed the execution.
Will England back it up against Japan?
Tactically, I loved the balance of the England performance; a really dominant set-piece, driving mauls and in-your-face defence.
England have maybe always been like that but have lacked the discipline to go with it.
Against Australia, they proved they have the capability to be disciplined and maintain concentration - and I want to see that over the next three weeks.
Can they, under more pressure - because they are going to face more pressure, particularly against New Zealand - still maintain that discipline and decision-making?
They have got the assets to overpower Japan, but can they do it by giving away fewer than 10 penalties? Can they do it by having 15 people on the pitch for 80 minutes?
All of the little things they have been after, can they do them against a team they should beat comfortably?
If they can, then when they go into the New Zealand game with it all to play for and when they are really testing themselves, they are going to have huge momentum.
Matt Dawson was speaking to BBC Sport's Phil Cartwright.

Kiara Advani has spoken about the online criticism she faced following the promotional rollout of Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups, particularly the scrutiny surrounding her intimate scenes with Kannada superstar Yash. During her appearance on the latest episode of Koffee With Karan alongside husband Sidharth Malhotra, the actress addressed the gendered nature of the backlash and explained how her partner’s response helped her deal with the commentary.
Koffee With Karan 9: Kiara Advani opens up on backlash over intimate scenes with Yash in Toxic; says Sidharth Malhotra was “never bothered” by online criticism
The controversy had sparked conversations on social media, with some users questioning Kiara’s decision to feature in bold sequences despite being married. However, similar personal scrutiny was largely absent in the case of Yash, who is also married and a parent. Discussing how the online reaction affected her and whether it became a subject of conversation at home, Kiara credited Sidharth’s attitude for helping her remain unaffected.

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.
The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.
The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.
The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.
In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.
With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.
Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.
The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.
With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

Rwanda's army team removed from Africa league after US sanctions, NBA says
- Published
The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.
The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).
However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.
The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March.
The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".
Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.
The BBC has asked Rwanda for comment.
- What is the Basketball Africa League? 
  - Published14 May 2021
- The evidence that shows Rwanda is backing rebels in DR Congo 
  - Published29 January 2025
In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda.
"What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked.
Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".
In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports.
The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.
The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the BAL in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.
The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba.
It is a professional league featuring 12 club teams from across the continent.
Rwanda has hosted all but one of the league's final and playoff matches since the inaugural match in 2021.
The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.
DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.
It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.

In November, a rumor spread that activists anonymously placed a golden statue of U.S. President Donald Trump rubbing his foot on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., referring to him avoiding the draft during the Vietnam War because he allegedly had a bone spur.
The claim and photographs of the supposed statue circulated on social media, including on Facebook and Reddit. An X post (archived) shared two images and said "The satirical monument, installed just ahead of Veterans Day, mocks Trump's Vietnam War draft deferment for bone spurs":
One of the photographs showed an epigraph at the base of the statue that read:
We honor the service and sacrifice of our commander in chief, Donald J. Trump. He's a soldier in spirit, who marched to the front lines of dodging the draft, armed with a perfect diagnosis of bone spurs.
We salute a leader who knows you can't spell sacrifice without "I," and a warrior who reminds us that sometimes when you're called to stand up, it's best to just sit down and rest your feet.
"I can be very military." — President Donald J. Trump
"The foot soldier," another inscription at the bottom said.
Meanwhile, Snopes readers searched our website, seeking confirmation that the statue was real.
It was. The statue appeared in a series of photographs on the reputable image bank Getty Images. Further, the organization responsible for putting it up confirmed it had in an email to Snopes. For this reason, we rated the claim true.
It also appeared on video news reports, including one by WUSA, a CBS affiliate in Washington:
The report said the statue was the work of an organization known as The Secret Handshake, an anonymous collective that also made the "Best Friends Forever" statue of Trump and late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein holding hands.
"We did put up the Bone Spur statue," The Secret Handshake told Snopes in an email.
The statue evokes the draft deferments Trump benefited from in the 1960s, during the Vietnam War. His disqualification in 1968 cited a medical reason, without providing details. In 2016, his campaign said it was because of bone spurs.
Three years later, Trump's former lawyer Michael Cohen testified that the president had not shown medical records proving the reason for his disqualification, according to a transcript of his testimony to the House Committee on Oversight and Reform:
Mr. Trump tasked me to handle the negative press surrounding his medical deferment from the Vietnam draft.
Mr. Trump claimed it was because of a bone spur. But when I asked for medical records, he gave me none and said that there was no surgery. He told me not to answer the specific questions by reporters, but rather, offer simply the fact that he received a medical deferment. He finished the conversation with the following comment. ''You think I'm stupid? I'm not going to Vietnam.'' And I find it ironic, Mr. President, that you are in Vietnam right now. And yet, I continued to work for him.
The statue is a humorous take on the suggestion that Trump allegedly dodged the draft without providing a real medical reason for not serving his country in Vietnam. It appeared on the National Mall on Nov. 9, two days before Veterans Day.
For further reading, Snopes has reported on other statues that derided Trump, including one that showed him naked in the European Parliament.

2 dead, 4 critically injured after building collapses in New York City
Firefighters dig through rubble of 3-storey building that fell at edge of construction site
Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-storey building in New York City's Brooklyn borough on Wednesday after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least two people and trapping others beneath the wreckage.
Firefighters were called to the scene in the Flatbush neighbourhood at about 4 p.m. News helicopter footage showed dozens of firefighters scouring the debris, with a group homing in on one area and appearing to use a saw to cut through the wreckage.
At least 17 people were hospitalized with injuries, including four in critical condition, officials said during a news conference.
New York City Fire Department (FDNY) officials said their search-and-rescue operations would continue into the night. "We do not know how many people were missing overall," said the FDNY's chief of department, John Esposito. It was unclear whether people might still be trapped.
"This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation, with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "This type of rescue is exactly what the FDNY trains for."
Firefighters search through the rubble on Wednesday. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
About 250 firefighters were working at the scene, Mamdani said.
At about 6:30 p.m., firefighters pulled a dust-covered person — still alive and moving — out of a hole they had dug into the rubble pile, hoisting them up on a stretcher and rushing them to a waiting ambulance.
The building that collapsed — a mixed-use structure with apartments sitting atop businesses — had been perched at the edge of a lot where another one-storey building had been torn down for a construction project. The site was being excavated, and the building that fell down filled the construction pit with bricks and wood.
New York City's buildings commissioner, Ahmed Tigani, said that at the time of the disaster, construction workers were on site doing excavation work adjacent to the building that collapsed.
A wall was shorn off an adjacent Brooklyn building, exposing a bedroom and closets filled with clothing inside. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.
A drone hovered over the site as firefighters dug by hand, tossing chunks of rubble aside. Rescuers also used dogs to sniff for survivors. As darkness fell, firefighters used flashlights to illuminate the area where they worked.
New York's fire commissioner, Lillian Bonsignore, said the rescue teams were performing "dangerous and perilous" work. "Every move is choreographed," she said.
One firefighter sustained minor injuries, fire officials said.
First responders rescue a person from the rubble of the collapse. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)
Phone and email messages seeking comment were left with the architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project.
One resident of the collapsed building, Anderson Velez, told the New York Post he was at work when his wife called and said she and their two children, aged 7 and 2, were trapped in the wreckage.
"She called me when the building collapsed while she was inside with rubble on top of her. She was screaming for someone to help get my son out and then the call cut off," he said.
Velez said he later learned that his family had been pulled from the rubble alive.

Recently listed furniture rental company Rentomojo reported a 62.6% year-on-year (YoY) decline in its profit after tax to ₹18.2 Cr in the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (Q2 FY27) from ₹48.6 Cr in the year-ago quarter. The decline was largely due to a deferred tax credit of ₹32.8 Cr recognised in the year-ago quarter, compared with a deferred tax expense of ₹6.2 Cr in Q2 FY27. On a sequential basis, the company’s net consolidated profit zoomed 133% from ₹7.8 Cr in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 52.8% YoY and 12% QoQ to ₹142.1 Cr in the quarter under review, driven by growth in customer orders, live subscribers and rental inventory. Including other income of ₹1.7 Cr, total income for the quarter stood at ₹143.8 Cr. Total expenses increased 53.2% YoY to ₹119.8 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹78.2 Cr in the year-ago period. Employee benefit expenses rose 38.3% to ₹19.5 Cr, while finance costs increased 46.7% to ₹9 Cr. The company said its normalised profit after tax, excluding exceptional items and deferred tax adjustments, increased 52.2% YoY to ₹24 Cr from ₹15.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. Normalised EBITDA also grew 52.7% to ₹58.8 Cr from ₹38.5 Cr a year earlier. Subscriber Additions, Higher Utilisation Drive Growth Rentomojo expanded its omnichannel network to 96 experience stores across 14 cities by the end of September, compared with 67 stores a year earlier. Customers ordered 3.8 Lakh gross items during the quarter, up 45% higher than last year's quarter. Besides, the company’s live subscriber base grew 42.5% to approximately 3.2 Lakh, while live item inventory increased 44% to 10.5 Lakh. Average occupancy grew by 61 basis points to 85.9% while average revenue per item (ARPI) increased 4.6% YoY to ₹1,650. The company also reported higher asset utilisation. Assets procured in the FY17 cycle generated cumulative revenue equivalent to 5.3X its original value, with around 54% of the cohort continuing to generate revenue. The FY18 cohort had generated 4.71X its original value, with 59.2% of its items still generating revenue. For context, higher utilisation of its rental assets allows the company to generate repeat revenue from its asset base. Purchase displaced, which measures the estimated retail value of consumer purchases replaced by customers choosing to rent furniture, grew 61% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹446.9 Cr. This was the company’s second quarterly results following its public market debut in September after it raised ₹1,255.6 Cr from an initial public offering. The company said it had utilised ₹90 Cr, or 63.7%, of the ₹141.4 Cr net proceeds allocated to the IPO's stated objectives as of September 30. This included the complete utilisation of ₹70 Cr earmarked for debt repayment, ₹8.1 Cr towards warehouse and experience store lease rentals, and ₹11.9 Cr for general corporate purposes. Commenting on the performance, founder, chairperson, managing director and CEO Geetansh Bamania said the company would continue focusing on subscriber growth, better asset utilisation and technology while maintaining profitability, cash generation and returns on capital. Shares of Rentomojo ended today’s trading session 3.30% higher at ₹610.9 apiece on the BSE.

Dutch antitrust regulators are investigating allegations that Biogen may have abused its dominant position in the market for multiple sclerosis treatments and associated blood tests.
The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets, also known by its Dutch acronym ACM, is probing whether the company reserved a test for patients who are treated with Tysabri, its MS drug, and refusing to make the test available to patients on rival medications, such as Tyruko, a biosimilar version that is sold by Sandoz.
Patients who are treated with Tysabri, Biogen’s biggest-selling medicine, must be regularly tested for the risk of developing progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, an infection caused by a virus that may be fatal or result in severe disability. Biogen developed a test for the virus and provides it free of charge — and exclusively — to patients receiving Tysabri.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
- Published
A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial".
The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines.
Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy.
The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns.
Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.
The BBC has asked the US department of health and human services for comment.
Here is what you need to know.
What was the trial?
The study was planned at the Bandim Health Project, a research centre that has operated in Guinea-Bissau since 1978.
It was designed to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving a hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth and the other half not being given the shot.
Bandim said the trial aimed to investigate whether the hepatitis B vaccine given at birth has broader health effects beyond preventing infection.
Previous studies in The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau have raised questions about a possible link to increased mortality.
Researchers argued that because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccinations at birth, despite WHO recommendations, they have a unique opportunity to study its effects before such vaccines are introduced in 2028.
But critics questioned the ethics of withholding the vaccine from some babies, particularly in one of the world's poorest countries, where the infection is widespread.
The Trump administration funded the proposed study, with the CDC awarding the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) $1.6m (£1.2m) in December 2025.
What did the WHO say?
Walter Kazadi Mulombo, the WHO representative in Guinea-Bissau, told the BBC they became concerned after receiving questions about the study and finding no publicly available protocol.
He said the main ethical concern was that the trial would withhold an intervention already proven to protect newborns against hepatitis B.
"The vaccine has been used for more than 30 years in more than 115 countries," he said. "A study that will withhold that intervention from other newborns is unethical."
He warned that babies could be exposed to the virus during childbirth if their mothers were infected, as well as later in life.
Nearly a fifth of the population of Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, a viral infection that affects the liver.
Those infected during infancy are particularly likely to develop chronic infections, which kill up to 25% of people, mostly through liver failure or liver cancer, according to data published in 2020.
The WHO is working with the government to bring forward the birth-dose vaccine.
"The country had been expected to add it to its routine immunisation schedule in 2028, but officials are considering introducing it in the first quarter of next year," Mulombo said.
Guinea-Bissau currently vaccinates children against hepatitis B at six weeks, which means it is less effective.
Why did Guinea-Bissau reject the trial?
Guinea-Bissau's government prohibited hepatitis B vaccine trials involving children in January. At the time, it requested a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study.
Health Minister Quinhin Nantote said in October that the suspension remained in force and had not been overturned by the Council of Ministers after reports emerged claiming that the trial would be taking place after all.
"We were surprised to learn from media reports that the study might proceed," Nantote said. "We are outraged because even I, as the minister responsible for this sector, was not informed."
The dispute intensified after the SDU said a revised study protocol had received ethical approval "from the relevant authorities in Guinea-Bissau", which Nantote denied.
Dr Gavin Yamey, a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in the US, criticised the proposal.
"The proposed trial reeks of neocolonialism," he told the BBC, questioning why the research was not being conducted in Denmark.
His criticism centred on the decision to withhold a recommended vaccine from some newborns in a country where hepatitis B is widespread.
SDU dean Jakob Grauslund said the trial had never started, no babies had been enrolled and no vaccinations administered as part of the research.
Was the trial approved by anyone?
The SDU said it had received a separate, positive assessment from the university's own research ethics committee.
Grauslund said the university had sought an additional independent assessment, although Danish law did not require one.
He added that the relevant Danish statutory research ethics bodies were unable to undertake the review.
Following the approval from the SDU's ethics committee, Grauslund decided that the project could proceed.
He, however, stressed that this did not replace the separate authorisation required from Guinea-Bissau's authorities.
What has happened to the vaccines?
On 19 October, Guinea-Bissau's Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project's facilities in the capital, Bissau, and seized a batch of hepatitis B vaccines.
Police said the batch was intended for vaccinating children but did not disclose how many doses had been seized or the specific grounds for the investigation.
They stressed that the seizure did not, in itself, mean the vaccines were defective or unsafe.
The police have not explicitly said whether their investigation relates to the proposed trial, the importation of the vaccines or other circumstances surrounding the batch.
Grauslund said he could not comment on the seizure of the vaccines.
Who is funding the research?
The proposed trial was funded by the US government at a time of significant changes to vaccine policy under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Kennedy.
Under Kennedy's leadership, a US vaccine panel attempted to end a longstanding recommendation that all newborns receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth, but a federal judge later blocked this, along with other changes to vaccine policy made by the Trump administration.
Critics have questioned whether the research could help support that policy shift, although the study's stated aim was to investigate potential effects of the vaccine beyond preventing infection.
Kennedy has praised the Danish researchers as "the deities of vaccine research", and cited earlier findings from their work in support of concerns about vaccine safety. A subsequent study by some of the same researchers, however, found no evidence of the previously reported effect.
There is no evidence that the proposed trial was designed to justify a change in US policy.

Quick Answer
Concat is a free, open-source CapCut alternative with offline AI captions, voice cloning, background removal, 100+ effects, and 4K exports. It runs locally, needs no account, and adds no watermarks. Available across major platforms, it’s promising but still in beta, with some rough edges.
When you think of video editing, CapCut is a popular name that would pop up. It has made short-form editing painless. However, it has now started to put more of its tools behind a paywall, and a few of them need an internet connection to work.
If you are looking for a way out, you have probably already seen OpenReel, the browser-based open-source editor, or gone through our list of the best free video editing software. This time we have something different. Concat takes a different route. It is a free, open-source editor that runs on your own computer and is loaded with features like captions, voiceovers, and background removal built in.
Table of Contents
What is Concat?
Concat is a video editor that is currently in beta. The idea behind its development is easy to understand: It wants to give people stuff that CapCut offers but for free, like auto-captions, text-to-speech, background removal, keyframes, effects, titles, and 4K export. Everything Concat has on offer comes without strings attached. You don’t need to sign up, no watermark stamped on your exports, and no premium tier waiting around the corner.
The other big difference is where the work happens. Concat does everything locally, on your machine. It is built on a native Rust engine with a GPU compositor, and the AI models it uses (for captions, voices, and cutouts) are downloaded once from the settings and then run offline. This means the raw footage that you upload never gets uploaded anywhere.
CapCut is still a great editor, and nobody is pretending otherwise. When we compared it with Instagram Edits, we pointed out that CapCut has the richer feature set, but also that some of its tools need a connection and that its template and music ecosystem is tied closely to TikTok, which owns it. And if you are in India, you already know CapCut is banned here. So, you have to download the modded version or depend on some ad-filled alternatives.
That is the gap Concat is trying to fill. Not a “lite” version of a big editor, but a free one that keeps the stuff you reach for every day and keeps it on your own PC.
Concat features that matter
The feature list is long. But here are the parts that stand out.
Auto-captions that work offline
Captions are quite important nowadays, as content is reaching every part of the globe. But it is a chore every Reels and Shorts editor knows too well. Concat handles them using Whisper, a speech-recognition model that runs locally. You pick a model size (you can choose larger models, which are more accurate but require a stronger machine), and styled captions appear straight on your timeline. No upload, no waiting on a server, and it keeps working without internet.
Text-to-speech and voice cloning
Concat gives you free voices for narration, which is handy for tutorials or faceless channels. You can also clone a voice from just a few seconds of recording. That’s nice to edit a flubbed line without re-recording a whole take.
Background removal
You might have removed people or objects from your images. For videos, most of the editors ask you to pay. But Concat lets you edit out people or objects from a clip for free. If the automatic cutout misses a spot, you can paint the mask manually.
Keyframes with a curve editor
With keyframes, you can animate almost anything over time: position, scale, rotation, opacity, volume, and the settings of effects. There is a built-in curve editor too. You can use this to make a zoom feel smooth instead of mechanical, something that a paid video editor offers.
100 effects, filters and transitions
Concat comes with about 100 effects, filters, and transitions. They are rendered by your GPU and show up live in the preview. This way you can see what you are doing instead of waiting for an export to find out.
Fast cutting and a proper timeline
You get everything like split, trim, ripple delete, merge, freeze frame, and speed changes. If you like clips snapping together without gaps, you can switch on a magnetic timeline. Additionally, you can stack as many tracks as you want for overlays and picture-in-picture, keep several timelines inside a single project, and use blend modes like screen, add, and multiply. Crop and flip tools are there as well.
Titles with real styling
You can change fonts, add strokes and shadows, and drop in a background plate behind the words. If you don’t have any ideas, you can start from the already available presets.
One-switch audio cleanup
If your video has bad audio because of a faulty microphone or nearby noise, it can spoil a good video more than bad lighting does. Concat has a simple toggle for noise reduction, voice enhancement, and loudness leveling. You can also change voice effects to chipmunk, robot, and telephone.
Export and performance
Now, the best part is that with Concat, there is no limitation on export. It supports H.264, HEVC, and AV1, up to 4K at 60 frames per second with 10-bit colour.
Which platforms does Concat support?
Concat is versatile and supports multiple operating systems:
- Windows
- macOS
- Linux
- Android
- iPhone and iPad
Moreover, the editor is available in 26 languages. Downloading and setting up Concat is simple. Here’s what you need to do:
- Open the official download page, which picks the right build for your device. You can also grab any version from the GitHub Releases page.
- Install it like any other app on your device.
- On Windows, your system may warn you because the builds are not code-signed yet. Click More info, then Run anyway.
- On macOS, if the system refuses to open the app, the project suggests running xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Concat.app in Terminal.
- Open Settings and download the AI models you want (captions, voices, cutout). After that, they work offline.
Concat vs CapCut
| Feature | Concat | CapCut | 
|---|---|---|
| Price | Free, no subscription | Freemium | 
| Who is behind it | Open-source project (AGPL-3.0) | ByteDance | 
| Internet needed | Only to download AI models once | Some tools need a connection | 
| Templates and music | Limited | Large library tied to TikTok | 
A few things to keep in mind
Concat is promising and has all the features you would need from a video editor that is trying to be an alternative to CapCut. But don’t forget that it is young, and there are a few caveats that you should know about.
- It is a beta. The repo had over 200 open issues at the time of writing this article. So, you may come across some rough edges. We would advise you not to trust it with a client deadline until you have tested it on your own projects.
- Unsigned Windows builds and the macOS quarantine step can feel sketchy to newcomers. But it is safe, even though they are expected for now.
- You do not get a stock library to lean on. You will need your own assets.
- iPhone users have extra work because you have to sideload it, and sideloading is not for everyone.
Once you have the clarity, you should give Concat a try and let its output help you decide if you should keep using it or not. Let us know in the comments below which editor you are currently using.

Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war
- Published
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.
The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.
Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.
We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.
More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.
Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.
More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.
The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.
For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.
When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.
"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.
Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."
Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."
Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.
"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".
Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.
Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.
Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.
"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.
She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."
Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.
Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.
"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time.
There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.
Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.
Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.
After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.
For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.
