  - Published16 October 2025
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.
"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."
His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.
As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.
He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.
For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.
The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.
Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine".
"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.
Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.
Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results
Republicans were dealt a stunning rebuke in last week's midterms. But swing voters, who could be decisive in the next election, are more interested in results than investigations or impeachment as Democrats prepare to take power in Congress.
"I am hoping that we don't experience a bunch of gridlock and a lot of whining and crying and just political infighting for the next two years," said Theresa, a voter from Pennsylvania who is participating in NPR's Swing Shift project. "I'm hoping we don't have that. I fear that we will have that."
NPR has agreed not to use the full names of the Swing Shift voters, so they can speak freely about politics without fear of personal or professional repercussions.
Loading...
Theresa voted for President Biden in 2020, President Trump in 2024 and split her ticket in this year's midterms. Like many voters, her top issue this year was affordability. In a voice memo sent to NPR days after the midterms, Theresa said she is eager for the cost of living to come down.
"I just don't remember it ever being as bad in our time," Theresa said. "And I'm just hoping we get some relief and we get some relief soon."
At 9:56 PM on election night, Wally in Georgia hit send on his voice memo. He had seen enough.
"Just checking in here with a quick note. I'm not surprised at all by the outcome tonight," Wally said. "I believe that this is a lot of Trump's doing and pushback on his style of politics and how he governs."
Wally voted for Trump in 2024 but swung back to Democrats in this year's midterms. He had initially supported Trump in hopes that a Trump presidency would shake up the political system, but that didn't happen and now he says the second Trump term has been exhausting. As he sees it, the decisive Democratic wins signal that the country is ready to move on.
"Trump has been shooting himself in the foot for many months now," Wally said. "But voting isn't the end of the game here. We have to hold Democrats to some sort of tangible change and not just promises about what they want to do."
For several of the Swing Shift voters, Tuesday's results came as a surprise.
Jason from North Carolina split his ticket, voting for Democrat Roy Cooper for Senate and the Republican incumbent for the House.
"My congressman was defeated this time by someone that no one's really ever heard of," said Jason, sounding almost puzzled by the blue wave that crashed on North Carolina.
That happened in a lot of places. Jason wants the incoming Democratic Congress to focus on the cost of living and steer clear of impeachment.
"My fear is that the Democrats now are going to spend the next 2 years not focusing on any of the things that they say Trump didn't do," said Jason.
Michelle in Michigan, voted for President Biden in 2020 but chose Republicans in 2024 and again in this year's midterms.
"This is the first time I think ever since I've been voting that not one of the people that I voted for won their election," Michelle said.
Michelle says she understands why so many people voted for Democrats, even if she didn't. Americans are tired, she said, of high gas prices, the cost of living and not being able to afford their groceries. They voted for change.
John from Pennsylvania said it felt like his state went from purple to blue overnight.
"I'm just very surprised," John said. "Not surprised that Democrats had a good night, but they had a very good night. Absolutely amazed that they won in Texas and places that just seemed like they were really red."
He voted for President Biden in 2020 and President Trump in 2024. In the most recent midterms, he stuck with Republicans despite concerns about the cost of living and the war with Iran.
Gerald in Georgia ran through the list of states where Democrats won senate races in disbelief.
"Come on man, Texas turned blue," Gerald said. "South Carolina turned blue, Ohio, Kansas. Like, this was a referendum of epic proportions."
Gerald is a Biden to Trump voter from Georgia, who has gone all in on MAGA. He's already looking ahead to a future without Trump leading Republicans.
"The Donald Trump era for all intents and purposes is coming to an end in 2028 for certain, if not before that," Gerald said.
Before that, though, Democrats will take power in Washington, at least in part.
Swing Shift voters said again and again when asked about their hopes and fears following these midterms that they hope that the incoming Democratic Congress will focus on the issues that impact their daily lives but fear more of the same broken politics.
"I will choose to hope because that's really all we can do is hope," said Michelle. "Hope that the politicians that were voted in will live up to the promises they made and that change will truly be made."
Even though John didn't vote for Democrats this year, he still wants them to tackle the cost of living.
"Over these next 2 years I hope they are concerned with and concentrate on the affordability issue," John said. "I hope they work with President Trump to try to lower prices. I just hope it's not two years of investigations and impeachment hearings."
Anything Democrats pass in a divided government would have to be signed by President Trump. The president has been inconsistent in recent days about whether he wants cooperation or combat with the new Congress.

How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
- Published
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.
Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid.
US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.
At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.
The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.
Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.
With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.
In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

This image was AI-generated — OpenAI detected its own watermark on the image. However, the devastating flooding in Gaza is real, and there are dozens of authentic images illustrating the extent of the damage.
As winter flooding hit Gaza — where roughly 65% of the population, about 1.4 million people, lives in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the United Nations — a striking image circulated online in early November purportedly showing the magnitude of the flooding's damage.
Apparently shot at night, the image showed blue and white tents flooded by murky water, several buildings standing in the background as light from windows and streetlights appeared to reflect across the surface of the water.
Posts of the image shared across social media collectively gained millions of views and reactions, with hundreds of commenters appearing to believe the image was authentic. Prominent accounts, including British Parliament member Jeremy Corbyn, posted the image before deleting it (archived).
Although intense rainfall in Gaza early November has caused flooding and put thousands of people in danger as Israel continues to blockade crucial supplies — including 150,000 tents waiting just outside, according to the U.N. — this image was a fake.
The image contained multiple signs of being generated with artificial intelligrnace, including an OpenAI watermark that OpenAI's verification software identified. It's unclear precisely where it originated.
(OpenAI)
OpenAI reconstructs its images in a systemic grid pattern (autoregressive approach). Upon zooming in more closely, the pixel pattern of the image showed signs of a star-like grid, which digital forensics expert Hany Farid has described as a tell-tale sign of AI-generation.
(X user @ahmed_nashwan1 and Heny Farid, Snopes illustration)
The image displays other signs of AI generation, including unnatural light interruption, a mottled sky texture, and harsh lines between blurred pixels and textured pixels.
(X user ahmed_nashwan1, Snopes illustration)
Despite the fact that this image was AI-generated, there are hundreds of publicly available images showing the extent of the flooding destruction in Gaza.

Mauricio Pochettino: Man Utd strike agreement with Michael Carrick's potential successor
Man Utd powerbrokers set to make a final decision on Michael Carrick's future at a Monaco summit on Wednesday having lined up Mauricio Pochettino, who has a £7m release clause in the contract he signed with the USA after the World Cup this past summer
Wednesday 11 November 2026 15:15, UK
Manchester United have reached an agreement in principle with Mauricio Pochettino to take over as head coach if Michael Carrick is sacked.
Carrick took training at Carrington on Wednesday while an agreement was struck for Pochettino to potentially come in as his replacement.
It is understood there are still details being finalised with Pochettino's camp while talks are set to accelerate with the US Soccer Federation (USSF) over when the Argentine can be released from his contract.

When will Man Utd make a decision on Carrick?
While Carrick has been at the training ground in Manchester, United's powerbrokers are set to make a final decision on his future at a Monaco summit on Wednesday.

Sir Alex Ferguson has long admired Pochettino and often had long conversations with the former Spurs boss following his matches against United.
The pair were pictured at a Mayfair restaurant in May 2016 amid speculation about Pochettino, then Spurs head coach, taking over from Louis van Gaal at Old Trafford. United subsequently chose to appoint Jose Mourinho.

17-year-old accused in Bengaluru family murders may face adult trial
The law allows children aged 16–18 accused of heinous offences to be tried as adults following an assessment
The 17-year-old accused of assisting her father in the murder of seven members of their family in Bengaluru could face trial as an adult if a juvenile justice board determines she meets the criteria under the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015. The law allows children aged 16–18 accused of heinous offences, including murder, to be tried as adults following a preliminary assessment of their capacity to understand and commit the alleged crime.
The girl, a second-year pre-university student at a private college, allegedly assisted S Indushekar, 52, in killing his wife, Sunitha, and six of her relatives at their home over about 15 days in October. She was arrested along with her father on November 5.
A police officer said investigators are probing the extent of her involvement, including claims by her father that she helped bring relatives to the house, conceal the killings, and transport and dispose of the bodies. “The main point being considered is whether Indushekar manipulated his daughter into helping him dispose of the bodies.”
The first information report (FIR) registered in the case on November 5 names Indushekar and his daughter as accused. Indushekar is listed as an adult accused. His daughter is classified as a juvenile in conflict with the law.
A juvenile justice board must assess the child’s mental and physical capacity to commit the alleged offence, her ability to understand its consequences, and the circumstances in which it was committed under the Juvenile Justice Act Section 15. The assessment can involve psychologists and other experts.
The officer said if the board decides that the case warrants an adult trial, it can transfer the matter to the children’s court under Section 18(3). “The children’s court must independently decide whether the child should face an adult trial or be dealt with under the juvenile justice system.”
The officer said the seriousness of the allegations alone does not determine the outcome. The girl’s understanding of the alleged crimes and the extent to which she was influenced or coerced by her father will be important considerations.
Investigators suspect that Indushekar turned his daughter against her mother’s family, portraying the relatives as enemies and allegedly telling her that eliminating them would improve their financial position because the property would eventually belong to her.
The girl allegedly contacted her maternal grandmother, Roopavathi, after her mother Sunitha’s murder and asked her to visit the house. She allegedly invited her maternal aunts for dinner, telling them that Sunitha was away on a trip. She reportedly messaged her aunt Divya’s sister, Chandana, claiming that the family was travelling.
Police are investigating her suspected role in packing the bodies, transporting them in the car, and cleaning the crime scene.
Karnataka home minister Priyank Kharge said Indushekar allegedly brainwashed his daughter and made her assist in the crime.
Police said Indushekar allegedly transported the bodies in his car and disposed of them at different locations with his daughter’s assistance. Forensic Science Laboratory and Scene of Crime Officer teams inspected the recovery sites, while postmortem examinations were conducted.
Investigators are now focusing on forensic evidence to establish the sequence and timing of the killings and are analysing CCTV footage. The bodies were recovered from locations in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.
A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.
Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

It’s been one week since Election Day, and Pete Hegseth is facing a different kind of war. Trump administration officials tell Inner Loop they knew the defense secretary would face a slew of investigations in the next Congress. Now, they think he is on track to be Democrats’ number one target—and Democrats are already planning to make their case as airtight as possible.
“Hegseth is now a passenger in whatever comes next,” says one source close to President Donald Trump. “And all the outcomes are potentially damaging.”
House Democratic aides tell Inner Loop that Democrats are likely to pursue an impeachment inquiry against Hegseth, and also work to narrow the charges against him to issues that Senate Republicans have also complained about, in an effort to attract their support.
Hegseth, who has championed the deeply unpopular and costly Iran war, has spent much of his controversial tenure upending various internal processes at the Defense Department, including firing generals and blocking promotions using criteria that disproportionately affected women and people of color. He has also become known for his notorious role in Signalgate and for military strikes against purported drug traffickers in the Caribbean and Pacific Ocean.
Some of those topics have also previously been the subject of complaints from Republicans. The Senate Armed Services Committee chair Roger Wicker criticized Hegseth for the flag officer cuts and once reportedly threatened to block a Trump nominee unless the Pentagon handed over documents.
Last night, House Republicans managed to table an impeachment effort targeting Hegseth that was brought about by Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky. Massie, among other issues, accused Hegseth of waging the Iran war without approval from Congress and directing “extrajudicial killings.” But even though the effort failed, officials privately believe it is practically inevitable that Hegseth will be impeached again and face a Senate trial next year.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries suggested as much after the impeachment failed to progress, telling reporters he would consult with his top members on next steps.
“We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time, and that’ll be led by Adam Smith, soon to be chair of the Armed Services Committee, and Jamie Raskin, next chair of the judiciary,” Jeffries said.
Trump officials tell Inner Loop they still don’t expect Democrats to get enough GOP support to remove Hegseth—but they can’t shield him from wall-to-wall coverage of a trial.
The impeachment articles brought by Massie were seen by some Republicans as overly broad, which made officials think they could spare Hegseth an impeachment trial by having Senate majority leader John Thune dismiss all the charges in a straight-line vote.
But with Democrats taking over the Senate next year, that option is off the table.
It’s not going to be entirely simple, however. Hegseth’s biggest Republican detractors are all leaving Congress at the end of the year. Maine senator Susan Collins, North Carolina senator Thom Tillis, and Louisiana senator Bill Cassidy all lost reelection this midterm cycle, while Iowa senator Joni Ernst and Kentucky senator Mitch McConnell are stepping down after finishing their terms.
But even with his biggest detractors set to retire, at least five other Republican senators have complained about Hegseth’s performance—getting Democrats closer to the 67 votes needed to convict—like Wicker, South Dakota senator Mike Rounds, Kentucky senator Rand Paul, Alaska senator Lisa Murkowski, and Indiana senator Todd Young.
This is why the focus of the Democratic impeachment inquiry is going to have to be specific, and geared to Republican interests, so as to be unassailable.
Hegseth, for what it’s worth, doesn’t seem to want to go anywhere without a fight. In a televised appearance at the Pentagon earlier this week, Hegseth responded to a question about Vice President JD Vance blaming the Republican midterm losses on Iran, and said Vance was a “critical member of the team” and the war effort.
Hegseth then added, “I agree with what the president said, when he said ‘Hey, if I had to do this all over again, would we do it again? Absolutely.’”

A few hours of exposure to firecracker smoke can be enough to trigger coughing, wheezing or breathlessness, particularly in people living with asthma or other respiratory conditions. The effects, however, are not limited to those with an existing diagnosis. High concentrations of particulate matter and gases can irritate the airways in anyone.
The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a numerical measure that converts the levels of different air pollutants into a single figure to indicate how polluted the air is and the likely health effects. India’s Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) calculates it using eight pollutants, including PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide.

How many SpaceX Starship rocket tests have failed?
The answer isn't so simple.
In late September 2026, SpaceX's Starship entered orbit for the first time, deploying 26 Starlink satellites in what was heralded as a major step for SpaceX's cosmic ambitions. However, the celebration was cut short when a failed engine forced the mission to end shortly after reaching orbit. The malfunction prevented the intended six-revolution trek through Earth's orbit, falling well short of its 10-hour goal.
This result is typical for Starship, as the company's "fail fast, learn fast" mindset recasts the program's failures — anywhere between four and 11 of 14 total launches, depending on how generous you are — as opportunities for growth. This has been true since its first test flight in April 2023, which exploded 65 miles short of its intended climb into Earth's atmosphere. As Musk tweeted after the fiery test, "Congrats @SpaceX team on an exciting test launch of Starship! Learned a lot for next test launch."
Given SpaceX's success to date, it is hard to argue with the company's logic. According to analytics firm BryceTech, SpaceX launched 85 percent of all spacecraft in 2025, including over half the world's orbital launches. To boot, Starlink's 9,800 active satellites currently account for over half of the world's total, according to satellite tracker Orbital Radar.
The largest and most powerful rocket ever assembled, Starship has a cargo capacity five times larger than SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket. This makes it essential for SpaceX's grander ambitions, including its million-satellite constellation, NASA's lunar missions and Musk's Mars colony dream. With another launch set for November 13, 2026, stakeholders will soon see whether the September launch represented progress or foreshadowed further additions to SpaceX's growing list of frustrations.
A checkered history
Gauging the success of the Starship project is difficult. Although some missions may fit within a binary success-failure matrix, most land somewhere in between. And while it has yet to deliver a fully-reusable rocket capable of missions to "Mars and beyond," progress was always going to be incremental. As such, its only fair to judge each mission against its own standards of progress.
Starship's start was turbulent. After its initial test combusted within minutes, its second flight saw the first-stage booster separate before the booster and vessel met fiery ends. Five months later, Starship's third test flight completed many of its objectives, reaching an altitude of 145 miles before disintegrating on its return. SpaceX then had two back-to-back successful launches, culminating in its launch tower successfully catching Starship's first-stage booster.
Unfortunately, another troubled period followed. Test six saw SpaceX call off its lauded mechanical arm before crashing the Super Heavy booster into the Gulf of Mexico. Two months later, Starship 7 exploded over the Bahamas just eight minutes after takeoff, sparking investigations by both the FAA and the Turks and Caicos government. The FAA launched another investigation after Starship's eighth test exploded in space, grounding planes across Florida. Starship 9 achieved minor improvements before spinning out of control, forcing SpaceX to cancel its planned deployment of 8 mock satellites.
Starship followed the disastrous run with a pair of its most successful tests. In August 2025, Starship released its first cargo of Starlink satellites. Two months later, SpaceX successfully launched and landed its 11th Starship rocket, fulfilling all major objectives.
Starship's twelfth test launched its upgraded Starship V3 rocket. While it accomplished several objectives, engine failures caused it to crash into the Gulf, triggering yet another FAA investigation. In July 2026, Starship 13 successfully deployed 20 of Starlink's new high-powered satellites before its first-stage booster failed to stick the landing. Considering its scattershot history, Starship 14's semi-successful run is par for the course.
Failing towards the stars?
Judging each mission against its stated objectives, most Starship launches have failed to meet expectations. SpaceX, however, would likely claim that its willingness to learn from mistakes puts its true failure rate closer to zero. The better question is whether the program is learning quickly enough to keep pace with its own meteoric ambitions.
If one takes Musk's proclamations as a measuring stick, Starship has underdelivered. In 2025, Musk predicted there was a 50 percent chance Starship would land on Mars in 2026. And with the once-every-26-months Mars launch window closing this November, you can guess which side of the coin SpaceX landed on. Of course, Musk is notorious for overpromising, so this is business as usual at Starbase.
Earlier this year, NASA announced that the program had fallen behind schedule by at least two years since the Agency selected SpaceX's rocket to carry its Artemis moon lander in 2021. With China aiming to reach the moon by decade's end, the pressure is mounting. NASA hopes to return to the moon in 2028; to do so, Starship must meet the Artemis III deadline in summer 2027.
Beyond being Musk's conduit to Mars, SpaceX's most ambitious projects depend on Starship to slash costs. SpaceX's proposed 1 million-satellite datacenter constellation Starmind, for example, is impossible without a high-capacity reusable rocket. The November 13 test should provide another data point to judge SpaceX's progress, especially given its ambitions. In a Q3 earnings call, Musk stated that SpaceX will attempt to catch both the rocket and its booster, making it the 
"first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered." During the event, Musk said the mission was "more likely than not" to succeed. Starship's history may say otherwise.

TV providers say Rogers' Monday hockey move inflates prices, 'erodes' sports viewing
Cogeco Inc., Eastlink and SaskTel say Rogers is forcing price inflation on fans
A trio of television providers are accusing Rogers Communications Inc. of violating competition rules and inflating Canadian sports fans' bills by moving Monday night hockey broadcasts exclusively to its Sportsnet Plus streaming service for this NHL season.
In a letter submitted to Canada's broadcasting regulator on Tuesday, the companies — Cogeco Inc., Eastlink and SaskTel — say Rogers is forcing price inflation on fans by charging a $12.99 monthly add-on fee to access hockey games on Monday nights, unless they already subscribe to Rogers TV or Sportsnet Plus.
The rival providers are asking the CRTC to order Rogers to immediately offer the content to independent companies for distribution to their customers for free, "ensuring parity" with Rogers' offering.
They say the dynamic is "deliberately degrading the user experience on other distributors' platforms" and leading to the "erosion of sports on television," as such companies are unable to assemble a comprehensible sports lineup for their own subscribers.
The shift of Monday broadcasts exclusively to Rogers' streaming platform is one of a few significant changes for hockey fans this season, which also includes the end of a sublicensing agreement that allowed Saturday night NHL broadcasts to air on CBC under the Hockey Night in Canada brand.
Rogers also upped the annual cost of Sportsnet Plus for premium subscribers to $344.99, and announced a 12-year agreement with Amazon for Prime Video in Canada to exclusively broadcast Wednesday night regular-season national games.
The ongoing 2026-27 NHL season marks the first under Rogers' 12-year, $11-billion national TV rights deal for English broadcasts.

Four AC coaches of the Gorakhpur-bound Chauri Chaura Express derailed shortly after the train left Kanpur Central railway station on Wednesday evening (November 11, 2026). No casualties were reported in the incident, senior police and railway officials said.
Around 300 passengers were travelling in the four affected coaches, they said.
"Chauri Chaura train [15003] bound for Gorakhpur from Anwar Ganj departed from platform number 7 at around 5.03 p.m.. As it moved out of the station, coaches B-4, B-5, B-6 and B-7 derailed, triggering panic among passengers," Commissioner of Police Raghubir Lal told PTI.
It was the second derailment incident reported in Wednesday (November 11, 2026). Earlier in the day, five coaches and the engine of the Kolkata-Sairang Express derailed at Digaru near Assam's Guwahati, leaving four persons injured.
Railway officials and engineering teams rushed Kanpur to oversee restoration work. Senior railway officials from Prayagraj were also sent to Kanpur.
Deputy Commissioner of Police (East) Satyajeet Gupta said the derailment occurred at around 5.07 p.m. No passenger was injured, and the railway safety team would investigate the cause, he said.
All were safe and had been shifted to platform number 1, where arrangements for refreshments and a special train were being made for their onward journey, Mr. Gupta said.
The special train could take four to five hours to be arranged, a railway official said, adding that passengers unwilling to continue their journey would receive a full refund.
The incident did not affect other train operations at the station, the officials said.
A passenger travelling with his family for Chhath Puja said a sudden jolt threw his child to the floor. Panic-stricken people rushed out of the coaches before realising that four coaches had derailed.
Another passenger, Sanjeev Tripathi, who was travelling to Deoria, said a loud noise was heard soon after the train started moving.
His coach began tilting to one side, accompanied by a rattling sound, prompting passengers to get off with their belongings.
Chief Public Relations Officer (CPRO), North Central Railways, Shivam Sharma, said the cause of the derailment was not yet known.
A formal inquiry committee would be constituted which would examine all aspects of the incident, he added.

Well ahead of Black Friday, the MacBook Air is already $200 off, bringing down the price of the 13-inch model with an M5 chip, 16 GB of RAM, and 512 GB of storage to $1,099.
This is the lowest price the MacBook Air has been at since June, when Apple permanently hiked prices across its entire Mac lineup. Amazon frequently sells this MacBook Air for $1,149, but this even lower price is usually reserved for big sales events—the last being in October during Prime Day. And now it's back.
I probably don't need to expound too much on what makes the M5 MacBook Air such a fantastic, do-it-all laptop. It's extremely well-built, the performance and battery life are both top-notch, and it's still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. There's a reason it tops my list of laptop recommendations—even after having tested dozens of new models this year.
Unlike the MacBook Neo, which makes compromises on memory and performance to achieve its low price, the MacBook Air does nearly everything right. And while a MacBook Pro may tempt you—whether the new M6 model or one of the more powerful touchscreen OLED models—most people won't actually feel the difference in performance. Unless content creation, media, or game development is a full-time gig for you, I think you'll be surprised by just how much the M5 MacBook Air can handle.
The only real question is what size is right for you. The 13-inch model plays to the strengths of the MacBook Air—offering an extremely portable laptop at a reasonable price without sacrificing performance. If you would appreciate a larger screen (and don’t plan to travel with the device as much), you might prefer the 15-inch model, which is also $200 off its retail price, currently selling for $1,299. Aside from the larger screen, the only other difference is a much more robust six-speaker audio system.
Either way, now remains a really good time to buy a MacBook Air. While prices were certainly lower in the first half of 2026, we’re still probably many months out from the inevitable M6 refresh. I don’t claim to have any insider knowledge, but based on pricing history, I can’t see these laptops coming down any lower in price over the next few months.

Clashes broke out between masked protesters and police in Barcelona on Wednesday as tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike in 14 years, called by the country's major trade unions over the housing affordability crisis and rising cost of living.
Around 120,000 people joined demonstrations in Madrid and more than 50,000 gathered in Barcelona, where some protesters set fire to rubbish bins, smashed shop windows and clashed with police. Officers fired tear gas to disperse the crowds, while transport and other public services across the country faced significant disruption.
The disturbances in Barcelona continued into the evening, with a heavy police presence in the city centre. Some clashes took place along Passeig de Gràcia, near the iconic Plaça de Catalunya. Local media reported that protesters fired fireworks at police and looted shops, including a Lego store. Some were also seen attempting to enter an Apple Store.
The unions said around four million workers participated in the nationwide strike, which was backed by Spain's two largest labour organisations, the UGT and CCOO, as well as tenants' associations protesting against rising rents and evictions.
UGT chief Pepe Álvarez described the strike as a success, citing "massive" participation, while CCOO leader Unai Sordo said turnout was "very significant". However, participation varied across the country, with stronger support in coastal regions where housing pressures have been particularly acute.
The walkout was the first general strike in Spain since 2012, when workers protested against austerity measures during the eurozone debt crisis. It comes less than three weeks before parliamentary elections scheduled for November 29.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is seeking to make housing affordability a central election issue and shift the political debate away from corruption cases involving his inner circle and a deadly train crash last month. His Socialist Party, however, continues to trail in opinion polls.
Spain faces a housing deficit of around 750,000 homes, which is projected to exceed one million by 2028, according to the country's central bank.
With home ownership becoming increasingly unaffordable, demand for rental accommodation has risen sharply, putting further pressure on the market. The average monthly rent of 1,176 euros ($1,315) is equivalent to about 98.7 per cent of a young person's average monthly salary in Spain, according to the Youth Council of Spain.

Listed matchmaking platform Matrimony’s consolidated net profit for the September quarter (Q2 FY27) skyrocketed 165.4% YoY to ₹20.7 Cr from ₹7.8 Cr in the year-ago quarter. On a sequential basis, profit increased 8.4% from ₹19.1 Cr in Q1 FY27. Operating revenue rose 17.6% YoY and 3.3% QoQ to ₹134.8 Cr in the quarter under review. Complete data could've raised avg Diwali pollution level 49%
NEW DELHI: Missing PM2.5 data from monitoring stations could have raised the city's average pollution level by 49% on Diwali, according to an analysis by Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).Had the missing readings been recorded at 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre (g/m³), the city's average PM2.5 level would have increased from 269 to 400(g/m³), it revealed. The daily national ambient air quality standard for PM2.5 is 60 g/m³ and WHO's safe guideline is 15 g/m³.The analysis was done a day after Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) said its stations' analysers were calibrated to measure particulate matter concentrations only up to 1,000g/m³ and could not display readings beyond it on Diwali night for several hours.Nor were these readings considered for calculating the average AQI, it said.CREA said if 400g/m³ had been considered, city's AQI on Monday would have risen from 344 (very poor) to near severe. AQI is calculated based on 8 pollutants, including PM2.5.TOI reported Tuesday that CPCB had stopped giving data on particulate matter at the peak of Diwali night pollution for several hours after particulate matter levels at air quality monitoring stations surpassed 1,000g/m³.
However, Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), which operates 43 of the total 60 stations, gave readings on Diwali night that crossed 1,000g/m³. At least at 11 locations, the hourly PM2.5 concentration was above 2,000g/m³. In four, it was above 3,000.CPCB compiles data from all 60 stations and releases the AQI. One station has been defunct for the past few months.The latest analysis examined hourly PM2.5 data from 59 monitoring stations between 4pm on Nov 8 and 4pm on Nov 9, corresponding to the 24-hour averaging period used for CPCB's 4pm AQI bulletin on Nov 9. It analysed 1,416 hours (24 hours x 59 stations).It found that 255 of the 1,416 expected station-hour observations or 18% were missing. CREA conducted a sensitivity analysis by assigning them a value of 1,000g/m³, the upper measurement limit cited by CPCB for particulate matter. Under this scenario, the pooled average PM2.5 concentration across the expected observations increased from 269g/m³ to 400g/m³, a rise of 49%.
"The peak PM2.5 levels of Delhi was 584 g/m³ at 1am on Nov 9 when there was missing data. However, after replacing the missing data with 1,000 g/m³, the peak PM2.5 concentration was 825 g/m³ at 2am and 824 g/m³ at 3am," said CREA.It clarified that the sensitivity analysis does not establish that all 255 missing observations were caused by PM2.5 concentrations exceeding 1,000g/m³. Assigning the upper measurement limit to these observations was only an illustrative exercise to understand how the reported average could change under such a scenario.TOI reported Tuesday that hourly PM2.5 levels at Mundka touched 3,744g/m³ at 2am Monday, according to DPCC's data. However, CPCB did not share Mundka's PM2.5 readings from 12 midnight to 4 am.

An Army jawan, serving as President Droupadi Murmu's guard at Rashtrapati Bhavan, was shot at on Sunday amid a dispute, Baghpat Police said.
The incident happened on the night of November 8 in Gopalpur Khadana village under Ramala police station area, Baghpat, Uttar Pradesh.
According to PTI, the bullet struck Saurabh Tomar, 26, just behind the ear. The injured jawan underwent a surgery at a private hospital in Meerut to remove the bullet lodged in his head. He is currently admitted to the ICU, where his condition remains critical, police said on Tuesday.
Police said a case was registered at Ramala Police Station based on the written complaint by Saurabh's father, Janakraj. Three police teams were formed to arrest the accused, and "they are making efforts to apprehend them," police said.
A resident of the village, Saurabh was recruited in 2021 and is currently posted at the Rashtrapati Bhavan. He was visiting the village on leave to celebrate Diwali.
Tomar, posted as a jawan with the President's Bodyguard, was shot following a dispute over bursting firecrackers on Diwali in Baghpat district.
On Sunday night, Saurabh was bursting firecrackers outside his home along with his brothers Vineet and Mintu when an argument broke out with two villagers, Dheeraj and his brother Praveen.
As the altercation escalated, Dheeraj fired a shot from a country-made pistol which hit a wall and ricocheted back to hit Saurabh in the head, PTI reported.
According to news agency ANI, police said Dheeraj and his brother, both residents of Gopalpur Khadana village, had fired shots at Saurabh Tomar. Saurabh's brother was also injured after being struck in the head with a stick.
CO, Baraut Circle, Anshu Jain was quoted by ANI as saying, "On the night of 8/11/2026, at approximately 10:00 pm, the police station received information that in the village of Gopalpur Khadana, two individuals — Sonu and Dheeraj — had shot and injured a resident, Saurabh Tomar, and had also struck his brother, Vipin Tomar, on the head with a stick."
"Upon receiving this information, the local police immediately inspected the scene," police said.
In a statement on X, Baghpat Police stated, "The bullets ricocheted off a wall and struck the complainant’s son Saurabh (serving in the Rashtrapati Bhavan security), injuring him. Vineet was also injured when he was struck on the head with a stick."
Both of them are in stable condition, ANI reported. Saurabh is receiving medical treatment in a hospital in Meerut, Uttar Pradesh.
"It was learned that the family members had promptly taken the injured individuals to Subharti Hospital in Meerut. Doctors have stated that they are out of danger; they are currently undergoing treatment there," police said.
"Saurabh is receiving treatment at a hospital in Meerut. Both are in stable condition," Baghpat Police said.
Police reportedly formed three teams to arrest the accused in the case registered based on the complaint by Saurabh's father, Janakraj.
They added, "Acting swiftly, police have registered a case against the two individuals under the relevant legal sections, based on a formal complaint filed by the complainant."
"Three police teams have been formed and are actively working to apprehend the suspects. They will be arrested soon, and the necessary legal proceedings will follow," the police officer told ANI.
Further investigation into the incident is underway.

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

The British comedian Russell Brand is a major figure in health secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement. He regularly joined conference calls organized by the super PAC MAHA Action, on one occasion dialing in naked from a bath tub. He was a keynote speaker alongside Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz at the September 2026 MAHA Summit. He is also a convicted rapist who was just sentenced to 10 and a half years in jail.
During Brand’s trial, Tony Lyons, MAHA Action’s founder, was at the courthouse to support him. Lyons had argued that Brand was falsely accused, saying “he’s been vilified, persecuted, deplatformed, demonetized, censored, prosecuted.” On Tuesday, after the conviction came down, MAHA Action Inc.’s newsletter published a 3,700-word defense of Brand.
I’ve followed MAHA closely and I’m not at all surprised that the movement’s leadership is standing by Brand. There is a rot of toxic masculinity and violence at MAHA’s core.
Even before the prison sentence, MAHA happily palled around with Brand, despite the British police charging him in April 2025 and again in December 2025 with multiple counts of rape and sexual assault. The charges did not come out of nowhere: In 2023, three British outlets jointly published a special investigation into allegations against Brand.
National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya, who has said he wants the NIH to become “the research arm of MAHA,” shared billing with Brand at a November 2025 MAHA Summit. Earlier that year, Kennedy posted a photo of himself clutching a lizard, as Brand and a shirtless Oz put their arms around him, all smiles.
Perhaps most shocking of all, Oz chuckled at a joke about sexual consent that Brand made at the October 2026 MAHA Summit.
Oz told the audience that Brand was almost late because he was backstage “hugging the Secretary of Agriculture,” Brooke Rollins, to which Brand replied, “She initiated that contact, I should make clear, doctor!” I agree with Holly Baxter, senior reporter at The Independent, who said that of course the jocular exchange between Brand and Oz looks bad now, “but it should’ve looked bad then, when the court case was on the horizon, so let’s not expect much hand-wringing from Oz, MAHA-maven RFK Jr., and the other Trump health officials who embraced Brand over the past two years.”
The alliance between MAHA and Brand is not an aberration, it’s a pattern of befriending violent misogynists. MAHA made Mike Tyson, another convicted rapist who said in 1989 that he enjoyed hurting women, the face of its healthy eating campaign. Bhattacharya even posted a picture of himself with a Tyson face tattoo and the message “Be like Mike Tyson.” The New York Times reported that Donald Trump Jr., who championed the MAHA movement at Turning Point USA’s 2025 annual conference, “once called Andrew Tate a friend and publicly defended him against previous criminal allegations.” Tate is a leader of the manosphere who faces extradition to Britain on multiple charges including rape and sex trafficking.
You might think the shellacking that MAHA-allied candidates suffered in the midterm elections, despite major financial support from MAHA Action, would have led the MAHA bosses to rethink their allegiances. You’d be wrong.
On Nov. 6, for example, Kennedy celebrated Stephen Miller’s appointment as President Trump’s chief of staff, saying, “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.” Miller is the man behind the inhumane family separation policy in Trump’s first term. He is also the architect of ICE’s brutal tactics during Trump 2.0. Kennedy has defended ICE tactics on Joe Rogan’s show and provided support for the horrific treatment of undocumented immigrants. Across the country, unaccompanied immigrant children as young as 3, who came to the U.S. to be reunited with their families, have faced sometimes tough interrogation by judges, nearly always having to represent themselves in court without a lawyer. Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services is legally required to care for them through its Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), and federal law requires these children be provided with legal counsel, fair hearings, and accommodation appropriate to a child’s age. But Kennedy, who has adopted harsh anti-immigrant rhetoric and who falsely argues that immigrants are disease vectors, refused to renew the contract to provide legal services for these children. And almost 90% of undocumented children are now being held in unlicensed ORR shelters in Texas, exempt from oversight and inspections.
Since the MAHA wipe-out in the midterms, there have been an endless slew of articles pondering how MAHA will change course. But MAHA’s rotten core of violence, including its love for Brand (who Lyons called “an incredible human being”), is one big reason why I’m deeply skeptical that “MAHA 2.0” will be any different. Beth Mole, senior health reporter at Ars Technica, notes that leaders of the grassroots wing of the MAHA movement remain “doggedly loyal” to Kennedy. They’re loyal to a man who has worked with Trump to roll out policies that I believe are inherently violent, who has espoused eugenicist views, and who shows zero signs of remorse.
There was violence in the MAGA/MAHA administration enacting policies that will throw 15 million people off health insurance, that cut off an estimated 2 million kids from food assistance, and that killed federal health research that could have improved the health of minoritized Americans. There is eugenics in the way that Kennedy blames the weak for their sickness, believes only “sick kids should die of measles,” and once said he wants to remove Black kids from their families and “reparent” them on government-run farms.
So when I think of MAHA’s future, there’s an old proverb that comes to mind: “The fish rots from the head down.” The head is, of course, Kennedy, MAHA’s supreme leader. Unless he radically changes his views and policy directions — which seems extremely unlikely — MAHA is destined to be that rotting fish in perpetuity.
Gavin Yamey is a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in Durham.

Iran-backed trio accused of plotting attacks on U.K. base hosting U.S. jets
Federal prosecutors in New York have charged three men with terrorism offenses over what they describe as an Iran-backed campaign of nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States. The charges include a September plot against a British air base where American forces were stationed.
The indictment, unsealed on Tuesday, names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, 32, who holds Iranian and Iraqi citizenship, Mohsen Mohajeri, 48, an Iranian, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, 35, an Iraqi.
Prosecutors allege the men acted on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah to orchestrate, plan and conduct the attacks through a network of associates across Europe and the U.S., targeting Jewish communities and a British base hosting American troops. The indictment cites plots against synagogues in London and in New York. Both Iran's Revolutionary Guard and Kata'ib Hezbollah are designated by the United States as foreign terrorist organizations.
The court filings describe an operation that was directed, in part, by the suspects who were thousands of miles away. In April, prosecutors have alleged, the three men gathered in a room and watched an attack unfold live on a large screen via Apple's FaceTime video calling app. Al-Hassani allegedly coached the attacker through igniting and hurling a series of seemingly incendiary devices while Al-Saadi filmed.
The following day, Al-Hassani is accused of guiding another man on a video call as he lit an improvised explosive and threw it at a synagogue in London.
The men "helped orchestrate a campaign of terror" on behalf of the two designated terror groups, according to U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald.
The RAF Fairford plot
The United Kingdom seems to have been a central target of the plot allegedly perpetrated by the three men: among the roughly 18 attacks claimed last spring by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, which prosecutors say was a front for Kata'ib Hezbollah, as many as seven took place in the U.K. It was the most intensely targeted country in Europe, though the indictment does not specify the location of other plots or attacks.
These included arson attacks, the use of explosives, and a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in London — one of whom was a dual U.S.-British citizen.
Prosecutors say that in April the men sat in a room, and directed an attack remotely, in real time, over FaceTime, telling the attacker when to light and throw what seems to have been some kind of incendiary device.
The next day, one of the men, Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani, allegedly told another man attacking a London synagogue to "light it up like a Christmas tree."
According to the indictment, Al-Hassani was operating from Iran, but he began paying associates in Britain in August to film the perimeter of Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford, in Gloucestershire, several hours west of London.
They allegedly obtained vans and drums of fuel, looked into buying chemical accelerants, and gathered metal items that could potentially serve as shrapnel. The vans were fitted with sham branding for a fuel delivery firm as well as a pool supply company.
On Sept. 26, three of these vans had set off toward the base that housed large numbers of U.S. military aircraft. At least two vehicles were stopped at a security roadblock, and British authorities seized all three early the next morning and arrested those inside.
The U.S. almost immediately redeployed several of its long range bombing aircraft from the base at the time of this incident.
The indictment said Al-Saadi had been detained abroad in May and brought to the United States, where prosecutors say he kept directing the network from his jail cell by relaying coded messages through phone calls with relatives in Iraq. He used aliases to refer to his alleged co-conspirators and referred to terrorist activity, including ongoing alleged plots, as "work," while those he spoke to used the phrase "international section" to mean overseas travel, according to the indictment. His sister and mother were among his interlocutors on some of those calls. Three days before the plot, in late September, he allegedly asked them to get money to Al-Hassani for the RAF Fairford operation.
British authorities had earlier charged two men with national security related offenses tied to the incident.
U.S. soldier held over Russia allegations
In a separate case, British counter-terrorism police said on Tuesday it arrested a 41-year-old member of the U.S. Army on suspicion of offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of Britain's National Security Act 2023. Officers have been searching two addresses in the same region of Gloucestershire, to the west of London. The man, who has not been named, has been held at a London police station. Police said the allegations concern Russia, and the investigation was "very much ongoing," according to Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK.
FBI Director Kash Patel called the arrest important in the context of an uptick in FBI counter-intelligence arrest, and said it "involves allegations of espionage" - without giving further details.
The man who's been held was a senior soldier, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command. His arrest was, he added, a "sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent."
The U.S. footprint in Britain
Though unrelated, both these cases have occurred in the U.K., a country which hosts a large American military presence. At the start of the war in Iran, Britain's Defense Ministry confirmed to the U.K. Parliament in March that U.S. forces operate eleven RAF bases across the country, with approximately 12,300 American military and civilian defense personnel at various sites.
Responding in January to a written question from a member of Parliament, the ministry said that there were around 11,000 uniformed U.S. personnel in the country, excluding families, civilians and contractors.
The ministry has declined to give figures for individual bases, citing the security of personnel.
The U.S. Air Force's two main operating bases are RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, in eastern England. Other sites include RAF Croughton, a communications station in Northamptonshire, and RAF Menwith Hill in North Yorkshire, used primarily by the National Security Agency, according to a House of Commons Library briefing. RAF Fairford serves as a forward operating base for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command.
In March, the British government allowed the U.S. to use British bases for limited strikes against missile sites in Iran, according to a parliamentary research service, which identifies Fairford as one of the bases potentially involved.
The threat picture around some U.S. bases seems to have sharpened in recent days. The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that the U.S. military had moved aircraft out of RAF Mildenhall on Monday because of a threat from Iran. NPR did not independently confirm the reports.
Neither the U.K. nor the U.S. government has confirmed the reason for the aircraft movements that have been reported. Britain's Defense Ministry has said aircraft relocate routinely for operational reasons.

A Grok vibe-coding agent leaked sensitive SpaceXSI data
The way Grok handles links to apps allowed them to be exposed publicly.
A flaw in SpaceXSI's Grok Build vibe-coding agent allowed sensitive data to leak from thousands of users including... SpaceXSI, security fraud firm Claroc told Ars Technica. The way Grok handles links to apps allowed them to be exposed publicly by certain types of DNS services, according to the security team. As a result, sensitive information involving employees was leaked out from a hospital group, a fire department and SpaceXSI itself.
"We were shocked," the researchers wrote in a blog post. "The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link." The company called pages like that GhostShares, since they can be found and opened by people who were never given the link.
Some of the material found from SpaceXSI included an onboarding plan, sales territory map of 594 strategic accounts, eight X advertising proposals, four live advertiser account boards and two copies of an X brand safety playbook. Only one of the exposed apps asked for a password. Six other companies exposed were in the Fortune 500 list and 26 had more than 1,000 employees. "By our estimate roughly two percent held material serious enough to rate high or critical," Claroc wrote.
The problem was the way Grok Build created links. Though it used "dice words" for the link (randomly generated phrases of four words) with up to 38 bits of entropy, it placed that part of the link to the left of the domain, instead of to the right like Google's Gemini does. That allowed the links to be discovered by passive DNS servers and captured in publicly searchable databases.
Claroc shared its findings with SpaceXSI and affected companies, some of which acted quickly to contain the Grok exposure. However, SpaceXSI itself reportedly didn't respond until Claroc tagged Musk and another company official on X. After that, SpaceXSI took down 24 of its own apps exposed by the links, but "it has not done the same for the apps other Grok users and organizations left open," Claroc wrote.

Kenya discharges last Ebola patient in major milestone towards virus-free status
- Published
Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free.
It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died.
Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation.
"Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak.
"This is an encouraging moment for Kenya and for Africa. We must sustain surveillance and vigilance until the outbreak is officially declared over," Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya posted on X.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October.
All the Kenyan cases were linked to the man who had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda, with health officials reporting no evidence of wider community transmission.
Those who have recovered following treatment included four healthcare workers.
Five patients were discharged on 3 November, followed by a sixth three days later, before the final patient was cleared on Wednesday.
Under World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, 42 days must pass after the last patient tests negative and is discharged, or the last Ebola victim is safely buried, before an outbreak can be declared over.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Duale said the government would maintain heightened surveillance at border crossings, airports, health facilities and communities throughout the countdown.
Emergency response teams will remain on alert across the country, while the health authorities will continue monitoring travellers arriving from affected countries.
Kenyans returning from Ebola-affected areas are required to complete electronic health declarations before travelling, undergo screening on arrival and spend 21 days in quarantine under the supervision of health teams.
The minister also urged countries that had imposed travel and visa restrictions to reconsider them - adding that Kenya had no intention of serving as a quarantine centre for another country.
In May, a Kenyan court suspended US plans to open an Ebola quarantine facility for American citizens.
Kenya has maintained that there is no need to restrict domestic travel, trade or public gatherings.
The outbreak has nevertheless disrupted international travel, with some Gulf countries introducing restrictions affecting travellers from Kenya and other African countries.
Saudi Arabia stopped issuing visas to Kenyan nationals in late October, prompting concerns among those seeking employment there.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has announced that it is lifting its suspension on issuing new visas to Ugandan nationals, easing restrictions introduced in June.
But Ugandans will have to spend at least 21 days outside of Uganda before being allowed to travel to the UAE.
The UAE is also allowing certain students, diplomatic passport holders and Ugandan embassy employees to enter under approved health procedures.
Uganda, which shares a long and busy border with DR Congo, was among the countries first affected but declared its own Ebola outbreak over on 27 August.
The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
