Sports Personality of the Year returns - with five awards decided by public
- Published
The 2026 BBC Sports Personality of the Year show will be held on Sunday, 13 December - with five winners decided by public votes.
Clare Balding, Gabby Logan and Alex Scott will again host the programme, which will be hosted in Salford and broadcast live on BBC One, BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app from 17:45 GMT.
Five of the nine awards to be presented on the night will be decided by public vote.
The show will celebrate another great year of sport, including Team GB's most successful Winter Olympics, England's best finish at a men's Fifa World Cup since 1966, and record-breaking displays at the European Athletics Championships.
There will be two new award categories at the ceremony this year - Men's Footballer of the Year and BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year.
The latter has been a BBC World Service award since 2015 but will now be presented as part of the BBC Sports Personality of the Year awards for the first time. Voting - for global audiences - opens on Tuesday, 10 November.
In addition to crowning the winners of both football awards, fans will also select the winners of the World Sport Star of the Year, Team of the Year and Sports Personality of the Year award itself.
An independent panel made up of industry experts, sports broadcasters, sports journalists and former sportspeople will determine the shortlists for the Sports Personality of the Year, Team of the Year and World Sports Star awards, with the winners chosen by public votes. The independent panel will also determine the winners of Young Sports Personality of the Year and Coach of the Year.
Separate panels of football experts will provide the shortlist of contenders for Men's Footballer of the Year and Women's Footballer of the Year.
Alex Kay-Jelski - director of BBC Sport - said: "What I love about BBC Sports Personality of the Year is that it brings together all those moments that stopped us in our tracks. The goals, the medals, the upsets, the records, the stories that had us talking at work, in the pub and around the dinner table.
"And what a year we've had. This year's shortlists will be packed with athletes and teams who have achieved extraordinary things, but what's especially exciting is that audiences will have a bigger say than ever before in who takes home the trophies."
The nine award categories are:
- BBC Sports Personality of the Year
- Helen Rollason Award
- Young Sports Personality of the Year
- Coach of the Year
- Team of the Year
- Lifetime Achievement award
- Men's Footballer of the Year
- Women's Footballer of the Year
- World Sport Star of the Year
Full voting details, dates and T&Cs will be announced in due course.

Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”
Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.
“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.
Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.
Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.
“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.
During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.
“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”
Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.
Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.
For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?
“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”
Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.
“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.
On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.
“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.
However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.
“No woman in the city is fully free,” Sinha says.
Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”
In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.
“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.
Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.
“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”
Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.
Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.
But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

India, Norway explore joint technology to turn industrial waste into construction material
The discussions follow the elevation of India-Norway relations to a Green Strategic Partnership during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Norway in May.
India and Norway are exploring joint research and technology initiatives to convert industrial and construction waste into valuable resources, with a focus on sustainable building materials, hazardous waste treatment and a circular economy.
The initiative was discussed at the India-Norway Dialogue on “Waste to Resource Solutions in the Cement and Construction Sector”, organised jointly by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), Norway’s research organisation SINTEF and the Research Council of Norway at the India Habitat Centre on Tuesday.
The dialogue brought together scientists, regulatory authorities and representatives of the cement and construction industries to identify opportunities for bilateral research and technology development.
The discussions follow the elevation of India-Norway relations to a Green Strategic Partnership during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Norway in May, with circular economy, clean technology and scientific research identified as key areas of cooperation.
India stresses circular economy, C&D waste potential
Addressing the inaugural session, CSIR-CBRI director R Pradeep Kumar emphasised the need to move from a linear to a circular economic model by converting construction and industrial waste into usable resources.
Kumar highlighted the potential of construction and demolition (C&D) waste, steel slag, fly ash, and red mud, while underlining challenges related to processing technologies, standardisation, economic viability, and market acceptance.
A key technical session examined the use of cement kilns for the environmentally safe treatment of hazardous waste, including persistent organic pollutants (POPs) and materials contaminated with DDT and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).
SINTEF chief scientist Kåre Helge Karstensen and CSIR-NEERI scientist Ramesh Kumar discussed how cement kilns, operating under controlled high-temperature conditions, could destroy hazardous organic contaminants while replacing conventional fossil fuels with waste-derived alternatives. The experts stressed the importance of emission monitoring, regulatory compliance and controlled industrial trials.
Research presented by CSIR-CRRI and CSIR-AMPRI highlighted the potential of fly ash, copper slag, red mud, plastic waste and steel grit in road construction, geopolymer concrete and specialised construction products.
Another session, led by SINTEF’s Christian John Engelsen, examined international practices in C&D waste recycling, including mobile recycling units and techniques to improve the quality of recycled aggregates.
The dialogue identified two to three joint India-Norway research proposals, pilot projects for hazardous waste treatment, technical guidelines for DDT- and PCB-contaminated waste and industry-academia partnerships as priority areas.
The initiative aims to accelerate the adoption of resource-efficient technologies in India’s cement and construction sectors.

AI unicorn Sarvam has appointed former Google Cloud India managing director Sashikumar Sreedharan as its president and chief business officer (CBO), as it looks to strengthen its enterprise and government business and scale the commercial deployment of its AI technology. In his new role, Sreedharan will lead Sarvam's business across enterprises and government institutions while expanding its engagement with digital-native companies, developers and partners. He will also oversee marketing, finance, forward-deployed engineering, service delivery and commercial operations, the company said in a blog post. Sreedharan will also join the company's board of directors. Before joining Sarvam, Sreedharan served as MD of Google Cloud India for over a year. Across a career spanning about 35 years, he has served across companies like Microsoft India, IBM, Wipro, Happiest Mind Technologies, among others. His appointment comes as Sarvam looks to move beyond developing indigenous AI models and build a larger enterprise business around its technology. The startup said it provides its full-stack AI offerings to over 100 enterprises and government institutions. “The next phase of Sarvam is about advancing our research, developing products loved by people around the world, and building a company that can operate at a much greater scale,” the startup said. Sarvam AI's Push To Build The India Stack Founded in 2023 by Pratyush Kumar and Vivek Raghavan, Sarvam develops foundational AI models, computing infrastructure, and enterprise applications. Its offerings target businesses and government agencies seeking tools tailored to Indian languages, data-security requirements, and local use cases. The new CBO appointment comes shortly after Sarvam expanded its AI portfolio with the launch of Prism. The "System One" decision model built on top of Sarvam AI's Sarvam 105B foundation model. Rather than generating open-ended text token-by-token like a conventional LLM, it evaluates a given context, a question, and a predefined list of options in a single processing pass to return calibrated probabilities for each choice. The startup has also released several other models in recent months, including Sarvam Vision 2.1, a vision-language model for processing documents and recognising text in Indian languages, and Saaras V4, its speech-to-text model. In October, it launched Bulbul V4 Flash, a text-to-speech model for generating natural speech across Indian languages. Earlier this year, Sarvam raised $234 Mn in the first close of its $300 Mn Series B funding round, which valued the company at $1.5 Bn. The unicorn minting round saw participation from investors HCLTech, Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners. It is now reportedly in talks with Nasdaq-listed IT services company Cognizant Technology Solutions to raise further funds for the round. It is looking to raise around $300 Mn at a valuation of around $3.5 Bn to $4 Bn.

Listed NBFC Kissht has secured board approval to raise up ₹832.2 Cr via a preferential issue of equity shares to 34 investors and entities. In a filing with the exchanges, the company said that its board has approved the issuance of 2.6 Cr fully paid-up equity shares to the investors at an issue price of ₹314.11 apiece. The NBFC did not disclose how it plans to utilise the fresh proceeds from the issue. The allotment is still subject to regulatory and shareholder approval. The company has also convened an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders to seek approval for the preferential issue. “Funds raising by way of a preferential issue on a private placement basis of up to 2,64,93,882 fully paid-up equity shares of the company… for cash, at an issue price of ₹314.11 per share… for an amount aggregating to ₹832.19 Cr to identified investors (non-promoters), in accordance with the provisions of… applicable laws….,” read the filing. Among the investing companies, Axis Flexi Cap Fund, Axis Multi Cap Fund and Axis Small Cap Fund together will receive 63.7 Lakh shares worth nearly ₹200 Cr. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, via two entities, will also receive 27.1 Lakh shares totalling ₹85 Cr. Envision Capital will also get 12.7 Lakh shares valued at nearly ₹40 Cr, while PE firm First Bridge will lap up 12.1 Lakh shares for a sum of ₹20 Cr. Kissht will also allot 23.9 Lakh shares to three entities linked to Ashoka WhiteOak Capital for a consideration of nearly ₹75 Cr. Other investors that will receive allotment under the preferential issue include 360 One, Alchemy Capital, Groww, Bandhan Small Cap Fund, Unity Small Finance Bank, among others. In terms of the other individual investors, Ameeta Rajendra Naik will receive 63,671 shares worth ₹2 Cr and Anil Shah will get 1.6 Lakh shares valued at nearly ₹5 Cr. The latest fundraise comes barely four months after the NBFC made a strong debut on the exchanges, listing at a premium of 11.7% on the BSE compared to its issue price of ₹171. Its public issue comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹850 Cr and an OFS component totalling ₹76 Cr. Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a lending tech platform that offers digital personal and business loans of up to ₹5 Lakh. It also offers health-related insurance products and secured loans through loans against property. In July, it also received regulatory approval to begin distribution of mutual funds through its wholly-owned subsidiary Invincible Minds. The NBFC claimed to have 45+ active lending and co-lending partners under its belt at the end of June 2026. It also operated 101 offline branches across eight states and union territories, and managed to more than double YoY its active customer base to 3.49 Mn in Q1 FY27. On the financial front, Kissht’s consolidated net profit zoomed 59% to ₹95.1 Cr in Q1 FY27 as against ₹59.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed nearly 45% to ₹669.5 Cr during the quarter under review as against ₹463.1 Cr in Q1 FY26. Shares of the NBFC closed Thursday’s trading session 5.08% higher at ₹359.7 on the BSE.

How to get this Siri camera upgrade for your iPad before its public release
You’ll be able to access Visual Intelligence from a new tab in the tablet's Camera app.
Apple users willing to install beta versions of its OS updates can get their hands on upcoming features sooner than most, as long as they're comfortable contending with the possibility of buggy software or apps breaking. And one such feature is the Siri Mode that's already available in the camera app on supported iPhones. It's also coming to compatible iPads as part of iPadOS 27.3 and will let you ask Siri AI questions about things you point your tablet's camera at.
We got our first look at this mode when Apple properly unveiled Siri AI at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June this year. It basically brings the company's Visual Intelligence tool for asking questions from photos to the camera app. But there's one distinguishing feature that's unique to iPads which isn't available on iPhones.
On iPads, Visual Intelligence includes Apple Pencil support. So, much like with Google's Circle to Search feature, you can snap a photo of something with your iPad, use your Apple Pencil to draw a circle around an item and learn more information about the object with the help of Siri AI.
It's worth noting that Visual Intelligence is already available on compatible tablets — iPad Pro and iPad Air with the M1 chip and newer, and iPad mini with the A17 Pro or A20 Pro chipset. As things stand, you can access it in the Camera app by long-pressing the Camera Control button or pressing the Action button if you've set it up to activate the feature (and your iPad has an Action button, of course).
In iPadOS 27.3, you'll have another way to access Visual Intelligence in the Camera app. All you'll have to do is swipe through the options in the viewfinder (i.e. photo, video and portrait modes) until you get to the Siri tab.
The company is expected to release the public version of iPadOS 27.3 in December. However, you can try it on your tablet right now, because Apple released the first beta in early November.
How to install the iPadOS 27.3 beta
To install the iPadOS 27.3 beta, open the Settings app on your iPad, then tap General > Software Update. If you haven't already done so, you'll need to enable beta updates. Tap the Beta Updates option, then iPadOS 27 Public Beta. After you go back to the Software Update tab, you should be able to install the iPadOS 27.3 beta.
Before you install the beta, it's best to create a full backup of your iPad using iCloud, a Mac or a Windows PC. Beta builds aren't the finished product, meaning they're more susceptible to bugs and errors. Backing up your data should be standard practice anyway, but it's especially advisable to do that before installing a beta version of an operating system, just to make sure your files and other information stay safe.
If you don't feel comfortable enough to install a iPadOS beta, that's perfectly fine! The public version of the OS update is likely coming soon. You can check out the Siri tab on your iPad's Camera app at that point.

Pope Leo XIV wrapping up Argentina visit before an emotional trip back to Peru, his adopted homeland
Pope Leo XIV is wrapping up his visit to Argentina with two poignant moments
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV told inmates at an Argentine prison with a dark history tied to the military dictatorship that there is always hope for redemption and reconciliation, as he spent his final morning in Argentina on Wednesday offering an uplifting message to a polarized country.
Leo visited Devoto Prison before celebrating his final Mass at Argentina’s national shrine, the Basilica de Nuestra Señora de Luján, where 1 million people were expected — the latest of the record-setting crowds that have welcomed Leo on the first papal visit to Argentina in nearly four decades.
Both sites have important sentimental connections to Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, who never returned home during his 12-year pontificate. But Leo’s final stops in Argentina pale in comparison to the emotional highlight of his South American trip, when he returns to his adopted homeland of Peru later Wednesday.
A massive national party is planned to greet the Chicago-born Leo, who spent more than two decades as a missionary priest and bishop in Peru and holds dual citizenship in the United States and Peru. He’s known to Peruvians as Padre Robert and beloved for ministering to poor communities, especially in times of crisis.
In Buenos Aires, Leo visited Devoto Prison, where Francis often ministered as the city’s archbishop, celebrating Mass, going into cellblocks housing inmates with AIDS and washing prisoners’ feet during the annual Holy Week ritual.
The prison, inaugurated in 1927, is being shut down permanently, with its more than 1,000 inmates moving to a new penitentiary complex. Only about 75 prisoners were on hand for Leo’s visit, chosen primarily because they were active in the prison’s religious programming, said the prison chaplain, the Rev. Matías De Martini.
Wearing identical white uniforms, they sat in rows in the prison gymnasium, facing a stage bearing the flags of Argentina and the Holy See, and a statue of the Virgin of Luján, which Francis had gifted to the prison during his years as archbishop.
The prison is grim and shows its age. Its corridors were dank, and harsh fluorescent light glinted off the worn bars dividing each wing. Red fire extinguishers lined the main hallway, and guards stood at attention, some holding plastic riot shields.
Leo heard stories from inmates of lives marked by drug addiction, crime and homelessness. He told them that their “troubling realities” are all too familiar.
“The sense of omnipotence produced by drugs, the false power that comes from easy money, the cowardly sense of security that comes from inflicting violence upon the weakest, and the impunity that results from corruption,” he said.
He urged them to use their time in prison, and the limitations they face, as a chance for redemption.
“The evil that assails the human heart wreaks havoc on society and on the lives of many people, sometimes reaching extremes of inhumanity,” he said. But he said that a light continues to shine.
“This means that even amid the evil, pain and deepest failures you may have experienced or caused, your present circumstances can become an opportunity to begin your lives anew,” he said.
Leo didn’t refer explicitly to the prison’s dark history, but his reference to impunity and corruption could be seen as directed not just at the current inmates and prison administrators but at past eras as well.
During Argentina’s last military dictatorship (1976–1983), Devoto functioned as a clandestine detention and torture center. It was designated a Memory Site in 2012 to ensure the military repression isn’t forgotten.
Human rights lawyers have petitioned the courts to block any sale or disposal of the prison’s land and facilities once all inmates are transferred, saying “the space must be preserved until the investigations regarding the crimes against humanity that occurred” there are finalized.
In 1978, during Argentina’s military dictatorship, 65 inmates held on ordinary criminal charges were killed at Devoto in what became known as the Seventh Pavilion Massacre. The military government described the killings as a riot and covered them up.
Nearly a half-century later, in December 2025, a federal court found that 153 inmates had been tortured, including the 65 who died in a fire that broke out as guards violently cracked down on the prisoners, and called the events grave human rights violations. It sentenced two former prison chiefs, Juan Carlos Ruiz and Horacio Martín Galíndez, to 25 years in prison. Both men were over 90.
Leo has carried on Francis’ practice of meeting inmates on his foreign trips, reminding them that they aren’t alone and remain beloved children of God. Leo’s last such visit, to a prison in Equatorial Guinea, produced some of the most chilling moments of his pontificate, when inmates were forced to sing and dance for him in pouring rain.
For Francis, that ministry began at Devoto, De Martini said.
“As pope, you’ll remember he sometimes said, ‘Whenever I walk into a prison, I always think, why them and not me?’” he said. “Well, that’s what he always said here. Everything he talked about as pope, he lived in this prison.”
After the prison visit, Leo was to make a pilgrimage to the Basilica de Nuestra Señora de Luján, dedicated to Argentina’s patron saint.
The municipality of Luján, about 72 kilometers (45 miles) northwest of Buenos Aires, urged pilgrims to arrive days in advance because of the sheer scale of the event and the extensive security and logistical deployment.
The basilica hosts one of the greatest demonstrations of faith in Argentina. Each October, hundreds of thousands of pilgrims walk there from Buenos Aires and nearby towns to give thanks or make requests to the Virgin of Luján, to whom Francis was particularly devoted. This year, despite persistent rain, more than 2.8 million people took part, a record for the shrine, municipal authorities said.
During the Mass, the bread and wine will be carried to the altar by community volunteers, among them Sara Ramírez, who works with young people in a poor neighborhood in Santa Fe province where she said hundreds of families lack drinking water.
“With these hands that I use to show my brothers and sisters that it’s possible to get ahead, I’ll bring the offerings to the pope,” she said.
Many of the pilgrims waiting outside the basilica hoped Leo’s call for unity would ease Argentina’s bitter political divide.
“I know it’s hard to move politicians,” said Enrique González, 47, who coordinates Hogar de Cristo addiction recovery centers in Patagonia. “But I think the pope strikes a chord on both sides, and that starts to change something.”

Apple is shutting down its online Support Community on November 20
It’ll remain online, but it will no longer accept new posts.
If you ever want to ask fellow Apple users anything about the company's devices in the future, you'll have to go on social media websites. The company is permanently shutting down the official Apple Support Community. As MacRumors has noticed, Apple posted a message on the community home page, which says that it's closing down on November 20. While the support website is still up, you can no longer post in it, and it's only available in a read-only state.
The community has gone through several changes over the years since it debuted in 1998. It was known as Apple Discussions for a time, before it was renamed to its current one. User responses on the Support Community are typically some of the first results to pop up whenever you search for technical issues you need an answer to or for instructions on how to use a particular feature. Some of those responses are helpful, but some are admittedly not. In its announcement, Apple says "you can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site."
In a statement, Apple told MacRumors that it decided to shut down down the Support Community "after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs." Maybe the community has just outlived its usefulness. Since people have other places online they can go to when seeking advice from other users anyway, Apple may have decided it was time to let the discussions forum go.

New Indian mega library rocked by scandal over 'AI-generated books'
- Published
An Indian court has ordered an investigation into allegations that a public library in the southern state of Tamil Nadu bought hundreds of books suspected of being generated using AI.
The controversy began after Tamil novelist Perumal Murugan raised concerns about books containing false information and questionable authorship at a newly opened library in Coimbatore city.
The Madras High Court has ordered the state's anti-corruption agency to investigate the purchases and freeze bank accounts linked to a publisher accused of supplying the books.
The state government has blamed the previous Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party-led administration for buying the books. The DMK denies allegations.
Tamil Nadu's School Education Minister A Rajmohan has described the allegations as potentially "India's first AI scam" and said the investigation would cover purchases at other public libraries across the state.
The case has raised wider questions about the growing use of AI in publishing, where tools can generate entire books quickly and cheaply, but also produce false information and invented references.
It has also highlighted the challenges facing libraries and publishers in checking the authenticity of books as AI-generated content becomes more widespread.
The controversy centres on the Periyar Arivulagam library, built at a cost of about 3bn rupees ($34m; £26m). Named after social reformer Periyar EV Ramasamy, it was inaugurated on 16 October by Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay.
Murugan, whose novels Pyre and One Part Woman have received international recognition, raised concerns after visiting the library last month.
Writing in an online magazine, he alleged that nearly 1,800 books in its Tamil section had been supplied by a little-known publisher called Agal Vilakku Pathippagam.
He said many of the books carried unfamiliar authors' names, unusually high prices and questionable International Standard Book Numbers (ISBNs).
One book cited in the controversy, Naladiyar Vaazhvin Vazhikatti (A Guide to Life through Naladiyar), was reportedly priced at 1,445 rupees for 300 pages.
It describes Naladiyar as a Tamil poet and philosopher, although Naladiyar is a classical Tamil work consisting of 400 four-line verses on morality and ethics.
Another book reportedly attributes the ancient Tamil poem Madurai Kanchi to an incorrect author. It remains unclear whether AI was used to produce any of the disputed books.
Questions have also been raised about a book found at another public library in Madurai which names renowned economist Jean Drèze as its author.
The book, Democracy and People's Rights in the Contemporary World, names renowned economist Jean Drèze as its author and was published by Phoenix Publishing House.
Drèze did not respond to BBC Tamil's request for comment but told The Hindu newspaper earlier this week that he had not written the book, raising concerns that his name may have been used without his permission.
BBC Tamil visited a Chennai address listed by Agal Vilakku and another publisher named in the controversy, Phoenix Publishing House, but found no signs identifying either business.
A woman at the address confirmed that Agal Vilakku operated there. Its proprietor, Mohan, declined to comment, saying the matter was before the courts.
The controversy has prompted writers, academics and publishers to question how the books were selected for public libraries.
More than 160 writers, researchers, artists and publishers have signed a joint statement calling for an independent inquiry, the release of procurement records and an audit of library collections across Tamil Nadu.
They have also called for the recovery of public money if the investigation finds that funds were misused.
The group questioned how the disputed books could have passed through a selection process involving expert committees, price negotiations and several levels of review.
The state government has ordered an internal audit of public library collections.
Rajmohan said 523 books had already been removed from the historic Connemara Public Library in Chennai city after preliminary checks raised concerns about their authenticity and quality.
Disputed books have also been removed from Periyar Arivulagam, while anti-corruption officials examine procurement records and inspect other libraries, he added.
The controversy also sparked a political row in Tamil Nadu. Rajmohan accused the previous DMK government of ordering the disputed books and said the state would seek to recover public money if the investigation found wrongdoing.
The DMK has rejected the allegations as politically motivated and has called for an investigation into the purchases.

Legally restrict heading a football in training, says MP
- Published
An MP is calling for legal safeguards to limit repetitive heading in football training, amid growing concerns about the risk of brain injury.
Grahame Morris, the Labour MP for Easington, submitted a parliamentary motion on Tuesday urging the government to take action to reduce the number of times a player can head the ball in training.
Researchers have found footballers are three and a half times more likely to die from a neurodegenerative disease than the general population.
The Early Day Motion (EDM) describes the need to protect players' brain health as a "significant public health and player welfare issue".
"The aim of this EDM is to raise awareness of the growing body of evidence linking repeated head impacts, particularly from heading a football, to an increased risk of neurodegenerative disease," Morris told BBC Sport.
The motion encourages the government "to take a more active role in prevention, education and player protection" Morris added.
Morris's motion supports a national petition submitted in September by the charity Head Safe Football, and calls on the government to take a number of actions:
- Impose legal limits on repetitive heading in football training
- Establish a cross-departmental task-force involving medical experts, players representatives, campaign groups and football authorities to develop "enforceable heading safeguards"
- Recognise chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) as a public health concern
- Create a national action plan to protect players' brain health
- Improve education and awareness of the risks associated with heading, including in schools and through the PE national curriculum
EDMs are seen as a means for MPs to express their opinion on a subject and to canvass support for their views. No matter how many MPs sign up to an EDM there is no guarantee that it will be debated in Parliament.
'Guidance is not enough'
Football does already have restrictions around heading.
The Football Association has phased out deliberate heading in grassroots football matches for children aged 11 and under.
It has also issued guidance recommending limits on heading during training of no more than 10 headers per week at amateur level.
In the professional game in England, clubs have been advised to limit players to 10 "high force" headers a week in training.
Scotland has gone further, banning heading in training on the day before and after matches in the professional game.
However, campaigners such as Dr Judith Gates, founder of Head Safe Football, believe that voluntary guidance is not enough.
"What we are finding is that coaches and parents don't know of the guidance, or the ban. Or they do not know why it exists," she told BBC Sport.
"There needs to be greater clarity and greater specific restrictions in order to protect players of today and tomorrow."
Dr Gates, whose husband the former Middlesbrough player Bill died with CTE, a degenerative brain disease associated with repeated head impacts, accepts that enforcing a legal limit would be challenging.
Prime Minister joins calls for compensation scheme
The calls for greater protection came as Prime Minister Andy Burnham called, in an interview with the Telegraph,, external on English football to formally recognise the game's dementia crisis and establish an "industrial injuries" compensation scheme for former players.
In a statement to BBC Sport, he said: "I've spoken to families affected by dementia and brain injury and heard what they have been through.
"Their determination to get this issue taken seriously has been extraordinary, and they should never have had to fight so hard to be heard."
Burnham's intervention follows inquests into the deaths of former England World Cup winner Nobby Stiles and Scotland defender Gordon McQueen, which found repetitive heading had contributed to their deaths.
The Professional Footballer's association (PFA) and the Premier League set up a brain health fund which has provided about £1m annually since 2023. However, campaigners say this is not enough to meet the costs of care.
The Football Association has not financially contributed to the fund, but said it continued to invest in research and had introduced guidance across professional and grassroots football.
"While the link between heading in football and long-term brain health remains the subject of ongoing scientific and medical research, we have consistently been at the forefront of efforts to help improve the safety of our game," an FA spokesperson said.

Religion no bar: Bombay High Court backs 21-year-old woman's choice of husband
The Bombay High Court granted relief to a Hindu woman seeking protection after marrying a Muslim man. The bench reaffirmed an adult woman's freedom to choose her partner without force or pressure.
The Bombay High Court has reaffirmed that an adult woman has the freedom to choose her life partner irrespective of religion, caste or faith, while granting relief to a 21-year-old Hindu woman who married a Muslim man and sought police protection over alleged threats from her family.
A vacation bench of Justices Advait M Sethna and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale was hearing a criminal writ petition filed by a woman who approached the court seeking protection to live with her husband.
The woman told the court that she had been in a relationship with the 21-year-old Muslim man for the past four to five years, and both families were aware of their relationship. The couple married on October 19, 2026, after which they approached the police seeking protection.
However, she alleged that the Dharavi police refused to take any action. She further claimed that her parents forcibly took her to Uttar Pradesh. After returning to Mumbai, she approached the High Court, expressing apprehension about her safety and seeking protection to reside with her husband.
Advocate R K Mendadkar, appearing for the woman, argued that she was a major and fully capable of making decisions about her life. He relied on the Supreme Court's 2018 judgment in Shafin Jahan vs Asokan K M, which recognised the right to marry a person of one's choice as an integral part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.
Agreeing with the legal position, the High Court observed that an adult woman was at complete liberty to exercise her choice and decide whom she wanted to marry, without force or pressure.
The petitioner's lawyer also raised concerns over the conduct of the police authorities. However, the bench declined to make any specific observations on the allegations, while making it clear that the police must act strictly in accordance with the law.
"At this stage, we do not deem it appropriate to make any observations in this regard. Needless to mention that the police authorities would act within the four corners of and strictly in accordance with law," the bench said while disposing of the plea.

Ottawa had been aware of Stellantis-Roshel talks for months, source says
Automaker announced plans to sell Brampton, Ont., plant to armoured vehicle manufacturer
The federal government had been made aware for months about the possibility that Stellantis would sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to a light armoured vehicle manufacturer, a source has told CBC News.
The automaker announced on Monday that it plans to sell the plant to Roshel Inc., a move Prime Minister Mark Carney characterized as a "betrayal of the workers as it is a betrayal of the obligations to Canada."
A source with direct knowledge of the sale of the Stellantis Brampton plant said the federal government had been engaged regularly on the deal since August. The source said both the Prime Minister's Office and Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's office had been briefed on the details of what was going to be announced. CTV News first reported the government's involvement in the talks.
More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when Stellantis halted operations in 2023 to refit the facility to produce the Jeep Compass.
Both Carney and Joly have blasted the potential sale to Roshel. The minister is expected to hold a meeting of all stakeholders in Toronto on Thursday in an attempt to find a way forward for the laid-off Stellantis workers.
Ottawa didn't facilitate deal: government source
A separate senior government source told CBC News that Joly didn't facilitate the deal between Roshel and Stellantis and that the minister would never have approved of a deal that wasn't supported by the union.
The minister was unable to block the deal before it happened, the source said.
In a deal announced by the former Trudeau government in 2022, Ottawa said it would inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them retool to increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.
The government source also said Joly wouldn't have approved of the deal with Roshel because it would break Stellantis's commitments under the 2022 deal.
That same agreement also saw Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government pledge to support the plants with an investment of up to $513 million.
CBC News confirmed on Tuesday that Ontario has not provided the company with any funding for its Brampton retooling initiative because it didn't meet conditions related to job creation and project milestones.
Ford cautions against Chinese 'knock-down kits'
Ford wrote a letter to Carney on Tuesday, a copy of which has been obtained by CBC News, warning against the possibility that the plant would be used to assemble "Chinese-made knock-down kits" — where a Chinese auto manufacturer imports parts from overseas just to be assembled in Canada.
"We cannot undermine the future of Canada and Ontario’s automotive sector by allowing the introduction of Chinese-made knock-down kits at the Stellantis Brampton facility," Ford wrote in the letter, adding that he is pleased the federal government is aligned on that position.
"The economic impact of introducing kits to Ontario’s automotive sector would be devastating to Canadian automotive workers and to the thousands of businesses and workers across the Canadian automotive and auto parts supply chain."
Ford has come out aggressively against the idea of the Brampton plant being used as an assembly station for Chinese vehicles since the possibility was first suggested in a February report by Bloomberg News. The outlet suggested Stellantis was in talks with Zhejiang Leapmotor Technology, a Chinese automobile manufacturer with headquarters in Hangzhou, China, at that time.
Asked about the Stellantis sale during an unrelated news conference on Monday, Ford again raised concerns about Chinese assembly kits.
"We can't bring in kits from China. Can't happen," the premier said. "That will bastardize the whole sector. Unacceptable. We need them to find a vehicle, a model that works."

"This next chapter is about embracing another part of who I am, falling in love with the journey and discovering what more I'm capable of.

Malaysia's disgraced former PM leaves jail for house arrest after embezzling millions
- Published
Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest.
There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy.
Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund.
The 1MDB scandal brought down his government and made headlines around the world when it came to light a decade ago, embroiling prominent figures from Malaysia to Goldman Sachs and Hollywood.
Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors.
Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large.
Najib's mansion in one of the capital's most exclusive neighbourhoods was declared a federal prison ahead of his homecoming on Tuesday.
Critics said his release from jail undermined efforts to fight corruption and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law made no provision for house arrest.
Najib, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2018, denied wrongdoing but was convicted at two separate trials.
In the first trial he was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal.
In September, the King of Malaysia granted him a conditional pardon to see out the remaining two years of his sentence at home.
The transfer to his mansion was to take place on Friday but put on hold after the attorney general sought clarification of the royal decree. On Tuesday the high court ruled the house arrest was effective immediately.
Najib's party paid a $12m fine as part of the terms of the royal pardon allowing him to serve the rest of his term at home.
He was sentenced after being convicted of abuse of power, money laundering and breach of trust over 42 million ringgit ($10m; £7.7m) transferred from SRC International - a former unit of 1MDB - into his private accounts.
Najib is appealing against a 15-year prison sentence, handed down at a second trial in December 2025, in a case involving much larger sums of money. In that case he was convicted of misappropriating nearly 2.3 billion Malaysian ringgit ($569m; £422m) from the nation's sovereign wealth fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
He is due to start serving that sentence after his house arrest ends, which is expected in August 2028.

Judoka determined to prove refugees belong at Dakar 2026
- Published
Arno Yafunga Botay was six when his family fled the Democratic Republic of Congo after threats to his father's life culminated in an attack on their home which claimed the life of his seven-month-old sibling.
Following a spell living in the Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya, the family settled in Nairobi. There, Arno used to watch his father Arnold practising judo and eventually asked him to teach him the sport.
Now, having coming through trials in East Africa, he will compete for the Refugee Olympic Team in the under-55kg category at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games.
"I didn't expect to be selected," the 15-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"I was so excited. I was crying tears of joy."
This is the first time that a team of refugees will appear at a Youth Games.
"It [means] a lot to me to represent other refugees, represent my community," Yafunga Botay added.
The family have been in Kenya since they were forced to leave DR Congo in 2017.
"There were people who wanted to kill me," Arnold said.
"At the time, I was detained somewhere when people came to our house and attacked my family. The situation led to the death of my child."

After finding safety, Yafunga Botay and his elder brother Christian would watch their father training before he headed out to work as a labourer.
Yafunga Botay began receiving instructions in judo rules and techniques at the age of seven.
However, life in their adopted East African nation provided its own challenges.
"I [did] not have the judogi clothes or transport fees for local competitions," he explained.
"It's been difficult going to school. There's no money for school fees.
"My father has no work. He needs to go to work and give us money to go and pay the school fees.
"And here we don't have support. As a refugee, to stay in Kenya, you need to have documents.
"[Thankfully] the IOC (International Olympic Committee) came with this programme of helping refugees achieve their dreams."
An Olympic first for refugees
The Refugee Olympic Team was first introduced at the Rio 2016 Olympics and Cameroon-born boxer Cindy Ngamba won the team's first ever medal at Paris 2024 when she claimed bronze in the women's 75kg category.
In a double first, the team will now make its Youth Olympics debut at Dakar 2026, which is the first Olympic event hosted on African soil.
"As a refugee, we have a right to compete," Yafunga Botay said.
"A refugee is a human being like other people."
Father Arnold says the team serves as a message of hope to people around the world who have been displaced.
"Being a refugee does not mean your life is over," he said.
"Refugees can also do things that surprise people.
"My message to fellow refugees is don't give up. Keep pushing until the end."
The six-strong team competing in Senegal is being mentored by two-time Olympic marathon champion Eliud Kipchoge.
"He teaches us [to] respect the coach, focus on what you are doing," Yafunga Botay said.
"I promised him I'll bring the gold medal [back] so he can see [what] I achieved."
Discipline and respect
Judo has become a central part of life for the family.
Arnold still coaches Yafunga Botay and Christian, now 17, occasionally serves as his younger brother's sparring partner.
The teenager describes his father as "strict" even at home, with a firm focus on the importance of discipline.
"Maintaining his weight is not easy. He [Arno] has to keep training consistently," Arnold said.
"Judo teaches him respect and helps him interact with others, whether at school or at home.

The owner of the dojo in the Kenyan capital where Yafunga Botay has trained since 2020 says his selection for Dakar 2026 has "changed perceptions" of judo in the community.
"It is helping parents understand that judo is not just a fighting sport - it has real value," Lawrence Karisa Nyundo told the BBC.
"I have received calls from parents who want to enrol their children.
"It is a big achievement for this club that one of our athletes is going to compete at the Olympics. We are praying that he performs well."
After Dakar, Yafunga Botay hopes other refugees can benefit from his experience in the future.
"In Kakuma, there are good judokas.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins on Friday, with the opening ceremony a day later and judo events running from 1-3 November.

Google’s Pixel phones get an update every month, but most are just security patches and bug fixes. The bigger changes are bundled into quarterly Pixel Drops, and one is rolling out today. The update brings a few new things, and many of the Gemini features previously exclusive to the latest Pixel phones will also expand to Google’s Pixel 10 lineup.
The Pixel 11 was Google’s first foray into “Gemini Intelligence” branding, something we’ll see a lot more of going forward. Some of the features under that heading were limited to Google’s newest phones (and in some cases, Samsung’s phones). The November Pixel Drop will expand these AI features to the Pixel 10 lineup, but importantly, that doesn’t include the budget-oriented Pixel 10a.
For starters, the Pixel 10 series will get the improved personalized suggestions (previously known as Magic Cue) that debuted on the Pixel 11. This enables things like sending grocery lists to Google Keep from other apps and generating summaries from the context menu. Rambler, Google’s AI-assisted voice input system, is also coming to the 2025 phones. Likewise, Gemini app automation will roll out on Pixel 10 with this update. This feature is still limited to select apps in rideshare, food delivery, travel, and a few other categories.
The AI-powered icon theming that Google added to Pixels back in March is also getting an update. Initially, this feature just matched icon colors to the system theme when developers didn’t include the necessary theming assets. With this update, Google says it has moved the feature to a more powerful Nano Banana model, unlocking 10 new icon styles for your home screen.

The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN.
 
The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.
Now, two more men fear becoming the latest victims of Beijing’s repressive crackdown against the largely Muslim ethnic group, condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity.
The girlfriend of one of the men said her boyfriend, whose name is being withheld for security reasons, told the Guardian he wanted to go “anywhere else but China”.
Human rights groups said two Uyghur men were at risk of deportation after recently being transferred to an immigration detention centre and they feared Thai authorities may once again give in to pressure from Beijing.
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” she said.
The men had been serving a seven-year prison sentence for offences related to an attempted escape from immigration detention in January 2020. They were part of a group of more than 200 Uyghur men, women and children who were apprehended by Thai police in 2014 near the border with Malaysia after they fled from China.
Since 2014, women and children in the group have been released to Turkey, while the men have been deported to China, in separate batches, attracting criticism from the United Nations and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.
Uyghurs, a Turkic minority mainly from the Xinjiang region in China, have been subjected to decades of oppressive and discriminatory treatment from the Chinese authorities. This has included the incarceration of hundreds of thousands of people in detention camps aimed at stamping out their cultural identity.
Beijing has defended its policies in Xinjiang as being aimed at poverty alleviation and counter-terrorism.
In July, Marzeyya Kasem’s (who asked to be referred to by her Islamic alias) boyfriend wrote to her in a letter that he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back to China. “Sometimes I thought why I’m a human being. What I do wrong against China … no want to go back to China,” he wrote. She shared the letter with a Thai rights group.
The two men facing imminent deportation reportedly pleaded their case to Thailand’s office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday.
Relatives of Uyghurs have said the Chinese government was “paranoid about Uyghurs going to a safe country in large numbers and living together”, and preferred to have them deported.
It is not clear whether China has issued a formal extradition request for the two men. But Chaipruak Doungprapat, Thailand’s national security council chief, told reporters that the men, along with three other Uyghurs who are still in prison, had arrest warrants outstanding in China.
Some have questioned whether criminal warrants could be credible considering that at least one of them, Kasem’s boyfriend, was a minor when he left China. “If they are really wanted for a crime in China, why didn’t China immediately issue a [Interpol] red notice [when they were detained in 2014]?” asked Kasem.
Kasem believes that because Thailand was criticised for last year’s mass deportation, this time the authorities were trying to establish a more credible legal basis for the move.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign affairs ministry said: “The cooperation between China and Thailand in combating cross-border illegal and criminal activities such as smuggling is consistent with the laws of the two countries, international law and international practice.”
A spokesperson for Thailand’s foreign affairs ministry declined to comment.
- Additional research by Rebecca Ratcliffe

Under its new global head Kunal Shah, WhatsApp is looking to expand beyond messaging. In a social media post, Shah said that the Meta-owned platform would focus on making services such as bill payments, financial transactions and international connectivity as seamless as sending a message. Shah, who took charge of WhatsApp earlier this year, said the messaging platform would focus on three broad areas — making communication more expressive, simplifying everyday tasks and using AI to improve user experiences. WhatsApp users could potentially complete tasks such as paying bills, borrowing money and staying connected while travelling without having to navigate multiple platforms or services. “We’re working with financial services and telecom partners so that finishing something feels as easy as starting it,” he said. Shah’s statement signals WhatsApp’s intent to deepen its push into financial services and commerce, building on its existing payments and business offerings. In India, the platform has been expanding its payments capabilities through WhatsApp Pay, although its adoption has remained limited compared with established UPI players. It also outlined plans to integrate AI more deeply into the messaging experience, with the technology expected to help users find relevant information, complete tasks and keep track of bookings and appointments. “The best technology saves you time, so you can get back to the connections that matter,” he said. However, Shah did not specify which AI capabilities the company plans to introduce or whether these would involve more advanced agentic features. It currently offers AI-powered features through Meta AI, including assistance with queries and content generation. WhatsApp's Three Priorities On the communication front, WhatsApp wants to make features such as voice notes, groups, stickers and video simpler and more expressive. Shah said users send more than 10 Bn voice messages and 4 Bn stickers on the platform every day, highlighting how communication habits continue to evolve. It also wants to reduce the number of steps involved in completing everyday activities that originate in conversations. This could involve deeper integrations with financial services and telecom partners, although Shah did not disclose specific partnerships or timelines. The third priority is the use of AI to make the platform more efficient by helping users retrieve information and manage everyday tasks. However, Shah emphasised that these changes would not come at the cost of user privacy. He reiterated that personal messages and calls on WhatsApp would remain end-to-end encrypted. “Whatever we build, WhatsApp must remain simple, reliable and private. These principles we’ve had for years aren’t changing,” he said. Shah's remarks come nearly five months after he moved from CRED to Meta to take over as the global head of WhatsApp. In June 2026, Shah announced that he would step down from day-to-day operations at CRED to join Meta. CRED cofounder Miten Sampat took over as interim CEO, while Shah retained his personal shareholding in the fintech startup. His appointment also marked a leadership transition at WhatsApp, with former head Will Cathcart moving to a new role within Meta. Shah's move came alongside Meta's investment in CRED as part of the fintech startup's ₹8,550 Cr Series H funding round, which valued the company at ₹43,239 Cr post-money. At WhatsApp, Shah now faces the challenge of expanding the platform's utility beyond communication while maintaining its simplicity and privacy standards. India, WhatsApp's largest market globally, has an estimated 535 Mn to 550 Mn monthly active users, with some industry databases putting the figure as high as 853.8 Mn. Globally, the platform has more than 3 Bn users. However, driving adoption of its payments, financial services and other offerings will remain a key challenge.

In a fresh legal challenge ahead of Cult.fit's proposed public listing, the Madras High Court (HC) has issued a notice on a petition seeking cancellation of the CULT trademark registration held by one of the company's subsidiaries. The rectification petition was filed by Deepak Poduval, who cofounded the CULT fitness business in Bengaluru in 2015. He has approached the court seeking cancellation of the trademark registration held by Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd, a subsidiary of Cult.fit, alleging that the documents used to establish ownership of the brand were forged. The court issued notice in the matter (OP(TM) No. 51 of 2026) on October 12, 2026. During a hearing on November 5, it adjourned the proceedings to December 2, allowing Cultfit Healthcare to file its response. Separately, Poduval has approached the Commercial Court in Bengaluru, seeking to have the 2017 deeds that purportedly transferred the CULT brand declared void. He has alleged that the signatures on these documents were forged. The matter is scheduled for its next hearing on November 16. How The CULT Trademark Dispute Began The dispute over the CULT trademark dates back to 2015, when Poduval first applied for the 'CULT – The Workout Station' trademark in August that year. Cultfit Healthcare filed a separate trademark application in November 2016, claiming usage of the brand from May 1, 2015 — the same first-use date mentioned in Poduval's application. When the Trademark Registry raised objections citing Poduval's earlier application, Cultfit Healthcare did not produce the alleged assignment deeds. Instead, it claimed to be the prior user and owner of the trademark in its own right. Poduval has since challenged the validity of the 2017 assignment deeds that purportedly transferred the brand to Cultfit Healthcare. He alleges that his signatures on the documents were forged and has cited a privately commissioned forensic examination that, according to him, supports his allegations. Cult.fit, however, has denied the allegations, maintaining that Poduval signed the assignment deeds. In a statement, Poduval said the dispute concerns the ownership of a brand that has become central to a company preparing to go public. He added that investors deserve transparency about how Cult.fit acquired the trademark. Trademark Dispute Part Of Larger Cofounder Row The trademark challenge is part of a broader legal battle between CULT's cofounders, Deepak Poduval and Rishabh Telang, over the transfer of the fitness business's assets and intellectual property to the Mukesh Bansal-led startup. In August 2026, Poduval filed an FIR against Telang at Bengaluru's Bellandur Police Station, alleging forgery, cheating and criminal conspiracy in connection with the 2016 transfer of certain assets and intellectual property from Cult Fitness Pvt Ltd to Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd. Poduval alleged that Telang forged his signatures on multiple documents used to wind up Cult Fitness, including board resolutions, shareholder consent documents and statutory filings. He also claimed that 50% of his shareholding in the company was extinguished without any consideration. Telang denied the allegations, maintaining that Poduval was involved in the transactions and the subsequent winding up of Cult Fitness. He further claimed that Poduval had received consideration for the transfer. Cult.fit also maintained that the transaction was carried out under appropriate contractual arrangements and that the consideration was duly paid and acknowledged by Poduval. The company added that neither it nor its subsidiary was an accused in the FIR. Following the FIR, Telang moved the Karnataka High Court seeking to quash the case. The court sought responses from Poduval and the state but did not stay the investigation. The latest petition before the Madras HC takes the dispute beyond the alleged transfer of assets, directly challenging the legal ownership of the CULT trademark held by Cultfit Healthcare. What The Dispute Means For Cult.fit's IPO The trademark challenge also raises questions about how Cult.fit has disclosed the ownership of the CULT brand in its draft IPO prospectus. In a written response dated October 14 to a complaint filed by Poduval with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), Cult.fit acknowledged that its draft prospectus did not correctly describe the ownership of the CULT trademarks. The company clarified that the trademarks are registered in the name of Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd and not Cult.fit Ltd. It also undertook to correct the disclosure in its final prospectus. With the subsidiary's trademark registration now under challenge before the Madras HC, the dispute could become a point of scrutiny for prospective investors. Poduval has also questioned the company's treatment of the CULT acquisition in its IPO disclosures. According to his complaint, Cult.fit has described the acquisition as 'not material'. While the draft prospectus does not name the acquisition, the company has made the deeds relating to Fitness First, another brand acquired by the group, available for investor inspection. However, the corresponding deeds for CULT have not been made available, Poduval alleged. The challenge is significant given the extent to which Cult.fit uses the CULT brand across its operations. According to its draft IPO prospectus, hundreds of fitness centres operate under the brand. It also extends to Cult Neo gyms and the company's Cultgear products business. If the trademark challenge succeeds, it could potentially affect the group's rights to use, license or transfer the brand, raising questions about the implications for its operations and brand ownership. Cult.fit has filed its draft IPO papers for a proposed public issue. The company plans to raise up to ₹950 Cr through a fresh issue of shares, while existing investors are looking to offload up to 17.86 Cr shares through an offer for sale (OFS). The total IPO size is expected to be around ₹4,000 Cr.

West Bengal BJP MLA Papiya Adhikari has defended her remarks claiming that bursting firecrackers helps kill germs and viruses, accusing her critics of deliberately twisting her statements to garner television ratings and online views. She later apologised for her comments and offered to withdraw them.
Adhikari said her remarks about firecrackers during Diwali and Kali Puja were based on traditional beliefs passed down by previous generations.
"Whenever I say something, people who oppose me use it to increase their TRP and views. Even if I cough or sneeze, the 'seku-maku' (a Bengali slang referring to secularists and Marxists) pick it up," she reportedly told a Bengali television channel.
"What I meant was that bursting firecrackers during Diwali-Kali Puja night kills germs, as told by our grandmothers and elders for generations. Lighting lamps drives away evil forces," she added.
Papiya Adhikari apologises, offers to withdraw remarks
The BJP MLA subsequently expressed regret over her comments, acknowledging that traditional beliefs may not be appropriate in the context of modern scientific understanding.
"There is an old saying from our ancestors regarding these traditions. In essence, this is a festival of lights - a festival of lighting lamps - meant to eradicate social evils. In the past, through rituals, many such evils were addressed. Now, however, we live in the era of firecrackers, and given how much science has advanced, perhaps that perspective is no longer appropriate," she said.
"If anyone has been hurt, I apologise. I am willing to retract my statement; consider it withdrawn. But the core idea remains: such social evils were - and still can be - eradicated," Adhikari added.
What did the BJP MLA say about firecrackers?
Adhikari triggered controversy at a Kali Puja pandal inauguration in her Tollygunge constituency on Saturday, when she claimed that bursting firecrackers could help cure diseases.
"You will see, bursting firecrackers also helps in curing several diseases," she had said.
She also said Kali Puja would be incomplete without green crackers.
"How can Kali Puja be complete without green firecrackers? We will definitely burst green firecrackers," she said.
However, the BJP MLA added that celebrations would be conducted in accordance with police guidelines.

New Zealand pacer Brett Randell earned his maiden international call up as he was included in the squad for the fourth and fifth ODIs against India to be played at the Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui.
The 31-year-old has 145 professional appearances, including five for the New Zealand A. He recently returned from a County Championship stint with Derbyshire.
Randell is also likely to make his debut in one of the remaining games.
All-rounder Josh Clarkson was also included in the squad.
“There’s been a few movements throughout the series so we’re fortunate to be able to bring in Brett and Josh,” New Zealand head coach Rob Walter said.
There’s also shuffling of the coaching staff with Northern Districts pathway coach Mitch Renwick and S&C coach Corey Mileys joined Walter and Martill Guptill for the ODIs.
Bowling coach Jacob Oram, batting coach Luke Ronchi, and S&C coach Chris Donaldson have left for Wellington for Test preparations.
India currently leads the five-match series 2-0 after no result was possible due to rain in the third ODI. The two-match Test series will start on November 19.

Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows.
The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.
You had one job
Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.
“We were shocked,” Claroc said in a Tuesday post. “The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it. Had the sales team bought a tool for this, it would have sat behind company sign-in, open only to the team. Built with AI, it went live open to anyone with the link.
Claroc notified SpaceXSI of the privacy spill on Sunday. When no one responded, a Claroc official took to X to tag both Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer about the threat. At the time this post went live almost all data remained available with one notable exception: the contents from the 24 SpaceXSI apps. All of them were exposing the information on Monday evening. SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending an email with questions for this article. At the time this post went live, links for all 24 apps returned an “app not found” error.
That's fine for Google Docs, because all the pages are running Google's JS code and Google can ensure it doesn't move data between unrelated documents. Similar for the simple documents shared on Claude/ChatGPT/etc. But it's no good for hosting multiple independent applications that are potentially running arbitrary JS, since even if one application is non-public and properly authenticated with session cookies, any other application could freely read sensitive data from it.
I think you'd need a unique (but non-secret) element in the domain name to keep each application on a separate origin, as a security boundary, and also put a secret element in the URL's path which won't be leaked over DNS.
