Your iPhone Duo can do more than multitask! These 10 quirky apps turn the foldable into a retro computer, cassette player, Nintendo DS, accordion, instant camera, virtual fridge, and even a grilled cheese toaster. Some are free, others paid, but all make clever, fun use of its folding design.
The iPhone Duo is perhaps the most radically different iPhone since the original iPhone. While its arrival was rumored for over a year, Apple finally launched it this September. The phone can fold in half to become nearly passport-sized and can be unfolded to shape-shift into a bigger, tablet-ish smartphone. Ever since its launch, we have been constantly hearing about its multitasking prowess, its computer-like processing abilities, how well it handles productivity apps, yada yada yada…
But all this is pretty basic, something we expect with all new iPhones, or rather flagship smartphones at this point. With the kind of price and specs these high-end smartphones come with, it hardly is a surprise that they can handle power-hungry tasks with ease. The foldable form-factor and the added display real estate make it a different experience, surely. But surely there is way more to the device than the same old tasks and apps? So, we are on a mission to make your iPhone Duo fun, using all that processing and multitasking magic that it possesses.
The result is these ten apps.
They are not at all useful. But they make the Duo a-not-just-another-serious (read: boring) device out there. They add an element to it that we all so need to survive – they make it fun. Got an iPhone Duo? Download! (Note: relax, all of these are optimized for the iPhone Duo)
Table of Contents
Top 10 Wacky and Fun iPhone Duo Apps
| Sl No | App | Price | What it does | 
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tiny Computer | $3.99 | Turns the Duo into a retro PC with vintage keyboards, games, and interfaces. | 
| 2 | Deck Man | $4.99 | Recreates a cassette Walkman with realistic tape controls and sounds. | 
| 3 | MD Vinyl | Free | Turns the screen into a vinyl turntable with spinning records and music controls. | 
| 4 | Fold Accordion | $2.99 | Uses the folding hinge as accordion bellows to create music. | 
| 5 | Delta | Free | Recreates the Nintendo DS gaming experience with dual-screen controls. | 
| 6 | Toastie | $2.99 | Turns the Duo into a virtual grilled cheese maker that works when folded shut. | 
| 7 | TypeDraw | $4.99 | Recreates a paper notebook with handwriting, page turns, and paper effects. | 
| 8 | Snapshots | $1.99 | Turns the Duo into a Polaroid-style instant camera with developing photos. | 
| 9 | Phridge | Free | Creates a virtual fridge you can decorate, stock, and mess around with. | 
| 10 | ChompDuo | Free | Adds six animated monsters whose jaws open and close as you fold the phone. | 
Tiny Computer (USD 3.99): Unfolding Retro computer feels
Imagine getting a vintage PC feel on something as new and pristine as the iPhone Duo? That is exactly what the app Tiny Computer can deliver. Using the half-fold setting of the iPhone Duo, the app turns your phone into a proper vintage computer. The upper half of the screen becomes the display while the lower half becomes the keyboard. You get to choose from ten different computers in total, including the Apple Macintosh, IBM PC, iMac G3, IBM ThinkPad, Windows XP, Amiga 500, and more.
It is not just all show; you can actually use some retro paint apps, run old command-line interfaces, play games like Solitaire, and even type on clicky keyboards. Each machine also hides secret commands and files paired with occasional crashes to make the whole experience even more believable.
Deck Man (USD 4.99): Go cassette crazy!
Another app that brings retro feels to the Duo is the Deck Man. It is one of the most visually appealing apps for the Duo because it essentially turns your iPhone Duo into a 1980s cassette Walkman player. The app uses the unfolded version of the phone as the collection of cassettes in your music library that you can browse. You then “insert” the cassette of your choice into the deck, and once you fold it, the secondary screen mimics the look of a cassette Walkman player.
The app has realistic mechanical clicks, background tape static, and if you fast-forward or rewind it too aggressively, the virtual tape inside can get all tangled and then would have to be untangled manually, just like a retro cassette player. “Tape” this one to your Duo!
MD Vinyl (Free): Spin those discs!
If cassettes are “too” modern for you, then you can go even further back in the music era with the iPhone Duo by installing MD Vinyl. This essentially turns the Duo into a virtual turntable with spinning records and album art. The record design determines the aesthetics of the app. The app allows you to pick and drop the needle to play or pause the tracks. It can pair with music apps like Apple Music and Spotify. It is not a new app and has existed for years, but it attains a whole new dimension on the Duo, adding a vintage touch to the modern audio experience.
Fold Accordion (USD 2.99): Fold and unfold to create music
If there is one app that makes the most use of the iPhone Duo’s form factor, it is the Fold Accordion. It literally turns the hinge of the iPhone Duo into working accordion bellows. When you launch the app, it places the keys on the display, which you can press with your right hand while opening and closing the Duo with the left hand to create music of your own. The app comes with a learning mode which highlights keys you have to press to create something pleasant, instead of getting straight to the chaos of keys. A great way to test that folding mechanism too.
Delta (Nintendo DS) (free): Double screen gaming magic, DS style!
Popular Retro Game emulator Delta has launched an updated version of its app, specifically for the iPhone Duo. The app brings specially designed skins for the iPhone Duo, and the most interesting one of the lot is the Nintendo DS portable gaming console, which interestingly was the world’s first mainstream foldable device. The app uses the inner display of the iPhone Duo to bring a DS-style layout and controls across the displays. The game even enters sleep state when the device is folded, similar to the Nintendo DS. Trust the Duo to bring back the magic of double-screen gaming.
Toastie (USD 2.99): Smartest thing since sliced bread!
Unleash the inner chef in you with the absolutely useless but equally fun app called Toastie. This app turns the iPhone Duo into a – wait for it – virtual grilled cheese toaster. You get 15 seconds to assemble your sandwich, and once you are done, you have to hit the ‘grill’ button and physically close the iPhone Duo shut. You then have to wait, listen to the sizzle, or get a slight peek to ensure your toastie is grilling well. If you open the phone too soon, the cheese won’t be melted; if you wait too long, it might end up getting burned. Once you are done with it, you serve it, and you get a star based on your accuracy, recipe, timing, and so on. Useful? Not. But definitely the smartest thing since sliced bread. Actually, the smartest thing done to sliced bread!
TypeDraw (USD 4.99): Paper-like Moleskine
The iPhone Duo looks like a handy pocket notebook or a passport, and TypeDraw literally converts it into a handy little Moleskine-like notebook. It even comes with a digital thread, just like you find on a notebook, which you have to move or swipe aside to open the notebook (or just open the Duo). You can write anywhere on a page using an Apple Pencil or your finger and can even fiddle and curl up paper corners, as well as choose fonts (you can convert your handwriting into one, if you wish), types of paper, and even plain, ruled, dotted, or grid patterns on paper. And the page turns on the internal display are absolutely paper-like. It is like carrying a real notebook.
Snapshots ($1.99): Unfold to Polaroid
Snapshots is an app that helps your Duo morph into an instant camera. It is one of the very first community-developed apps optimized specifically for the iPhone Duo. When bent in half (90 degrees), the top half of the primary display becomes the viewfinder while the bottom half holds the controls. Once you hit the shutter, the photo captured on the upper half of the viewfinder is virtually printed on the lower half with the same mechanical sound and effect as on an instant camera. Just like with a real instant camera, the photo does not appear right away but takes a few seconds to develop, giving us those Polaroid feels.
Phridge (free): Chill…literally!
This is perhaps the most quirky and our personal favorite app in the list. It turns the iPhone Duo into a – wait for it – refrigerator. When folded, you can decorate the ‘door’ of this fridge with magnets, to-do lists, photographs. And when you open it, you can see groceries and food and drink inside and arrange them. This is when the real fun happens, because you can topple something over, drop a fizzy drink, or break a glass jar or bottle. You can also place your hand in a slingshot to shoot stones at the shelves, or get a sword to slice things in half, if you feel like some chaos. You can only close the fridge when you fold the phone shut, making the hinge integral to its operation. How cool is that? Just chillin…
Chompduo (Free): Jaw-dropping (and closing) stuff!
We all need an app that adds six hungry monsters to your iPhone Duo. Well, we do, anyway. That is exactly what ChompDuo does. When installed, it unleashes six hungry monsters on your Duo that open their huge mouths when the device is unfolded, making the inner display a giant mouth. You can tap on the open mouth to make it bite or drag it to squeeze it shut. When you fold the phone, the jaws close shut with a chomp sound, and a pair of googly eyes appear on the outer display, which can jump when you tap on them. What more does one need on a foldable?

World's fastest ocean liner is sunk to break another record: largest artificial reef
The fastest passenger liner in the world crossed the Atlantic Ocean in less than four days. On Wednesday, it sank in five hours.
The SS United States, launched in 1951 and longer than the RMS Titanic, once transported four presidents, the Mona Lisa and a slate of 20th century movie stars. After decades spent rusting, and facing the scrap heap, its minders settled on a deal to turn the vessel into what's expected to be the world's largest artificial reef off the coast of Okaloosa County, Fla.
Crews removed plugs in the ship's hull, allowing it to fill with water without the use of explosives. After hours of delays, its final moments went quickly. The ship tilted onto its side and dipped below the waves.
The sinking marks a bittersweet coda to the era of gleaming behemoths that crossed the seas in elegant fashion. It is also the latest in an ongoing effort by coastal communities to lure thrill-seeking tourists away from international destinations, one that has so far generated surprising economic benefits.
"For those of us who love shipwrecks and love ships in general, it was way more tragic to see it sitting and rusting away at the dock," wreck diver and maritime enthusiast Karen Flynn told NPR.
Her diving club, the Maryland-based Atlantic Wreck Divers, booked tickets and a charter boat just days after a date for the ship's "deployment," as the sinking is diplomatically described, was set.
"We've dove everything that you can around the world," Flynn said. "This will just be one more unique, new thing for us to dive."
A potential tourism boom
In many ways, Flynn and her club are the exact type of visitor that Okaloosa County is hoping to attract: divers planning to stay overnight who will spend a fair amount of money on equipment, food and lodging during their travels.
The Florida panhandle county has sunk hundreds of artificial reefs, many of which are ships or boats.
"Certainly this is the biggest that we've done," said Okaloosa County tourism director Jennifer Adams.
The United States, which is nearly 1,000 feet long, is now the centerpiece of that watery collection.
Reefs bring in roughly $10 million to $12 million in annual economic benefits for the county, Adams said. She expects that number to climb now, and for the county to recoup its $10 million investment in the United States in "a couple of years."
To fulfill that promise, the liner's transformation was designed to appeal to tourists, marine life and federal regulators, Adams said. Its hull was stripped of toxic materials and bulky components, and the ship itself was placed just over 20 nautical miles from the city of Destin's beaches.
"It should rest at a place where its upper decks … are not outside of the recreational diving limits," said Flynn, the diver.
Panhandle counties now have a claim to several big-ticket ships that could draw tourists. The SS United States joins the USS Oriskany — a 888-foot post-war aircraft carrier sunk by the U.S. Navy off Pensacola in 2006 — and is set to make the area home to the first and second largest artificial reefs globally.
Since 1940, Florida alone has created more than 4,000 artificial reefs, according to a state fish and wildlife commission tally. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration analyzed 2017 data on diving tourism around artificial and natural reefs. It calculated that visits to just a few of those reefs generated almost a billion dollars in annual economic benefits.
Economist Andrew Ropicki, at the University of Florida, says Okaloosa and its surrounding counties have something of a "critical mass" of these planned shipwrecks.
"You can capture more of those tourism dollars than [other areas]," he said.
But Ropicki also warned that an overinvestment in reefing might eventually lead to diminishing returns, as visitor interests shift or they become overwhelmed by choice.
Adams, the Okaloosa tourism director, told NPR plans are already in the works to sink "five or six" additional artificial reefs after the SS United States.
For now, however, she hopes the sight of such a unique ship below the surface of the Gulf of Mexico is enough to draw crowds.
Sovereign of the seas
Wednesday's sinking carries a far more complicated set of emotions for Susan Gibbs. She's head of the SS United States Conservancy — custodian through much of the ship's ill-fated stretch moored in Philadelphia.
"I'm full of a complex mix of sorrow but gratitude and pride and hope," she said prior to the sinking.
Gibbs is the granddaughter of William Francis Gibbs, who worked obsessively on the ocean liner almost a century ago. For a short period, after the end of World War II and before the age of the passenger jet, his creation was the pride of the American transportation industry.
"He would freely admit that he loved this ship a thousand times more than my grandmother," she said.
Now, seeing her grandfather's crowning achievement stripped and scuttled feels "complicated." Her organization sold the SS United States to Okaloosa County for $1 million in 2024, a fraction of its original cost.
But for Gibbs, it's a better fate for the vessel than a scrapyard.
"We felt that reefing was by far the more dignified solution," she said.
Karen Flynn, the wreck diver, agrees. She says even below the waves the ship will still have a sense of grandeur.
"There's something about looking out over that bridge … and seeing the nose of the bow and then seeing just the blue out in front of it," she said. "That is going to be a spectacular shot."

- The claim that Christians and MAGA supporters are planning to protest the 2026 midterm election results at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 3, 2027, is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from an event poster that advertises a "Peaceful protest & Christian unity against the rigged midterms" at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 3, 2027. The event's organizer is Jake Lang, a Jan. 6 Capitol rioter who spent four years in prison before being pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump.
- At the time of this writing, it is unclear whether Lang had permission to hold the protest at the Capitol and who would attend. Though the event poster includes Christian imagery and references, it is unclear whether the event has any connection to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement. It is also unclear whether the event has the potential to devolve into a "sequel" to the Jan. 6 Capitol attacks, as some social media users and Snopes readers speculated.
- As was the case with the 2020 election, there is no evidence that widespread election fraud affected — or "rigged" — the results of the 2026 midterms.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have contacted the Capitol Police, which issues permits for protests at the U.S. Capitol, and Lang for more information about the protest and await replies to our queries.
In November, a claim (archived) circulated online that Christians and MAGA supporters were planning to protest the 2026 midterm election results at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 3, 2027.
One X user who posted about the alleged protest included what appeared to be a flyer for the event, titled, "The Million Crusader Cross March."
According to that flyer, the event described itself as "Peaceful protest & Christian unity against the rigged midterms" and encouraged attendees to "Bring your cross."
Posts about the alleged protest also circulated on Facebook and Instagram (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim. One reader asked whether the flyer showed that "there is another Insurrection planned at the Capitol on January 3rd 2027."
While the event flyer featured in the X post above did appear to advertise a real protest (archived) organized by Jake Lang, a Jan. 6 Capitol rioter who spent four years in prison before being pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump, it was unclear exactly who would attend or whether it had the potential to devolve into a "sequel" to the Jan. 6 Capitol attacks, as some social media users and Snopes readers speculated.
The event's connection to Christianity was clear from its use of Crusader and cross imagery and references in the event poster but it was unclear whether there was any connection to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement. CNN reported in February 2021 that Lang did not vote in the 2020 election despite protesting to overturn the results months later. At the time of this writing, one of the listed speakers said on X (archived) that he would not be speaking at the event.
A Facebook page for the event that listed Lang as an organizer showed fewer than 200 attendees at the time of this writing.
We contacted the Capitol Police, which issues permits to protests held at the U.S. Capitol, to ask if Lang had applied for and received such a permit, and, if so, how many people he had estimated would attend. We asked Lang the same questions. We await replies to our queries.
In the meantime, because we could not confirm the size of the event, its likelihood of taking place or its exact connection to the MAGA movement, we leave this claim unrated.
It is important to note that, as was the case with the 2020 election, there was no evidence that widespread election fraud had affected — or "rigged" — the results of the 2026 midterms.
In a Nov. 10 article, the technology magazine WIRED investigated the possibility that activists on the far right would seek to lure disappointed Republican voters to embrace their groups and ideologies.
WIRED suggested Lang's protest was part of this movement, describing him as a "far-right activist."
Lang organized other protests across the U.S. with crusader imagery before the midterms.
For example, he hosted an anti-Muslim "Christian Crusade" in Dearborn, Michigan, on Aug. 18, in which Michigan Public reported protesters "gripped rifles, chanted 'U.S.A.' and argued with many local residents." Michigan Public reported that the Dearborn Police Department made 22 arrests in connection with the protest.
Lang also organized a protest in Bridgeview, Illinois, in October. The area is also known as "Little Palestine" because of its large Arab American population. NBC Chicago reported that Lang led a protest at the Palestine Fest event on Oct. 4 where protesters "wore military-style gear and held up anti-Palestinian messages."
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Lang crashed a Seattle cat convention to condemn furries.

Nations worldwide have spent the last few years obsessing over bigger models and the compute power needed to train them. However, as models move into everyday products, it is becoming difficult to run AI models faster, cheaper and reliably at scale. This is where inference platforms are emerging as saviours. Now, before we dive into the topic, let’s first understand what inference actually means. Simply put, inference is the process through which a trained AI model uses what it has learned to respond to new inputs, such as questions, images or instructions. For context, when you ask an AI model to summarise a health report or a business document, it uses its existing capabilities to process your request and generate a response. But achieving this is not as simple as it reads. Now, the challenge is that every interaction with AI requires computing resources, whose costs can quickly add up as millions of users interact with AI-powered products every day. This is where inference platforms have found their niche. These platforms deploy, manage and optimise AI models without having to build and maintain the entire infrastructure themselves. In India, companies such as Simplismart, Pipeshift and E2E Networks are building different layers of the inference stack, betting that businesses will increasingly pay for faster, cheaper and more reliable AI. But with global cloud giants and AI providers competing for a share of this growing market, where do Indian startups stand? And what will it take for them to build sustainable businesses? Let's explore in today's edition of The AI Shift… Why Inference Became A Business Problem The need for inference platforms becomes clearer when we look at how businesses are using AI in their everyday operations. After integrating an AI model into their product, businesses want to make sure that it is delivering reliable results at the right speed and cost. Take Apna, a jobs and professional networking platform and a customer of Indian inference startup Simplismart. The company uses AI for tasks such as improving candidate profiles and onboarding employers. The challenge for Apna's CTO, Abhishek Ranjan, is to make its AI faster, more efficient, and economically viable. Apna uses inference platforms to run smaller open-source and proprietary models for relatively simple tasks. As the number of AI interactions grows, even small differences in cost and response time can add up across millions of requests. "But this does not mean businesses need to depend on external inference platforms for every task," said Ranjan, who is also the CTO of Blue Machines AI, a subsidiary of Apna that has built its own inference platform for conversational AI applications. Unlike some recruitment-related tasks, conversational AI needs much faster responses and must be able to handle many users at the same time. Even a small delay can affect the experience of someone interacting with a voice AI assistant. This is why Blue Machines has built its own inference platform, allowing it greater control over speed and performance. Depending on the task, it can use advanced AI models, open-source models or models it has fine-tuned itself. Apna uses an external inference platform when it wants flexibility across models without having to manage the entire serving infrastructure. Blue Machines, meanwhile, offers more specialised requirements around response times and concurrent workloads. Simplismart's examples show how the problem changes by workload. The startup claims it has reduced inference costs by 53% while retaining 99.99% accuracy through model quantisation and latency optimisation for voice AI platform Sanas. When it comes to customer support platform Exotel, Simplismart claims to have reduced inference costs to ₹0.90–₹1.30 per minute from ₹2.10 for a closed-model API, while cutting latency from 1.1 seconds to under 300 milliseconds. The common thread is that inference is not about finding the cheapest or most powerful model but finding the combination of model, hardware and serving configuration that fits the business. Inference Comes In Different Flavours The term “inference platform” can sound like one product, but businesses can consume inference in very different ways. The choice depends on how much control they need, how much traffic they handle and how much of the infrastructure they want to manage themselves. “Inference platform is too generic a term,” said Vishnu Subramanian, founder at JarvisLabs, an AI infrastructure company, acquired by E2E Networks. He pointed to four broad ways businesses can consume inference: Shared model APIs: Ready-to-use models accessed through an API, with the infrastructure managed by the provider. Managed inference: Dedicated model deployments where the provider handles much of the technical setup. Self-managed inference: Businesses bring their own models and decide how those models are deployed and scaled. Dedicated infrastructure: Reserved capacity for workloads that need predictable performance, latency or reliability. The simplest option is a shared model API, according to Subramanian. JarvisLabs' Token Factory, for instance, lets businesses access hosted open models through an API and pay for the tokens they consume. The GPU capacity is managed by the platform, allowing a company to start using a model without building its own serving infrastructure. For businesses with larger or more specific workloads, managed inference offers more control without requiring them to manage every technical layer. Therefore, a startup experimenting with an open model may be comfortable with a shared API, while a high-volume voice application may need dedicated capacity. Similarly, a regulated enterprise may want greater control over its models, data and deployment environment. Why Are Startups Betting On Inference? It is a no-brainer that inference has created infrastructure opportunity, with startups building different layers of the inference stack rather than simply competing to offer more GPU capacity. In India, Simplismart is one of the companies trying to capture this opportunity. The startup raised $14 Mn in Series B funding in October, with participation from NVIDIA, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. Its software helps application companies run AI within their cost, performance and deployment requirements, while also allowing cloud providers to turn GPU capacity into managed AI services. Listed company E2E Networks is approaching inference through both managed and self-managed offerings, while startups like Pipeshift are focusing on production inference for open-source models, particularly workloads where latency matters. Pipeshift recently partnered with Neysa to bring its managed serving layer together with Neysa's sovereign AI cloud for Indian businesses, targeting use cases such as voice agents, coding agents and enterprise copilots. The same fragmentation is visible globally. YC-backed startups are building businesses around increasingly specific inference problems. Hopper, an AI inference platform for voice agents, for instance, focuses on optimising inference for real-time agents and post-training open models on production traces, while RouterPlus is building an inference marketplace that selects models and providers based on a company’s actual traffic, cost and capacity requirements. As of now, the inference opportunity is unlikely to settle into a single category. For Indian startups, it could mean opportunities across low-latency voice AI, open-model serving, sovereign inference, agent workloads and specialised enterprise deployments. Therefore, the white space for the next big opportunity is right there — make that intelligence faster, cheaper and easier to scale. The Weekly Buzz: OpenAI Builds An Emergency Kill Switch OpenAI introduced a new internal safety system this week called Control Room. Think of it as a master emergency brake for every experimental AI project running inside the company. As researchers test increasingly powerful models and let groups of AI agents work on their own for hours or days, the risk of something unexpected happening grows. Control Room keeps a constant watch on all of these experiments. The moment staff spot unusual or potentially dangerous behaviour, they can hit a single stop button and shut the entire job down in roughly 35 seconds. This is not a public product for everyday users. It is an internal tool designed to give OpenAI tighter real-time control over its own most advanced research. In an era when AI systems are becoming more independent and capable of long stretches of unsupervised work, even the labs building them need reliable ways to stay in charge. Control Room is OpenAI’s latest answer to that challenge — a fast, company-wide kill switch that keeps humans firmly in the driver’s seat. Startup In The Spotlight: Vecton AI Founded in 2025 by Himanshu Goyal and Gaurav Mandlecha, Bengaluru-based Vecton AI is building an AI transformation platform for banks, financial services and insurance companies, helping them move AI projects from experimentation to production. Financial institutions handle large volumes of structured data and repetitive workflows, but deploying AI at scale can be difficult because of regulatory requirements, legacy systems and the cost of integrating new technology into existing infrastructure. Vecton AI aims to address these challenges with AI consulting and strategy, process automation, custom-trained models and autonomous agent development. The startup uses a forward-deployed engineering model, with its teams working alongside financial institutions through implementation rather than limiting its role to consulting. It builds production-ready AI agents and machine learning workflows designed to meet BFSI regulatory requirements, with applications across sales acceleration, customer engagement, document processing and intelligent copilots. Vecton AI is targeting India’s growing ‘AI in BFSI’ market, which is projected to reach $9.4 Bn by 2034. The startup’s focus is on helping financial institutions operationalise AI across high-volume processes while navigating the compliance and infrastructure constraints of the sector. Prompt Of The Week What prompts and hacks are CTOs, CEOs and cofounders using these days to streamline their work? Here’s Praveen Ojha, chief technologist at EPAM India, with a prompt he relies on to assess a client’s AI maturity before recommending an agentic AI modernisation roadmap. “I am the EPAM India CTO, working across AI delivery, consulting and presales. I serve as a bridge between our global technology teams and the India tech center, and I lead a team of senior architects to support delivery and consulting. For this, think like an AI modernisation expert. Here is the problem statement: Enterprise clients want to adopt agentic AI, but most don’t have a clear view of how ready they are. Before I recommend a modernisation roadmap, I need an honest assessment of the client’s AI maturity. Here is the client as I see it: . These are the inputs I have: . These are the rules the client must comply with: . First, assess the client’s AI maturity across five areas: business process, data, technology, operating model and governance. Score each one and explain in detail. Then recommend the agentic use cases that should go on the modernisation roadmap. For each one, name the human-oversight point, lay out the ROI logic and show how it aligns with the client’s governance and regulatory rules. Next, separate what stays constant in every assessment from what changes for this client, and turn the constant parts into a reusable Skill with its own instructions, templates and checklists. Finally, list the checks that should run automatically every time the Skill is used.” Editor’s Note: Some prompts may need to be adjusted by users for best results or may not work as intended for certain users.

The World Test Championship match-ups for the 2027-29 and 2029-31 cycles will be proposed, while major men’s events for 2028-35 are set to be submitted for approval during the International Cricket Council’s (ICC’board meetings, which began here on Wednesday.
In all, eight ICC Committees will meet across the four-day programme.
Running from Wednesday till November 15, the final set of meetings of 2026 will bring together ICC Board and Committee representatives from around the world.
“ICC World Test Championship match-ups will be proposed for the 2027-29 and 2029-31 cycles, while windows for all established ICC major men’s events for 2028-35 will be submitted for approval,” stated a press release from the world body.
Discussions will also include the first feedback from the Franchise League Review Group and Governance Review Committee, which were both established at the ICC Annual Conference in July this year.
“The Franchise League Review Group has set out to consider ways to enhance the current ICC sanctioning framework of regulations that further protect and strengthen the ecosystem to address new challenges arising from the increasing number of franchise leagues,” the ICC said.
The Governance Review Committee will report its initial recommendations after being tasked with undertaking a thorough review of the ICC’s governance.

The Task Force for Afghan refugee women cricketers will present proposed next steps for the Development Pathway Programme to the ICC Board.

Indonesia hosts the meetings at a time of significant growth for cricket in the country, with Persatuan Cricket Indonesia making considerable strides in participation, international competition and developing infrastructure.
Indonesia’s men’s team played more T20Is than any other country in 2025, while their senior women’s team made its Asia Cup debut this year and its Under-19 women’s team qualified for the Under-19 Asia Cup for the first time.
The country is currently investing in new facilities, including the development of the Bali International Oval, which is set to host the ICC Women’s T20 World Cup East Asia-Pacific Qualifier in 2027.

Cardiologists have called for a review of a recent order issued by the Director General of Health Services (DGHS), strictly prohibiting the sterilisation and re-use of single-use devices and disposable surgical items used in critical specialties like cardiology and cardiothoracic and vascular surgery, citing issues of patient safety
At the annual conference of the Cardiological Society of India (CSI), Kerala chapter, here on Sunday, the CSI Kerala Chapter president Asokan P.K. said the association would seek a review of the order by DGHS as the exorbitant cost of medical devices and accessories would make crucial procedures such as angioplasty unaffordable and inaccessible to many.
Prathap Kumar N., organising chairman of the conference, said the rising cost of complex angioplasty, particularly procedures requiring multiple specialised devices, had become a major concern. Reimbursement package rates under government-funded health insurance schemes were often inadequate to cover the actual cost of advanced cardiac interventions.
With an increasing proportion of the population requiring advanced cardiac interventions, making complex procedures affordable to ordinary patients was a major challenge. Permitting the regulated re-use of select interventional devices, wherever scientifically proven safe, could help reduce treatment costs and extend the benefits of modern cardiac care to a wider section of the population, Dr. Prathap Kumar pointed out
He said cardiologists had sought a review to determine whether selected catheters, guidewires and other equipment could be safely re-processed under scientifically validated protocols and re-used for patients.
“Patient safety must remain paramount. Any proposal for re-use must be supported by scientific evidence, validated sterilisation, functional testing and strict regulatory oversight,” Dr. Prathap Kumar said.
He called for wider consultation among medical specialists, infection-control experts and regulatory authorities to develop an evidence-based policy regarding the sterilisation and re-use of medical devices, balancing affordability with patient safety.
The order by the DGHS said the practice of re-using single-use devices and disposable surgical items was a serious concern from the perspective of patient safety, infection prevention and control, regulatory compliance and healthcare expenditure. It said such re-use may also expose patients to significant risks, including cross-infection, device malfunction, loss of performance and other procedure-related complications
However, it is a fact that sterilisation and re-use of medical devices, ensuring the integrity of the devices and patient safety, is a common practice in both private and public sector hospitals across the country.
The Cardiological Society of India had in 2017 brought out a consensus document, “Guidance on reuse of cardio-vascular catheters and devices in India”, which clearly endorsed re-use, but set out certain requirements which had to be met for re-use to be safe and effective.
The devices, which can be reused, should be clearly defined, a meticulous process for disinfection and sterilisation followed and its functionality ascertained before use. Also, “an appropriate consent should be obtained where necessary” and the cost saving entailed should be directly passed on to the patient, the document said.
The CSI(K) conference also featured discussions on the evolving roles of drug-coated balloons and drug-eluting stents in coronary angioplasty, leadless pacemakers, laser-assisted coronary interventions, invasive coronary function testing, newer cholesterol-lowering therapies, complex valve procedures and advances in heart failure management.

Revised Maximum Retail Prices (MRPs) of 1,364 anti-cancer formulations have come into effect from Monday (November 9, 2026), a move projected to save consumers an estimated ₹3,540.38 crore annually, according to an official release.
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), functioning under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, capped trade margins on the MRP of 137 anti-cancer drugs based on recommendations submitted on October 17, 2026, by an Expert Committee constituted by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.

According to the Ministry, 85 pharmaceutical companies have reported revised MRPs for 1,364 anti-cancer formulations across 121 drugs as of November 8, 2026.

New Delhi, Nov 11: Dairy major GCMMF, which sells products under the Amul brand, has raised milk prices by Rs 2-4 per litre effective Thursday, citing a sharp increase in input costs.
In a statement on Wednesday, Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation (GCMMF) said it has increased prices of fresh pouch milk by 4-5 per cent in major milk variants/packs across India effective November 12, 2026.
“The price of our largest-selling Amul Taaza toned milk with 3 per cent milk fat has been increased by only Rs 2 per litre (3.3 per cent increase) and Amul Gold Milk with 6 per cent milk fat by Rs 4 per litre (5.5 per cent rise),” GCMMF said.
It had last raised rates in May this year.
The price is being hiked due to a steep rise in input costs of milk production and processing, it said.
GCMMF pointed out that there has been a significant increase in the cost of green and dry fodder, cattle feed ingredients like oil cake, maize and molasses, milk packaging film and fuel during the year.
“In the current challenging environmental circumstances due to low and uneven rainfall in Gujarat, as well as many parts of India, we are constrained to increase the consumer price of milk to pay better prices to our producers and support them in these difficult times,” the co-operative said.
GCMMF said its member unions have increased farmers’ procurement price by 4-5 per cent in the last one year, and a similar revision will further support our farmers.
It highlighted that 80 per cent of the revenue collected from consumers through the Amul co-operative structure is returned to 36 lakh milk producers.
A major portion of the increase in milk retail prices will go back to milk producers, and they will continue to be encouraged to increase milk production, GCMMF said.

A post is being widely circulated on social media (here, here) claiming that Members of Parliament (MPs) in India are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. It also claims that MPs are entitled to toll tax exemptions and free train travel. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Indian MPs are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. They are also entitled to toll tax exemption and free train travel.
Fact: MPs are entitled to free train and air travel, as well as toll fees exemption. However, they are not exempt from paying GST on purchases of cars and air conditioners. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
First, according to the details of benefits available to MPs on the official Parliament website (here and here), each MP is entitled to 34 free single air journeys per year anywhere within India. They can use these tickets to travel with their spouse, relatives, or friends.
Additionally, MPs are entitled to free first-class AC or executive-class train travel anywhere in the country. Their spouse or another accompanying person can also avail of this facility. An accompanying assistant is entitled to a free AC two-tier (2-Tier) train pass.
According to the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) regulations (here and here), vehicles used by MPs are exempt from paying toll fees on national highways. MPs are also entitled to toll-exempt FASTags for two vehicles during their tenure.
However, there is no evidence to suggest that MPs are exempt from paying GST on cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase. Neither the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954, which outlines the benefits and entitlements of MPs, nor any official government notification mentions such a GST exemption.
To sum up, while MPs are entitled to certain travel benefits, they do not receive any GST exemption on the cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase.

Why your Roku might be plugged into the wrong HDMI port
Your Roku might lose a few features if you plug it into any old HDMI port on your TV.
Depending on your smart TV, an add-on media streaming device isn't necessarily essential, but they can still provide a lot of value. Perhaps your TV's processor can't keep up with the latest apps and features, or you might prefer a specific ecosystem. That's what Apple is banking on to sell the 2026 Apple TV 4K, which is now an extremely pricey box at $299.
Roku streamers are far cheaper, but can still come with other concerns. You might be worried about your Roku monitoring what you watch, for example, or the implications of Fox's pending takeover. On a more mundane level, there's an issue applicable to any connected device: getting the best possible performance from your TV.
To do that, it's vital to you select the right HDMI port and cable. It's hard to go too far wrong with Roku devices, but a mistake could still mean getting inferior video or sound.
Picking the right HDMI port for your Roku
The reason it's hard to go wrong is that for the most part, Roku devices don't exploit any features unique to HDMI 2.1 or later, and all modern TVs support at least HDMI 2.0. Standards like 4K, HDR10+, Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision can all work over 2.0, if not necessarily in their optimal form. Optimal would include 120Hz-plus refresh rates — but even Roku's top-of-the-line Ultra is capped at 60Hz, regardless of which port you plug it into.
That's acceptable, since 24fps is the most common playback speed for TV and movies while 30fps is used for news. 60fps content (equaling 60Hz) is common on YouTube, Twitch and many live TV streaming services; any modern Roku will support this. 120Hz would simply enable clearer motion, which is mostly relevant for gaming.
The Roku Ultra does support an HDMI 2.1 feature called Quick Media Switching (QMS). This allows refresh rates to shift up or down seamlessly, like if you're flipping from the 30fps evening news to the 24fps cinematic standard. Without QMS, you're going to run into temporary blackouts when a frame rate shift occurs.
In some cases, only certain HDMI ports on your TV will support HDR standards like Dolby Vision. Or if that barrier doesn't exist, you might have to go into your TV's input settings to flip a port over to the appropriate "enhanced" option. Ports are often set to reduced capabilities by default for the sake of compatibility. But since it's unlikely that you'd run into conflicts, you might as well enable modern functionality across the board. Check your manufacturer's website to figure out which ports support HDR and which menus you might need to navigate.
On sound, cables and similar
Another important point here is that you shouldn't plug a Roku into your TV's ARC or eARC port. While that technology is essential for some audio features like Dolby Atmos, labeled ports are intended for compatible output devices like soundbars, receivers and other speaker systems. If a TV supports ARC or eARC, it's automatically pulling audio from every HDMI 2.x input, regardless of how it's marked.
Along with the right ports, it's also important to choose a matching cable. If your Roku does support HDMI 2.1 features, a 2.0 cable will prevent them from working. If there's any doubt about what you have, HDMI 2.1 and even 2.2 (also known as Ultra96, which is not in wide use yet) cables are easy to find at low prices.
Computers and game consoles should always get priority for available HDMI 2.1 or 2.2 ports, since they can fully take advantage of high refresh rates and VRR (variable refresh rate). Streamers like Rokus are further back in the line, at least until manufacturers start taking advantage of everything newer TVs are capable of.

Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
- Published
A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.
Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.
His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.
Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.
He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.
Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.
When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.
Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín.
However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.
A nationwide manhunt is now under way.
Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.
Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.
However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office.
Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims".
He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s.
Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom.
The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro.
Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling
In northern Ethiopia, conflict pushes a strained healthcare system to the brink
"It was a mess, it was chaos, and that continued for almost seven, eight days. Without (cell) network, without electricity," recalls a surgeon in Ethiopia.
On September 24, a two-year ceasefire between rebels and the Ethiopian government began to collapse. As injured people streamed in from the countryside, this surgeon and his colleagues treated as many as they could at a hospital in Mekele, the capital city of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Fearing repercussions for treating rebel fighters, the surgeon asked NPR not to publish his name.
"The whole emergency (room) was flooded with war trauma patients," he recalls. "The floors were all filled up, there was no place to step."
For the past several weeks, the violence has continued at a steady pace, raising concerns that Ethiopia could again face a civil war. The Ethiopian military has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of backing Tigrayan militants, who have aligned themselves with seven rebel groups in Ethiopia with the goal of ousting Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
After drone strikes in late October killed at least 15 people, including children, the director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, posted on X that the violence in northern Ethiopia "is pushing an already fragile health system closer to collapse."
During the initial outbreak of violence in September, the surgeon in Tigray says he spent days operating on victims of gunfire, drone attacks, and mortar shells. Some were clearly civilians, but others were fighters in uniform. Complicating matters, he recalls, there was no way to know how many patients were coming because cell service and the internet were cut.
"We don't know where they're from — you just go ahead and do whatever you can, you know?" he told NPR.
There had been signs that the war between Ethiopia's federal government and rebel groups could reopen. In May, Tigrayan rebels ousted regional leaders and installed their own. In response, Ethiopia's federal government cut funds to Tigray — including to hospitals run by the regional administration. Doctors, he says, haven't been paid in months.
"It's an open wound, which was never closed, you know. Left for healing and never healed," he says. "I guess now it's infected."
For Tedros of WHO, the situation is deeply personal. He is Tigrayan and previously served as Ethiopia's minister of health. In his social media post, he wrote that hospitals are facing shortages of workers, medicine and ambulances, and that WHO and the U.N. are working to deliver medical supplies to the affected regions.
"As fighting continues, more people are likely to lose access to essential healthcare … civilians must be protected," Tedros wrote. "The most courageous choose peace."
A worldwide worry
Public health experts say targeted attacks on healthcare —– generally considered a war crime —– have become a growing concern in conflict zones around the world.
So far in 2026, attacks on health care facilities and workers in 19 countries led to more than 960 deaths, according to data collected by WHO. While the largest mass casualty event occurred in a Pakistani airstrike on a drug rehabilitation center in Afghanistan, hundreds of people have died in attacks on healthcare settings in Sudan, Lebanon, and Ukraine.
Complicating matters are funding cuts to global health initiatives, including the dismantling of USAID shortly after Donald Trump took office in 2025.
"The continual attack against healthcare is eroding the norm of healthcare being a protected part of conflict," says Lindsey Green, a researcher focused on Ethiopia for the U.S. nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights.
The Tigray war lasted two years, killing an estimated 600,000 people. The majority of Tigray's health facilities were only partially functional, as the Ethiopian government imposed an aid blockade on the region — home to more than 7 million people.
Attacks continued, despite a peace agreement
The government struck a peace agreement with Tigrayan rebels in 2022, ending most hostilities, but attacks on healthcare continued. In August of this year, Physicians for Human Rights worked with the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa to publish a report detailing these attacks.
Of more than 600 health workers surveyed across three regions of northern Ethiopia, 63% reported attacks on ambulances, some as they tried to reach injured patients, and 57% reported witnessing an armed takeover of their clinic or hospital between 2020 and 2024. One health worker in Mekele recalled Ethiopian forces occupying a hospital and placing the uniforms of Tigrayan rebels on the floor and forcing staff to step on them. "Nonsense stuff," he said.
"Armed groups were occupying facilities to take resources or to destroy resources, to destroy machines and equipment, really with the goal of making healthcare harder to access," Green says.
In the report, researchers confirmed targeted attacks on health care workers perpetrated by both rebels and government forces – often as retribution for a community's perceived alliances or against doctors who treated an enemy. But there has been no way for victims to seek justice from either party.
"It's very clear that this ongoing pattern of attacks on healthcare links back to impunity for these violations," Green says.
NPR reached out to Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry and Office of the Prime Minister, but did not receive a response.
Doctors in northern Ethiopia say the one-two punch of a war that specifically targeted healthcare, followed by foreign aid cuts, have left the region without a chance to recover.
A health worker in Tigray counted more than 100 women who died in childbirth over the past year. He attributed their deaths to the dire state of the health system. He spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity, due to fear of being targeted for speaking out.
"They died during delivery because of a lack of medicine, lack of health care providers, a lack of fuel. So the ambulances are not functional," he said.
An independent review of birth data during the Tigray war from 2020 - 2022 showed that the maternal mortality rate per 100,000 live births increased fivefold, compared to prewar data. Researchers in 2022 found that 83% of clinics and hospitals were no longer able to serve pregnant women. Additionally, systemic rape and sexual violence were regularly used as a weapon of war.
"They told us, the people should be punished, because we are supporters of the TPLF (Tigrayan rebels)," the health worker says.
Ayoda Werede, a California-based physician with the nonprofit, Health Professionals for Tigray, says that since the latest outbreak of violence, the Ethiopian military has not targeted health centers. But other unidentified groups have stolen supplies, "including medication, equipment, even mattresses off of patient's beds," Werede says. "This was just the opportunistic vacuum space that was created because of this conflict."
Her fear is that Ethiopia's healthcare system is already stretched beyond its capacity — and as the conflict reignites, injured people will have nowhere to go. The surgeon in Mekele has similar concerns. Many of Tigray's doctors, he says, have already left the country.
"We've lost our sense of being secure," he says. "It's a repeat of what's happened in the past."

This past August, Joe Hancock, a Kentucky plumbing and heating contractor, opened a just-delivered box packed with hundreds of sheets of paper. Leafing through them, he read seven words no small business owner wants to see: “A lawsuit has been filed against you.”
The complaint, from air ambulance firm PHI Health, claimed Hancock was on the hook for almost $27,000 in medical helicopter bills. They were tied to one of his now-retired employees, who needed an emergency flight after a heart attack.
Hancock, who owns Whitehead-Hancock Plumbing, Heating & Cooling, a family-run business in Frankfort, Ky., that has been around for more than a century, didn’t understand why he was being roped into a lawsuit that featured 31 other companies — for medical charges he was never aware of.
“I was terrified,” Hancock said. “I was like, ‘What in the hell is going on here?’”
He’s not alone. The PHI lawsuit highlights an evolving tactic by health care providers in a raging battle over out-of-network bills. Previously, providers targeted health insurance companies to pay outstanding amounts that were awarded through federal mediation. Now, they increasingly are dragging the insurers’ clients — employers — into court, claiming they are responsible for bills that insurers haven’t fully paid or have delayed paying. The practice is introducing a new shock that could further torch the affordability of workers’ health coverage.
“These big suits naming dozens of employers at a time is really an escalation,” said Garrett Hohimer, a vice president at the Business Group on Health. “And it will cause employers to incur expenses that [come directly] out of their health care plans.”
A 2022 law called the No Surprises Act shielded patients from the financial trauma of many types of unexpected medical bills, but it has also given rise to a vast industry that’s driving up costs across the health care system. The law uses an arbitration process to determine how much health care providers should get paid for out-of-network emergency care, like helicopter rides, for people who have some type of commercial health coverage. STAT has reported that providers are winning most of these arbitration awards, which often are far higher than the amounts in-network providers receive for the same services.
Already, high payments tied to this process have added approximately $20 billion in extra costs to the health care system, Georgetown University researchers have estimated. A large portion of those costs inevitably come out of the bank accounts of America’s employers and consequently lead to higher premiums, emphasizing how even well-intentioned health reforms can add to the financial pressure that’s crushing workers and businesses.
PHI Health, a national chain, is arguably the most aggressive company suing employers, which it claims are not “passive” bystanders in insurers’ refusal to fully pay awards. Other regional physician practices have sued some employers as well. But PHI and its army of attorneys have filed lawsuits against hundreds of companies, demanding they collectively pay tens of millions of dollars in unpaid out-of-network claims that it won in the federal arbitration process.
PHI isn’t just suing small, local firms like Hancock’s. It’s also taking legal action against some of the largest corporations — Amazon, Walmart, Eli Lilly, United Airlines, General Motors, PepsiCo, State Farm, and Toyota, to name a few — as well as unions, counties, cities, states, public school districts, and universities.
PHI has sued other health care organizations, including hospitals, nursing homes, and medical billing firms. It also has gone after nonprofits, such as the Catholic Diocese of Cleveland. In each instance, a worker or family member at these companies took an emergency medical helicopter, often at a cost of tens of thousands of dollars per trip.
In some cases, PHI wasn’t sure what company it should be suing, but sued anyway. Several lawsuits named specific health insurers and employers as defendants, and then added “ABC CORP” or “XYZ CORP” as a placeholder. If the insurer or employer “is not in fact the plan sponsor … that covers the patient transported by PHI, then the identity of the plan sponsor is unknown to PHI, and this action is instead brought against ABC CORP,” one lawsuit reads.
Katie Keith and Ellie DeGarmo are attorneys at Georgetown’s Center for Health Policy and the Law who have tracked No Surprises Act lawsuits, including those filed by PHI. They said the scores of cases reinforce the bloat in the health care system: above-market prices that providers are winning for not participating in an insurance company’s network, attempts from insurers to not pay at all or profit off lowball offers, and a booming revenue stream for arbitrators.
But trying to wring money out of employers — and, ultimately, from their workers — is a stark divergence from the public statements of physician groups and air ambulance companies, which have painted health insurers as the bad guys for not following the rules.
“It kind of undercuts the narrative that this is provider versus insurance company,” Keith said. “In this case, this is about provider versus everyone who pays for health care and is now stuck with the bill for [arbitration] awards that have gone totally off the rails.”
STAT reached out to more than two dozen employers that were listed in PHI’s lawsuits. Most did not respond to inquiries. Of those that did, most declined to comment.
“Because this matter involves pending litigation … we will not be providing any interviews,” said Clint Mitchell, the division superintendent of Spotsylvania County Public Schools in Fredericksburg, Va. PHI Health is suing Spotsylvania County’s school system for almost $28,000.
Jay Litten, the town manager of Bridgewater, Va., told STAT the town’s health insurer, Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, retained counsel and was handling the case. PHI sued Bridgewater in October for more than $37,000 in unpaid awards.
PHI has boasted about its success in the law’s arbitration process. In 2024, it told prospective investors that it was “able to maintain our profitability” by winning more than three out of every four arbitration claims, and it expected “this trend of favorable” outcomes from the process would continue.
The company has some private equity backing, according to financial filings from when the company considered going public in 2023. Its largest shareholder as of 2023 was Q Investments, a family office that has a private equity firm.
PHI declined to make anyone available for an interview. In a statement, CEO Scott McCarty defended the company’s lawsuits, saying the employers PHI has sued “have a duty to their employees and a responsibility to health care providers in their communities to abide by the law and pay for services delivered.”
McCarty said health insurers are asking their employer clients to choose between paying the unpaid arbitration amounts or authorizing the insurer to continue refusing payment.
“Once an employer is on notice of nonpayment and affirmatively endorses that practice, it is no longer a passive bystander,” McCarty said in the statement. “It has made a conscious decision to allow its insurance company not to pay binding federal awards in violation of federal law.”
In PHI’s lawsuits, the company alleges insurers, and now employers, are using an “unlawful scheme to ‘low pay, late pay, or no pay’ providers, including PHI.” All the cases are still pending.
The company also claims insurers float the money from unpaid awards, which are binding decisions, on the stock market as a way to earn extra interest or investment income.
James Gelfand, CEO of the ERISA Industry Committee, a lobbying group that represents large employers, said companies don’t condone insurers delaying payments as a way to make extra money. But he said under the federal law known as ERISA, employers are legally obligated to make sure they spend their health plan assets wisely on behalf of workers. If employers believe the awards are tied to ineligible claims — or are egregiously high compared with what they normally would pay — those payments could violate that obligation.
As a result, the employers’ health insurers “are operating with our blessing when we say, ‘Hey, if the [arbitration] award is inappropriate and wrong, do not pay it,’” he said. “How can we claim to be responsible stewards of people’s money if we’re just like, ‘Oh, here you go!’ That would be crazy.”
Jenny Goins, who is CEO of the National Alliance of Healthcare Purchaser Coalitions and used to oversee health benefits for Kentucky state employees, said “slow-walking the payments” to providers is one of the only ways employers can push back if they believe the awards are based on ineligible or incomplete claims. Medical claims are not eligible for arbitration if, for example, the employer or its health plan doesn’t cover a certain service or if there is certain information or data missing.
PHI has frequently named Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, owned by Elevance Health, as a defendant in the lawsuits against employers. Elevance did not make anyone available for an interview. The company said in a statement that PHI is charging prices for air ambulance services that are 700% of what Medicare pays and mileage rates that are 1,500% more than Medicare rates.
“We have already paid PHI substantial amounts for services provided to our members,” Elevance spokesperson Janey Kiryluik said in a statement. “We dispute whether additional amounts are legally owed for claims that were ineligible” for the arbitration process.
PHI said only arbitrators can determine the eligibility of claims. It added that the rates Medicare pays don’t cover the full cost of emergency air care, nor can those prices be considered during the arbitration process.
The bigger issue revealed by the lawsuits, Goins said, is how “broken” the law has become, even though she believed it was well-intended. The issue has now attracted interest in Congress, where lawmakers are proposing various plans to overhaul the arbitration process.
“Greedy people see an opportunity to make more money,” Goins said. “I also see there’s a true opportunity to shine a light on this.”
In September, PHI dropped Hancock’s company as a defendant, one month after its attorneys served him with court papers. Hancock said his heating, cooling, and plumbing business of 30 employees is not self-insured — meaning he buys his health insurance from Anthem, which takes on all the risk of his employees’ medical care.
PHI’s McCarty blamed Anthem in a statement, saying it “does not always receive clear or consistent information from insurers identifying whether a plan is self-funded or fully insured. In this case, after the lawsuit was filed, Anthem’s counsel confirmed that Whitehead-Hancock was fully insured, and PHI promptly dismissed it, without settlement.”
Other businesses are getting released from PHI’s lawsuits, too. It’s unclear if they were wrongfully lumped in, like Hancock’s company, or if they are paying PHI’s demands to clear a costly legal headache.
PHI’s legal team “threw a handful of darts, and they’re going to try to rattle as many cages as they can,” Hancock said. “It’s not right. It shouldn’t be legal.”

On 4 November 2026, the results of the 2026 US midterm elections were announced, with the Democratic Party winning a majority in the House of Representatives & the Senate. Against this background, a video is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows US President Donald Trump destroying his office following the Republican Party’s defeat in the 2026 US midterm elections. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing US President Trump vandalizing his office after the Republican Party’s defeat in the midterm elections of 2026.
Fact: We found no credible reports confirming such an incident. This is an AI-generated video by a creator named Iman Rus. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
We found no credible reports confirming such an incident. A reverse image search using keyframes led us to the original video, which was uploaded on 4 November 2026 by the Iranian Embassy in Lebanon on X. The video clearly carries the label “AI Generated” in the upper-right corner. It also credits the creator, Iman Rus, at the end.
A keyword search based on the information gathered above led us to the same video uploaded on the YouTube channel ‘Iman Rus’ on 4 November 2026. The video title clearly identifies it as AI-generated. Additionally, YouTube’s AI disclosure in the video also confirms that the content was created using AI.
We also analysed the viral video using AI detection tools, Hive AI and SynthID, both of which indicated the video was AI-generated.
To sum up, the viral video claiming that Trump vandalised his office following the Republican Party’s defeat is AI-generated.

New South Wales police have launched a homicide investigation after a human torso was found in bushland on Sydney’s lower north shore.
Police were called to Lane Cove North about 2.30pm on Wednesday after reports of human remains.
Police had “received a number of reports from members of the public” regarding a strong odour in the area, Supt Paul Devaney told media on Thursday morning.
Officers found a sofa containing a human torso located about five metres off the roadway.
The remains consisted of “a torso … devoid of head, arms and legs”, Devaney said. There were signs the body had been there for “at least a couple of days”.
A crime scene was established, with forensic specialists seizing the human remains – believed to be that of an adult male – for a postmortem examination.
“It’s a very, very quiet street in Lane Cove, an area that has probably nil crime rate, so it’s a very unusual activity,” Devaney said.
Detectives together with the state’s homicide squad launched an investigation, with the Aviation Command (PolAir) and cadaver dog deployed.
Members of the public with information, including dashcam or security camera footage that may be relevant, were urged to contact police with information.
Devaney sought to reassure Lane Cove residents that there was no apparent threat to locals.
“There is no indication that this person met foul play within the area of Lane Cove. But it is very early stages in the investigation and we are still undertaking numerous and comprehensive inquiries,” he said.

The state has recorded 206 farm fire incidents across 23 districts this season, with crop residue burning confirmed in 89 cases, according to an official statement issued late on Wednesday.

Farmers adopting crop residue management practices are also being given an incentive of Rs 1,200 per acre. About Rs 500 crore will be disbursed to farmers under the scheme, the spokesperson said.
The administration inspected all 206 locations where fires were reported. In confirmed cases of stubble burning, fines totalling Rs 3.55 lakh were imposed through 62 challans, of which Rs 2.30 lakh has been recovered, Press Trust of India reported.
Authorities have also registered 74 first information reports, or FIRs, while red entries have been made in the revenue records of the fields concerned in 19 cases.
Paddy procurement begins on October 1, while monitoring of farm fires starts a few days earlier and continues until the end of November.
According to district-wise data, no stubble-burning incidents have been reported in Bhiwani, Charkhi Dadri, Gurugram, Mahendragarh, Nuh and Rewari. One fire was reported in Panchkula, but crop residue burning was not confirmed. Six incidents each were reported in Hisar and Hansi.
The government has also sought to fix responsibility among officials to strengthen monitoring. Show-cause notices have been issued to 109 nodal officers for alleged negligence in carrying out their duties.
As part of its technology-based monitoring system, the state has installed 79 sensors in villages identified as hotspots. It is also using 36 drones to continuously monitor various districts. District-level officers have been assigned responsibilities to ensure effective monitoring.
The spokesperson appealed to farmers not to burn stubble and instead use modern agricultural machinery and government schemes to manage crop residue. The statement said scientific management of crop residue helps maintain soil fertility, protect the environment and ensure cleaner air.
Overall, the state is combining subsidies, direct incentives, machinery distribution, technology-based surveillance and enforcement measures to curb stubble burning and encourage sustainable crop residue management.

Militants ambush police vehicles in northwestern Pakistan, killing at least 10 officers
Police say militants have ambushed vehicles carrying police officers in northwestern Pakistan, triggering a gunbattle that killed at least 10 officers
PESHAWAR, Pakistan -- PESHAWAR, Pakistan (AP) — Militants ambushed vehicles carrying police officers in northwestern Pakistan on Wednesday, triggering a gunbattle that killed at least 10 officers, officials said.
The attack took place in Kohat, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which borders Afghanistan, local police official Faisal Khan said.
He said two senior police officers were among the dead and an exchange of fire between security forces and the attackers was ongoing He provided no further details.
No group immediately claimed responsibility, but suspicion is likely to fall on the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has stepped up attacks on security forces in the region in recent months.
Pakistan has seen a surge in violence in recent years, much of it blamed on the TTP. The group is separate from but closely allied with the Afghan Taliban, who returned to power in neighboring Afghanistan in 2021.
Pakistan frequently accuses Afghanistan’s Taliban government of sheltering TTP militants, an allegation Kabul denies.

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
- Published
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.
Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."
After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.
But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
Huang's position vulnerable unlike other tech bosses
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.
Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.
Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.
