Before arriving in Budapest as rivals, Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Magnus Carlsen spent part of October working together in Spain. For the 22-year-old Uzbek, it was an opportunity to exchange ideas with the world No. 1, and the beginning of a collaboration he hopes will continue.
“I think it’s a very uncommon thing among top players to work with each other. But I was very happy to join the camp with Magnus. We played a lot of training games, and we shared ideas, our visions for chess,” Abdusattorov told Sportstar on the sidelines of Total Chess.
The arrangement followed a conversation with Carlsen’s longtime coach, Peter Heine Nielsen. Abdusattorov had expressed his interest in training camps or practice games with the Norwegian. Carlsen subsequently extended an invitation during an esports event, and the two agreed to meet in Spain.
Abdusattorov still considers himself an improving player, with much to gain from such an exchange. He hopes the work will help his results in Budapest, where the Total Chess pilot brings together 24 players for a competition spanning fast classical, rapid and blitz.
The format appealed to him, as did the strong field and the opportunity to earn FIDE Circuit points towards Candidates qualification. His ambitions in the World Championship cycle remain clear, though he wants to approach them differently this time.
Abdusattorov’s successes this year include titles at the Tata Steel Masters and Prague Masters. But his assessment of the previous qualification cycle, in which he missed out on a Candidates place, was less about the games than the expectations he carried into them.
“I don’t want to make the same mistake again. In the previous cycle, I tried really hard; I wanted it very badly. In the end, this kind of mindset didn’t bring me a lot of benefits, and it didn’t work for me,” he said.
His immediate priorities are to improve his chess and his rating. Meanwhile, a teammate is preparing for the match Abdusattorov hopes to reach himself.
Javokhir Sindarov will challenge India’s D. Gukesh for the World Championship crown in Geneva, with the first game scheduled for November 24. It comes fairly soon after Sindarov and Abdusattorov helped Uzbekistan win the Chess Olympiad on home soil in Samarkand in September, adding to the country’s first title in Chennai in 2022.
For Abdusattorov, those achievements are part of a shared ambition.
“We are very motivated. We have a clear goal to make Uzbekistan the number one country in chess. We are working on that goal,” he said.
He credited sustained investment and support from the government and the national federation for making the country’s results possible.
“I’ve said this many times, that without the support of government, I think it’s very tough to achieve big results. It’s truly an immense responsibility and effort to make it all possible,” he said.
Abdusattorov also wants to contribute beyond his tournament appearances. Sindarov already runs a chess academy, he said, and he plans to open one of his own.
He did not set out a timeline, but sees the growing interest in Uzbekistan’s leading players as an opportunity to bring more children into the game. There are now many chess clubs in the country, he said, with success at the highest level giving parents a reason to consider the sport for their children.
“When you have big results, when you have big attention, the parents will be motivated to send their kids to chess clubs,” he said.
“But our job, I think, is to supply our people with our results, with our achievements. And I think that’s the most important part.”
His understanding of a leading player’s responsibilities also extends to helping chess reach a wider audience. New events offer more opportunities, he believes, but players have a part in sustaining that interest through their games, interviews and promotion of tournaments. Greater involvement from the elite, he said, can help attract both spectators and financial support.
Some of that attention already follows him away from competition. Asked what people might not yet know about him, Abdusattorov pointed to the interest in his engagement.
“I think the news of my engagement went viral on social media. So, with time and with patience, they will get to know me even better,” he quipped.

Italian authorities evacuated some 300 schools across Italy on Wednesday after receiving an emailed bomb threat, the latest disruptions affecting European institutions following hoax bomb threats against airlines and broadcasters in recent weeks.

At Rome’s Mamiani high school, students poured into the streets thinking the alarm was the recess bell and only learned there was a bomb threat after they were outside.

How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles
Measles spreads incredibly fast. For the last few months, so has Dale Weiser's phone number.
Weiser is the clinical services supervisor for the Chester County Health Department in south-central Pennsylvania. Since August, she's been driving out to Amish homes to vaccinate people against measles. She says it usually starts with a phone call.
"I was at a house, like, at 4:30 in the afternoon, and I had a phone call at 8 the next morning saying, 'hey, I heard you were down the street. Can you come do that at my house?'" she says of a typical request she gets from Amish families. So far, she's administered more than 400 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in Amish homes.
The house calls are part of the state of Pennsylvania's strategy to wage war on measles by flipping the script on traditional public health messaging. Instead of advertising vaccinations loudly, health officials have launched a quiet word-of-mouth campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been particularly hard hit by the country's worst measles outbreak in 35 years. The state has confirmed six measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases so far — though the true count is likely much higher, since many people who get sick don't seek medical care.
Lower vaccination rates
Surveys suggest only about a third of Amish families in the region vaccinate their children. That's left the Amish community especially vulnerable to measles, one of the most contagious diseases.
There's no religious edict against vaccination among the Amish. It's very much seen as a family and individual choice, says Weiser. Often, she says, these decisions are driven by practical and cultural factors.
"They don't have health insurance. They're not interacting with the mainstream medical society. And measles wasn't a problem for 30 years, so there was no real risk to not being vaccinated, at least for measles," Weiser says.
But as measles cases have piled up in Pennsylvania, Weiser says many Amish families have changed their minds about getting the MMR vaccine. And when they do, she hops in her car and brings the shots to them.
"When I arrive at their home, there's usually a small child that will run from the back of the house to the barn to tell the men that there's somebody strange in the driveway, or that the nurse is here," she says.
A patient, personalized approach to outreach
Some days, Weiser will vaccinate a single family in their kitchen. Other times, she'll find dozens of people gathered to get the shot. She's also fielded a lot of questions. Some, like what's in the vaccine and potential side effects, are things anyone would ask, she says.
"But I was caught off guard when I was asked if there were tracking chips in the vaccine, and I was like, whoa. Flashback to COVID. Where did you hear that?" she recalls.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
As with the general population, vaccine misinformation has made its way to the Amish community. And when she encounters it, Weiser takes the time to explain why the rumors are false.
Chester County Public Health Director Jeanne Franklin says this kind of patient, personalized approach has helped build trust among the local Amish – who, along with conservative Mennonites, are known as the Plain community because of their simple way of life.
"That's why we said it has to be boots on the ground in the communities. It's not just because they were a Plain community, it was because we needed to be seen as caring people," Franklin says.
Instead of relying on traditional top-down, rigid public health messaging, her staff has spent a lot of time quietly visiting Amish church leaders and businesses, introducing themselves and asking community leaders if they would hand out flyers advertising vaccine clinics. "One of them said, 'Come on back with a clinic' at his restaurant. And he helped spread the word," Franklin says.
Vaccine questions and misinformation
When I stopped by the restaurant, Honey Brook Barbecue in Honey Brook, Pa., an area with a sizable Amish community, I found the manager grilling chicken in an outdoor tent. Like many Amish people NPR talked to, he spoke on the condition of anonymity in keeping with his community's tradition of not drawing attention to oneself.
The manager says 24 people showed up to get vaccinated at his restaurant back in August, all drawn by word of mouth. He says he decided to host the clinic for two reasons: to protect the general public and to protect his own community. He said he didn't want people blaming the Amish for spreading measles.
But he says other people in the Amish community who don't regularly interact with the public aren't getting vaccinated. For some, it's because of cultural reasons, but he says others are concerned about what they've heard is in the MMR vaccine.
"In my community, a lot of it has to do with what people think is in it," the manager says of the MMR vaccine. One concern he's heard repeatedly is that the vaccine contains parts of aborted fetuses.
That is a myth often repeated by anti-vaccine forces, and it is one heard in conversations with Amish people in Lancaster County, home to around 45,000 Amish people. It's also the county with a third of the state's measles cases — more than 500 confirmed cases.
At the Amish-owned Gordonville Book Store, where a buggy is parked outside, I meet a shopper named Lydia Esh. She says she, her husband and six adult children had all previously been vaccinated against measles. But none of her 13 grandchildren have gotten the shot, because their parents had heard that the MMR vaccine had changed and now contained aborted fetus parts — which is false.
There is some evidence that anti-vaccine groups have been targeting the Amish in recent years, says Steve Nolt, a professor at Elizabethtown College who has written numerous books about Amish history and culture. For example, he points to an advertisement questioning the safety of childhood vaccines published in The Pennsylvania Busy Beaver, an advertising publication with a large Amish readership.
But in conversations around Lancaster, I also find evidence that public health outreach efforts are working. One member of the Plain community, a visibly pregnant woman outside an Amish-owned hardware store, says her husband and two children recently got vaccinated to protect her and her unborn child. She asked NPR not to use her name, as did an Amish man working at a produce stall in an Amish market. He says he recently got vaccinated because "measles is scary."
Linda Beth Fisher, an 18-year-old Amish woman behind the counter at the Gordonville Book Store, says she is concerned that several Amish people in her area have died in the measles outbreak, but she's not sure what to believe about the MMR vaccine.
"Personally, I'm kind of leery of it. I'm not sure why," Fisher says. "I guess I've just kind of heard that they're not good, but I've also heard that they are good. So I just feel like it's two sides of the story. Would you encourage people to get it?"
"They almost always come back"
These types of concerns often surface at pop-up vaccine clinics like one recently hosted at the Christiana Fire Company in Lancaster County. The Pennsylvania Department of Health hosts these events in Lancaster three or four times a week — all advertised by word of mouth, says Dr. Jennifer Wallace. As medical director for the department's Bureau of Community Health Systems, she oversees pop-up clinics and outreach to vulnerable communities across Pennsylvania.
Wallace says when members of the Plain community come with questions, "We're here to give them that information and then let them ponder it. They can ask any questions they want to and then let them either get vaccinated if they choose or take that information home. Think about it. Talk with their bishops. Talk with their community. They almost always come back."
Wallace says many who end up coming are families with multiple children. Tables set up around the firehouse are strewn with crayons, coloring books and bubble wands to keep young ones entertained while parents fill out paperwork.
"And then you see the kids get vaccinated and you can almost see the mother's shoulders relax over time as each child gets that shot," she says. "We've had some mothers cry afterwards because they're just so relieved."
The state health department says 30 people attended the Christiana firehouse clinic, 24 of whom got vaccinated. That included a father and his three sons who arrived for their second doses.

For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.
Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.
“I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them. The work he had taken up to help his family has left him dependent on others, with no certainty about what his future will look like.
By some estimates, Panipat processes more than 1m tons of used clothing from across the world every year, making it one of the world’s largest textile recycling hubs. In the city’s 20,000 factories, employing about 300,000 people, discarded clothes are shredded into yarn and made into finished products, including home furnishings for brands such as H&M Home, Ikea, Primark, Tesco and Walmart.
But the fast-fashion industry, built on buying more and more clothes and wearing them less, carries a devastating cost for workers tackling its waste. Ramesh Chaudhary, an environmental activist who has worked in Panipat’s labour department, has been tracking reports of injuries and amputations across the city for the past five years. He estimates that at least one worker a day loses a limb, rising to as many as five on some days.
“Every day, we come across cases of workers injured inside factories, sometimes losing a hand or a leg, and sometimes even dying,” Chaudhary says. He gathers his information through a network of labour contractors who supply workers to factories across Panipat. But not all news of injuries reaches him, he says, suggesting the scale of the problem could be greater.
Between 17 and 24 August this year, the Guardian monitored reports from 11 private hospitals and two government hospitals in Panipat. In that period, six cases of textile workers with severe limb injuries were reported: two had lost an arm, another man lost both, one lost a hand, one lost a leg and the sixth their fingers.
Such injuries are common in Panipat’s factories, says Chaudhary, because machinery often lacks the necessary safety mechanisms. If a worker gets caught in a spinning machine, he says, cutting the power may not stop it immediately. By the time the machine comes to a halt, a worker may already have catastrophic injuries.
During numerous visits to spinning units and factories, the Guardian did not see anyone wearing any kind of safety gear. None of the workers interviewed reported having safety training.
India’s 1948 Factories Act places a duty on factory owners to protect workers’ health and safety. It requires serious workplace accidents to be reported to the authorities. But the effectiveness of safety oversight remains a concern, says Sandeep Sachdeva, co-founder of the Safe in India Foundation, which works to reduce industrial injuries.
“Factories are often audited by buyers, especially where quality and critical components are involved, and inspected by government industrial safety and health departments. Buyer audits tend to focus more on commercial requirements and product quality than on workplace safety or working conditions,” he says.
“Government inspections are selected through a central software system, but inspectors are now required to inform factories before visiting. Their role is now that of a facilitator-cum-inspector – a shift that undermines the effectiveness of inspections, particularly in factories with unsafe working conditions.”
For workers, losing a limb means losing their livelihood. Ramashankar Singh, who is in his fifties, from Chapra in Bihar, spent 18 years in Panipat’s factories before an accident last year led to him having a leg amputated.
It happened when a hot ball bearing fell on his foot. Ramashankar’s injury was first just wrapped in discarded cloth, before the factory owner sent him to a pharmacy.
The wound worsened as the infection spread. When Ramashankar approached his employer again, the owner agreed to arrange treatment and admitted him to a private hospital. By then, the infection had progressed so far that doctors had to amputate his leg above the knee.
“The factory owner said he would give me another job, possibly as a cook or a security guard at the factory,” Ramashankar says. “But that never happened.” The owner also said he would help him secure a government disability pension, but he has received no pension since the accident and relies on a prosthetic leg provided by a charitable organisation.
After so much of his life spent in a factory, Ramashankar says: “I have almost forgotten how to live without work. Much of my day now passes lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling fan.”
He also struggles with guilt that he has become a burden on his family.
India’s textile industry is the country’s second-largest source of employment after agriculture, directly employing more than 45 million people. An estimated 92% of its workforce is informally employed. In Panipat, more than 90% of workers are employed informally, says Ina Bahuguna, programme manager at the Estonia-based Reverse Resources, which monitors the city’s textile waste.
“Formal employment contracts and the social security benefits that accompany them, including pensions, are largely limited to workers in management, clerical roles and some specialised jobs, such as tailoring,” says Bahuguna.
Most workers on the factory floor lack these protections, leaving those who suffer serious injuries particularly vulnerable. Without formal employment or adequate social security coverage, they are left without employer-backed compensation, rehabilitation support or a source of income.
The Guardian asked several factory owners why they hired workers on a contractual or piece-rate basis rather than in permanent positions, and most cited the workers’ seasonal migration, saying some did not return to Panipat after travelling home.
For workers who sustain life-changing injuries, getting employers to pay for medical treatment can be a struggle. Indrapal Singh, who lost his arm in 2017, had worked in Panipat for 15 years, two and a half of those at the factory where he was injured. His hand was caught in a Chinese-made carding machine, which tore away the skin. He was given a painkilling injection but, as the infection worsened, his arm had to be amputated. The factory owner refused to pay his hospital bills.
Indrapal spent six years fighting his case through the courts, but says he received no compensation. The police told him that he had signed documents withdrawing his complaint, something Indrapal, who says he cannot read or write, disputes.
“I lost my arm, fought for six years, and in the end, all I got was a government pension of 5,700 rupees [£45]. The factory owner has faced no consequences, and the factory continues to operate as before,” he says.
Chaudhary says: “Workers have very little bargaining power when they are up against factory owners who are not only financially powerful but sometimes politically influential too. For many workers, taking them on in a legal fight is simply not an option.”
Arvind Kumar, the officer in charge at one of Panipat’s 12 police stations, says three workplace injury cases have been registered at his station so far this year. One involved the death of a worker. “Fewer than 1% of workplace injury cases reach the police and are formally registered,” he says.
Most cases, the officer says, are settled outside the formal legal system. Workers may receive a one-time payment towards medical bills, but then are generally left to manage the long-term consequences of their injuries on their own. The police rarely get involved.
For now, Suraj Kumar’’s family are grateful that the factory owner covered his hospital bills. They are not sure whether to register a police complaint.
“He [the owner] is like God to us. He is paying for our boy’s treatment,” says his mother, Sita.
Suraj struggles to imagine what comes next. “I thought that if I worked hard for two years, I could buy myself a motorcycle. I had so many things I wanted to do with my life. I never thought I would have to start by figuring out how to live without my arms.”

South Africa's ANC records worst-ever results in local elections
- Published
South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic".
While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 30.76% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 64.82% 20 years ago.
The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. In 2021 it won six. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.
The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second in the overall vote with 24.64%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party came third overall with 9.76%, unseating the ANC as winner in the city of Durban, while the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6.22%.
"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC," said secretary-general Fikile Mbalula on Saturday. "We knew this disaster is coming, we're staring at it. As we got into elections, the cost of living of our people was too high. The middle class have turned on the ANC in big numbers."
Entering the count centre tonight, South Africa's president and leader of the ANC Cyril Ramaphosa said: "We accept the will of the people however concerning it might be, we accept that this is how the people of South Africa in our towns, in our cities, in our metros have spoken - and this is their verdict, we accept it with humility. It is a decline that is concerning, that is how I characterise it."
It's a continuing decline for the ANC, which lost majority rule in the national elections in 2024 for the first time in its history. It then had to form a coalition government with a raft of other parties in what is now known as the GNU, or government of national unity.
While the Democratic Alliance made significant gains in the cities in these local elections, its overall vote share rose marginally from 21.83% in 2021, and was below the 26.9% it gained in 2016.
Voter turnout was 52.29%, an increase from 45.9% in 2021, when elections were held during the Covid pandemic.
"This election is delivering a devastating message to the ANC", said political analyst Susan Booysen. "It's an ANC in decline at local municipal level, at the metropolitan level, and when the results are reflected provincially and nationally, we see severe declines in ANC levels of support all around."
The reason for that decline in support is largely due to poor service delivery and infrastructure across the country, from water and power to sanitation. "These are huge problems," says Booysen, "and have really been affecting the lives of ordinary people, in the suburbs, in the townships, and in very dramatic ways."
The big picture looks even more bleak for the ANC. The party will elect a new leader next year as Cyril Ramaphosa comes to end of his term. He is due to stay on as president of the country until the next national elections in 2029, but there are few candidates lined up to succeed him in either role.
- ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline 
  - Published4 days ago
"It is sort of the end of the liberation movement era in South Africa," said political analyst William Gumede, "and the dominance of the liberation movement since the end of apartheid. So the ANC is going to be a party that by 2029 could be the second biggest rather than the biggest party. It may actually spiral into a long period of just total infighting. This is a new era for South Africa's politics and also the ANC."
The elections also saw a significant shift in voting patterns, with the DA, traditionally known as the "white party" for attracting a largely white vote, gaining more black votes. "We're moving towards a post-racial voting pattern in South Africa," added Gumede.
South Africa now faces days of local coalition building, with the three metropolitan municipalities in the province of Gauteng, the country's powerhouse, under particular scrutiny. The ANC may even find itself shut out in the cities of Johannesburg and Pretoria.
"We are now in a coalition country," said Gumede. "Essentially, what the voters are saying is, "Well, the ANC has dominated the last three decades, they didn't use their power to change the society for the good, so we don't want the dominant parties anymore, whether at national level, provincial level, or rather now at a local level. We actually want coalitions. We want people to work together."
Parties now have 14 days from the moment results were announced to negotiate coalitions.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

India’s retail inflation is likely to hit 6% in October, a two-year high that would push the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to keep interest rates elevated and possibly raise them again in December.
The Consumer Price Index is projected to rise 6%, from 5.5% in September, according to a Mint poll of 15 economists. If the forecast holds, inflation would breach the RBI’s upper tolerance limit of 6% for the first time since October 2024. Economists’ estimates range from 5.9% to 6.2%. Official data is scheduled to be released on 12 November. The increase is expected to be driven primarily by food prices and an unfavourable base effect.
Elevated oil and commodity prices are adding to inflationary pressures, potentially raising the prospect of another rate increase in December. The central bank raised the benchmark repo rate by 25 basis points in its October policy review.
Expectations of higher interest rates have also pushed yields on the benchmark 10-year government bond to a four-year high in late October. Although Brent crude prices have eased on expectations of a de-escalation in West Asia tensions, they remain elevated. Drought conditions in several parts of the country could add to price pressures.
“We expect the RBI to hike policy rates by 25 bps. We don’t see the need for a bigger, 50 bps hike in December as rupee/dollar exchange rate has stabilized post the central bank measures” said Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at IDFC First Bank.
High food inflation
The food and beverages division, which accounts for a significant share of the consumer inflation basket, is expected to record inflation of more than 8% in October, according to Icra. The increase is likely to be broad-based across food sub-segments, said Aditi Nayar, chief economist at Icra.
“Part of the increase in headline inflation is also attributable to the unfavourable base following the rationalisation of goods and services tax (GST),” Nayar said.
The expected increase marks a departure from the relatively benign inflation environment towards the end of 2025, when retail inflation fell to 0.04% in October. Since then, inflation has steadily firmed up, with food prices playing an increasingly important role.
In its October monetary policy review, the RBI turned more cautious about the inflation outlook, raising its inflation projection for 2026-27 to 5.2% from 5% earlier. The central bank cited deficient monsoon rainfall, ongoing El Niño conditions and elevated energy and commodity prices as risks to the outlook.
The RBI expects inflation to average 6% in October-December before moderating to 5.7% in January-March. Its projection for core inflation for the full financial year stands at 4.4%.
The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) also flagged the broadening of food price pressures, including sharp increases in items such as sugar and onions. It warned that the continued pass-through of higher energy and commodity prices could add to supply-side inflationary pressures.
Against this backdrop, the MPC unanimously voted to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% and shifted its policy stance to calibrated tightening. The change signals that rate cuts are unlikely in the near term, with future decisions depending on how growth and inflation evolve.
With food inflation expected to remain elevated in the coming months, the trajectory of prices following the kharif harvest and any moderation in energy costs will be key to determining whether headline inflation retreats from its October levels.
The increase is expected to be led by food prices, which have risen across several categories. “Inflation will be mainly driven by food prices which have shown a rise. This will continue for the next few months too, being aligned to the kharif harvests of various crops,” said Madan Sabnavis, chief economist at Bank of Baroda.
The increase in headline inflation will also reflect an unfavourable base effect, alongside continued pressure from food prices.
This also marks a departure from the relatively benign inflation environment seen towards the end of 2025, when retail inflation had fallen to a historic low of 0.04% in October. Russell Brand, who was convicted of rape and sexual assault, posted on Elon Musk’s X that Meta had taken down his Instagram account.
After being sentenced to 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault, Brand has now found himself without a social media platform.
“We disabled your account. You no longer have access to russellbrand,” read the screenshot the sex offender shared on X.
In the explanation as to why his account was deleted, the screenshot read, “Your account, or activity on it, doesn’t follow our Community Standards. No one can see or find your account, and you can’t use it. All your information will be permanently deleted.”
Meta also noted that Brand would not be able to “request another review of this decision,” but allowed him to download all the information he had previously shared.
Watch on Deadline
Brand’s Instagram account had over 5M followers, and he had shared more than 6,500 posts.
The sex offender’s Facebook Page was also removed, with the screenshot reading, “We suspended your page. This is because Russell Brand goes against our Community Standards.” On the Facebook page, Brand had 6.2M followers.

The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
- Published
As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.
This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.
Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.
Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes.
"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.
The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara.
But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers.
Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea.
Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity.
"Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says.
At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species.
Guiding tours runs in Sucdi's family. Her father worked in the profession for over three decades, taking journalists, photographers and visitors from different countries around Somalia.
He introduced her to the business nearly three years ago.
"I started this job as a hobby, but it has become something that I like and am passionate about," she says.
She now works alongside her father and a team of guides, building on his experience while using social media to reach a wider audience.
She shares videos of her tours on TikTok, offering people outside Somalia a glimpse of places they may never have imagined visiting.
She is also considering producing content in English to reach audiences who do not speak Somali.
Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu.
The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow.
However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security.
Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down.
But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation.
Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital.
Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life.
About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department.
Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city.
But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive.
"What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says.
Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue.
She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen.
"I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says.
Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.
Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade.
For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking.
American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice.
His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media.
"I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says.
What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere.
"It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says.
During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes.
"The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says.
Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage.
"If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines."
But visiting the country challenged those perceptions.
"Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says.
Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia's natural beauty.
Although she has spent only a few hours in Mogadishu, she has already visited the sand dunes and taken in the Indian Ocean coastline.
"The desert was so beautiful to see. I have also enjoyed the beach, and the ocean. It is inspiring," she says.
Having travelled to Somalia from neighbouring Ethiopia, she says she has been struck by the people's friendliness.
"I don't see anything dangerous. I feel safe and the people are warm," she says.
An experienced traveller, Mihaela says she prefers to visit new countries without having preconceived ideas.
"I travel the world to see new places, to see countries, to see the differences. I don't take a picture in my mind to compare the reality with. I'm just expecting the new to come to me," she says.
She hopes to share her experience and encourage others to visit Somalia.
"I'm going to post my pictures and say good things about what I'm experiencing. I'm going to promote it," she says.
For Sucdi, that potential is personal.
She is continuing a family profession while building a business in an industry with few women and using digital platforms to reach audiences far beyond Mogadishu.
"Somalia still has a long way to go before tourism becomes a major industry," she says.
"Through my tours, I am giving visitors an opportunity to experience its landscapes, our culture and people beyond the familiar negative headlines."
For her, every visitor is another opportunity to tell a fuller story of Mogadishu.

Amazon is betting that many Ring customers will also want an AI-powered security drone and robot patrolling their homes or offices. But the company’s upcoming Ring Robotic products are also certain to intensify privacy concerns previously raised around a prior Amazon attempt to popularize a flying security camera.
The Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10. Amazon describes the devices as relying on an AI Pilot system that uses each device’s cameras along with “specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing” to plan patrol routes while autonomously navigating around obstacles such as furniture.
Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor plan of the customer’s home or business. This setup process occurs after the customer carries the Ring drone through their indoor spaces or allows the Ring Rover to do some autonomous exploration.
The AI Pilot can supposedly use that guided- or self-tour information to identify specific rooms and suggest patrol points near side doors, windows, or even sensitive locations such as a cash register in the case of a business.
However, flying and roving cameras with AI-enabled features could introduce new privacy risks for homes and businesses, on top of existing concerns involving fixed Ring cameras installed in room corners or as doorbell cameras.
Return of the Ring drone
Amazon’s Ring Drone appears to be a direct successor to the company’s Ring Always Home Cam that was only temporarily available for purchase by invitation as a “Day 1 Edition” product in September 2021—even having the same starting price of $250.
But the Ring Drone still requires authorization from the Federal Communications Commission before going on sale. Assuming that comes through, Amazon aims to make the drone available on January 27, 2027, with customers able to register for email updates through the product page.
The drone can supposedly follow a set route and schedule for customers who subscribe to the Amazon Ring Protect plan. It can automatically fly along those set routes when responding to a notification from a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm.

Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak
BUNIA, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease.
According to the latest health ministry data, 11,042 people have been infected with the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387 — nearly half of those infected in what has been Congo's deadliest outbreak.
The outbreak was declared in mid-May, and since then, Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to several factors, including armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.
The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces.
The resurgence of violence in the two major hotspots in Ituri and North Kivu provinces has sparked worry among health authorities who are calling for a halt to the fighting to allow health workers unhindered access to the sick.
Health facilities and medical professionals have also been targeted by many in communities skeptical of the virus, and there have been several attacks on health workers.
Experts have called for more efforts to slow and contain the disease in Congo, while it has spread to multiple African countries including Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.
Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared, compared with the West Africa outbreak.

Update | November 11, 17:18 IST Months after Inc42 exclusively reported on Greenjoules’s fundraise, the cleantech startup announced the closure of its Series B round at ₹150 Cr ($16 Mn). The round was co-led by Amazon’s Smbhav Venture Fund and Climate Pledge Fund, with participation from Rainmatter and Singularity’s Strategic Autonomy Fund. The startup said that the fresh funds will support its new plant at Pune’s Khed City with the capacity to produce 2 Lakh litres of biocrude a day from agricultural waste. The facility will be developed in phases from 2027, which is expected to be the largest of its kind in India. Additionally, Greenjoules also secured a ₹100 Cr debt from Technology Development Board (TDB), under the Government of India’s Department of Science and Technology. “Greenjoules was built without a map; every step forward meant first inventing the path. We took two things that looked irreconcilable — low-energy-density agricultural waste and specification-grade fuel — and spent more than six years proving they were one and the same. With the concept proven and partners such as TDB and our Series B investors behind us, we are ready to make a deep impact on the global energy market, and to carry that pioneering spirit into sustainable aviation fuel,green hydrogen and sustainable materials.” said Shweta Viraraghavan, cofounder and chief technology officer, Greenjoules. Original | August 21, 18:58 IST Pune-based green energy startup Greenjoules has raised about ₹62 Cr ($6.5 Mn) in what appears to be an ongoing Series B funding round. While Amazon’s investment arm, Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings, is leading the funding round, Singularity AMC’s Singularity Strategic Autonomy Fund also participated in the round. As per MCA filings accessed by Inc42, the startup’s board allotted 40,338 Series B1 compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) at ₹11,155.5 apiece for ₹45 Cr to Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC. Separately, it also allotted 15,238 Series B1 CCPS to a sum of about ₹17 Cr to Singularity Strategic Autonomy Fund. Greenjoules declined to comment on Inc42’s queries regarding the total size of the round. Founded in 2018 by S Viraraghavan, V Radhika, VS Shridhar and R Sethunath, Greenjoules converts farm residues into renewable fuels that can be used in existing diesel engines and industrial equipment, effectively substituting crude oil with agricultural waste. The startup is developing green fuels that can cater to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), green hydrogen and biomethane areas. Prior to the ongoing round, the climatetech startup raised $4.5 Mn in a combination of equity and debt from Blue Ashva Capital in 2021, to set up commercial scale waste to energy plants and invest into new R&D initiatives. The investor interest in the eight-year old startup aligns with India’s broader push to scale renewable fuel sources in a bid to attain the country’s net zero goals. India aims to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by the year 2070. Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced this target during the COP26 climate summit in Glasgow, backed by a climate plan known as the "Panchamrita". The country's long-term low-carbon development strategy rests on seven key transitions to low-carbon development pathways. These include low-carbon development of electricity systems, enhancing forest and vegetation cover consistent with socioeconomic, development of CO2 removal and related engineering solutions, among others. Amid this push, India’s cleantech market is projected to become a $152.5 Bn market by 2030, creating a suitable market opportunity for new and emerging players as well as more established industrial players to leverage the opportunity.

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

Scientists have long known how to make cells younger—at least in the sense that adult cells can be converted into pluripotent stem cells very similar to those found in embryos. While this capability has been foundational for biological research, these methods aren’t viable for anti-aging technologies, for a few reasons.
“You don't want to have a pluripotent cell in your body, because it can become all types of cells,” says Oliver Brüstle, a professor who studies stem cells at Germany’s Bonn University.
Additionally, the few key genes involved in the stem cell conversion process can drive the formation of cancer if left active. That’s why Brüstle and his team have looked for other ways of de-aging cells without going through a pluripotent state. In their recent study published in Aging Cell, the researchers started with blood cells from people of various ages, including an infant and a 101-year-old donor.
They guided these cells into a younger state but not all the way toward becoming embryonic-like stem cells. And as this transformation progressed, the chemical signals in the DNA that help estimate a cell’s age also changed. In less than two months of reprogramming, one biomarker in particular was set back as far as 60 years.
Aging continued to reverse even when the scientists drastically reduced the cells’ ability to multiply. Therefore, the apparent rejuvenation can’t be explained solely by the fact that the cells were dividing and producing new cells over and over again. However, the mechanism that did erase these signs of aging is still unclear.
“The hope is that you actually can do this systemically in the entire animal,” Brüstle says. “But if you think about applying it in a patient, then you want to be sure this is not a lab experiment, so it's about finding the mechanism.”
The researchers also shifted the blood cells specifically into a kind of cell that produces neurons. One caveat is that blood cells and neurons age on different timelines, so the extent of the reversal could be exaggerated by the use of a different measuring stick. The authors acknowledge this limitation in their paper, though this discrepancy couldn’t account for all the age-associated biomarkers that reversed course.
Blood cells getting brainy also would not be a desirable result if you gave a patient a de-aging drug, but it would be useful for other regenerative medicine purposes. However, what Brüstle sees as one of the most exciting outcomes of the study is the information gleaned about the process of de-aging.
Usually, making stem cells is quick. That’s useful for many experiments, but it doesn’t give researchers the chance to study cells as they shed the markers of age. In this recent study, since the scientists were able to slowly turn back the cells’ biological clocks, they could track each step of de-aging. “Now we can actually try to dissect the process much more easily than having an instantaneous event,” Brüstle says.
Scientists began converting adult cells back into stem cells two decades ago, but we’ve known very little about how the subsequent de-aging occurs. This means when clinical researchers test potential medical interventions for age-related conditions, they haven’t always had a reliable measure to compare against.
“Now we have a model” Brüstle says. “You can work along this, and now you can probe a zillion things. What impacts the process? This will lead you to the mechanisms. That’s our hope.”

Hoax note on Air India Kolkata-Mumbai flight sparks hijack scare
The note was found by the cabin crew of flight AI 2772, an Airbus A320 (VT-TNH), at around 10.37am, when it was scheduled to depart.
A hijack threat to an Air India flight from Kolkata to Mumbai triggered a security scare at the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport in Kolkata on Wednesday after a handwritten warning was found in the aircraft’s lavatory before take-off, prompting security agencies to carry out mandatory checks, officials aware of the matter said.
The note was found by the cabin crew of flight AI 2772, an Airbus A320 (VT-TNH), at around 10.37am, when it was scheduled to depart. It warned that the aircraft would be hijacked at 11.10am, officials said.

Safety drill initiated
The Air Traffic Control (ATC) was immediately informed, after which all concerned agencies swung into action, they said. “The aircraft was moved to an isolation bay and the mandatory security drill was initiated,” an airport official requesting anonymity said.
All 105 passengers and seven crew members were deboarded and security personnel thoroughly searched the aircraft to rule out any potential threat “as per established protocols,” the official quoted above said.
In its initial statement, Airports Authority of India (AAI), confirmed that a hijack note was found and that concerned agencies were carrying out checks.
An updated statement in the evening said, “Following the completion of all necessary checks as per established protocols, boarding for Air India flight AI 2772 (Kolkata–Mumbai) is complete at NSCBI Airport, Kolkata. The expected time of departure (ETD) is 1700 hrs.”
The aircraft eventually took off for Mumbai at 5.38pm, the airport authorities confirmed. The threat was later declared a hoax, they said.
The incident comes less than a month after two other flights faced hijack scares.
Similar hijack hoaxes
On November 7, an IndiGo flight (6E 451) from Bengaluru to Lucknow returned to Bengaluru after a passenger found a threat note inside the aircraft’s lavatory. A full emergency was declared at Bengaluru airport and checks were carried out. The threat was later declared a hoax, and the flight resumed its journey.
Earlier, on October 14, an Air India flight from Frankfurt to Delhi was diverted to Jaipur after it transmitted Squawk Code 7500, the internationally recognised code for hijacking. The alert was subsequently reported to be false, and a possible technical glitch is being examined.

As Delhiites burst firecrackers well past the 10 p.m. deadline set by the Supreme Court for Deepavali night, air pollution shot up to over 50 times World Health Organisation (WHO) limits in parts of the city, official data showed.
The level of PM2.5 (a major pollutant) in Akshardham was 760.99 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) data. This is about 50.73 times the WHO permissible limit of 15 micrograms per cubic meter for a 24-hour period.
Deepavali 2026: All you need to know about Supreme Court-permitted time slots, green crackers and other directives
PM2.5 (Particulate Matter 2.5) are fine inhalable particles, which can get into lungs and bloodstream and lead to a range of respiratory and other diseases.
The level of PM2.5 in Anand Vihar was 767 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per DPCC data — This is about 51.13 times the WHO permissible limit.
The level of PM2.5 in Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium was 702 micrograms per cubic meter, as per DPCC data, which is about 46.8 times the WHO permissible limit.
The overall air quality of Delhi continued to be in the “very poor” category while many parts of the city continued to reel under “severe” air quality.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

Actor Sidharth Malhotra has revealed that he was once set to collaborate with filmmaker Aditya Dhar on a project backed by Dharma Productions. The actor shared the information during his recent appearance on Koffee With Karan, where host Karan Johar brought up the long-discussed collaboration while asking him about directors he would like to work with.
Koffee With Karan 9: Sidharth Malhotra was to headline an Aditya Dhar film at Dharma Productions – Karan Johar makes SURPRISING revelation!
During the conversation, Johar named several filmmakers, including Aditya Dhar, Mohit Suri, Sandeep Reddy Vanga and Sanjay Leela Bhansali, and asked Malhotra, “Aditya Dhar, Mohit Suri, Sandeep Reddy Vanga, Sanjay Leela Bhansali, the directors of the moment. Is there anyone you're willing to do anything to work with?” Responding to the question, Malhotra said, “Oh wow, I think all of them are extremely exciting. Maybe Aditya, because I've interacted with him in the past.”
Johar then brought up their earlier association, reminding the actor of a project that had been planned several years ago. “You were meant to do a film many moons ago.” To which Sidharth replied, “Yes, in Dharma itself.”
The brief exchange brought attention to a collaboration that never materialised. The project was reportedly in development during Aditya Dhar’s early years in the industry, before he made his directorial debut with Uri: The Surgical Strike in 2019. Although the film with Malhotra was to be backed by Dharma Productions, it did not progress to the shooting stage. Neither the actor, nor the filmmaker shared further details about the proposed project during the conversation.
Interestingly, both Malhotra and Dhar have since explored stories rooted in action, military operations and national security, albeit through different projects. Malhotra has essayed defence personnel and characters associated with national security in films such as Aiyaary (2018), Mission Majnu (2023) and Yodha (2024). His performance as Captain Vikram Batra in the 2021 biographical war drama Shershaah earned him considerable appreciation and remains a notable film in his career.
Dhar, meanwhile, established himself as a filmmaker with Uri: The Surgical Strike, which went on to become a significant milestone in his career. His subsequent work in Dhurandhar and Dhurandhar The Revenge has further strengthened his association with large-scale action narratives and technically ambitious storytelling.
While the Koffee With Karan conversation did not indicate whether the two are considering working together in the future, Malhotra’s revelation offers a glimpse into a collaboration that was planned long before either had established their current standing in the industry.

The Enforcement Directorate (ED), Chennai, has provisionally attached movable and immovable assets worth approximately ₹14.2 Cr in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment fraud operated by Pan India Cryptocurrency, HashPe. The attachment was made on October 30, 2026, under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002. The ED has also filed a prosecution complaint before the Special Court (PMLA), Puducherry. According to the ED, Hashpay allegedly operated a fraudulent cryptocurrency-based ponzi investment scheme that lured investors with promises of daily returns of 1%, returns of up to 3X the invested amount, referral commissions and rewards such as luxury cars and foreign trips. The agency said the attached assets include immovable properties in Tamil Nadu, Haryana and New Delhi, a BMW car and funds deposited in bank accounts. The investigation was initiated based on an FIR registered by the Cyber Crime Police Station, Puducherry, under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, and the Information Technology Act, 2000. How The Ponzi Scheme Worked ED's investigation found that HashPe operated through a website, hashpe.io, and a multi-level marketing network. Its promoters allegedly used cash payments, bank transfers and cryptocurrency transactions to mobilise investments from the public. The scheme reportedly used USDT (Tether), a stablecoin, and Bitcoin to facilitate transactions. However, the agency found that the purported trading activities were not backed by actual cryptocurrency trading. Instead, money collected from new investors was allegedly used to repay earlier investors and pay commissions to agents. Withdrawals were eventually stopped and the platform was frozen, leaving investors with financial losses. The ED further found that the promoters allegedly created fictitious cryptocurrency tokens, including TCX and HashPe, at an almost zero acquisition cost and assigned artificial values to them. The platform displayed profits to investors despite the absence of genuine cryptocurrency trading activity to generate the promised returns. To attract investors, the promoters used celebrity endorsements, promotional events featuring luxury cars and gold, and foreign cruises to build credibility. They also established a multi-level marketing network, with agents designated as 'Leaders' receiving commissions for bringing in new investors. The ED said approximately ₹112.91 Cr was collected through the scheme, a portion of which was returned to investors. The remaining funds were transferred to bank accounts of ‘HIFY Circle’ and other related entities before being converted into cryptocurrency. The proceeds were allegedly diverted towards personal expenses, loan repayments, hefty commissions and promotional activities, among other purposes. The agency has identified approximately ₹49.54 Cr as proceeds of crime in the case. The development comes after the ED conducted search operations at premises linked to HashPe, its promoters and associates on September 1. Following the searches, four individuals namely Imran Basha, Hitesh Kumar, Syed Usman alias Babu, and Dharmendra were arrested under Section 19 of the PMLA, 2002. All four accused are currently in judicial custody while the investigation is ongoing. The investigation revealed that Usman handled large cash investments and operated the HIFY Circle bank account, while Dhamodharan managed HashPe's software, database and cryptocurrency operations, including its wallet functions. Heightened Crypto Crackdowns Branches of ED across the country have stepped up the heat on suspected illegal cryptocurrency activities in recent months. On November 7, the ED in Bengaluru conducted searches at premises linked to crypto exchanges CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India (DEI) over alleged unauthorised cross-border transactions involving crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks. India is considering giving regulated private credit funds greater loan-recovery powers to boost lending and widen funding options for businesses. A high-level panel, headed by Niti Aayog member Rajiv Gauba, is weighing a proposal to grant them secured creditor status under the loan recovery law, two people aware of the discussions said.
Easier credit recovery could reduce these funds’ risks, lower borrowing costs and boost loan flow to small and medium enterprises, the people said on the condition of anonymity. For the funds, easier loan recovery could offer some parity with banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), and help them find new funding sources.
“The panel is considering the pros and cons of such a proposal. It will take a final call soon,” said one ofthe persons cited above. Any such relaxation may require an amendment to the Sarfaesi Act (Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002), the person said, adding the relaxation may come with some safeguards to ensure the status isn’t misused.
The proposals, once finalized, will be shared with relevant ministries and departments for necessary action, the people added.
Queries emailed to Gauba’s office remained unanswered. Gauba heads two high-level committees to suggest reforms in the non-financial sectors and also on the action plan for the Viksit Bharat goal. The committees, set up in August 2025, reckon that for India to become a developed economy by 2047, all credit channels need to fire together to ensure adequate and cheaper loans for sustained economic growth, said the people cited above.
Hard recovery
Private credit funds pool money from wealthy individuals and institutions to lend directly to businesses, mainly mid-sized, often those struggling to secure bank loans. Regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi), these close-ended category-II alternative investment funds (AIFs) lend through privately negotiated deals, usually held to maturity. They do not qualify as “secured creditors” under the Sarfaesi Act, and hence cannot enforce security against a defaulter as easily as other lenders. Unlike banks or NBFCs, they can’t take possession of assets in the case of a default without a complex legal process.
This higher recovery risk forces such funds to either charge more for funds or remain cautious in lending, which pushes up borrowing costs, especially for mid-sized companies that often require customized funding solutions and struggle to get them from banks.
Experts welcomed the move to ease private credit recovery.
“Sarfaesi access for regulated private credit funds is a pragmatic, long-overdue reform,” said Eshwar Karra, deputy managing director at Kotak Alternate Asset Managers.
AIFs don’t lend in the traditional sense; they invest the money. “But secured high-grade investments should carry the same enforcement rights as secured bank loans. Parity would remove an artificial risk premium, speed up resolutions, and strengthen LP confidence,” he said, also pitching for opening pension and insurance funds to private credit.
The change to Safaesi Act is long overdue, said Vivek Iyer, partner and financial services risk advisory leader at Grant Thornton Bharat. “Today, the rules are uneven. A bank, an NBFC or the debenture trustee of a listed secured NCD can enforce security without going to court. A category-II AIF holding the same loan through an unlisted instrument usually cannot.”
Small share
In India, private credit is mainly used for refinancing, growth capital, acquisition financing, structured credit transactions and special situations. Some of India's prominent domestic AIFs with private credit funds are Edelweiss Alternatives, Kotak Alternate Asset Managers, Motilal Oswal Alternates, 360 ONE Asset and ICICI Prudential.
While India’s private credit market doubled over the five years through December 2025, it remains small, with $25 billion in assets under management (AUM), about ₹ 2.34 trillion, according to Moody’s. For perspective, India’s current commercial bank loan market is at ₹227 trillion.
Rakshat Kapoor, head of the private credit business & chief investment officer at Motilal Oswal Alternates, said that India’s private credit industry has grown to a sizeable scale warranting greater regulatory attention. “Historically, when these acts, laws and regulations were made, private credit funds did not exist at this scale. But now, private credit funds have become a sizable segment, and these amendments may be carried out,” he said.
“Private credit today is not simply credit capital; it increasingly serves as ‘growth capital’, which is much needed to accelerate economic growth and help entrepreneurs expand their businesses,” said Manish Aggarwal, partner and leader (financial services and infrastructure transactions) at Deloitte India.
Sunil Gidwani, partner (financial services) at consultancy firm Nangia Global, said: “This would address an enforcement gap, rather than create a recovery framework.” He added that any extension of powers should define eligible funds and exposures, while ensuring “borrower safeguards, transparent valuation and sale processes, and effective judicial oversight”.
According to the EY Private Credit Report H1 2026, the market remained resilient despite the West Asia crisis, with investments reaching $3.5 billion in the first half of 2026, broadly in line with $3.4 billion recorded in the second half of 2025. Some notable private credit transactions in the first half of 2026, as per the report, were $176 million raised by Kalpataru Properties for refinancing; $156 million raised by HyFun Foods Group for refinancing and working capital requirements; $150 million secured by the GMR Group to fund group firms; $124 million raised by the Manipal Group for refinancing; and $113 million raised by Inspira Group’s Lenexis Foodworks for acquisition financing.
India’s private credit market is projected to nearly triple from $21.8 billion in 2025 to $56-65 billion by 2030, with a CAGR of 21-24%, according to a CareEdge report dated 2 November.
The penetration of this credit pathway remains weak in the country. According to a Kotak Mutual Fund study in March, private credit in India accounted for roughly 1% of the total credit as of 2025, about one-tenth of the level in the US.
(Mansi Verma contributed to this story)

BJD questions SIR credibility over alleged dual voter IDs in villages bordering Odisha, Andhra Pradesh
The BJD alleges residents of Kotia and Jumdang villages hold voter ID cards issued by both Odisha and Andhra Pradesh despite the completion of the SIR exercise.
The Biju Janata Dal (BJD) on Wednesday questioned the credibility of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Odisha, alleging that residents of villages along the Odisha-Andhra Pradesh border continued to hold voter ID cards issued by both states even after the exercise. The party also sought an explanation from the state’s election authorities over the alleged duplication.
Raising the issue at a press conference, senior BJD leaders Devi Prasad Mishra and Bijay Nayak questioned how residents of Kotia in Koraput district and Jumdang village in Malkangiri district could remain registered as voters in two states despite the completion of the SIR exercise.
Mishra said the law did not permit an individual to be registered as a voter in two places and demanded that the chief electoral officer (CEO) of Odisha seek details from the Andhra Pradesh government on the number of Odisha residents who had voted in the neighbouring state’s elections.
He also questioned why Andhra Pradesh had not removed duplicate and allegedly ineligible voters from its electoral rolls despite the alleged violation of electoral rules.
Meanwhile, Koraput Collector Manoj Satyawan Mahajan said that some residents of Kotia had crossed into Andhra Pradesh to vote in the neighbouring state’s panchayat elections last week.
Around 10% of voters from Kotia had exercised their franchise in the Andhra Pradesh rural elections, he said, adding that the 40% polling figure cited by Andhra Pradesh officials was based on the combined turnout at a polling booth catering to several villages, including those in the neighbouring state.
“We have information that people from four to five villages went to cast their votes in Andhra Pradesh. The population of these villages is smaller than what the voting percentage claimed by Andhra Pradesh officials would suggest,” he said.
The district administration had two objectives — preventing Andhra Pradesh from setting up a polling booth inside Kotia and discouraging residents from participating in elections in the neighbouring state, the collector said.
“We were completely successful in preventing the setting up of a polling booth inside Kotia. However, a few villagers still went to vote. The booth also catered to several villages in Andhra Pradesh. Therefore, the claim of 40% polling cannot be attributed to Kotia residents alone,” he added.
Odisha law minister Prithiviraj Harichandan said the state government would look into the matter.
“The Revenue Department needs to identify people who have dual voter identity cards and initiate legal action against them. Our government prevented Andhra Pradesh from setting up polling booths on Odisha soil. Despite that, some people crossed over to Andhra Pradesh and cast their votes,” Harichandan said.

Senior NASA officials held a lengthy news conference last weekend, laying out a series of lunar contract awards, new contract opportunities, and mission decisions. They followed one after the other: landers, nuclear-powered rovers, scouting drones, power generation, storage, and communication satellites.
It never seemed to end.
“Hopefully, we’re keeping industry on their toes trying to catch up to all the solicitations we’re doing,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program, more than 90 minutes into the news conference. “This is what it takes to do the Moon Base in the timeline we have set forth.”
The rapid-fire announcement of awards tells us a few things about NASA’s efforts to return to the Moon and establish a durable settlement there during the next decade.
First, the agency is serious about this effort—the Artemis Moon Base program represents the most credible effort to establish a permanent outpost on another world in NASA’s history. Second, NASA is reaching out to all corners of the US commercial space industry, casting an extraordinarily wide net to reach companies that have yet to fly any hardware into orbit. Third, NASA is getting creative about how it’s buying these services, and this may matter most of all.
Changing way NASA buys stuff
There was a lot packed into the announcements this weekend, so to make sense of it all, I called Mike Gold, a lawyer and former NASA associate administrator who set up the Artemis Accords, who is now the president of Redwire Space. He was at NASA at the beginning of Artemis and understands what it takes to get the government moving. He said he was blown away. During a period of seven days, Gold said, NASA put out five proposals for lunar contracts.
“The pace that’s occurring, and the nature of the procurements is unprecedented,” Gold said. “You are seeing an all-hands-on-deck approach. Big companies, small companies, new companies, old companies.”

Swabbing public transport to identify urban microbiomes, a city’s microbial signature
A recent study in the Chennai Metro Rail showed a wide range of microbes found on high-touch surfaces, though researchers said there was no cause for fear and no immediate reason to act
A team of researchers from IIT Madras swabbed 96 samples from 12 stations and trains on Chennai Metro’s Blue and Green Lines in December 2021 and January 2022, targeting four high-touch surfaces: station handrails (bannisters), ticket-vending kiosks, train handrails (rods), and ticket counters.
