From waste-water surveillance to public transport surfaces, mankind is constantly on the lookout for diverse microbial sources to test, to understand anti-microbial resistance patterns in a particular society. The latest in the urban transport systems sweep, performed at Chennai Metro Rail stations, showed that Chennai had a distinctive ‘transit biome’ - influenced by the city’s coastal climate, humidity, urban density and relatively nearby agricultural activity.
A team of researchers from IIT Madras swabbed 96 samples from 12 stations and trains on Chennai Metro’s Blue and Green Lines in December 2021 and January 2022, targeting four high-touch surfaces: station handrails (bannisters), ticket-vending kiosks, train handrails (rods), and ticket counters. The team swabbed 96 samples from 12 stations and trains and after quality control, 47 samples were sequenced using whole-genome metagenomic sequencing. Metagenomics is defined as the direct genetic analysis of genomes contained with an environmental sample.

Sourabh Chandrakar: CBI likely to seek further custody today; ED may have to wait
According to ED, Mahadev began its illegal operations in 2019-20 and continues to run across India, despite ban on multiple apps linked to the racket
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is likely to seek Mahadev online betting fraud mastermind Sourabh Chandrakar’s further custody on Thursday from a Raipur court, where he will be produced upon completion of his eight-days’ remand, people familiar with the development told HT.
The above people added that they need to unearth details of his accomplices and public servants he allegedly bribed in Chhattisgarh to safely run the illegal betting empire.
This development means that the Enforcement Directorate (ED), which is conducting a parallel money laundering investigation in the Mahadev fraud and has identified proceeds of crime worth ₹94,000 crore, may have to wait more before it could get Sourabh’s custody and interrogate him.
“We have identified some of his associates in India who helped him run illegal betting panels but we need to get to the bottom of the entire conspiracy and identify the conniving public servants in Chhattisgarh. So, we may ask for his further remand at the Raipur court on Thursday,” said an officer, who asked not to be named.
As exclusively reported by HT, Chandrakar was extradited from Oman on November 1 and taken into custody by the CBI.
Also Read: Mahadev case: Promoter brought back from Oman
Since then, he has been questioned in Delhi and Raipur and confronted with crucial evidence in the multi-crore fraud.
Alleged protection payments
While seeking his custody last week, CBI had said that it was crucial to identify police and administrative officials in Chhattisgarh who allegedly received huge amounts of money to allow the illegal operations to continue.
The CBI alleged that Chandrakar, other promoters and associates of Mahadev Book secured the protection of police and administrative officials and influential politicians by regularly paying them.
The CBI has alleged that hawala operators were used to arrange and distribute the alleged protection money. Police officers and employees were also allegedly engaged to channel these payments to police and administrative officials.
Also Read: Mahadev app: CBI arrests key accused Abhishek Kumar after he arrives from Dubai
How the betting network operated
Investigations have indicated that Chandrakar, co-founder Ravi Uppal and their associates promoted the Mahadev Book app and ran online betting operations through an extensive network of panel and branch operators.
The promoters allegedly retained 70-80% of the illegal earnings, while the remaining amount was distributed among panel operators, according to the CBI.
The accused, CBI has said, arranged hundreds of bank accounts using forged documents to facilitate transactions involving the proceeds of crime. These accounts were operated on a commission basis, while betting proceeds were transferred by panel operators to Chandrakar and other promoters in the UAE through multiple bank accounts, the agency alleged.
A substantial portion of the illegal earnings was also allegedly spent on advertising betting websites and organising lavish annual events attended by celebrities. The agency claimed that celebrities were paid from the proceeds generated through online betting
According to the CBI, Chandrakar left India in 2022 to evade the process of law and deliberately remained abroad without joining the investigation.
Following his extradition from Oman, he was taken to Raipur in a private aircraft last Tuesday for production before the trial court.
Scale of the alleged operations
According to ED, Mahadev began its illegal operations in 2019-20 and continues to run across India, despite a ban on multiple platforms and apps linked to the racket. The operations allow people to place illegal bets on poker and other card-based games, cricket, badminton, tennis, football matches and even election outcomes.
According to ED, there are at least 3,200 betting panels across India and the UAE and around 1,000 WhatsApp operators at the main call centre in the UAE. Around 70% to 80% of the profit gained by a panel is shared with the head office and the estimated earnings per month turn out to be ₹950 crore, the ED has alleged.
The anti money laundering probe agency has estimated the proceedings linked to Mahadev Online Betting (MOB) and some linked platforms to be worth around ₹94,000 crore, out of which ₹4,000 to ₹5,000 crore has already been remitted to the promoters abroad.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.
- This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

Quick Answer
Samsung’s latest Galaxy Z Fold 8 ad mocks Apple’s iPhone Duo at a difficult time. Reports of cracked displays, long delivery delays, and missing features have raised concerns about Apple’s first foldable. With its reputation for hardware excellence at stake, Apple needs more than silence to restore confidence.
Believe it or not, Samsung might finally have landed an ad glove on Apple. While the two brands have been taking digs at each other for years, Apple has kept things subtle, while Samsung has never been shy about being more direct. So when Apple finally decided to join the foldable race with the iPhone Duo, it was hardly surprising to see Samsung going all out against its rival – from Apple’s late arrival to the foldable party, the Duo name, the features, the price, you name it, and Samsung probably has tried to make fun of it. But as in the past, these attempts seemed just that… attempts to ruffle a leading brand on a perceived weakness, and to reassure their own fanbase. But very recently, we think Samsung struck a bit of a serious nerve in the Apple nervous system.
The Samsung Z Fold 8 slices up an apple (no, really!)
Samsung released a 32-second video on Instagram that shows an apple (duh) with a “new” sticker on the open screen of the Galaxy Z Fold8. The phone folds, and the apple gets sliced. This slice rolls down the floor, through all the old versions of the Z Fold in the past to show how many foldables Samsung launched before Apple made its first.
The video also boasts about the Z Fold 8 being thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo, all while comparing it to a slice of apple. This is not the most clever or cinematic Apple attack we have ever seen, but it is entertaining and thankfully is not over the top (unlike some others). What it also is, is a direct jab at something that Apple rarely has had to face – a perceived hardware problem with the iPhone.
iPhone Duo: from potential elixir to possible albatross
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, we thought it would be just the thing the foldables needed. Foldables have been a regular part of tech news and product portfolios since pre-COVID times (the first Galaxy Z Fold came in 2019), but even after years of iterations and multiple devices from multiple brands, the foldable segment was actually running out of steam.
So, when Apple launched the iPhone Duo, we thought that foldables would finally get some serious momentum. After all, once Apple launches something (even if it has been in the market for some time), it usually becomes more desirable and eminently “inspirational” for the competition: we have seen new features, specs, and design get picked up by the competition from Apple products, and become mainstream. From accepting touch to rejecting 3.5 mm audio jacks, it has all happened. So you could hardly blame many for thinking that Apple would launch a foldable phone, and voila! All foldable phones would start selling like hotcakes.
That scenario, however, does not seem to be playing out.
When Apple launched the iPhone Duo, the tech world went abuzz, which is business as usual when a new iPhone launches. But when the iPhone Duo became available for purchase, all the news that came in was not good. In many markets, due to supply and production issues, consumers had to wait for two months or more to get a device even after paying an advance. The brand’s decision to limit sales to two devices per person was also not well-received in some markets. It would have been understandable in the case of a new brand launching its first product, but from the first trillion-dollar company in the world, it just seemed unusually odd. The fact that it came with a super premium price tag did not help matters.
All those who have got their hands on Apple’s first foldable phone have not been thoroughly impressed with it either. There has been talk of users missing the speed and convenience of Face ID, the lack of app optimization, the new placement of the status bar, and more. And as if that were not enough, there was news that landed Apple in perhaps the hottest soup it has been in a very long time – reports have started coming in of the internal display cracking at the hinge, and a line of dead pixels appearing on it.
Often coming late to the party and rocking it…but perhaps not this time!
Once again, such problems from a new brand’s first product might have been treated with more patience. But imagine spending Rs. 2,99,900 and getting a device whose display has hardware issues. Imagine also being a person who has booked the device and is waiting for their unit, which is two months away. While Apple has acknowledged the issue, insisted that the issues exist in a small number of devices, and has assured users that all devices facing the issue will be replaced, a lot of damage has been done.
Apple’s reputation has, in some ways, worked against it. With Apple, the tech world has become accustomed to waiting for features, functions, and form factors that were seen on other devices. Android users have mocked Apple fans for getting the features that were on Android after years. But while Apple has delayed the addition of a feature or an entry into a segment, it has generally delivered an excellent performance. And that has been the defense of many Apple fans – Apple might not be the first to make a certain kind of device or bring a certain feature, but its implementation (whether it was capacitive touchscreens, Touch ID, App Store, and more) has been excellent and often an industry benchmark.
With Duo, that belief is being rocked. The brand has stepped into the foldable zone almost seven years after others, and launched a device with what seems to be a hardware flaw– not a software bug that can be fixed with an update, but a problem that can only be fixed with replacement.
Is silence golden for the communication wizard?
Apple’s handling of the issue so far has been a little unusual. The brand has found itself in trouble in the past as well with issues such as Antennagate and Bendgate, both of which generated a storm of criticism. But Apple officially addressed those issues publicly – Steve Jobs himself came out with an explanation in the case of the iPhone 4 when its stainless steel band interfered with the phone’s cellular performance, and the company also issued a very detailed statement on BendGate, famously pointing out that the issue had occurred with only nine users.
While there has not been radio silence from Apple with regard to Duo’s screen, no major management figure has come out to explain the issue or build back confidence – even in his first earnings call, new Apple CEO John Ternus limited himself to saying that while the issue existed, it affected a very small percentage of units. This relative silence could be (mis)interpreted by many in the public. To many, it does not seem as if the brand is working out solutions, as it has actually been launching devices left, right, and center since the Duo was launched.
To see management showcasing new products and talking of record earnings, even while complaints trickle in about a high-profile flagship does not make for great optics. We hope that changes soon, or alternatively, Apple comes out with a strong defense of its first foldable – it needs it. The longer it keeps silent, the more space it gives to its competitors to score points off its perceived weakness. And Apple cannot really afford to let cracks develop not just on the Duo, but in its own reputation for hardware excellence. As Samsung has shown, its competitors will not hang back in taking potshots at it. And unless credibly explained, these shots will start to hurt.
Given its potential and the hype around it, the Duo could still prove to be the elixir the foldable sector needs, but Apple needs to address the issues around it swiftly and effectively. This is a challenge unlike any other the brand has faced in recent times. Even the relative failure of the Vision Pro was more about a product being too futuristic (almost a prototype of sorts for an elite audience). The Duo, however, is supposed to redefine how we use foldables in particular and even smartphones in general. Many have even called it Apple’s most radical iPhone since the OG iPhone. How John Ternus tackles the issues surrounding the Duo could well define the tone of his tenure.

Top chip manufacturer TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI. That would give the Taiwanese chipmaker direct stakes in leading AI developers, even as its own contract chipmaking business has profited enormously from the AI data center buildout.
The chipmaker’s board approved plans to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at the latter’s expected IPO price, according to Reuters. Such an investment may give markets “a shot of confidence as the artificial-intelligence trade shows signs of strain,” The Wall Street Journal reported.
But analysts also warned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers, and customers has made it difficult to evaluate real market demand for AI-related hardware and services, according to the Journal.
TSMC’s chip fabrication plants physically produce the vast majority of Nvidia’s chips designed for AI data center workloads and make most of Apple’s custom chips used in iPhones, Mac laptops and desktops, plus Apple’s planned AI computing server. Most of these fabs are located in Taiwan, but TSMC also operates fabs in Japan and China, and it has an expanding US manufacturing cluster in Arizona. It is also building a new fab in Germany.

Anduril Industries has announced the successful demonstration of a new satellite-based sensor designed to track other spacecraft that may be hiding their maneuvers in Earth’s shadow.
Funded with Anduril’s internal capital, the company’s oven-sized satellite launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission in July with a package of tech demo payloads: an edge-compute processor, a power-management system adaptable to different mission types, and a long-wave infrared space sensor capable of detecting other objects in orbit.
Anduril reported on the success of the tech demo mission Tuesday. The company’s satellite, named Anduril-216, flies about 590 km (366 mi) above Earth, spending about one-third of each orbit in darkness. Anduril-216’s night passes allow its infrared imager to shine.
“This is a unique sensor that allows us to take imagery in long-wave [infrared],” said Gokul Subramanian, Anduril’s senior vice president of engineering. “What’s unique about that is it’s got a huge dynamic range. It has very low solar exclusion, so we’re blocked by the Sun very rarely, and we can see things in full dark.”
Filling a gap
The US military and a growing number of commercial data providers use a network of radars and optical sensors on the ground and in space to monitor satellite traffic. Anduril acquired one of the commercial satellite-tracking companies, ExoAnalytic Solutions, earlier this year. But there’s a gap in optical tracking as satellites fly in Earth’s shadow, so space traffic monitors could temporarily lose track of a spacecraft if it performs a maneuver in orbital night.
The Space Force is charged with tracking satellites for two primary reasons. First, military commanders want to know if an adversary moves its satellite in a threatening manner. Second, the Space Force issues traffic alerts to global satellite operators if there’s a risk of a collision.
“Right now, we don’t have ground sensors in our adversaries’ sovereign lands, and then in the eclipse period where we are relying heavily on visible sensors, the satellites that are not illuminated by the Sun, we can’t see those,” said Adam Thurn, vice president and general manager of orbital systems at Anduril. “With the long-wave infrared space sensor, we’re looking to close that gap.”

T-Mobile violated a New York state law by imposing a 50GB-per-month data cap and reducing speeds to less than a megabit per second on home Internet plans it is required to offer people with low incomes, New York government officials alleged.
T-Mobile agreed to a settlement requiring it to scrap the data and speed limits, to offer the required low-income plans to more parts of the state, and to make it easier for customers to find information about the plans. The settlement requires T-Mobile to eliminate the speed limits and expand availability of the plans within 120 days.
The alleged legal violation and the settlement are related to T-Mobile’s wireless home Internet service, not the company’s mobile plans. Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the settlement on Monday, saying that a state investigation found T-Mobile violated the New York Affordable Broadband Act (ABA).
The state law doesn’t specifically mention data caps, but it requires home Internet providers with at least 20,000 customers to offer plans at specific prices and minimum speeds to people who meet income-eligibility requirements. T-Mobile’s policy of reducing speeds after customers exceed a monthly data cap violates the law, New York officials said.
“An investigation by the Office of the Attorney General (OAG) found T-Mobile’s offerings did not meet the ABA’s requirements, which mandate that home Internet providers offer high-speed broadband to income-eligible households for $15 per month at speeds of at least 25 Mbps, or $20 per month for speeds of at least 200 Mbps,” the press release said.
Speeds reduced from 25 Mbps to 600 Kbps
New York says in the settlement with T-Mobile that “after the data cap is reached, the customer’s maximum download speed is reduced from 25 Mbps to 600 Kbps.” New York’s press release said “a typical customer could hit the data cap after about four days of usage.”
Data caps and speed limits aren’t the only restrictions. T-Mobile also “only offers ABA Internet plans to customers in homes that are eligible for 5G home Internet,” preventing residents in 4G-only areas from accessing the plans, the settlement says. The company also prevented search engines from indexing the webpage that provides detailed information about eligibility for and enrollment in ABA plans, it says.
“T-Mobile did not fully comply with the New York Affordable Broadband Act,” New York said in the settlement.
T-Mobile’s ABA webpage confirms that customers are provided only 50GB per month and that speeds after using the allotment are merely “up to 600 Kbps.”
Although the settlement includes a list of the New York AG’s findings, T-Mobile did not admit to any violation. “Respondent neither admits nor denies the OAG’s Finding in paragraph 1-14 above,” the document says.
New York beat industry attempt to kill law
New York started enforcing the Affordable Broadband Act in January 2025 after winning a nearly four-year court battle against broadband industry lobby groups that tried to kill the law. The groups that sued New York in a failed effort to block the law included CTIA, the wireless industry association that represents T-Mobile and other carriers. The law finally took effect a month after the Supreme Court rejected the broadband industry’s challenge.
When contacted by Ars, T-Mobile did not explain why it imposed the restrictions on low-income plans.
“We have a long history of helping customers in New York stay connected through low-cost broadband, and we’re updating our plan to meet the state’s requirements while maintaining the same low price,” T-Mobile said in a statement. “We’ve reached an agreement with the New York attorney general that builds on that commitment, provides greater clarity around our offering and makes the plan available to more eligible customers.”
The settlement with New York applies to T-Mobile’s fixed wireless Internet plans, which can be used for home Internet service as an alternative to wired broadband. The fixed wireless Internet relies on T-Mobile’s cellular network but provides access at a single location, delivering wireless signals to receivers installed at customer homes.
It took almost 18 months for New York to investigate T-Mobile’s compliance and reach a settlement with the company. “In June 2025, the New York Department of Public Service contacted the OAG and relayed concerns about certain features of the plan that T-Mobile was offering to customers eligible for reduced-price Internet service under the ABA,” the settlement said.
T-Mobile only offered plan in 5G areas
It seems that ISPs have generally offered the required plans, though cable company Optimum failed to comply until Ars made some inquiries on behalf of a customer who could not obtain the plan he was entitled to shortly after the law took effect. ISPs knew about the law long in advance due to the multiyear court case that they initiated, but Optimum wasn’t ready to comply with the requirement and rejected the low-income man’s request twice.
New York officials said the AG’s office “found that T-Mobile was only offering ABA plans in areas where it had deployed 5G wireless service, even though it offered full-price Internet plans that could deliver 25 Mbps download speeds in areas where it had 4G service. In addition, T-Mobile specifically coded its website to hide its ABA plan information from search engines, making it difficult for New Yorkers searching for low-priced Internet to find their plans.”
The settlement requires T-Mobile to stop intentionally limiting download speeds, and says the “temporary reduction of download speeds due solely to network congestion shall not constitute a violation of this Assurance.” There’s also an exception in the state law, which says ISPs shall provide 25Mbps “subject to exceptions adopted by the Public Service Commission where such download speed is not reasonably practicable.”
Extending the low-cost service to 4G areas, T-Mobile agreed to provide the low-income plans “at every address at which Respondent offers residential fixed wireless Internet service.” Speeds lower than 25 Mbps would not violate the settlement if T-Mobile “would be unable to provide a minimum download speed of 25 megabits per second to a residential fixed wireless Internet service customer enrolled in a non-ABA Plan at the same address.”
The document says that “T-Mobile offers 5G home Internet to roughly 40 percent of homes in rural areas of upstate New York and 4G (LTE) home Internet to the remainder of homes in the regions where T-Mobile offers fixed wireless service.”
To make its ABA webpage more accessible, the settlement says T-Mobile “shall not include a noindex tag on the webpage, or otherwise prevent search engines from indexing the webpage or presenting a link to the webpage in response to search engine queries.” T-Mobile must also prominently link to the ABA webpage on the part of its website that lists or describes its standard home Internet deals.
New York could sue T-Mobile if it violates the settlement. The ABA’s enforcement mechanism requires the attorney general to sue a broadband provider on behalf of residents. Such lawsuits can recover restitution and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.
ISPs that want to raise another challenge to New York’s law could get help from the Trump administration, which asserts that states must not enforce price regulations or net neutrality laws against any ISP that obtains grants from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. The grants have not been distributed yet, and California argues that the Trump administration does not have authority to preempt such laws.
T-Mobile’s violation of price-lock promise
In addition to this week’s settlement, New York struck a deal with T-Mobile last month over the carrier violating its promise to never raise prices on certain mobile plans that came with a lifetime price guarantee.
A state investigation “found that from 2017 to 2019, T-Mobile advertised ‘Price Guarantee Plans’ to its 4G customers, promising to ‘never change the price you pay,’” the New York attorney general’s office said on October 20. “However, in 2024, T-Mobile changed course and began raising the price of these plans by approximately $5 per phone line. New Yorkers enrolled in approximately 252,957 of these Price Guarantee Plans saw their phone bills increase.”
T-Mobile agreed to give affected customers several reimbursement options and a price lock until May 2029. The attorney general’s office estimated that the agreement would provide up to $38 million in value to customers affected by the price hikes. T-Mobile also agreed to pay the state a fine of $98,834.75.
T-Mobile provided a statement on the price-hike settlement.
“The $38 million cited in the press release is an estimate of potential benefits that a group of long-standing T-Mobile customers may choose to take advantage of, not the amount in refunds or payments,” T-Mobile said. “The agreement provides for approximately $98,000 paid to the state and a range of optional customer benefits. We’re glad to have this matter resolved and remain focused on delivering value to our customers.”
Jon is a Senior IT Reporter for Ars Technica. He covers the telecom industry, Federal Communications Commission rulemakings, broadband consumer affairs, court cases, and government regulation of the tech industry.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast rainfall and snowfall across several parts of the country on Thursday, November 12, with isolated heavy rainfall likely in Jammu and Kashmir. Delhi is expected to witness a partly cloudy sky, with mist or shallow fog at most places during the morning hours.
In its weather bulletin issued on Wednesday, November 11, the IMD said a western disturbance is likely to bring fairly widespread to widespread rainfall over Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and adjoining regions on November 12 and 13. Isolated heavy rainfall and hailstorm activity are also likely over Jammu and Kashmir on Thursday.
The weather agency has also forecast isolated thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds, with speeds reaching 40-50 kmph and gusting to 60 kmph, over Jammu and Kashmir during November 12-13.

On 02 November 2026, three BSF personnel, including an Assistant Commandant, were injured after a group of people allegedly attacked them during an anti-smuggling operation in Ashabari, Boxanagar, Tripura. The attackers allegedly assaulted the personnel, damaged their vehicle, and snatched a service weapon. By 08 November 2026, police had arrested 21 people, including two key accused, Rabiul Hossain and Mahabul Hossain. Chief Minister Manik Saha also chaired a security review meeting and directed strict action against those involved. Subsequently, authorities launched land demarcation and ownership verification near the Ashabari Border Outpost, while security agencies intensified identity checks and patrols along the India-Bangladesh border (here, here, and here).
Following the incident, several videos are being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming to show BSF personnel retaliating against the attackers by identifying and assaulting them, along with bulldozer action against their properties. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The video shows BSF personnel in Tripura retaliating against those involved in the attack by assaulting them.
Fact: The videos do not show BSF personnel retaliating against those involved in the 2 November 2026 attack in Tripura. The first video dates back to a lathi charge during local election counting in Tripura’s Khowai district on 5 October 2026. The second shows police action against garment workers protesting in Mirpur, Bangladesh, on 1 November 2026. The third is from a protest against a proposed land port in Jaigaon-Gotibari, West Bengal, on 3 November 2026. The fourth shows an eviction drive in Baburhat, Chandpur, Bangladesh, during which illegal structures were demolished. None of these videos are related to the BSF attack in Ashabari, Tripura. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1 & 2
In our investigation, we found that the first video, which shows security personnel lathi-charging people as they run away, dates back to 5 October 2026. It shows an incident during the vote-counting process for local elections in Tripura’s Khowai district. According to local media reports (here, here), the video was recorded near a counting centre in the Champahawar area, where workers from several political parties had gathered to hear the Gram Sabha election results. Tensions escalated during the counting process, prompting security personnel to use lathis to disperse the crowd. One person reportedly died in the ensuing stampede.
The second video, which shows a man being assaulted by security personnel, is also unrelated to the BSF attack in Tripura. We found that it shows police chasing and assaulting garment workers during a protest in Mirpur, Dhaka, Bangladesh (here, here, and here). According to local media reports, garment workers in the Mirpur-10 and Mirpur-11 areas staged protests on 1 November 2026, demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka. Police used batons and tear gas to disperse the protesters, leading to clashes, stone-pelting, and chases between the two sides. A police vehicle was also reportedly set on fire near the Mirpur-11 metro station (here, here, and here).
Video 3
In our investigation, we found (here, here, and here) that the video is from a protest held in the Jaigaon-Gotibari area of Alipurduar district, West Bengal, on 03 November 2026. Local tribal residents were protesting against a proposed land port, demanding rehabilitation and compensation. The situation escalated when police arrived to clear the road blockade, resulting in clashes between the protesters and police. Following the incident, police arrested 11 people.
Video 4
In our investigation, we found that the video shows an eviction drive in Baburhat, Chandpur, Bangladesh, during which more than 200 illegal structures were demolished. According to media reports (here, here, and here), local authorities launched a joint eviction campaign to remove illegal structures along the Chandpur-Comilla highway, between Khajuria and Border Bazar. Officials had issued prior warnings and public announcements before carrying out the demolition drive, which was scheduled to continue for three days, with the possibility of extension. The Roads and Highways Department and district administration also planned to plant trees in the cleared areas and construct a dedicated traffic intersection to ease congestion. Police and administrative personnel were deployed to maintain law and order during the operation.
To sum up, unrelated videos are being shared showing BSF personnel retaliating against attackers in Tripura.

The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 combines a stylish translucent design with smooth linear switches, a compact 75% layout, multi-device connectivity, and excellent battery life. It’s great for everyday typing, but limited customization, closely packed keys, and a premium price may put some buyers off.
ASUS has a wide range of product categories, and its mechanical keyboards are quite popular among gamers.
ASUS also offers standard mechanical keyboards for regular users. The company recently sent us its recently announced Jelly75 keyboard for review. It features a 75% layout, a unique translucent design, and multi-device connectivity. The keyboard also comes with a slightly higher price tag of Rs 7,999 (US $129.99)
I have been using this keyboard for the past several days, and in this review, you will learn everything about the keyboard, including the good and the bad things, and also learn if this Jelly75 keyboard is worth the price for what it offers.
Table of Contents
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Review: Design, Typing Experience, and Everyday Use
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Unboxing
You get a fairly simple package when you unbox the ASUS Jelly75 KD201. Inside, you find the keyboard, a USB-A to USB-C cable, a 2.4GHz wireless receiver, a quick start guide, and warranty documentation.
However, ASUS doesn’t provide a keycap puller or even a switch puller out of the box.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Design and Build Quality
The ASUS Jelly75 keyboard is available in two colors: Volt Green and Orange Meadow. I received the Volt Green variant of the Jelly75, which comes with a translucent chassis and a combination of white, black, and mint green keys. This color combination makes it very attractive for a vibrant and unique desktop setup.
If you don’t like contrasting looks, the Orange Meadow color variant, which offers muted colors and a retro-looking design, is the best choice, which I personally prefer.
But the Volt Green variant also looks good in person and stands out more than the regular black-and-white finishes on most mechanical keyboards.
The standout feature on both variants is the translucent design, so you can see parts of the internal keyboard structure through the casing.
However, the body and keys are made of polycarbonate, but it’s solidly built, and the weight adds extra rigidity.
The steel plate inside the keyboard adds to its weight, bringing it to about 1.19 kg.
While the weight helps the keyboard stay stable during typing, it can be inconvenient if you plan to carry it often.
Since the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard uses a 75% layout, it measures about 326.2 x 142.1 x 39.5 mm, which takes up less space than traditional full-size keypads but more than smaller percentage keypads.
If you are not familiar with keyboard percentages, here is a detailed visual guide we created to help you understand different keyboard layouts.
The keys are densely packed together, and there is not much space between them; also, there is no gap between functional keys and the regular keys, especially around the arrow key cluster, where, until you get used to this layout, there is a high chance that you can accidentally mispress the other keys.
Also, the keyboard doesn’t have any knobs, which would have been a nice addition for direct volume control. Additionally, the Caps Lock key doesn’t come with any light indication to show it’s active.
The rubber pads on the bottom help it stay stable and in place without sliding on a smooth desk surface.
The keyboard also comes with adjustable kickstands that let you set three typing-angle positions.
While the design is attractive, the translucent, lighter-colored keycaps make dirt more visible. It also supports a wireless receiver, but the keypad doesn’t have a dedicated compartment to store it, which is inconvenient, especially if you plan to carry it between workspaces. It won’t be much of a concern if you plan to connect it via Bluetooth, but it’s something you should know.
Continuing with the design, you will find the ASUS logo on the bottom right, a toggle to switch between connection types on the top, and a USB-C charging port on the top left.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Keyboard Layout and Ergonomics
The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 uses a 75% keyboard layout, which is a sweet spot between portability and functionality.
Unlike smaller 60% or 65% layouts, it includes a function row at the top and navigation keys on the right.
However, it doesn’t include a separate number pad, which full-size keyboards often have.
This compact layout has all essential keys and doesn’t miss anything, especially if you are coming from notebooks or a Mac.
This layout works for writing, programming, office work, and even standard gaming.
Although you get a dedicated number row below the function keys, a dedicated number pad is still more convenient, especially if your work involves entering numbers regularly.
However, the keys are densely packed, with negligible gaps between them.
ASUS has also included a dedicated Copilot key near the arrow key cluster, which could accidentally launch Windows Copilot, especially until you get used to this densely packed layout.
In terms of key design, ASUS used tall, squarish-rounded keycaps instead of the flatter options found on many keyboards.
While this makes them look unique, it may take time to get used to, especially if you are switching from a MacBook or another low-profile keyboard.
Since these keys are taller, I recommend a separate wrist rest, especially if you plan to use the keyboard lying flat.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Switches, Keycaps and Typing Experience
Typing experience is one of the most important things to consider when buying a mechanical keyboard, since you spend several hours every day writing, coding, or working on documents.
The ASUS Jelly75 comes with linear mechanical switches that offer 4mm of total key travel.
However, you won’t get tactile feedback when you press the keys. Unlike tactile switches, which have a noticeable bump when pressed, the Jelly75’s linear mechanism presses the keys gently, creating a smooth typing experience.
I personally prefer tactile feedback because I am used to my MacBook keyboard, but many also prefer smooth switches for longer typing sessions.
ASUS also rates the switches at 50 million keystrokes, which should last longer with regular use.
The keyboard also offers a gasket-mounted structure. ASUS calls it Uni-cushion technology, where it uses cushioning between the internal keyboard layout assembly and the outer body to help absorb vibrations.
This is especially useful if you press the keys harder, as the chassis absorbs vibration and stays steady overall.
The keycaps have a rigid feel. You won’t get rattling, wobbling, or uneven keypresses even on the larger keys like the spacebar.
As a mechanical keyboard, the ASUS Jelly75 offers hot-swappable switches, so you can remove and replace individual switches without soldering.
If you prefer tactile switches, you can also replace linear switches with tactile options.
However, ASUS doesn’t include a switch puller in the box, so you will need to buy it separately if you plan to swap the keys.
The ASUS Jelly75 keyboard comes with a white backlight instead of RGB backlighting. It keeps the keyboard looking cleaner.
You can adjust the white backlighting to four brightness levels using the dedicated keys on your keyboard, including Fn + F9 shortcuts.
You can also turn off the backlight completely, which can help extend battery life further.
However, the backlight illuminates the area around the keys and doesn’t illuminate the letters and symbols printed on the keys; instead, it glows around them.
This won’t be an issue if you are already used to this keyboard layout and type without looking at the keyboard, but if you look at the keys while typing, the lighting may not be as helpful in low light.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Connectivity and Multi-Device Switching
Another big advantage of the ASUS Jelly75 KD201 keyboard is its connectivity. If you use multiple devices, such as a Windows PC, MacBook, or iPad, you can connect this keyboard to all of them wirelessly and switch between them easily.
The Jelly75 keyboard supports three connectivity options: Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless, and a wired USB connection, and it can connect up to five devices using all three connection types.
The Jelly75 keyboard supports Bluetooth 3.0 and 5.0, and it can remember up to three Bluetooth devices.
To pair your devices, switch the keyboard to Bluetooth mode and hold Fn + 1, 2, or 3 for more than three seconds.
Once paired, you can easily switch between devices using the corresponding shortcuts.
You can pair up to three devices via Bluetooth. It also supports a 2.4 GHz wireless connection using the included USB receiver. ASUS says the wireless range is about 10 meters.
You can also connect the keyboard using the USB cable provided in the box.
The USB cable is long and suitable for any desktop layout, and its braided design lets you fold it easily and keeps it tngle-free.
However, as I said before, the main limitation is that it lacks a dedicated compartment for storing the 2.4GHz receiver if you plan to carry the keyboard between workplaces.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Customization
You won’t get much customization on the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard. Instead, ASUS kept it simple with a plug-and-play design.
It supports dedicated shortcuts to switch between Windows and MacBook layouts and offers several function-key shortcuts.
You can use Fn + F1, F2, and F3 to mute or adjust the volume, and F6-F8 to control music playback. It also includes shortcuts for switching between applications, searching, and launching Launchpad on macOS and Windows Search and Spotlight on macOS.
The keyboard also includes a dedicated Microsoft Copilot key, which lets you launch Copilot directly from your keyboard.
However, one noticeable downside is that, unlike other mechanical keyboards, it doesn’t include dedicated software for advanced key-mapping customization, so you can’t set custom shortcuts.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Battery Life
The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 has a 4000mAh rechargeable battery. ASUS rates the keyboard as lasting up to 8500 hours on a single charge with the backlight off, which translates to roughly 354 days.
It can last days without needing to charge. I used this keyboard with the backlight on throughout the entire two-week review period. I didn’t have to charge it once.
Regarding charging, the Jelly75 uses a USB-C port and includes a USB-A to USB-C cable in the box. It supports up to 5W charging. You can also charge the keyboard by connecting it directly to your device. It also includes a useful wired USB mode, which can be convenient if you suddenly run out of battery.
The keyboard uses battery light indicators to show the remaining battery. When the battery level drops to 20%, the status light slowly flashes red and reminds you to charge it. While charging, the indicator flashes, and when it’s fully charged, the light turns solid white. You can also check the remaining battery life in the Bluetooth settings for the connected device.
Asus MD105 Wireless Mouse Review
Along with the Jelly75 keyboard, ASUS also sent the MD105 wireless mouse, which pairs well with it. Interestingly, it comes in two color variants: Volt Green, which perfectly matches your keyboard if you picked up the Volt Green variant, and Milky White, which suits the Orange variant.
In terms of design, the MD105 mouse looks like a conventional mouse with a slightly wider body, and it comes with a dedicated thumb rest designed for right-hand users that offers great support, especially if you are a creator and plan to use the mouse for several hours a day.
It feels very light and weighs just 66 grams without a battery, and although it’s slightly wider, it isn’t as travel-friendly as other compact mice.
One feature I particularly like is the silent-click mechanism, which reduces clicking noise. This can be especially useful in shared offices and libraries, or when you’re working late at night.
The MD105 uses an optical sensor with three adjustable DPI settings, including 1200, 1600, and 2400. You can switch between them using the DPI button. Lower DPI settings offer more controlled cursor movement, while higher settings let you move the cursor faster.
For my big hands, the mouse feels perfectly compact, and my right finger rests comfortably on the support, making it comfortable to use.
Since it is lightweight, it is also quickly responsive and easy to move. For connectivity, the MD105 supports Bluetooth 5.0 and also offers 2.4 GHz wireless through the included USB receiver.
You can pair up to three devices: two via Bluetooth and one via the wireless receiver.
It also offers a wireless compartment in the mouse. If you are planning to use it with Bluetooth, you can safely store the wireless receiver in the compartment.
Since it supports multiple devices like the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard, it is also useful for switching between Windows and Mac computers.
A few months ago, I switched to a mouse with a built-in battery, but the MD105 comes with a single AA battery included in the box.
You need to replace it whenever you want, without waiting for the mouse to recharge. However, I prefer a rechargeable mouse, as mine also comes with a battery level indicator, so I can charge it.
If you can, this MD105 mouse suggests you need to keep an AA battery on hand in case it suddenly runs out of battery
The ASUS MD105 mouse is priced at Rs 1,699, which is a good value considering the ergonomics, comfort, and portability it offers.
It also has dedicated left-side switches for extra shortcuts, and its quiet operation, adjustable sensitivity, and multi-device connectivity make it a great buy if you are planning to get it alongside the Jelly75 keyboard.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Review Verdict
At Rs 8,999 (US$129.99), ASUS faces stiff competition from brands like AULA, Royal Kludge, and Keychron, which offer feature-packed mechanical keyboards with hot-swappable switches, RGB lighting, and dedicated volume knobs.
Some keyboards, like Royal Kludge, also offer a small dedicated display that shows useful information such as battery status and connection mode.
However, ASUS Jelly75 bets on its design, with colorful, translucent, rounded keycaps that make it one of the most distinctive-looking keyboards.
The gasket-mounted construction, linear switches, and multi-device connectivity also make it a great everyday companion with a simple plug-and-play device for a productive and attractive-looking desktop setup. However, if you want a fully customizable keyboard experience with a dedicated knob and customizable software, this might be a limitation.

- Comfortable typing experience
- Hot-swappable switches
- Multi-device connectivity
- Excellent battery life

LONDON — Millions of people would have their obesity diagnoses flipped — from having obesity to not, and vice versa — if an alternate way of defining the disease supplanted the standard body mass index measure, according to a new study that argues such an approach could lead to better care for patients.
The study, published Wednesday in the journal Nature, is the latest volley in a debate about the limitations of the body mass index, and what could possibly replace it. BMI is deeply entrenched as a metric, dictating everything from regulatory decisions to insurance coverage to who is eligible for certain medical treatments. But it is a blunt measure that fails to take into account other health issues and differences in body composition, such as where fat is stored.
The new research stems from an effort to come up with a different diagnostic framework. Last year, a Lancet commission proposed a pathway that aimed to identify people whose health is currently being hurt by their weight and who are more likely to have dire outcomes going forward.

As Delhiites burst firecrackers well past the 10 p.m. deadline set by the Supreme Court for Deepavali night, air pollution shot up to over 150-200 times World Health Organisation (WHO) limits in parts of the city, but fell through the early morning hours of Monday (November 9, 2026) due to better weather conditions, show official data.
At the peak of pollution, following the bursting of firecrackers on Sunday night, crucial air quality data were missing from several monitoring stations managed by government authorities. Experts say missing data on peak values of air pollution will artificially show better air quality than the reality.
Though the Supreme Court allowed only green firecrackers during fixed windows on November 7 and 8, traditional firecrackers, which are more polluting, were also available in the markets of Delhi.
As per the Delhi government’s Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) data, the level of PM2.5 (a major pollution) in Patparganj of East Delhi was 2,597 micrograms per cubic metre at 1 a.m. on Monday — about 173.13 times the WHO permissible limit of 15 micrograms per cubic metre for a 24-hour period.
Similarly, the level of PM2.5 in NSUT West Campus was 3,008.4 micrograms per cubic metre at 5 a.m. on Monday — about 200.5 times the WHO permissible limit. PM2.5 (Particulate matter 2.5) are fine inhalable particles, which can get into lungs and bloodstream and lead to a range of respiratory and other diseases.
Favourable wind
Gufran Beig, chair professor, National Institute of Advanced Studies, said though the air pollution spiked around 12 midnight on Sunday to 5 a.m. on Monday due to bursting of firecrackers on Deepavali, both wind direction and speed were very favourable for faster dispersion of air pollution.
“The wind direction was earlier north westerly, originating from stubble burning areas in Punjab and Haryana. But around Sunday afternoon, it changed to easterly and south easterly and also picked up speed by Sunday evening. The reversal of wind direction led to almost negligible effect of stubble burning in Delhi,” said Mr. Beig, who is also the founder-director of the Central government’s SAFAR (System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting Research).
The 24-hour average overall Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 344 (“very poor”) at 4 p.m. on Monday, lower than 376 (“very poor”) a day earlier, according to the CPCB’s daily bulletin, which is considered the day’s AQI. A higher AQI means worsening of air quality. The overall AQI of Delhi which stood at 370 (very poor) at 9 a.m. on Monday, improved through the day to reach 344 by 4 p.m.
Meanwhile, both the AAP and the Congress attacked the BJP government over the missing data, with the former alleging that it was “data fraud”. Hitting back, Delhi Labour Minister Kapil Mishra alleged there was a “conspiracy” by AAP-governed Punjab to set stubble on fire on Sunday evening.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.
Stubble burning in Punjab
Meanwhile, Punjab recorded 1,152 stubble burning incidents on Sunday — the highest this paddy harvest season, according to the Indian Agricultural Research Institute’s (IARI) daily bulletin. But it dropped to 198 on Monday, taking the total this harvest season to 4,657, the second lowest since 2020 (till November 9), the data show.
The contribution of stubble burning in neighbouring States to PM2.5 (a chief pollutant) in Delhi on Sunday was 5.1%, according to the Union Ministry of Earth Sciences data.

How valuable is a CEO? Often, it's hard to say. Sometimes, though, a series of unusual events provides a crystal-clear answer.
On Wednesday afternoon, the New York Times reported that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a subordinate, following revelations earlier this week that he had a romantic relationship with a possible Chinese spy.
Right after that, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia's board was preparing to oust Huang.
That one-two punch knocked Nvidia shares down about 8% in after-hours trading, wiping more than $300 billion off the company's market value.
The Chinese spy allegations were already known days ago. The new news today is that Jensen Huang is likely to be ousted as CEO.
So we have our answer: Huang is worth at least $300 billion. That's more than Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs, the world's most important investment banks.
And quite right, too. Huang is "the architect of the US AI trajectory," Stacy Rasgon, a top chip analyst from Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors earlier this week.
This is the most powerful new technology to emerge since the dawn of the internet 30 years ago. And the US is in the lead — well ahead of China in second place.
Now, with Huang likely out, and no obvious successor, America's AI lead looks shakier.
"We can't even begin to speculate as to who they might find to fill Jensen's shoes," Rasgon wrote in a note to investors Wednesday evening. He slashed Nvidia's price target to $200 from $400.
Earlier in the week, Rasgon warned of the geopolitical risks if Huang was forced to step down.
"The primary beneficiary of Jensen's removal as Nvidia's CEO would clearly be China; we hope cooler heads prevail," he wrote.
On Wednesday night, other analysts shared similar concerns.
"This would be a setback for the US, particularly as China continues aggressively investing in its own AI capabilities," Brad Gastwirth, global head of research at Circular Technology, told me.
"Removing Jensen would be a tremendous mistake," he added. "Nvidia is central to America's AI leadership, and losing Jensen at this stage could create unnecessary disruption."
Nvidia's board has serious questions to answer about Huang's conduct, especially his relationship with a possible Chinese spy. If they do nothing, the directors expose themselves to legal risk as representatives of the company's shareholders.
One of the few real powers a public company board holds is the ability to hire and fire executives, so actions often involve tough decisions like this.
But the board also has to weigh the enormous cost of losing the man who built Nvidia into the engine of the AI boom.
Tonight, that cost is at least $300 billion.
"The board obviously needs to take the allegations seriously, particularly anything involving national security," Gastwirth said. "Unless the investigation uncovers something that makes his position untenable, I believe the board would be making a major strategic mistake by removing him."

'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
SEOUL, South Korea — Until she fled North Korea three years ago, Kim Yumi felt deeply frustrated whenever state TV showed leader Kim Jong Un with his young daughter. The message, she felt, was clear and worrying: North Korea was laying the groundwork for an eventual hereditary transfer of power, this time to Kim's daughter.
Publicly questioning the Kim dynasty's hold on power would mean severe persecution. Already angered by draconian pandemic regulations that ruined her family's fishing business, she defected to South Korea by boat with her family.
"My husband and I didn't want our children to live under a fourth-generation dictatorship. As parents, we thought the best thing we could do for our children was to give them freedom," said Kim Yumi, 32, who now lives in Seoul.
North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty, with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession. There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions — from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011.
This time, North Korea is apparently trying something radical.
Kim Jong Un's repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years have led to speculation that she's being groomed as her father's heir.
The question of who will become North Korea's next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge — governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.
North Koreans have no say in the selection of their future leader, and analysts and defectors say they will passively accept a third dynastic succession — at least publicly.
To gauge North Koreans' private views, The Associated Press spoke with nearly a dozen defectors who still have contacts in North Korea or witnessed the country's previous power successions, as well as several experts.
Most defectors believe the girl is Kim's heir
Not much is known about Kim's daughter except that she's reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae.
Since late 2022, she has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim's "most beloved" and "respected" child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father.
South Korea's spy agency says she is Kim's likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by the AP shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North's deeply patriarchal culture.
"During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un," said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea's Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. "They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un," when he accompanied his father as his heir.
Kang Mi-Jin, a defector who runs a company analyzing North Korea's economy, said her contacts inside the North told her over smuggled phones that they think Kim Ju Ae is in line to succeed her father.
Jung Gwang-il, a defector who specializes in smuggling outside information to North Korea, said the North Koreans he meets as they visit Chinese border towns also hold the same belief.
Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity, holding her as a baby during a 2013 trip to Pyongyang.
Doubts remain about a woman becoming North Korea's leader
Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn't been confirmed.
Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers' Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un's influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry.
"My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader," said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009.
Lee Si-young, a defector who heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station, said that some of her older contacts in North Korea aren't happy with a woman taking power. But she said members of the Kim family "are like gods reigning over humans so gender really doesn't matter."
Kim's push for hereditary power transfer faces little resistance at home
Whether or not the girl succeeds her father, observers agree that Kim Jong Un, 42, is likely to designate one of his children to prolong his family's rule, a move they expect would face little resistance at home. South Korea's spy agency recently assessed that Kim is extremely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease but shows no other signs of poor health.
North Koreans will passively "accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with," said Ahn Chan-il, a defector and scholar who heads the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul.
During North Korea's first leadership transition, in 1994, the new leader, Kim Jong Il, then 52, had already spent two decades as the official successor working alongside his father to run the country.
The second succession, in 2011, was more uncertain. Kim Jong Un, who was then 27, was seen by outsiders as too young and inexperienced. He quickly consolidated his grip on power, however, by orchestrating high-profile executions and purges, including the 2013 killing of his powerful uncle Jang Song Thaek.
"A hereditary power succession system has been institutionalized in North Korea, just like presidential elections in our system," said Oh Gyeong-seob, an analyst at Seoul's Korea Institute for National Unification. "North Korea's ruling elite accepts it as a matter of course. So do its general citizens."
Choi Song-juk, who fled North Korea in 2015, said she had been so brainwashed that she had no complaints about the North's two earlier power successions. She now calls them "nonsense."
Defector Jeon Jae-hyun said North Korea's pervasive surveillance apparatus keeps people from voicing their discontent with the government and helps enforce political loyalty.
Defector Kim Yumi said she had never heard about the girl until Kim Jong Un publicly introduced his daughter at a long-range missile launch site in November 2022.
"Ordinary people know absolutely nothing about private lives of the Kim family," said Kim Yumi, who now runs a YouTube channel on North Korea. "They don't really try to know about it and don't pay attention to it because doing so could put them in danger."

A baby girl born into a financially struggling family in Punjab turned out to be a source of unexpected fortune for her parents. Just a day after 24-year-old carpenter Yudhvir Singh welcomed his daughter, he won ₹1.5 crore in a state lottery. The win came after some relatives had told him, ‘We wanted a boy’. Singh now credits his daughter for changing the family's fortunes and has named her Barkat, meaning prosperity. According to a report by The Tribune, Singh, a resident of Bareta town in Punjab's Mansa district, bagged the first prize in the Punjab State Dear 200 Monthly Lottery. His daughter was born on November 6, while the lottery results were declared on November 7. The proud father chose the name Barkat, which means prosperity, for his daughter following the unexpected windfall. Singh had bought the winning ticket on November 4 from a lottery stall in Budhlada. He was accompanying his pregnant wife, Harman, to a hospital in Mansa for a medical check-up when he made the purchase. The carpenter had not intended to buy a lottery ticket that day. He had stopped at the stall while getting his mobile phone number ported and decided to try his luck. However, the decision did not go down well with his wife initially, particularly given the family's financial difficulties. The couple was already repaying a loan taken to build their two-room house and had additional medical expenses to manage ahead of their first child's arrival. Singh recalled that Harman had questioned why he was spending money on a lottery ticket when they needed funds for hospital bills. He also said that the private hospital had declined to offer even a ₹5,000 reduction in their bill. For the family, which was struggling to meet its expenses, the lottery ticket had been an unplanned purchase. Little did Singh know that it would eventually bring him a prize worth ₹1.5 crore. The lottery announcement, coming just a day after his daughter's birth, made the win particularly special for Singh. The celebrations also changed the way some relatives viewed the arrival of the baby girl. Singh believes his daughter's birth and the lottery win are closely connected, and considers her arrival a blessing for the family. “I have named her Barkat (prosperity). She has brought good fortune to our home. How can we name her anything else?” he said. Despite the sudden change in the family's financial situation, Singh said he has already decided where the prize money should go. His daughter's education and future remain his biggest priorities. “My daughter has changed my fortune. She has brought her own luck with her. I want to spend the money on her education and future so that she can stand on her own feet and get a good job,” he said. Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150 mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards South Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85 mph (140 km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of over 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150 mph (240 km/h), with winds gusting over 185 mph (296 km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100 mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150 mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.
