New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc.
On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by the prime minister, Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside its traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.
But with some seats won by very slim margins, and special votes yet to be counted, that success is precarious, resulting in an election too close to call until official results are released on 27 November.
Special votes include overseas votes and ballots cast outside a voter’s electorate. In 2023, 600,000 such votes were made, 21% of the total. These votes tend to favour the left – in 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) and the Greens gaining three seats between them.
With nearly 100% of the regular votes counted on Saturday night, National secured 42 seats, Act 13 and New Zealand First 12. The combined 67-seat majority is wafer thin, with the left bloc just three seats behind.
Speaking to a room full of the party faithful at Auckland’s Viaduct events centre just before midnight, Luxon said the results were “too close to call” and the special votes would need to be counted before negotiations could begin.
National was still the largest party in parliament, he said, and had “a pathway to forming the next government”. National pipped Labour by 0.02% in the party vote.
Labour, led by Chris Hipkins, secured 35 seats, while its traditional coalition partners the Greens won 16 and Te Pāti Māori five. Even with the seven seats from the centrist newcomer party, Opportunity, the left bloc is three seats short of forming a government.
Before a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, Hipkins joked that New Zealand had spoken but “it may take a bit longer to work out what they’ve said”.
“As things stand tonight, it is clear that we are not going to know the shape of our next government for a little while longer yet,” Hipkins said, promising that Labour would get “straight to work” should the final count land in its favour.
The collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties, including Act, New Zealand First and the Greens. It is also helped propel Opportunity into parliament for the first time.
Opinion polls in the lead-up to the election had Opportunity placed to become the kingmaker. At this stage, the right bloc does not need the party to govern, but if special votes change the landscape, its predicted role could come to fruition.
Currently at 5.9%, the centrist party has met the threshold needed to enter parliament, a historic first. Since New Zealand adopted the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996, no new party has been able to meet that threshold – all the other minor parties have been born from MPs or groups splintering from larger parties.
The party’s leader, Qiulae Wong, told her supporters in Auckland she was “stoked”.
“It’s looking very promising for us,” she said. “Let’s just see how the rest of the votes fall.”
In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote.
However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.
National won more seats that its party support allows for, meaning it could gain an extra five seats to make up the balance.
That will be good news for its path to power, but comes with some significant trade-offs for the party. Four of its most senior ministers, including Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Chris Bishop and Gerry Brownlee, will not return to parliament because they did not win a seat, or the party didn’t win enough votes to bring in list-only MPs.
On the other side of the house, Te Pāti Māori picked up five overhang seats.
With all the extra seats, there could be 130 in the next parliament – a record under MMP – which means 65 seats are needed to form a coalition.
The country faces a two-week wait until special votes are announced, followed by the possibility of weeks of negotiations. Luxon said caretaker government conventions would apply in the meantime.
“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well-established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.

Gaming, social media, and e-commerce platforms are facing a fresh wave of sweeping European Union rules that aim to make “your online experience fairer.” The newly proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) published by the EU Commission on Wednesday is designed to tackle practices that exploit consumers into spending more of their time and money online, including misleading prices or availability, addictive design features like gaming loot boxes, undisclosed influencer marketing, and more.
Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
The proposed Digital Fairness Act seeks to bolster consumer protections for online users.
“The Act will protect consumers of all ages shopping and browsing for goods or services online,” the EU Commission said in a news bulletin. “It will also mean fairer competition for businesses, which are expecting to save EU consumers up to €13.7 billion ($15.1 billion) a year.”
Here’s an overview of what the DFA proposal includes:
- A ban on manipulative marketing practices and so-called “dark patterns” that push consumers into making decisions they might not otherwise make, such as fake claims about a product almost being sold out.
- A requirement to give consumers the choice to turn off addictive features, such as persistent prompts, endless scrolling, and autoplay of videos. Restrictions around addictive design also apply to “AI companions and general conversational chatbots.”
- Restrictions on unfair practices that encourage overspending, such as banning gambling-like features (pay-to-win and pay-to-progress, for example) for minors.
- Requiring influencers to clearly disclose advertising content, and restrictions to prevent them from exploiting the trust of children.
- Restrictions on unfair personalised ads and prices that target minors or take advantage of sensitive data.
- Making subscriptions and digital contracts easier to cancel, with prompts to remind customers about upcoming automatic renewals and free trial periods coming to an end.
- Requiring clear and transparent pricing, especially around dynamic pricing and purchases using virtual in-app currency. When consumers wait in virtual queues for cultural and sports event tickets, companies will have to show the current price in real time and at the highest possible price.
- Giving consumers the right to communicate with a human customer service representative, and clear rights using an AI agent to make purchases.
The scope of the restrictions being proposed is broad, and could have a significant impact on major parts of the online digital landscape, from the “rabbit hole” algorithms across YouTube, TikTok, and Meta platforms, to AI chatbots and apps like DuoLingo that relentlessly nudge users to keep interacting with them. Some gaming organizations have already slammed the DFA proposal, describing its restrictions around virtual currencies, loot boxes, and offering micro-transactions to minors as being “unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate.”
Given this is a draft proposal, the DFA will undergo various approvals through the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union before being passed into law, and its current measures could be changed or removed entirely as part of that process. When (or if) it does come into force, the EU Commission says companies who violate the regulations could see fines of up to six percent of their worldwide annual turnover.
“Our consumer protection rules will help ensure that businesses compete on the merits of their products and services - not on their ability to exploit consumers or evade the rules. We are not making it harder to do business. We are making it harder to do business unfairly,” EU Commissioner Michael McGrath said in remarks following the DFA draft publication. “We cannot have 21st-century consumers protected by rules that have not kept pace with the 21st-century economy.”

In 1924, Dutch physician and physiologist Willem Einthoven was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine “for his discovery of the mechanism of the electrocardiogram (ECG)”.
His work made it possible to record the electrical activity of the heart with greater accuracy. By developing the string galvanometer and establishing a standard method for interpreting its recordings, Einthoven helped turn electrocardiography into an important tool for studying heart function. Today, the ECG is routinely used to investigate irregular heart rhythms, detect signs of reduced blood supply to the heart muscle and identify evidence of previous heart attacks.

Famed ship SS United States to be sunk off coast of Florida
- Published
A ship that was once the fastest in the world and is longer than the Titanic will be sunk off the coast of Florida and turned into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will soon become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.
Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.
Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it will be added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, as a land-based museum detailing the ship's history is also planned.
Before its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities from the US the Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969.
A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.
The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work. On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will be sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives.
Stars including Marlon Brando, Coco Chanel, Duke Ellington, Salvador Dali, Walt Disney, Judy Garland and Cary Grant also boarded the ship during its sailing lifetime.
Before its purchase by the municipal Florida government, a number of proposals that would have seen the ship live a second life as a museum or a floating hotel failed.
Instead, the famed ship sat at various docks with various owners as legal battles played out.
The SS United States Conservancy group repeatedly attempted to keep the ship above water, but was unsuccessful.
Conservancy President Susan Gibbs - whose grandfather helped design the SS United States - said she was glad that the story of the ship would live on.
"[The ship] has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together," Gibbs told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

A claim is spreading online that Jan. 6 Capitol rioter Jake Lang, who was pardoned by U.S. President Donald Trump, crashed a cat convention in Seattle because he appeared to believe the event was for furries — people who identify with or enjoy dressing as anthropomorphic animals or creatures.
Videos of the alleged event and jokes about Lang's apparent mistake spread on X, Facebook and Threads. (Warning: Lang uses profane language and homophobic slurs in the video below).
Lang did, in fact, post videos of himself at Sea-Meow, a Seattle cat convention, with captions that claimed he "BUSTED UP" a "furry convention." Of course, it's impossible to know whether Lang actually believed Sea-Meow was a furry convention, or if he simply said that it was. 
Either way, however, it is accurate to say that Lang crashed a cat convention while publicly claiming that it was for furries. As such, we have rated this claim as true.
The video shows Lang yelling slurs at people wearing pink shirts and cat ears who appeared to be convention staff. Lang accused them of "sexualizing children" and spreading "homosexual and transsexual ideas." Lang also claimed the organizers were "mislabeling" the convention before one of the people in pink shirts stepped in.
"This is a convention for cats," the person tells Lang in the video. Lang, in response, doubles down, asking why there were furries at Sea-Meow. (Being a furry is not inherently sexual, and academic research indicates that furries are more likely to identify as such for nonsexual reasons, like social belonging.)
The "Sea-Meow" sign is clearly visible in Lang's videos, and there is no evidence the videos were generated using artificial intelligence.
While at least one person in a fur suit — the costumes furries are known for — was visible in Lang's video, Sea-Meow is clearly about cats, not furries. The convention describes itself as "the premier cat convention of the Purrcific NW, the mecca of cat people." Sea-Meow's stated mission makes it clear that it's focused on supporting cats, not furries:
Our mission is rooted in the celebration of our love of cats by bringing together all the cat people under one roof and supporting feline organizations around the United States in meaningful ways. We aim to connect our community, educate and spread feline awareness, inspire people to participate in the animal welfare community, and help cats conquer the world, one home at a time!
Programming for Sea-Meow, which ran Nov. 7 and 8, included panels with cat rescuers and a presentation by Jackson Galaxy, a cat behaviorist and YouTuber perhaps best known for hosting the now-defunct Animal Planet show "My Cat From Hell." Sea-Meow's website also said that 15% of ticket proceeds went to charities like the Seattle Animal Shelter and Feral Care, a nonprofit organization that provides food and shelter to "unadoptable cats."
Videos on Sea-Meow's social media largely show people of all ages cuddling cats, with nary a fur suit in sight. Sea-Meow's sponsors include Weruva, a cat food company, and BluePearl Pet Hospital, which operates specialty and emergency vet hospitals across the United States.
Sea-Meow's programming did include a "cat cosplay contest," but photos of example cosplays did not show any fur suits, instead depicting people dressed like Hello Kitty, a "taco cat" and other non-furry costumes.
We reached out to Sea-Meow to ask if the convention had any programming or policies about furries and if Lang ever actually made it past the doors, given that his videos are filmed outside of the actual convention building. We await a response.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has cautioned students and parents against enrolling in medical colleges without verifying their statutory recognition and regulatory approvals, warning that fraudulent institutions could be misleading aspirants through advertisements, websites, social media promotions and unauthorised admission offers.
In a recent advisory issued in compliance with directions from the Supreme Court, the NMC has urged students to independently verify a medical college’s approval status, permitted student intake, and admission permissions for the relevant academic year before seeking admission or making any payment.
The advisory follows the Supreme Court taking cognisance of the issue in Ayesha Jain v. Amity University, Noida & Ors., an ongoing case in which the Court directed regulatory bodies, including the NMC, to caution students and parents against dealing with unauthorised educational institutions. The directions came in the context of a reported instance of a purported fake medical college operating from a farmhouse and claiming to offer various courses.
The Commission has clarified that a medical college’s presence in an official list, or its previous operation, does not automatically establish that it has permission to admit students in subsequent academic years. Candidates must check the approval granted for the particular year and the number of seats sanctioned through official NMC and Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) records.
Verify with regulatory body
It has also cautioned students against relying exclusively on prospectuses, websites, advertisements, social media posts or documents such as purported Letters of Permission and approval certificates circulated by institutions or their representatives. Any doubts regarding the authenticity of such documents should be verified directly with the concerned regulatory authority.
For admissions governed by counselling procedures, candidates have been asked to use official channels, including the Medical Counselling Committee (MCC), wherever applicable, or the competent State and Union Territory counselling authorities. The Commission has also advised students against making admission-related payments to unauthorised agents, personal bank accounts or unverified intermediaries.
Highlighting the importance of distinguishing between regulatory approvals, the NMC said affiliation, registration or recognition granted by one authority for a particular purpose should not be construed as permission from the Commission to conduct an MBBS course. Each statutory requirement must be independently satisfied.
Extraordinary claims
The advisory also asks students and parents to exercise caution when institutions make extraordinary claims about clinical training, hospital facilities and admission opportunities. The existence of a building, office or website, it said, does not establish that an institution is legally authorised to impart medical education.
Suspected fake medical colleges, unauthorised MBBS courses, forged permission letters and fraudulent admission offers can be reported to the NMC through its official communication channels. Complaints may also be made to the State or U.T. medical education departments, relevant regulatory authorities, and local police. Students have been advised to preserve advertisements, payment receipts, correspondence and website details as supporting evidence.
The Commission has separately clarified that courses in pharmacy, nursing, Ayurveda, and allied healthcare programmes fall under different statutory or competent regulatory authorities. Their recognition and approval must be checked with the respective regulators.
The advisory asks the public to refer to the NMC’s official website and relevant regulatory and counselling portals for updated information before proceeding with admissions or payments.

Britain should not be permitted to act as a 17th-century colonial power treating the waters around the Falkland Islands as a Dominium maris Britannici, Argentina has told an international tribunal.
Marcelo Kohen, representing Argentina at a hearing in Hamburg, mocked Britain for apparently believing in the historic doctrine that the British crown has sovereignty over expansive parts of the oceans.
Argentina has applied to the international tribunal for the law of the sea (Itlos) for a ruling that would force Britain to suspend the drilling for oil in the North Basin of the Falkland Islands ahead of further arbitration.
The Sea Lion oilfield is about 130 miles north of the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory over which Argentina has a longstanding sovereignty claim.
Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, reportedly shared among his cabinet a photograph of the Argentinian legal team in Hamburg, describing it as “tremendous”, adding that “we are working on the Falklands issue like no one else in history”.
Addressing the tribunal on the second day of hearings, Kohen said that the dispute over the archipelago of 700 islands in the south Atlantic – known in Argentina as the Malvinas – did not mean that the area was a “legal black hole” and that the UK could do as it wished with its natural resources.
“The fact that the parties dispute sovereignty does not turn the areas surrounding the Malvinas into some kind of Dominium maris Britannici,” he said. “We are not in the 17th century … We are in an era where we should put an end to the last vestiges of colonialism.”
Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, told the tribunal’s panel of judges on Tuesday that Argentina was seeking to further its sovereignty ambitions by applying for suspension of the drilling.
She claimed that such a move would kill the Sea Lion project, with “disastrous consequences” for the Falkland Islanders and the companies involved. The UK claimed that the tribunal, which adjudicates over maritime matters, does not have jurisdiction to wade into matters of sovereignty.
Kohen, switching from French to English, said the UK had failed to mention in its submissions the “elephant in the room” or the “whale in the bathtub”. The UN regarded the Falkland Islands as a non-self-governing territory, he said, and had called in 1976 for both sides to refrain from taking decisions that would unilaterally change the situation before the sovereignty dispute was settled.
The exploitation of hydrocarbons would put the islands among the “highest ranks of wealth just below the principality of Monaco” while depriving Argentina of its rights to those resources, Kohen told the tribunal.
Argentina’s legal team claimed that suspension of the drilling, which is due to start in March next year and which could double the GDP of the islands, was urgent given the irreparable damage to Argentina’s rights.
The UK has claimed there is no urgency as oil extraction would not take place until 2028, before which an Itlos arbitration panel would have come to a conclusion on the future of the oilfield.
In his closing remarks to the panel of 20 judges, Mario Oyarzábal, a legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, said they rejected the UK’s attempt to characterise the proceedings as an attempt to litigate the sovereignty dispute.
He said: “The question before this tribunal is a much narrower one: whether, while the underlying dispute remains unresolved, the UK may unilaterally authorise or carry out new drilling for the exploitation of hydrocarbons in the disputed maritime area.”
Milei described the reclaiming of the Falklands as a “national cause” during his recent speech at the UN general assembly. Argentina invaded the islands in 1982 on the orders of the dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri. The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
The UK will offer further submissions on Wednesday.

The Indian men’s football team is currently stationed in Auckland, waiting to kick off the first of its two friendlies against New Zealand.
Meanwhile, on Wednesday, thousands of kilometres away in Dhaka, a second-string side wore the national colours and is closer to adding another milestone to the nation’s SAFF Championship history.
Led by India Under-23 coach Naushad Moosa, the Blue Tigers edged Maldives 1-0 to book their spot in the semifinal and keep the dream of winning a record-extending 10th title alive.
Control is key
Unlike Jamil’s 4-4-2 team, which uses long balls to find wide players, Moosa opts for a standard 4-3–3 shape and expects his players to keep the ball on the floor.
India held over 55 per cent possession against both Pakistan and the Maldives, spending several sequences doing the same thing: passing from one end to another before attempting to pierce through the middle. The idea has been fruitful so far, with Suhail Bhat and Manglenthang Kipgen’s goals against Pakistan a testament to it.
His high defensive line aids this tactic, as any time the ball is lost, players are stationed close enough to try to win it back immediately.
However, while Moosa’s style of football has been effective on the pitch, the physical toll of always being on their toes has been evident in the players. Both against Pakistan and the Maldives, India’s intensity dropped towards the fag end of the match, with Moosa having limited options on the bench.
Pakistan bagged two goals in added time while Maldives had the same number of big chances to equalise, but were denied by some adept goalkeeping from 20-year-old Priyansh Dubey.
Logistical challenges
The main cause for India’s dip throughout a match, perhaps, is the changes in the roster. The tournament’s clash with the ISL and the New Zealand friendlies left the coach with just 17 players out of the 28 picked for the opener against Pakistan.
Following that 3-2 win, three players (Bijoy Varghese, Muhammad Suhail and Liston Colaco) joined the senior squad, three (Farukh Choudhary, Noufal PN and Hmingthanmawia Ralte) went back to their clubs, while Ronney Willson Kharbudon and Suresh Singh Wangjam did not travel to Dhaka due to injuries.
ALSO READ: Form over reputation: Khalid Jamil’s India squad has no guaranteed places
Only four players who started against Pakistan were named in the lineup against Maldives, leaving Moosa to reform the side in six days. And the rule that no changes can be made to the contingent after competition has left Moosa with just 20 players to work with.
A six-day gap between the first two games has helped to some extent, but now a semifinal and a possible final are coming up in the next six days. And with Moosa seeming to have been handed the short straw, he will have to dig deep and find that extra spark if India is to defend its title.
Does Suhail Bhat need more game time in the ISL?
Suhail Bhat has had a dream start to the tournament, netting three goals in two games, including the winner against Maldives. The goals come as a perfect statement of intent for the 21-year-old who has been occasionally popping up in the headlines over the past few seasons, with his limited performances for Mohun Bagan Super Giant.
His hard-working mentality and awareness of situations in front of goal have made him a useful asset for Moosa, while he remains a work in progress at his club. Having been with the Mohun Bagan since 2023, Suhail has been overlooked for vastly experienced and foreign strikers and has made just 19 appearances across four seasons in the Indian Super League, with just one start.
Moreover, Moosa has not been able to get more than 65 minutes out of the youngster, who seems to lack match fitness, playing just five minutes out of Mohun Bagan’s five games this season.
This begs the question: does the 21-year-old need to push for a move away and establish his credentials, especially as Indian football continues its endless search for a prized forward like Sunil Chhetri? And with Jamil picking forwards David Lalhlansanga and Muhammad Suhail for the New Zealand tour after a good start in the ISL, Suhail will have to ensure that he gets a fair chance as well.

Analysts weigh how Democrats’ midterm wins could shift Trump’s Latin America policy
Analysts are examining how recent Democratic wins in the U.S. midterm elections might impact Latin America during President Donald Trump's final two years
MEXICO CITY -- U.S. President Donald Trump's impact on Latin America in the last two years has been enormous, from immigration and deportations to boat strikes that have killed hundreds to the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
Now analysts are trying to get a read on whether the sweeping wins by Democrats in the midterm elections will signal changes ahead for the region in Trump's final two years in office.
Initial signals from the White House have been contradictory. Trump has given mixed signals on immigration policy, at one point describing his past policy as “too tough,” but then suggesting a hard line on immigration would continue. He appointed Stephen Miller, the primary architect of his immigration agenda, as his new chief of staff.
A U.S. House effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fell short Tuesday. The key figure shaping priorities for the hemisphere, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, remains a key member of Trump's Cabinet.
Here is a look at the key areas that might be impacted by the political shifts in the U.S.
The first postelection message on X from the Secretary of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, was unequivocal: “Deportations will continue.”
But two Texas cities — Houston and Austin — already have announced plans to limit police cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, a trend that could extend to state-level law enforcement once Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, a vocal critic of ICE’s practices, takes office in January 2027.
Former Mexican Ambassador Martha Bárcena expressed hope that increased collaboration among mayors, members of Congress, governors and their Mexican counterparts will help to “limit and curb the cruelty of ICE and discrimination against the Hispanic population.”
Mexico could be the place where pressure intensifies the most, as it offers the United States the best opportunity for tangible, short-term results, specifically more arrests and extraditions, while the Justice Department continues to investigate cartels, Mexican analyst David Saucedo said.
On Monday, the heads of Mexico’s security apparatus and the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration posted messages about their meeting last week to strengthen collaboration against the cartels.
Further south, the U.S. military, including the Army and the Navy, is expected to maintain its focus on joint operations under the “Shield of the Americas” initiative with Latin American partners to combat criminal gangs. Saucedo noted that this approach does not require significant Congressional funding. Additionally, crime remains a top priority for most Latin American countries, most of them led by Trump allies who won elections based on promises to crack down on criminals.
Boat strikes in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which have killed at least 240 people, are likely to face increased scrutiny, as Democrats already have called for an investigation into the legality of these actions.
Some analysts believe that Trump will maintain his aspirations to assert U.S. dominance in the region, although his capacity to act could be limited.
Venezuela stands out as a top Latin American priority for the Democrats, as it touches upon a key voter concern: corruption.
There are already specific calls from Democratic lawmakers to investigate who has benefited from oil agreements signed between the Trump administration and Caracas.
Christopher Sabatini, of the London-based think tank Chatham House, expects Democrats in Congress to pursue hearings on oil deals and also anticipates increased pressure for the holding of elections in Venezuela. That said, he believes the tense relationship between the Democrats and opposition figure María Corina Machado, a Trump ally, could hinder concrete progress.
Some believe pressure on Cuba will not ease. Two days after the election, Rubio announced further sanctions against the island.
José Briceño, a professor from the Mexican Center for Research on Latin America and the Caribbean (CIALC), considered a military operation against the island unlikely, given the complexity and risks involved. But no one wants to rule it out.
“A secretary of state with presidential ambitions has every incentive to seek a quick result in Cuba,” wrote Orlando J. Pérez, a professor at the University of North Texas.
Brazil will stand as the main counterweight to Washington as Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's win served to check the region’s growing shift to the right and denied Trump a powerful ally. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, who also leans to the left, has been less outspoken and has walked a fine line with the Trump administration.
The economy proved a key issue for U.S. voters, opening the possibility for changes in trade policy, particularly in areas where tariffs have fueled inflation for U.S. businesses and consumers, said Mariana Aparicio, an expert in international political economy at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.
Nevertheless, she predicted Trump will continue to use tariffs as a tool for political leverage.
Mexican Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard said tariffs are unlikely to change significantly, but he suggested the new Congress could make adjustments to the North American Free Trade Agreement.
Analysts also agree that economic support for Latin American governments aligned with the White House will continue; however, it is highly unlikely that Trump will be able to repeat actions such as the $20 billion in support for Javier Milei’s Argentina in late 2025.

GoKwik’s Golden Handcuffs GoKwik has added a contentious twist to its ESOP policy. Under the new rules, current and former employees could forfeit their unvested and vested-but-unexercised options if they join any of GoKwik’s nine rivals. Can the startup use ESOPs to restrict where its talent goes next? A New Kind Of Restriction: GoKwik’s amended ESOP Plan 2021 names Razorpay, Shiprocket, CRED, Cashfree Payments, BiteSpeed, Snapmint, WebEngage, Shopflo and Pine Labs as restricted companies. Employees cannot join, advise and invest in them without risking the loss of outstanding options. Crucially, the restriction applies retroactively to previously issued grants and extends for two full years after an employee’s departure. Employees In Limbo: For GoKwik employees with significant ESOP holdings, the new policy has created a difficult choice between career mobility and potential wealth loss. Many are weighing offers from larger or better-known companies against the risk of forfeiting ESOPS they have already earned the right to exercise. The timing has added to concerns. GoKwik has seen several senior-level departures in the recent past, while the recent layoff, earlier this year, is further adding to the staff’s concerns. A Legal Gray Area: Non-compete clauses are common in Indian employment agreements, but explicitly linking rivals to the forfeiture of vested options is unusual. Legal experts believe that GoKwik’s amendment could face legal scrutiny if it is used to penalise employees for joining a competitor. The issue also raises governance concerns. By converting earned equity into an aggressive retention tactic, startups risk eroding the trust that underpins employee wealth creation. So, will GoKwik stand by its restrictive ESOP policy or roll back the controversial clause? - After the 2026 midterm elections, posts on social media combined two separate claims about voter fraud into one copypasta.
- The posts claimed that Wisconsin had 7.1 million registered voters but a population of only 4 million people old enough to vote, and that Texas was beginning to arrest people for committing voter fraud.
- The claim about Wisconsin is false. Data from the Wisconsin Elections Commission shows the state had 3.6 million active voter registrations, while the Wisconsin Department of Health Services estimated the state's voting age population at about 4.8 million in 2025.
- The claim about Texas is a mixture of true and false information. It's true that on Oct. 31, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton — who went on to lose his bid for U.S. Senate against Democrat James Talarico — announced he had ordered the arrest of an unknown number of people who allegedly voted in the 2026 election but had been convicted of felonies and therefore did so illegally. It's also true that on Nov. 2, the U.S. Department of Justice announced five people in Texas had been arrested and charged with "election-related crimes."
- It's false, however, that Texas had "just started arresting people," as some posts claim, and no additional election-related arrests been announced in Texas as of this writing.
After the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party won a massive number of seats at both the state and federal levels, copypasta posts spread on social media alleging that the election results in Wisconsin and Texas were fraudulent.
"Wisconsin found 7.1M registered voters when they only have 4M population," read a Nov. 8 X post, for example. "Texas just started arresting people.. it has started!"
(X user @PaulGoldEagle)
Snopes readers contacted us looking for a fact-check on the two separate claims — one questioning the number of registered voters vs. total population in Wisconsin and the other claiming Texas was arresting people for voter fraud.
The Wisconsin claim is false, based on data from the Wisconsin Elections Commission.
The Texas claim is a mixture of true and false information. While recent news releases did indicate several people in Texas were arrested, or had warrants issued for their arrest, on election-related charges, the number of people targeted was too small to affect the outcome of an election.
Wisconsin voter registration
First of all, searching for Wisconsin's voter registration figures revealed that this particular claim has been around for quite some time.
The Associated Press disproved a similar claim suggesting the state had counted more ballots in 2020 than it had registered voters (that claim used an outdated voter registration figure). We also found a February 2026 fact-check from the nonprofit news organization Wisconsin Watch disproving a claim spread by President Donald Trump that the state had more voter registrations than adults.
Checking the latest numbers revealed the claim remains false. According to the Wisconsin Elections Commission, the state had 3.6 million active registered voters as of Nov. 1. Meanwhile, Wisconsin had an estimated population of just under 6 million in 2025, according to the Census Bureau and the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, and about 4.8 million voting-age adults.
It's unclear how the post arrived at the figure of 7.1 million registered voters.
According to the WEC and Wisconsin Watch, the state also maintains a list of inactive voter registrations, around 4.7 million additional entries. However, voters cannot cast a ballot if their registration is inactive, meaning that it's improper to consider those additional 4.7 million entries as active, registered voters.
The WEC's frequently asked questions page describes those inactive records as follows, noting that state law requires it to maintain the ineligible list, which also helps it catch potential fraudulent cases:
People are made inactive (ineligible) when they die, move and register in another state, are convicted of a felony, are adjudicated incompetent to vote, or are made inactive through statutory voter list maintenance processes.
Adding the 3.6 million active registrations to the 4.7 million inactive ones that shouldn't be counted produces a total of approximately 8.2 million total records, larger than the state's population, and more in line with the misleading claim.
Texas voter fraud arrests
As for the posts' claim about Texas, Snopes found two news releases showing that at least a few people were reportedly arrested, or had warrants issued for their arrest, on election-related charges.
On Oct. 31, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced his office had issued arrest warrants for an unspecified number of people with felony convictions suspected of voting illegally in the 2026 midterm elections while on parole. (Paxton went on to lose his bid for U.S. Senate against Democratic state Rep. James Talarico.) The people allegedly cast ballots in Harris County, home of Houston, though the warrants were issued in Montgomery County, the suburban county directly north of Harris County.
Under Texas state law, a person convicted of a felony loses their right to vote while serving their sentence, including while on parole or probation. They regain their voting rights only when their sentence is fully served.
Paxton's news release did not say how many warrants had been issued or how many people had been arrested on the charges. We contacted his office for clarification but had not received a reply at time of publication.
Meanwhile, on Nov. 2, the day before Election Day, the Department of Justice announced new election-related charges against five people located in Texas. It's unlikely that five illegal votes could be enough to sway a statewide election. None of the DOJ arrests appeared to be related to the 2026 midterms, either.

The US military is taking a new approach to prop up commercial launch companies as SpaceX looks to wind down its Falcon rocket program, suggesting defense officials see the workhorse rocket’s retirement as a potential national security risk.
The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital has twice in the last two weeks announced it was sending cash to two of SpaceX’s competitors in the launch business. First, on October 26, the office announced a $150 million conditional loan commitment to Stoke Space. Military officials revealed a second $150 million Pentagon loan Tuesday for Rocket Lab.
Stoke Space and Rocket Lab are the first two launch companies to receive significant support from the Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), an organization established in 2022 to infuse companies developing “vital” national security technologies with capital. OSC has been on a loan spree in recent weeks, committing hundreds of millions of dollars to companies specializing in batteries, drones, and semiconductors. In the space sector, the office also provided a $150 million loan to LeoLabs, a commercial satellite tracking company, for production and deployment of radar units.
SpaceX, the Pentagon’s leading launch provider, has stopped taking commercial orders for Falcon 9 launches after 2028 as the company shifts its focus to the next-generation, super-heavy-lift Starship rocket. Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launches for government customers, including NASA and the US Space Force, are expected to continue a while longer. The Space Force’s launch contract with SpaceX allows the military to place Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy orders through 2029, with the actual launches extending through 2033.
Then, if Starship is fulfilling its promise, SpaceX plans to retire Falcon for good. Starship may eventually be capable of launching national security payloads, but SpaceX’s near-term priority is using the rocket’s massive cargo capacity for its own Starlink Internet satellites and Starmind orbital data centers.

A team of scientists at the CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB) has identified critical weaknesses in the bacterium that causes Tuberculosis (TB), a finding that could pave the way for the development of new treatments against one of the world’s deadliest infectious diseases.
The discovery is particularly significant for India, which accounts for nearly a quarter of global TB cases and about a third of drug-resistant infections, according to the World Health Organisation’s Global TB Report 2025. Drug-resistant TB remains a major public health challenge, as treatment requires a combination of antibiotics taken over several months and is becoming increasingly difficult due to the emergence of resistant strains.
Led by CCMB Director Vinay Kumar Nandicoori, the research team mapped the protein export machinery of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the bacterium responsible for TB. The study sheds light on how the pathogen transports proteins within and outside its cells, a process essential for its growth, survival and ability to cause disease.
The research was carried out by joint first authors Priyadarshini Sanyal and Jagadeeshwari Uppada in collaboration with scientists from the Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Chennai, led by Areejit Samal, and the Translational Health Science and Technology Institute, Faridabad.
Using a combination of computational modelling and laboratory experiments, the researchers identified 92 key components and nearly 200 molecular reactions involved in the bacterium’s protein transport network. These included the general Sec pathway, the Twin-Arginine Translocation (Tat) system and the specialised ESX secretion systems unique to this group of bacteria.
“Protein secretion acts like a delivery system inside the bacterium and is vital for its survival,” said Dr Uppada. The team focused on two major secretion pathways, SecA1 and Tat, employing CRISPR-based gene-silencing technology to reduce their activity. The results were striking: bacterial growth declined sharply both in laboratory cultures and inside immune cells, demonstrating that both pathways are essential for the pathogen’s survival.
Dr Priyadarshini Sanyal said further analysis revealed that disrupting these systems affected the export of more than 100 proteins in the SecA1 pathway and around 140 proteins linked to the Tat system. Researchers also observed structural damage to the bacterial cell membrane, making it unstable and more permeable. Proteins that normally remain inside the bacterium began leaking into the surrounding environment.
Dr Nandicoori said that these changes highlight the close connection between protein secretion and the maintenance of the bacterial cell envelope, a key factor behind TB’s persistence and resistance to treatment. The findings, published in the peer-reviewed journal Molecular & Cellular Proteomics, could help researchers identify new drug targets, although translating the discovery into effective medicines will require several more years of research.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
- Published
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.
Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.
"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.
But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.
For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.
I think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.
- Could this be the end of 'Jensanity' 
  - Published1 day ago
The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.
We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.
China denies that she was engaged in espionage.
Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.
China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.
Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.
He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.
Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.
But can he survive?
At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.
He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.
While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.
And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

SRINAGAR: Chilling CCTV video of the moment CRPF personnel came under fire in a suspected terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir's Kulgam district has gone viral.
The five-minute footage shows a CRPF jawan sitting on the pavement outside a row of closed shops. At around 2.06 pm, a sudden burst of gunfire rings out, with bullets striking the ground just metres away from him. Dust and debris can be seen flying into the air as the rounds hit the pavement.
The jawan immediately jumps to his feet and runs towards the right for cover. Another trooper enters the frame from the left as gunfire continues. The first jawan soon reappears, carrying his weapon, and moves towards the direction of the firing, apparently trying to assess the situation.
For nearly a minute, the audio captures sustained gunfire, frantic shouting and the confusion among security personnel.
At around 2.07 pm, another jawan, dressed in full combat gear, is seen rushing onto the roof of the shuttered shops.
"Hame goli lagi hai. Jaldi aao (We have been hit. Come quickly)," an injured trooper can be heard shouting, although he remains out of the camera's frame.
It is unclear whether all the shots heard in the footage were fired by the attackers or whether some were return fire from the security personnel. 
However, the audio captures nearly 25-30 rounds being fired.
According to news agency PTI, two suspected terrorists riding a motorcycle opened fire on a CRPF checkpost near Mir Bazar in Kulgam district, injuring three personnel. One of the injured jawans is in critical condition, officials said.
The attack took place around 75 km from Srinagar and less than a kilometre from the heavily guarded Jammu-Srinagar National Highway, PTI reported.
The injured personnel were rushed to a hospital in Anantnag, around 22 km from the site of the attack. One jawan sustained a gunshot wound to the stomach and is in critical condition. The other two suffered injuries to the arm and foot.
Visuals from the hospital showed the injured personnel being wheeled in on stretchers as medical staff rushed to attend to them.
The attackers fled on their motorcycle after opening fire, triggering a massive security operation in the area. Security forces have cordoned off the site and launched searches to track down the assailants.
Investigators are also examining CCTV footage from shops and other establishments in the area to reconstruct the sequence of events and identify the attackers.
