2027 Chevrolet Bolt Review: RIP to the GOAT of low-cost electric motoring
Like a budget-minded phoenix, the Bolt is back — but not for long.
Since its debut a decade ago, the Chevrolet Bolt has offered a value-minded EV in a simple, practical package. Today, at $28,995 (including destination fees), the 2027 edition is the cheapest EV on the American market. It's about $10,000 less than that original Bolt, and a killer deal.
A deal that is, sadly, more or less dead. This stalwart EV is not long for this world, risen from the ashes of a disastrous, multi-billion-dollar recall and eventual production hiatus, but set to return to them in just a few months' time. That's a shame, because this is no-frills, no-emissions motoring at its finest.
History lesson
The current-generation Bolt is the latest in a line of notable, electrified hero cars with a bowtie on the front. Chevrolet got in the game with the EV1 way back in 1996, but it was the 2010 Volt that signaled the brand's intent to find new, affordable ways to propel our cars.
When the Bolt came along in 2016, it not only forced vehicle pundits worldwide to improve their enunciation, but showed that Chevrolet was just getting started on its electrification journey. Starting at under $40,000, the Bolt was a compelling package, and it got even better in 2021 with the release of the second-generation model and its upscaled version, the Bolt EUV.
Then came the fires, the recall, and before long all that brand equity Chevrolet had been building went right out the window.
Current-gen
That stop-sale of the Bolt was a painful thing, so much so that I figured we'd never see another one. But here it is, the 2027 edition, with a few choice updates meant as a strong send-off for this significant but sadly stymied machine.
The biggest upgrade is a wholly new, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack. It's rated for 65-kilowatt-hours of capacity, providing an EPA-estimated 262 miles of range for the LT trim I tested. It has a single motor that delivers 210 horsepower and 169 pound-feet of torque to the front wheels.
Quickest EV on the road? Hardly. Fun and torquey? Yes indeed, just like the earlier Bolt and even Volt before it.
It now charges via NACS port, so Supercharger support is baked in, and it should go without saying that the unfortunate battery woes that plagued the model have now been fixed. But otherwise it's much the same as it was before, in the same hatchback shape that's every bit as practical as the various crossover SUVs swarming dealership lots.
Buttons are still here
The Bolt you see here is about as basic as it gets. Its only option is the $995 Comfort Package, which provides a few extra features like heated front seats and a heated steering wheel, things that, even at this price, feel like they should come standard.
There's not much luxury to be found here. Textured rubber is as good as it gets from a materials standpoint, with hard plastics dominating the interior. That said, I genuinely like the shadows cast by the patterned lines on the inside of the doors and storage cubbies, along with the matching pattern on the upholstery. I just wish the other surfaces weren't all covered with the same pebbled leatherette texture.
There's plenty of room in the second row, and the flat floor means fitting three across is realistic for short distances. Or, drop the 60/40 split rear seat and open up 56.3 cubic feet of cargo space. That's comparable to Volvo's EX40 SUV. With the seats up, you still get 16.2 cubic feet.
Front seating is even more generous. I'm six feet tall with short legs and had plenty of headroom, and while some would lament the lack of a sunroof on my test car, I don't miss it.
On the dashboard, the 11.3-inch touchscreen is of average size for a modern car, but more importantly, the Bolt still offers a good selection of physical buttons for everything from toggling those (extremely toasty) heated seats to enabling the lane-departure system.
Even the steering wheel has real buttons and rollers at play, not the unfortunate capacitive touch controls that have swept the industry. Some will call it all a bit old-school, but I appreciate the tactility.
Software experience
That 11.3-inch touchscreen is running a flavor of Chevrolet's Android Automotive-based infotainment system, which means Google Maps is built right into the car. So too is the Google Play Store, enabling you to install car-optimized apps directly into the dashboard.
What's missing, sadly, is Android Auto or Apple CarPlay. Unfortunately, the Bolt is one of the cars swept up in Chevrolet's curious crusade against phone projection. Want to use a media app that hasn't been updated to run directly in Android Automotive? You're stuck pairing your phone over Bluetooth and streaming the old-fashioned way.
Beyond that frustration, Chevrolet's software is a bit sluggish to use, and while Google's Gemini AI assistant is baked into the dashboard, I still wish I could run it from my phone.
On the go
Suffice to say, the stuff running in the dashboard is my least favorite part of the 2027 Bolt. Everything else, though, I really like. You have a few different drive modes here, and while I confess I couldn't really tell the difference between Normal and Sport, either way I found the car punchy and fun zipping from one intersection to the next.
It's no Lucid Air Sapphire, and its acceleration does start to feel flat as you approach highway speed, but the Bolt still has plenty of power for anyone's needs. Likewise, the handling won't win any awards, but it offers reasonably good ride quality for a car in this category. It's perfectly pleasant cruising over road work or highways with separation joints.
The adaptive cruise control works well too, as do the auto-dimming headlights, but the lane-keep assist system is disappointing. Even on well-lit, well-painted roads, the Bolt struggled to identify lane markings. This left the little EV wandering way over the line before the car applied any corrective feedback.
If you want more support, hands-free Super Cruise is available, but it's sadly locked in a big bundle of options, including ventilated seats and automatic wipers, that costs $6,600. That's a shame considering Super Cruise is a standalone option on many other Chevrolets, usually costing less than $2,500.
When it comes to all-important efficiency, this Bolt is again officially rated for 262 miles on a charge. That's a nice boost from the 238 miles the Bolt originally promised. In my mixed testing, with some highways and some secondary roads, I saw 4.0 miles per kilowatt-hour, for a theoretical maximum range of 260 miles on a charge. So, right on the money.
Wrap-up
The dodgy lane-keep assist function is frustrating, but the lack of smartphone projection is the big bummer here. Otherwise, the Bolt remains a solid car. Maybe it's because I've driven so many variations of these things over the past decade, but cruising around in the Bolt just feels easy and familiar.
It's comfortable, simple and best of all, it's cheap. The average transaction price of a new car this year is knocking on the door of $50,000. That makes the 2027 Bolt a downright steal. I'm sure that value will continue forward on the second-hand market, which is sadly where you'll have to go if you don't get one soon.
Production of the Chevrolet Bolt ends early next year, which is unfortunate, as in many ways it feels like it's finally hitting its stride. But that doesn't mean the age of the affordable EV is dead. The Slate Truck enters production soon, with Ford's Fathom following not too terribly far behind. The market is about to have even more compelling and cheap EVs, and that's a very good thing.

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) held that laws penalising having more than two children have lost their relevance due to the falling fertility rate in India.
“We are of the strong opinion that laws that penalise having more than two children have lost their relevance. The foundation of such laws, that is, the fear of overpopulation, has crumbled due to demographic changes in the past few decades,” a Bench headed by Justice P.S. Narasimha observed in a 37-page judgment.
The court said its 2003 judgment (in Javed versus State of Haryana) which upheld such penal laws, needed a revisit by a larger Bench. India’s Total Fertility Rate (TFR) had fallen from 3.02 to 1.9. A TFR of 2.1, known as the replacement rate, would allow one generation to completely replace itself.
“Even though India’s population is not yet declining, the TFR falling below the replacement rate will soon result in a demographic transition towards an older population with a declining share of the working-age population. Therefore, laws aimed at limiting population growth have now lost their significance,” Justice Narasimha observed.
The 2003 judgment in the Javed case had referred to the situation that existed in China as of 2000 and drew inspiration from the measures that it had undertaken to control the population.
Justice Narasimha said the decades-old view that population explosion was an impediment for progress was outdated.
Healthy growth
“The earlier perception that population harms development does not hold water anymore. Rather than society and the courts being concerned about the negative consequences of high population, it should instead focus on the need to encourage a healthy growth of population,” the judgment, by a Bench comprising Justice Alok Aradhe, said.
The judgment pointed out that the share of persons aged 60 and above had already risen from about 8.3% in 2014 to 9.7% in 2024, and government projections place that share at nearly 15% by 2036.
India’s falling fertility rate, the court said, would necessarily mean a smaller proportion of younger persons in the future, and, correspondingly, a larger ageing population. It said the issue had been of significant concern in recent years.
The court said the failure to take notice of demographic changes would lead to only serious consequences for India. Failure to adapt not only produced injustice, but was also an abuse of power.
The judgment was based on a petition filed by Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, whose election as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat in Maharashtra was set aside on the ground that she had more than two children. The lower courts and State authorities found that she had given birth to a third child in 2014, but still contested and won the panchayat elections in 2022. They had held that she acted in violation of Section 14(1)(j-1) of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959, which upheld the two-child norm.
Justice Narasimha found such laws linking motherhood to political representation a violation of Article 21 (right to life) under the Constitution.
“Allowing such laws to stand excludes an entire class of citizens from political representation on grounds bearing little rational connection to their capacity to hold public office. It compels an unconscionable choice between bearing children and democratic participation, impinging on the right to reproductive autonomy under Article 21,” Justice Narasimha observed.
Seeking an immediate re-visitation of the Javed judgment of 2003, the court permitted the appellant to continue in her elected position as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat while staying any proceedings against her.

Eight people have tested positive for Shigella infection in Malappuram district, with five cases linked to a wedding feast at Korakkuthu in Elamkulam panchayat near Perinthalmanna.
The outbreak has prompted the Health department to step up surveillance and preventive measures in the area.
The five patients attended a wedding held on October 31, 2026, in ward 12 of Elamkulam panchayat. Around 80 people who attended the function have since reported symptoms of diarrhoea. A child from the area is also suspected to have Shigella infection and is under special observation.
The other confirmed cases include a four-year-old girl who ate food from a snack shop at 5th Mile at Amarambalam near Nilambur, and two people who ate mandi rice from a restaurant at Palunda near Chungathara, Nilambur.
The girl and the two patients from Chungathara are undergoing treatment at Government District Hospital, Nilambur. Several others, including the girl’s mother, have also reported similar symptoms.
The Food Safety department has collected samples of food and drinking water served at the wedding and sent them for testing. Stool samples of those affected will be examined at the laboratory at Government Medical College, Manjeri.
A special health team has begun surveillance and field-level interventions. The Health department has advised people to drink boiled and cooled water and eat properly cooked food. Drinking water sources should also be superchlorinated using bleaching powder, said health officials.
The health authorities, in coordination with the panchayat, will intensify inspections at local establishments and public functions. Event organisers have been asked to follow public health guidelines.

Top of the morning to you and a fine one it is. Blue skies, cool breezes, and plenty of chirping birds are enveloping the comfy Pharmalot campus, which is cause to fire up the coffee kettle for yet another cup of stimulation. Our choice today is pistachio. Meanwhile, we have assembled the latest menu of tidbits for you to peruse. We hope you have a wonderful day and please do keep in touch. Once again, we will note that our settings have changed to accept postcards and telegrams …
The Food and Drug Administration approved a Bayer drug to reduce recurrence of stroke, making available the first in a novel class of medications that hold the promise of preventing blood clots more safely, STAT notes. Many blood thinners are not used in this setting due to the increased risk of bleeding, but the drug, which will be sold under the brand name Sunharbo, uses a mechanism that is thought to stop the formation of bad clots without increasing the risk of bleeding. Experts say the data showed a significant advance in an area that has seen little innovation over the past few decades. Secondary strokes are estimated to affect about 20% of people who have had a first stroke and can cause severe disability or death.
The FDA warned that GLP-1 drugs carry a potential risk for a rare but serious eye condition and required pharmaceutical companies to inform patients and doctors of the risk, STAT writes. The condition, called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, is sometimes referred to as an “eye stroke” and is caused by insufficient blood flow to the optic nerve. It typically causes sudden vision loss and, in severe cases, can lead to blindness. There are currently no proven treatments for the condition. The FDA said it started looking into this risk after researchers in 2024 published an observational study linking Ozempic and Wegovy to the eye condition.

Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.
Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.
More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn’t have critical vulnerabilities.
Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind’s Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.
“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.
The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead.
Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent.
Police and the public prosecutor’s office have not said much about the case, and little was known about the killers except that they were armed and then fled the scene. It was also unclear whether the crime was linked to Beltrán’s work, though he had previously reported allegations of corruption involving local authorities.
Regardless, many press freedom groups already cite his murder as the latest example of how conditions for journalists have deteriorated dramatically in Ecuador. Six journalists were killed in the country last year alone.
Artur Romeu, Reporters Without Borders’ Latin America director, said in a statement that months ago Beltrán had told the organisation “about his fears and the threats he was receiving”.
“We took part in efforts to get him to safety,” he said, adding that Beltrán had been placed in a protection programme run by the public prosecutor’s office, although it was not known whether that protection was still in place when he was killed.
“Reporters Without Borders calls on the public prosecutor’s office to investigate as a priority whether there is a link to his journalistic work, identify any possible masterminds and protect his family and colleagues,” said Romeu.
The Ecuadorian civil society organisation Fundación Periodistas Sin Cadenas (FPSC) reported that at least 19 journalists have had to go into exile since gang violence exploded in 2023. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, it has become a major trafficking hub, particularly through the Pacific.
Journalists have received death threats with photographs of their homes and details of their routines and families.
“Practising journalism in Ecuador is now an extremely high-risk job,” said María Fernanda Almeida, a project coordinator at FPSC, adding that all of last year’s killings of journalists “remain completely unpunished”.
“And one of the many terrible effects of this violence is self-censorship: at least in the coastal provinces, colleagues no longer want to report on violence,” she added.
Almeida said another problem for journalists has been the stance of the government of the far-right president Daniel Noboa, who has responded to the surge in crime with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, repeatedly declaring states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces in measures that have been widely criticised by human rights groups.
While covering military operations, reporters have had their phones confiscated, a search warrant was executed at a reporter’s home and a journalist was threatened by soldiers simply for filming them stopping university students.
There have also been several reports that Noboa, one of US president Donald Trump’s key allies in Latin America, has pressured media organisations to dismiss journalists critical of him, including the columnist Roberto Aguilar, who said he was fired from the newspaper Diario Expreso after the government reportedly threatened private advertisers with audits if they continued advertising with the outlet.
Noboa’s administration did not respond to requests for comment.
“I don’t think there is complete freedom of expression in Ecuador today,” said Almeida. “And that is very worrying because the more violence and silencing there is, the more journalism is needed.”

Brazil fines Facebook $1.3M for failing to comply with court orders during election
Brazil’s top electoral court fines Meta’s Facebook $1.3 million for not fully complying with judicial orders during the recent presidential election runoff campaign
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazil’s top electoral court fined Meta’s Facebook $1.3 million for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during last month’s presidential election runoff campaign when the company was accused of political bias by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ’s team.
Justices ruled late Tuesday that Facebook had failed to adequately meet court demands related to allegations that its platform treated content from Lula and challenger Flávio Bolsonaro differently but said there was no evidence so far that the company attempted to influence the election’s outcome.
“Such a conclusion would require compelling evidence of intent, to be presented in full proceedings through the appropriate legal channels,” Justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze said in his decision that was unanimously accepted by his colleagues.
Ahead of the runoff vote, Lula’s campaign filed a lawsuit claiming that the company owning Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp was using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favor Bolsonaro.
The accusation gained traction among Lula's supporters and sparked a protest in front of Meta's offices in Sao Paulo.
Meta said in response that a series of recent platform issues stemmed from unrelated global technical glitches, strict anti-fraud measures and regulatory compliance rather than targeted suppression. The tech giant also told the court that it had adopted measures to ensure equal treatment of the two campaigns.
But Bellizze said that while the company had submitted statements and documents regarding the measures, some court orders were not followed or were fulfilled incompletely or late.
The fine of 7.5 million reais ($1.3 million) relates to the “conduct of the defendant in relation to the court order as a whole, considering, in particular, the delays, incomplete information and the difficulty verifying certain data,” according to a statement on the decision by the country’s top electoral court.
The amount corresponds to three days of fines of 500,000 reais ($90,000) between Oct. 17-19 and six days of fines of 1 million reais ($180,000) between Oct. 20-25, the statement added.

Why India and Pakistan's stock markets are rallying after the US midterms
Stock markets in India and Pakistan have rallied following the US midterms, buoyed by hopes of easing tensions with Iran and lower oil prices. But analysts say the gains are driven by different factors, and lasting economic relief remains uncertain.
BENGALURU/KARACHI: Investors in India and Pakistan are hoping that the outcome of the United States midterm elections held last week will ease geopolitical tensions and bring down oil prices, offering relief to two economies grappling with high energy costs.
Stock markets in both countries posted some of their biggest gains in months last week after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress, raising hopes that President Donald Trump could face greater checks on his trade and foreign policies.
The rally extended into this week, with India's benchmark index Nifty 50 rising 0.84 per cent on Wednesday (Nov 11), while Pakistan's KSE-100 slipped 0.14 per cent after surging 3.13 per cent the previous day, amid easing geopolitical tensions, lower oil prices and strong remittance inflows.
For India and Pakistan, which rely heavily on imported oil, lower energy prices could help ease inflation and reduce pressure on businesses and households.
But analysts say the rallies are being driven by different factors.
In India, stronger corporate earnings and renewed foreign investor interest have helped lift markets, while Pakistan's rally has been fuelled largely by hopes of easing US-Iran tensions.
Global oil prices fell nearly 12 per cent between the US midterm elections and Nov 10, according to Reuters price data, amid hopes that easing tensions with Iran would reduce supply disruptions.
But analysts caution that lasting economic relief will depend on whether oil prices remain low and diplomatic hopes lead to concrete progress.
For now, it remains unclear whether the stock market rallies signal a broader economic recovery or merely short-lived optimism.
INDIA'S STOCK MARKET RECOVERY GOES BEYOND US ELECTIONS
Anita Gandhi, head of institutional equities at brokerage Arihant Capital Markets, said Indian stocks had been declining since September 2024 amid slowing economic growth and weakening investor confidence.
India's benchmark index Nifty 50 fell nearly 16 per cent from its September 2024 peak to March 2025, according to stock exchange data.
US tariffs, rising oil prices and geopolitical tensions subsequently added to the pressure, she said.
But Gandhi believes the prolonged sell-off has also created opportunities, as share prices have become more attractive to investors. She pointed to better-than-expected corporate earnings in the July-to-September quarter and recent efforts to make Indian markets more accessible to foreign investors.
These developments, alongside "good earnings and reasonable valuations", have helped improve foreign investors' perceptions of India, she said.
Gandhi considers the US election outcome an additional boost rather than the main driver of the recovery.
Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, founder and CEO of investment advisory firm HST Wealth, was more cautious about whether the recent surge in foreign investment would last.
He said some international investors who had previously bet on further declines in Indian stocks appeared to be buying to close those positions as prices recovered, rather than making fresh, long-term investments in the market.
"A few strong session cannot establish a lasting change in allocation," he said.
Radhakrishnan said a more convincing turnaround would require sustained foreign buying over several weeks, investment across a wider range of industries and stronger corporate earnings.
PAKISTAN'S MARKET RALLY RIDES ON PEACE HOPES
In Pakistan, analysts attributed the market rally following the US midterms largely to hopes of easing tensions between Washington and Tehran.
Muhammad Waqas Ghani, head of research at brokerage JS Global, told CNA that investors were betting on easing geopolitical risks.
Pakistan's benchmark index KSE-100 rose for two consecutive sessions after the US midterms before falling 0.85 per cent on Nov 6 as oil prices climbed and investors sold shares to cash in on earlier gains.
The index rose again on Tuesday after a long weekend as oil prices eased, but slipped the following day, highlighting the fragility of investor confidence.
Ghani said a sustained recovery would depend on concrete progress towards a ceasefire or de-escalation of the US-Iran conflict, rather than expectations alone.
For Pakistan, the benefits could extend beyond the stock market.
Ghani estimated that easing war-related pressures could reduce projected inflation by 1 to 1.5 percentage points.
JS Global raised its inflation forecast for the year ending June 2027 from 8.2 per cent to 9.8 per cent because of the conflict.
Ghani warned that even with lower energy prices, inflation was unlikely to return to Pakistan's central bank target of 5 to 7 per cent anytime soon.
Mohammad Sohail, CEO of Pakistani investment firm Topline Securities, said rising oil and gas prices could slow economic growth, fuel inflation and affect interest rates and stock markets.
However, he believes Pakistan is better placed to withstand such shocks than in previous crises, thanks to an improved economic position.
The country’s foreign exchange reserves have risen to about US$26.8 billion, according to central bank data, while the government's budget shortfall has narrowed to its lowest level in more than 20 years.
Still, much depends on what happens next in the Middle East.
Hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough are growing, with Trump meeting Qatar's prime minister on Monday as efforts to end the war in Iran intensify.
But US and Gulf officials have cautioned that an agreement is far from certain, according to media reports.
"A sustained decline in oil prices and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz would be positive. But we still need to await the details of any US-Iran deal," said Priyanka Kishore, a Singapore-based economist.

Sachin Tendulkar will gift 26 of his prized cricketing bats, including those with which he scored some of his 100 international centuries, along with other memorabilia for display at the Mumbai Cricket Association’s (MCA) Sharad Pawar Cricket Museum.

One of the most essential pieces of technology that makes your phone’s camera work was created in 1974, and it hasn’t changed much since.
When you snap a photo with your smartphone, the camera captures light and converts it into electrical signals to build a digital image. But the Bayer filter—a red, green, and blue layer that sits above the sensor and adds color to your images—absorbs and wastes around 60 percent of that light before it can reach the sensor. To make a red pixel, the filter blocks and throws away blue and green light.
Now, the Boston company Metalenz has acquired an Israeli startup called PxE Holographic Imaging, which has developed a new optical layer called a HoloCoder. This microscopic structure sits directly on top of the image sensor and diffracts light, bending the light waves rather than absorbing them.
With the HoloCoder redirecting the light waves toward the sensor’s pixels instead of blocking them, the camera sensor can collect up to a claimed 2.5 times more light. Such a leap in light-gathering ability could dramatically improve a smartphone's low-light photography and dynamic range.
There's a surprising secondary benefit too: HoloCoder technology can capture 3D depth information at the same time. Most smartphones use secondary cameras, dedicated depth sensors, or AI guesswork to figure out the distance between the camera and the subject in order to judge how much depth should be shown in features like portrait mode. By merging light sensing and depth sensing into one layer, the HoloCoder promises to simplify the electronics on the back of your smartphone, saving space and processing power.
The acquisition of PxE—details of which were not disclosed—makes sense for Metalenz. The company launched publicly in 2021 and pioneered the commercialization of metasurfaces, a flat-lens system with nanostructures that bend light, reducing the need for multiple lens elements over the camera sensor while also capturing more light. The company has shipped more than 300 million of these metasurface optics to consumer devices today.
The technology can also capture polarization data, and Metalenz is working with Qualcomm to create a more effective, secure facial biometric authentication system for Android called Polar ID to rival Apple's Face ID, expected to arrive on consumer devices at the end of 2027.
Rob Devlin, Metalenz CEO and cofounder, tells WIRED that PxE's approach mirrors his own company's by patterning microscopic structures directly onto an image sensor to unlock light data that conventional camera systems throw away.
“Apple, Samsung, Google—everyone is fighting to improve the visible camera every year, right?" Devlin says. "A lot of what they're doing is investing hundreds of millions of dollars into software to try to somehow improve it, but the downside of that is that once information is lost when you're absorbing all of that light, you can't really buy it back, even if you're throwing all of the software into the world at it.”
Low-light photography and night-time video capture could see dramatic improvements with the HoloCoder system. In high-contrast scenes—like taking a selfie in front of a bright window—the sensor can capture more light and better re-create the scene without blowing out highlights or drowning shadows in noise.
PxE's technology isn't on the market yet, but as Metalenz has already developed a supply chain, processed an image pipeline, and set up machine learning algorithms on how to take advantage of these new data streams, Devlin thinks PxE's HoloCoder will be able to fit neatly into its platform and “completely disrupt" the visible sensing market. While the HoloCoder functions as a diffractive optic rather than a true metasurface, Devlin says Metalenz has already replicated the technology in the lab using its own metasurface optics.
“It's really then bringing all of that information together through a single approach," Devlin says. "We would do a metasurface design where now from a single image sensor, you're getting all of the information that is in light: You're getting polarization, you're getting color without filtering, and you're getting this depth channel. It's like the one sensor to rule them all.”
For now, Devlin says the two technologies will be separate products for different markets, but in the long term they could fuse into one Metalenz system. He expects we could see PxE's HoloCoder used in consumer electronics as early as late 2027 or early 2028.
Simplifying and shrinking the hardware with metasurface optics was just the first phase for the company—the real goal has always been to unlock that new information channel, which Devlin thinks can be transformational for other categories, like autonomous robots and autonomous vehicles. Instead of relying on large modules with multiple sensors and computationally expensive chips to align all that spatial data in real time, a single-sensor system could do the job in a smaller, cheaper design while using less computing power.
“It is a real problem in the sense that, in the color filter, you lose a lot of light,” says Arka Majumdar, who researches low-energy opto-electronics at the University of Washington. He points out that other industry heavyweights, including Samsung and a startup called Eyeo, have been actively researching their own alternatives to Bayer filters, called “color routers.”
While he agrees that ditching the filter can meaningfully improve smartphone photography in low light, he is skeptical that it can revolutionize categories like robotics and self-driving cars. Unlike phones, vehicles have plenty of space to mount stereo cameras or lidar. The bottleneck isn't low light or image clarity, but the computational power needed to make split-second decisions.
“In fact, arguably, if you get better data, it's actually worse,” he says.

Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
- Published
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.
It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.
The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.
Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.
Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.
Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.
All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

Ahead of its long due IPO, adtech unicorn InMobi has bolstered its marketing by securing a naming rights for Bengaluru's Ibbaluru Metro Station for the next 30 years via a ₹65 Cr deal. The partnership will see InMobi support Namma Metro over a 30-year concession, and Ibbaluru Metro Station will be known as InMobi Ibbaluru Metro Station. "Bengaluru is one of the world’s leading technology hubs. InMobi was born here, and over the last 18 years, we’ve grown alongside the city, continuing to build from India for the world. This partnership is our way of giving back to the city that gave us our start," the company said in a statement. The deal will contribute to BMRCL's non-fare revenue, which includes income from commercial activities such as station branding and advertising, alongside its core passenger fare collections. BMRCL said the partnership would support metro infrastructure development and encourage more corporate participation in the city's public transport ecosystem. The naming-rights deal comes as InMobi continues to work towards a public listing in India, a plan first reported over two years ago. In July 2024, reports said the company was targeting a 2025 IPO at a valuation of around $10 Bn. However, the proposed timeline has since slipped, with InMobi yet to file its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP). The delay in the proposed listing has coincided with changes in InMobi's shareholding structure. In December 2025, InMobi's cofounders bought back around 25-30% stake from early investor SoftBank, bringing the latter's holding down from approximately 35% to less than 8%. The transaction was backed by $350 Mn in debt raised from Varde Partners, Elham Credit Partners and SeaTown Holdings. The reshuffle in InMobi's cap table continued in 2026, with private equity firm True North reportedly acquiring a 2-3% stake through a secondary transaction valued at around $50-60 Mn. The company has appointed JPMorgan Chase, Jefferies, Kotak Mahindra Capital and Axis Capital as merchant bankers for the IPO. Earlier reports pegged the proposed issue at around $1 Bn, although subsequent valuation estimates have varied. While the IPO remains a work in progress, InMobi has continued to expand its advertising technology capabilities through acquisitions. In May 2026, the company acquired San Francisco-based mobile app marketing and analytics platform MobileAction to strengthen its capabilities in app discovery, user acquisition and advertising optimisation.

United is restricting AI agents from booking flights
The airline believes AI poses security risks and may violate DOT and FAA rules.
United Airlines has announced it will change ticking policies to restrict AI agents' from booking flights through its website, third-party travel agencies and flight aggregators. The airline joins a growing number of businesses, including JPMorgan Chase and Amazon, which block agents from using their products to avoid the security and privacy issues associated with them.
Giving something like your payment details or log-in credentials to an agent can expose sensitive information and lead to "unintended purchases, account changes or use of MileagePlus miles," United says. Allowing an AI agent to complete a booking could also violate existing airline regulations from the Department of Transportation and Federal Aviation Administration. For example, United says only a human can acknowledge that their bag doesn't contain explosives during flight check-in.
United would like to avoid association with any agent-based embarrassments, for instance when Meta's Muse leaked a user's address online. Like other companies, it also wants to keep AI from getting in the way of its relationship with customers. The Wall Street Journal reports that United CEO Scott Kirby has been open about the company's reluctance to jump into agentic commerce. "To be honest, I don't want to create another middleman," Kirby said at an event on Tuesday. Not every airline feels the same way: Southwest created a plugin so users can book flights with ChatGPT.
Luckily for United and other companies blocking AI agents, agentic commerce might not be taking off with regular people. During its recent third-quarter earnings call, Uber shared that it handled 320 million trips and deliveries during the week of Halloween; of those, AI agents were responsible for 500 Uber Eats orders and only four rides. Those aren't exactly industry-destroying numbers.
Handing an AI your credit card is very different from handing it your email login, and both are different from just asking it to send you a news summary every morning. Even if a large number of people are downloading apps like Muse, it seems like letting an agent shop for you isn't as frictionless or foolproof as it needs to be to catch on.

Indonesia's VP offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.
Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.
It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to "continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents," Hadi said.
As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.
"I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place," Raka said. "I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy."
The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.
Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.
The developments come amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo. The popular former president backed Prabowo's presidential bid after he chose Raka as a running mate.
The controversy over Raka's academic qualifications escalated last month after the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements.
The ruling intensified political pressure on Raka and fueled calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment.
Widodo faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

Owaisi and Chandrashekhar Azad are set to join hands ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections, seeking to consolidate Dalit and minority votes
NEW DELHI: All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Azad Samaj Party (Kanshiram) president Chandrashekhar Azad are likely to announce an alliance for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections at a joint press conference in Lucknow on Thursday, November 12.The proposed tie-up could mark an attempt by the two parties to build a political front outside the BJP-led NDA and the Samajwadi Party-Congress alliance. John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, the progeny of one of America’s most famous and wealthiest families, who during three decades in the U.S. Senate sought expanded healthcare for the poor and excoriated President George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq War, died on Friday (November 6, 2026) at his home in Washington, the Washington Post reported. He was 89.
His family did not provide a cause, the newspaper added.
Mr. Rockefeller, a tall, soft-spoken Democrat with liberal views, was elected in 1984 to the first of his five six-year terms representing West Virginia in the Senate after two terms as Governor of the poor coal-mining State.
Mr. Rockefeller voted in 2002 in favour of the Republican Bush’s measure authorising the Iraq war, which began with a U.S.-led invasion in 2003. He later expressed regret over that vote and, as head of the Senate intelligence committee, accused Mr. Bush of taking the nation to war on “false premises.”
He was a great-grandson of oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller and the scion of a family that formed a political dynasty that included his uncle, New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller.
Initiatives in public office
New York-born Jay Rockefeller’s life changed direction after he graduated from Harvard and served in a national service program in impoverished rural West Virginia from 1964 to 1966.
When he was put in public office, he worked to increase healthcare access, fight poverty, provide health benefits to coal miners and assist military veterans. As a senator, he had a role in shaping the programme created in 1997 under which the U.S. government helps States provide medical coverage for millions of uninsured children.
Mr. Rockefeller backed Democratic President Bill Clinton’s failed proposal for near-universal health insurance coverage in the 1990s and then fought for Democratic President Barack Obama’s successful quest for a healthcare overhaul law, signed in 2010.
In the debate over Mr. Obama’s measure, Mr. Rockefeller unsuccessfully sought to have the federal government offer a medical insurance program to the general population — in addition to existing programs for the poor and elderly — as an alternative to private insurance plans that could be costly and exclusive.
“Championing those most in need has been my life’s calling and I will never stop fighting to make a difference for the people who mean so much to me,” Mr. Rockefeller said in 2013 when he announced at age 75 he would not seek a sixth Senate term.
On the Iraq war
Before the Iraq invasion, Mr. Bush’s administration built the case for war by touting intelligence indicating Iraq owned an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction — they actually did not exist — and alleged ties between Iraqi leaders and the al Qaeda network responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks on the U.S.
“If I had known then what I know now, I would have voted against it,” Mr. Rockefeller told the Charleston Gazette newspaper in 2004, referring to the 2002 war authorization measure.
“I think the intelligence was shaped,” he continued. “And I think the interpretation of the intelligence was shaped. You had a president who we now know was determined to go to war.”
‘Fundamentally misleading’
A report from the intelligence committee issued in 2008, when he served as its chairman, asserted that Mr. Bush, Vice President Dick Cheney and other leading officials exaggerated intelligence findings and ignored disputes within U.S. intelligence circles about Iraq’s weapons and the hotly disputed ties to al Qaeda.
The report rejected pre-war statements by Mr. Bush and Cheney that Iraq might give al Qaeda weapons of mass destruction.
“Representing to the American people that the two had an operational partnership and posed a single, indistinguishable threat was fundamentally misleading and led the nation to war on false premises,” Mr. Rockefeller said as the report was released.
During his Senate tenure, he also headed the Commerce, Science, and Transportation and Veterans Affairs committees.
Wealthy family
Mr. Rockefeller was born on June 18, 1937, weeks after the death of his great-grandfather, who had been America’s richest man.
The Rockefeller name came with high expectations. His father was a famous philanthropist. His uncle Nelson served as U.S. vice president, as well as Governor of New York. His uncle David Rockefeller headed Chase Manhattan Bank and uncle Winthrop Rockefeller was governor of Arkansas.
He was elected to West Virginia’s legislature in 1966 before age 30, then elected West Virginia’s Secretary of State in 1968.
He lost a bid to become Governor in 1972, then served as a college president before being elected Governor in 1976. Mr. Rockefeller, who became one of the wealthiest members of the U.S. Congress, spent millions of dollars of his own money to bankroll his successful campaign for the US Senate in 1984.
Mr. Rockefeller sometimes found himself overshadowed by his State’s other senator, Robert Byrd, who died in 2010 at age 92 as the longest-serving member of Congress in U.S. history.
He usually backed his State’s coal and steel industries but angered coal executives in 2012 by fighting Republican efforts to prevent regulation of emissions from coal-fired power plants.
He was married to public television executive Sharon Percy Rockefeller, with whom he had four children.

Ousted Press Secretary Katie Zacharia melts down in BBC interview
The broadcast comes weeks after Zacharia was dismissed following five days as press secretary

Katie Zacharia, who briefly served as White House press secretary last month, repeatedly redirected questions about the 2026 midterm election results during an interview on the BBC’s “Newsnight,” focusing instead on an ongoing Senate race in Alaska.
During the interview, presenter Victoria Derbyshire asked Zacharia about statements made by President Donald Trump following election losses that handed control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate to Democrats.
Derbyshire noted that Trump had initially expressed a desire to work with congressional Democrats before raising concerns about election integrity days later.
In response, Zacharia raised questions about the Senate contest in Alaska, where the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan Sullivan, faces a challenge from Mary Peltola, a Democrat, as well as an independent candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan.
"Do you think that Dan Sullivan in Alaska is fair?" Zacharia asked.
Derbyshire questioned why Vice President JD Vance did not cite the Alaska contest in a recent social media post attributing the Republican Party’s midterms performance to the war in Iran.
"Why didn’t JD Vance mention the Sullivans and Alaska?" Derbyshire asked. "Does questioning if the election was honest mean that the president is now at odds with his vice president, who clearly said, in a long social media post, it was because of the Iran war, why Republicans lost?"
Zacharia said that Derbyshire was avoiding the subject of the Alaska ballot structure.
"You don’t want to answer the question because you know it’s not fair," Zacharia said. "You know that, that was a set-up! It is so clearly a set-up, and that is why it is being investigated right now.
“And that should be across the pond being questioned just as much as anywhere else in the world. This is not some random obscurity. This is two Dan Sullivans that were on the ballot in Alaska."
Republicans have asserted that the presence of the independent candidate was intended to confuse voters. Allegations of Democratic involvement in the independent candidate’s campaign have been denied.
As ballot counting continued Wednesday morning with 84 percent of votes tabulated, Peltola’s lead exceeded the combined vote totals of both other candidates on the ballot.
When Derbyshire attempted to return to Vance’s comments regarding the Iran conflict, Zacharia asked: "Who put Dan S. Sullivan on that ballot? Who did that?"
She added: "The New York Times had an answer. Did you read that? Did you read what The New York Times came out with? Yes or no?"
Zacharia also addressed potential policy differences within the administration.
“The president has been very clear; there is not any kind of ‘at odds’ right now,” she said. “He made those statements very clear, both in his interview and across the board. Any kind of insinuation that there’s this massive division happening is not actually understanding the relationship between the president and the vice president.”
The exchange also covered Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who was the subject of an impeachment resolution introduced by Representative Thomas Massie, Republican of Kentucky, over the administration’s authorization of military action in Iran. House Republicans voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to refer the eight articles of impeachment to committee, effectively blocking the measure from reaching the House floor.
In the interview, recorded prior to the vote, Derbyshire asked whether Hegseth should resign to relieve political pressure on the White House.
"Pete Hegseth should absolutely not resign," Zacharia said. "He’s been a wonderful secretary of war, and he absolutely did what any other secretary of war or secretary of defense would do in these circumstances."
She added: "And history will prove that not only President Trump, but also Secretary Hegseth will be thanked for ensuring the U.K. and the rest of the world won’t have to deal with nuclearized Iran."
Derbyshire also asked whether the midterm results indicated that Trump had lost political momentum. Zacharia rejected the characterization, citing historical trends where the sitting president's party typically loses congressional seats during midterm cycles.
"Regardless of the outcome, he is the fighter in chief," Zacharia said, describing the midterms as "not even a setback" for the president.
"Absolutely not a loser,” she said.
Zacharia served five days as press secretary in October before being replaced following a 14-minute briefing in which she took questions from three news organizations. The position has remained vacant since Karoline Leavitt stepped down in August.

National Drugs Act's stringent restrictions cannot override personal liberty, says Supreme Court
The court noted that the accused, Arshdeep Singh, had been in custody since May 2020, and although charges were recently framed, the trial was yet to commence.
Keeping an accused behind bars for more than six years without the trial even beginning amounts to “punishment in itself”, the Supreme Court has held, terming the state of affairs “unacceptable” and reminding courts that even the rigours of special laws must yield to the constitutional right to personal liberty.
“Keeping an accused incarcerated without trial for more than six years itself amounts to punishment, which is unacceptable,” said a bench of justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu in a recent order, as it granted bail to a man arrested in a narcotics case.
The bench was categorical that the stringent restrictions under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act cannot override the constitutional guarantee of personal liberty.
Court takes note of case
The court noted that the accused, Arshdeep Singh, had been in custody since May 16, 2020, and although charges were recently framed, the trial was yet to commence. It also noted that he had no prior criminal antecedents. It pointed out that in such a case, the rigours of Section 37 of the NDPS Act must yield to Article 21 of the Constitution, which protects the right to personal liberty.
Setting aside an Allahabad High Court order from July 28, 2025, which had rejected Singh’s second bail application, the apex court directed his release on bail subject to conditions imposed by the trial court.
Section 37 of the NDPS Act imposes stringent twin conditions for granting bail in cases involving commercial quantities of narcotic substances. Where the prosecution opposes bail, the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the accused is not guilty and is unlikely to commit an offence while on bail. The provision is designed to make bail difficult in drug-trafficking cases. However, the Supreme Court’s intervention underscores that these restrictions cannot become a justification for indefinite pre-trial incarceration.
Interception of the accused by NCB
Singh was arrested by the Narcotics Control Bureau on May 16, 2020, after a truck in which he was travelling was intercepted on GT Road. Investigators claimed to have recovered 31kg of opium concealed in plastic bags in the truck. The prosecution alleged that the contraband was in his conscious and constructive possession, while Singh maintained that he was merely driving the vehicle and had no knowledge of the substance allegedly concealed in it.
His first bail application was rejected by the high court in July 2022. When he approached the court again, he argued, among other things, that the mandatory procedure under Section 52A of the NDPS Act, governing the disposal and documentation of seized narcotic substances, had not been followed.
The high court rejected this argument, relying on a Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling, which held that delayed compliance or non-compliance with Section 52A, by itself, would neither vitiate a trial nor constitute a standalone ground for granting bail. It also found no fresh ground warranting reconsideration of Singh’s plea, apart from the period of incarceration.

Apart from emphasising the quantum of recovery and that Singh was allegedly in conscious possession of the contraband, the high court also relied on the statutory restrictions under Section 37 and rejected his plea.
The Supreme Court, however, considered the prolonged incarceration and the absence of progress in the trial decisive, underscoring that the severity of an accusation cannot, by itself, justify keeping an undertrial in prison for years without bringing the case to trial.
The bench also made Singh’s liberty conditional on his diligent attendance at trial and directed that any breach of bail conditions, including attempts to influence witnesses, could lead to cancellation of bail.

- KitKat released a GTA 6-inspired teaser on November 10, featuring its missing chocolate truck driving through Vice City-style streets.
- The campaign references the real March 2026 theft of approximately 12 tonnes of KitKat.
- There is no confirmed partnership between KitKat and Rockstar Games yet.
KitKat seems to have tracked down its missing chocolate shipment, and it’s clearly pointing to Grand Theft Auto 6. The brand-new mysterious teaser takes the real-life chocolate heist to the neon-lit streets of Vice City.
The famous chocolate brand shared a teaser on November 10, 2026, on X with a cheeky caption: “About those missing KitKats… Stay tuned.” While Rockstar Games hasn’t announced any collaboration between GTA 6 and KitKat, the video has caught fans’ attention, who have started connecting the dots between the missing truck and the upcoming blockbuster.
KitKat Is Turning Its Real-Life Heist into a GTA 6 Marketing Stunt
The KitKat teaser opens with a missing truck announcement before showing a red KitKat-branded big rig meandering through a cityscape that looks straight out of GTA 6 Vice City. Soon, you spot the palm trees, colorful buildings, and a distinct Miami-inspired sunset atmosphere.
Eventually, the teaser wraps up with a stylized shot of the truck, a hand sticking out of the window, and a mysterious “Stay Tuned” message. Look, it’s too early to speculate that it’s Jason’s hand sticking out of the rig. But the partial hairstyle and the face profile, matching the official screenshots for Jason in GTA 6, suggest that the assumption might be true.
Back in March 2026, approximately 12 tonnes of KitKat chocolate bars were stolen while they were being transported from a Nestle facility in Italy to Poland. Even Nestle confirmed the theft and launched a Stolen KitKat tracker to help identify the missing products using their batch codes.
Fast forward to today, with just a week left till GTA 6’s release, and KitKat comes up with a teaser themed around Vice City; the incident has sparked several speculations among fans.
Apart from pointing out the similarities of the neon-lit theme in the teaser, some are joking that the stolen chocolates have finally made their way into Vice City. Others are wondering if the entire situation was secretly building towards this enormous GTA 6 and KitKat marketing campaign.
However, KitKat is not an official GTA 6 marketing partner, and there’s currently no confirmation from Rockstar Games yet. So, if you’re curious about the GTA 6-themed KitKat chocolate bars, we might need to wait longer for that.

Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy on Wednesday said the first phase of the Musi rejuvenation project would begin shortly, asserting that the river had to be cleaned up and restored rather than merely beautified. He said the government would ensure that no one suffers losses in the process and called for the cooperation of all political parties.
Speaking at the inauguration of the revived Thammidikunta Lake, he said Musi river pollution was causing hardships to people in Nalgonda district, who were paying the price for the neglect of successive governments. The lives of Hyderabad residents were closely linked to the river, he said.
Recalling the construction of Osmansagar and Himayatsagar reservoirs by the Nizam to protect Hyderabad from floods, he said the Musi riverfront had been developed nearly a century ago, but the water body had now become polluted.
Describing Hyderabad as a city of rocks and lakes, Mr. Revanth Reddy said it had 1,372 lakes, but nearly 50% had disappeared due to various reasons. Encroachments had resulted in waterlogging on roads and flooding of residential colonies during rains. He stressed the need to free lakes from encroachments as part of efforts to protect nature and establish Hyderabad as a global city.
He said Thammidikunta Lake had been expanded from 14 to 30 acres, keeping the future of coming generations in mind, even if some people suffered losses in the process. Actor Akkineni Nagarjuna had voluntarily handed over two acres of land to the government, he said, describing him as a hero in real life as well as in films.
The Chief Minister said the lake would become a new destination alongside Shilparamam and called for developing a lake economy around it. He directed police officials to ensure adequate security and suggested planting a Jammi tree on the lake premises so that lakes could become venues for Dasara celebrations and help preserve cultural traditions.

Islamic State group-affiliated rebels kill at least 22 in Congo's eastern region
A rebel group affiliated with the Islamic State group has killed at least 22 people in Congo's eastern Ituri province
ITURI, Congo -- At least 22 people were killed in a series of attacks by a rebel group affiliated with the Islamic State group between Tuesday and Wednesday in Congo 's eastern Ituri province.
The attacks were carried out by the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) across eight locations in the Mambasa territory in Ituri, according to two civil society and human rights monitoring groups.
At least 10 people were also abducted.
“The death toll remains provisional. In addition to the 22 civilians killed, the perpetrators abducted other individuals, and motorcycles and homes were set on fire,” said Marie-Noelle Anatobe, coordinator of the Civil Society of Congo in Mambasa territory.
The attacks happened in nearly inaccessible locations near the border between Uganda and Congo.
The ADF grew out of Uganda and was pushed to the border region with Congo, where it has operated for years, targeting civilians. It pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group in 2019.
Both the Ugandan and Congolese armies have been jointly attacking the group, but they have long struggled against it.
Locals often say the military is usually absent during the attacks. Last year, the group killed dozens of people in Irumu territory in Ituri province, which the United Nations described as a “bloodbath.”
“This morning, we were left only to count the dead. It is truly deplorable,” Rams Malikidogo, a coordinator of the Association for the Protection and Defense of Vulnerable Children and Women in Mambasa territory, said.
