Kennedy relatives join the fight against Trump's arch, alleging harm to JFK's grave
One of America's most prominent political dynasties has waded into the growing fight against President Trump's proposed arch in Washington, D.C.
Nine members of the Kennedy family filed suit in federal court on Tuesday to block the 250-foot structure, saying it would obstruct their relatives' gravesites — including the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame — at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.
"A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come," Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said in a statement on behalf of the family.
The plaintiffs include children of Sen. Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy and a son of Sen. Edward M. Kennedy, all three of whom are buried at Arlington National Cemetery. There is one noticeable absence: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., did not join his siblings in the lawsuit against his own administration.
"It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in a statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."
The Kennedys' motion, filed hours before Veterans' Day, adds a highly personal layer to the ongoing legal fight.
"[The arch] constitutes nothing less than a permanent denigration of the Kennedy Gravesites and the final resting place for Plaintiffs' parents and grandparents," they wrote in their 27-page filing. "Plaintiffs would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended."
The Kennedys seek to join the existing federal lawsuit against the arch, which combines two cases: one brought by Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian earlier this year, and another filed by the governments of D.C. and Virginia late last month. The Arlington County Board has also filed a lawsuit in Virginia.
Loading...
The Trump administration has raced its arch through the federal approvals process over the past year, culminating in a final green light from the National Capital Planning Commission on Thursday. Officials had previously said they could break ground in Memorial Circle that same day.
But within moments of the late-night approval, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan stepped in with an order blocking construction for two weeks while she evaluates the broader legal challenges.
One of the main arguments against the arch is that its construction is unlawful without congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. The administration maintains that the arch is justified by a century-old authorization of two never-built columns at that same location, which did not seem to convince the judge: Chutkan wrote last week that "merely to state this argument is to reveal its flaws."
The administration has also argued that the case should be thrown out because of plaintiffs' lack of standing, which was the Supreme Court's reasoning in the White House ballroom case. But Chutkan has said D.C. and Virginia likely have standing to sue over the arch, given the financial and logistical harms they would suffer.
David Super, a Georgetown University law professor, told NPR in an email that he believes the Kennedys' involvement only strengthens the plaintiffs' standing.
"I can imagine ... that a judge on any level would feel uncomfortable denigrating their concerns over their family graves the way the Supreme Court denigrated the plaintiffs' interest in the White House ballroom case," he wrote. "And coming at a time when the Administration is hinting that it might tear down the Kennedy Center, this certainly makes the President look insensitive or even hostile to his revered predecessor."
Several Kennedy family members have spoken out against Trump's attempted takeover of the Kennedy Center, which is the subject of a separate lawsuit.
Arlington National Cemetery is central to the arch fight
The cemetery says JFK's gravesite is one of its two most-visited locations, along with the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
The Kennedys explain in their legal filing that JFK's family chose Arlington as his final resting place so that his gravesite could be accessible to the public.
"President Kennedy himself visited the Cemetery and stood where he is now buried," they wrote. "The vista looking back toward the District from the spot where his grave now stands was one of his favorites. While looking out, he remarked, 'I could stay here forever.'"
The grave was intentionally placed on the same axis as the bridge connecting Arlington House (the former home of Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee) to the Lincoln Memorial, with Kennedy's personal secretary remarking that he was "the link between Lincoln and Lee."
Kennedy's gravesite is topped with an eternal flame, which has burned since his funeral in November 1963. The Kennedys said their ancestors were "assured that all aspects of the design would safeguard visibility of the Eternal Flame" from the bridge, even with its intentionally low profile to preserve views of Arlington House.
The arch, they say, would block those views. The Trump administration has acknowledged that the arch would disrupt the historic significance of many nearby memorials, but has said building it anywhere else would defeat its purpose.
The Kennedy complaint goes a step further, citing a recent forensic analysis by the Washington Post that shows the arch would cast shadows over tens of thousands of graves. It would darken JFK's memorial on 50 days of the year, and briefly block the eternal flame on almost half of those.
The Trump administration has said the arch will be topped with its own eternal flame, per the controversial lighting recommendations of the Federal Aviation Administration.
The Kennedys said they often visit their family's graves in the morning for extra privacy — exactly the time of day that the Post analysis found the shadows would be most pronounced.
"Plaintiffs' visits to these would literally be shadowed by the Arch, an unlawfully-created structure," the filing reads. "The shadow the Arch would leave over the Kennedy Gravesites would fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the Gravesites."
Arlington National Cemetery is the final resting place for more than 400,000 service members, veterans and their relatives.
The White House has characterized the arch as a tribute to the nation's military heritage, saying it will "enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike."
But many of those veterans and their family members have spoken out vehemently against the arch: at protests in Memorial Circle, in tens of thousands of written comments as part of the federal review process, over nearly nine impassioned hours of public testimony during last Thursday's planning commission meeting.
Critics say the arch would disrespect those buried at Arlington and disrupt the solemnity of the space for the loved ones who visit them. They say construction — which the Trump administration estimates would involve 20-hour days — would interfere with the 24 to 27 funeral services held there every weekday.
Veterans have said that if Trump — who got five draft deferments during the Vietnam War — really wants to honor their service, he would stop cutting resources for them.
A flurry of court filings argue for a more permanent ban on the arch
The Trump administration has also recast the arch as a military structure (on a public-facing website and in recent court filings), though the plan that received final approval last week has no details about national security. The judge did not seem to find that late-stage argument compelling in her order last week.
In a 10-page declaration filed Tuesday, a retired military general argued that the arch would actually endanger national security.
Ret. U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Steven Anderson warned that storing ammunition in a tourist attraction would constitute a "tremendous risk," and that launching drones in that area — especially so close to D.C.'s airport — "poses clear hazards" to civilians.
"Not only is the Arch not suitable for any practical military facility, but it actually degrades security in the National Capital Region by placing a high-payoff target for our enemies just a few meters from a major road network and the traffic circle that surrounds the Arch," Anderson wrote.
He pointed to bombings in Beirut in 1983 and Oklahoma in 1995 as "two examples of the danger posed by allowing vehicles within close proximity of comparable military or law enforcement targets."
Anderson's declaration was part of a slew of documents that the veterans filed this week in their quest for a more permanent ban on the arch.
Democrats have also vowed to use their forthcoming majority in Congress to block Trump's construction projects and investigate potential wrongdoing.
But experts told NPR earlier this week that given Trump's veto power, Congress is better positioned to tackle that fight through oversight hearings and funding restrictions. The future of the arch, they say, will likely be up to the Supreme Court.

US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
- Published
An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.
A majority of the House of Representatives agreed to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky - for now.
In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".
The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.
Massie was the only Republican to vote against moving the resolution to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.
His effort failed in a 211-204 vote, with more than a dozen members, including 11 Democrats, missing the vote.
The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress before Democrats take control in January.
President Trump celebrated the vote in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort "has miserably FAILED".
"Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot," Trump said, referring to Hegseth.
After the vote, Massie said he "wasn't surprised" but "was disappointed", according to BBC's US media partner CBS.
"My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do," he added. "They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."
Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.
The Kentucky congressman also said that removing Hegseth now would give the Senate time to approve a replacement while Republicans were still in power.
Impeachment resolutions can be carried past the end of a congressional term, meaning Democrats would be able to take it up next year.
The Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in January following a successful midterm election that allowed them control of both chambers.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, had predicted earlier in the day that the impeachment bid would fail.
In the eight articles of impeachment formally introduced in the House on Monday, Massie said Hegseth was "breaking the law and must be held accountable" for fighting a war in Iran for more than 90 days without lawmakers' approval.
The impeachment articles also accused Hegseth of overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the US campaign against boats alleged to be carrying drugs in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth called efforts to impeach him a political stunt by a Trump administration opponent who was "disgruntled and defeated".
Hegseth also argued Massie's resolution endangered national security, because it communicated to US adversaries "that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations".
"This is not patriotism. This is sabotage," he said.
He echoed some statements Trump had made during a surprise appearance at the White House briefing room on Monday, including touting a rise in military recruitment levels.
But Hegseth said Massie was motivated by policy differences and "not high crimes, not misdemeanours, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offences the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause".
Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year to a Trump-backed opponent, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it began in February.
He had already incurred the president's ire for demanding the Trump administration release files on deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
While Hegseth has survived politically for now, many lawmakers - including some Republicans - have questioned how long he can last in the administration.
Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a Republican, said on Tuesday he expected Hegseth to resign or be fired by Trump.

The role of family physicians in ensuring accessible, affordable and patient-centred healthcare came into focus at the premiere of the documentary ‘The Doctor Next Door: A Legacy of Care’, screened at the Indian Heritage Academy in Bengaluru earlier this week.
Through accounts of veteran physicians, patients and young medical professionals, the film examines the decline of neighbourhood family practices and the growing fragmentation of healthcare. It highlights how long-standing doctor-patient relationships built on trust, familiarity and personal attention remain central to effective primary care.
The documentary draws attention to the rising dependence on specialised and corporate hospital-based treatment, making a case for strengthening family medicine as the foundation of India’s healthcare system.
Swetha Reddy, project manager of the documentary, said the film features perspectives from young medical students and practitioners considering careers in general practice, highlighting the need for changes in medical education and healthcare policy to encourage family medicine.
Directed by Ganesh Shankar Raj of Mindia Films and produced in collaboration with the Academy of Family Physicians of India (AFPI), the non-profit documentary explores the enduring relationship between family doctors and patients, and the importance of continuity of care in an increasingly specialised healthcare system.
The screening was followed by a panel discussion featuring scientists, medical professionals, senior family physicians, and community health advocates. The discussion centred on the challenges facing primary healthcare, the need to strengthen family medicine, and the importance of human relationships in medical practice.
Veteran family physician B.C. Rao was among the contributors to the initiative, alongside representatives of AFPI and other healthcare professionals.
The organisers said the documentary was intended to initiate wider conversations on reviving primary healthcare networks in urban and rural communities, and recognising neighbourhood doctors as an integral part of the healthcare system.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

The Child Development Centre (CDC), Thiruvananthapuram, has received an Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)-approved grant of ₹35 lakh for a three-year research project titled “Development and Validation of a Tool for Assessing Grief among Parents of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.”
The project, led by CDC director Deepa Bhaskaran, aims to develop and validate a culturally relevant tool to assess grief among parents of children with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD).
“The study will use focus group discussions and in-depth interviews involving parents of children with ASD, bereaved parents, professionals working with children with ASD, and members of the general population to understand the dimensions and cultural expressions of grief in the Indian context,” Dr. Bhaskaran said.
According to her, parents commonly experience shock, denial, fear, guilt, anger, sadness, and helplessness following their child’s diagnosis. The grief, described as chronic sorrow or non-finite grief, can recur at different stages of the child’s development, particularly when expected developmental milestones are not attained.
“The findings will help facilitate the identification of grief-related concerns among parents and support the development of appropriate grief counselling protocols and support group interventions, ultimately contributing to improved psychosocial well-being among families of children with ASD,” she said.
Inadequate social support compounds parental distress, she noted.
“There is a need for healthcare professionals to recognise and assess parents’ emotional well-being alongside the rehabilitation needs of children with autism. Early diagnosis, psychological support, and training for professionals to identify grief and help families develop coping strategies are vital,” she added.

Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, had an extramarital relationship with CEO Jensen Huang, according to a New York Times report on Wednesday that cited five company sources.
Powell, 48, reports to Huang, 63. The Times reported that the duo was "captured on video being affectionate" at an Nvidia conference hotel in San Jose in March, and that Powell is also married.
Huang is already under investigation at Nvidia on whether he was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." The Times had reported that US officials believed another woman he grew close with, tech executive Alice Huang, may have been recruited by the Chinese government to spy on the chip giant. The Nvidia CEO admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife in a note to staff on Sunday.
Here's what to know about Powell.
Powell steered Nvidia's healthcare efforts
Powell joined Nvidia as a director in 2008 and has steadily risen through the ranks. According to her corporate profile, she was originally responsible for promoting the use of Nvidia's AI chips for medical imaging.
She'd previously worked as an engineer and then in product at an electronics startup and ended up getting ahold of Nvidia to talk about their computing chips. Once the company realized its technology would have healthcare applications, it got back in touch to hire her, she said on an episode of the Lifers podcast published this August.
Powell called the job a "dream come true" on the podcast.
Her LinkedIn says she was promoted to senior director in 2016, and she led a business development team focused on AI. Powell's authority was growing — in 2017, she became vice president of healthcare, her profile says.
Her corporate profile now says she is responsible for both the hardware and software sides of the company's healthcare business, including technology for medical imaging, life sciences, and drug discovery.
"I pretty much live and breathe healthcare. So I'm talking about it all the time," Powell told Business Insider in 2025.
Kimberly Powell's ties to Jensen Huang
Huang, one of the entire tech industry's best-known representatives, has led Nvidia since he founded the company in 1993, so he and Powell have worked together for over 18 years.
In the August interview with Lifers, Powell credited Huang's healthcare ambitions.
"Jensen has been passionate about the healthcare industry going back 20-plus years, and that was really fueled by seeing just researchers who had dreams and aspirations to do something very, very meaningful and impactful in the healthcare domain and us potentially having the tools to do it, to achieve that goal," she said.
Nvidia's code of conduct, which begins with a letter from Huang, includes personal relationships among the activities that can create a conflict of interest.
It also says, "We promptly investigate reports of misconduct."
Neither Powell nor Nvidia responded to requests for comment from Business Insider.
CNN reporter Meg Tirrell posted on X that she'd been planning to moderate a conference panel featuring Powell on Thursday morning, but that Powell had cancelled.

- Twitch streamer and left-leaning political commentator Hasan Piker has filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative commentator Scott Jennings, seeking $72.5 million.
- The lawsuit pertains to a heavily edited video that Jennings reposted in August, to which he added his own commentary falsely presenting the clip as Piker saying he had a "plan of returning our country to lynchings," as well as that Piker "is out there calling for Black people to be lynched." The text of Jennings' post also falsely claimed, not as a direct quote, that Piker indicated "the USA should resume lynchings against black people."
- As Snopes previously reported, a full review of Piker's unedited remarks about lynchings confirmed he was sarcastically mimicking other people's opinions. The video's fragmented excerpts from three different streams presented Piker's words without full context, and in some cases out of order. As such, it was misleading.
- Piker's complaint, filed Oct. 27 in a U.S. district court in Washington, D.C., cites Snopes' reporting. The complaint accurately says Jennings had not responded to our email, in which we asked whether he researched the original clips from Piker's past streams and if he wished to provide further comment.
- We once again emailed Jennings and Piker for comment. A statement from one of Piker's attorneys appears later in this article.
Editor's note: On Nov. 10, Scott Jennings' attorney Benjamin Chew filed a motion to dismiss Hasan Piker's defamation lawsuit against Jennings. Jennings' staff emailed Snopes a statement from Chew reading, "Mr. Jennings' filing today puts great trust in the U.S. Constitution, the truth, and the right of Americans to speak … even if Mr Piker doesn't like what they have to say."
On Oct. 27, Bloomberg Law reported that Twitch streamer and left-leaning political commentator Hasan Piker — who campaigned for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Party's U.S. Senate candidate in Michigan — had sued conservative commentator Scott Jennings, seeking $72.5 million for alleged defamation.
The lawsuit concerns a heavily edited 41-second video that Jennings shared in his own commentary video (archived) on Aug. 11. The edited clip shows Piker appearing to make several offensive statements targeting Black people, such as, "I don't give a f*** what Black people care about," and mentions going "back to a better time when lynchings were happening." Others (archived) shared the video, as well.
In Jennings' commentary, he falsely claimed the video shows Piker saying he had a "plan of returning our country to lynchings," as well as that Piker "is out there calling for Black people to be lynched." The text of Jennings' post also falsely claimed, though not as a direct quote, that Piker said "the USA should resume lynchings against black people."
The edited clip consists of genuine sentence fragments stitched together from three of Piker's streams out of context and out of order, twisting their original import. In one of the original streams, Piker's remarks on lynchings were sarcastic reactions to a user's chat comment and opinions expressed by someone else in a separate video.
A review of Piker's full, unedited remarks found he was speaking of a desire to prioritize winning elections over concentrating on matters that he believed resulted in past electoral losses.
Piker's complaint, filed Oct. 27 in a U.S. district court in Washington, D.C., alleges two counts of defamation and one count of false light, claiming Jennings "knew the portrayal was false or acted with reckless disregard for its falsity," as well as that, as a result, "Piker has suffered injury to his reputation, public humiliation, emotional distress, mental anguish, and damage to his professional interests."
Piker is seeking $27.5 million in compensatory damages, $45 million in punitive damages, attorneys' fees and other relief.
The complaint cites Snopes' reporting from August, specifically on pages 5, 29 and 30, including accurately stating that Jennings had not responded to our email in which we asked whether he researched the original clips from Piker's past streams and if he wished to provide further comment.
Piker spoke about the lawsuit during his stream on Oct. 27, saying Jennings "certainly messed up" and that the case was about "truth in the media." He added of Republican commentators, "I don't think you should be able to get away with lying like this, and if I don't put a stop to it they're going to continue maliciously defaming others as they have done so this entire time."
Daniel Watkins, one of several attorneys representing Piker, emailed Snopes the following statement:
Scott Jennings accused Hasan Piker of calling for Black Americans to be lynched. That is an extraordinary accusation. And it was a lie. Jennings took a manipulated video, put words in Hasan's mouth that he never spoke, and then held those words up as proof of something Hasan never said or believed. There is something especially disgraceful about exploiting this country's history of racial terror to destroy another man's reputation. Scott Jennings has every right to disagree with Hasan Piker. He has no right to invent what Hasan said. We brought this case because the truth matters, reputation matters, and there comes a point when lying must have consequences.
Snopes once again emailed Jennings and Piker for comment about the lawsuit and will update this article if we receive further information.
Transcript of the edited video
Days prior to Jennings' post, the National Republican Senatorial Committee posted (archived) the same video compilation.
The transcript, featuring heavily edited excerpts from three different streams, reads as follows:

Ian Nepomniachtchi and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave took outright leads in Groups C and D respectively after the opening round of the Total Chess World Championship Tour pilot’s Fast Classic stage here on Wednesday.
Alireza Firouzja and Jan-Krzysztof Duda shared the Group A lead, while Fabiano Caruana and Liem Le were level atop Group B. All six collected four points from their two games, with Firouzja and Caruana placed first in their groups on the strength of their preliminary blitz rankings.
The opening day produced 10 decisive results from 24 games. Each player faced the same opponent twice with colours reversed, earning three points for a win and one for a draw.
For the Indian contingent, R. Vaishali recovered from a first-game defeat to draw her return encounter with Vachier-Lagrave, while R. Praggnanandhaa and Arjun Erigaisi drew both their games against Vincent Keymer and Hans Niemann respectively.
Vachier-Lagrave’s victory over Vaishali was the only decisive result in Group D. Playing with Black, the Frenchman capitalised on a late error in a balanced endgame to win their first encounter. The subsequent draw took him to four points, two ahead of Arjun, Niemann, Wesley So and Bibisara Assaubayeva. Vaishali finished the day with one point.
In Group C, Nepomniachtchi defeated Abhimanyu Mishra before drawing their second game to move into the lead. World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen and Anish Giri drew twice, finishing with two points each.
Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and Haik Martirosyan exchanged victories, both winning with Black, to occupy the next two places behind Nepomniachtchi on three points apiece.
Firouzja began with a victory over Nodirbek Abdusattorov, exploiting a critical mistake before defending the return game to secure a draw. Duda matched his four-point tally by drawing his first game against Andrew Hong and winning the second with White.
Levon Aronian and Jorden van Foreest split their encounters, with Black winning both games, to finish the day on three points each.
Caruana opened his Group B campaign by beating Hungary’s Richard Rapport with Black, before a draw in the return game secured his share of the lead.
Le followed the reverse sequence against Vladislav Artemiev, drawing first and then winning.
Praggnanandhaa and Keymer remained two points behind the leaders after neither could break through in their two meetings.
The second round on Thursday will again feature two games per player. Only the four group winners will advance to the knockout bracket that decides the Budapest title, the remaining players will contest separate placing brackets.

At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of Cairo, authorities have said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles (5okm) south of the capital, when a train travelling to the south-western Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. It said one of the trains had derailed.
The health ministry said at least four people had been killed and 88 injured. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.
The president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.
A train driver and his assistant were injured in September last year when two freight trains collided in the same district.

Mohalla Tech, the parent of social media platforms ShareChat and Moj, reported a 78.5% YoY increase in its consolidated net loss to ₹1,978.4 Cr in the financial year ended March 2026 (FY26), weighed down by higher share-based payment expenses, foreign exchange losses and finance costs. The loss for the fiscal year widened despite a 40.4% jump in operating revenue to ₹1,016.3 Cr from ₹723.4 Cr in FY25. Further, the startup also reported an improvement in its operating performance. ShareChat’s management claims that it managed to narrow its FY26 EBITDA loss by 58% YoY to ₹91 Cr and recorded its first EBITDA positive quarter in Q1 FY27. The company reported an EBITDA profit of ₹9.5 Cr and a margin of 0.3% in the June quarter. Its EBITDA margin improved to over 2% in Q2 FY27, the management claimed. QuickTV Subscription Drives Revenue Growth The startup’s management said its FY26 top line growth was led by the launch of QuickTV, its subscription-based microdrama platform launched in February 2025. The subscription vertical, which accounts for subscriptions from both Quick TV and Moj (Moj+ and Moj Blue), raked in a revenue of ₹292.7 Cr in the fiscal, accounting for almost 30% of the top line in the fiscal. Mohalla Tech had counted advertising and livestreaming as its two major pillars for revenue generation since its inception over a decade ago. In the previous fiscal year, it aggressively expanded into monetising the content on its platform amid a growing fervour for microdramas in the Indian content landscape. Hailed as the "next phase of evolution for the entertainment industry", Microdrama adoption picked pace in the Indian market early in FY26. ShareChat had launched its vertical microdrama platform, QuickTV, earlier in February 2025. Since then, the app has been downloaded by over 5 Cr users from the Google Play Store. As its content monetisation took shape, the social media unicorn faced some operational turmoil for its long-set revenue driver — advertising. Advertising revenue dipped 13% YoY to ₹251.8 Cr in the fiscal year. This decline came as advertisers from the real money gaming (RMG) stopped promotional spends. To note, ShareChat had already diversified its offerings for clients across FMCG and mid-market advertisers. Hence, it managed to offset the dent anticipated from the RMG ban. On the other hand, ShareChat’s livestreaming segment grew almost by 9% YoY to ₹471.8 Cr. This segment registers revenue from paying users on both ShareChat and Moj platforms. ShareChat’s FY27 Outlook For the fiscal year FY27, Mohalla Tech is targeting an EBITDA profit of ₹25 Cr, including at least ₹15 Cr in the second half of FY27. The startup reported around ₹740 Cr in revenue in the first half of FY27, while its Q2 FY27 annualised revenue run rate reached approximately ₹1,500 Cr. It did not disclose its bottom line performance for the September half of the ongoing fiscal. To fuel this financial improvement, the startup is expecting both of its content monetisation models — subscription video on demand (SVOD) and advertising-based video on demand (AVOD) — to shoulder its next phase of growth. ShareChat is expecting its advertising to make a stronger contribution in FY27, growing by 40% YoY. While it is expecting its AVOD revenue to surpass the ₹350 Cr mark, this particular revenue stream touched ₹160 Cr in the first half. The management didn’t share any projections for revenue from SVOD in the fiscal. It believes that most Indian internet users are unlikely to pay for microdrama subscriptions, with the number of paying users for the format expected to remain below 100 Mn even as the market matures, making advertising an important monetisation opportunity. The Microdrama Dillema Mohalla Tech's push into microdrama comes as the format draws growing interest across businesses. EloElo Group, the parent of microdrama platform Story TV, recently raised $80 Mn (around ₹756 Cr) in a Series C round led by Hornbill Capital and NBCUniversal. The company plans to invest in original content across Indian languages, expand Story TV internationally and strengthen its AI-powered production capabilities. Story TV has more than 5,000 microdramas across six languages, while EloElo claims over 40 Mn monthly active users across its apps. The space has also attracted startups such as Kuku TV, Flick TV, ReelSaga and Chai Shots, alongside larger platforms including JioHotstar's Tadka, Zee Entertainment's Bullet and Amazon MX Player's MX Fatafat. Businesses and platforms are utilising the short-story format to plug in marketing and products while capitalising on the rise in vertical content consumption. What's New: ShareChat parent Mohalla Tech's consolidated net loss widened 78.5% YoY to ₹1,978.4 Cr in FY26, even as operating revenue jumped 40.4% to ₹1,016.3 Cr. Why It Matters: Subscription revenue from its microdrama push helped offset declining advertising revenue, while the company narrowed its EBITDA loss by 58%. The Details: Higher ESOP expenses, forex losses and finance costs weighed on profitability, with total expenses jumping 65.6% YoY. However, rising customer acquisition costs and the difficulty of converting free viewers into paying subscribers continue to weigh on the economics of standalone microdrama platforms. For instance, Mohalla Tech said acquiring a user on its free-to-use platform Moj costs around ₹14-15 per download, while acquiring a paying subscriber for QuickTV costs hundreds of rupees, given the latter's newer brand and subscription paywall. It claimed that competing subscription platforms could be spending upwards of ₹1,000 per subscriber. Owing to this, platforms like Mohalla Tech are instead banking on advertising revenue and marketing plug-ins to increase monetisation. Where Did ShareChat Spend In FY26? Mohalla Tech’s total expenses surged 65.6% to ₹3,083 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,862.1 Cr a year earlier. During its FY26 earnings call, management said the reported loss was largely driven by non-cash and notional accounting items, including provisions for interest on hybrid debt instruments, unrealised foreign exchange losses and ESOP expenses. Employee Benefit Expenses: Expenses under this head more than doubled to ₹959.5 Cr from ₹445.8 Cr in FY25. A large part of the increase came from share-based payments, which climbed 302% to ₹739 Cr in FY26 from ₹183.8 Cr in FY25, following an expansion of the company's ESOP pool and additional grants to key employees. Foreign Exchange Losses: Owing to rupee-dollar depreciation, non-cash expenses under this head rose more than fourfold to ₹566.9 Cr from ₹128 Cr in FY25. The increase was largely driven by unrealised forex losses of ₹566 Cr. Business Development: Expenses under this head, which usually covers functions like marketing, promotions and customer acquisition, surged 7.7X to ₹334.8 Cr from ₹43.4 Cr in FY26.

The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6, 2026) termed vehicular emissions a major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR and said immediate, medium- and long-term measures were needed to curb the rising air quality index.
Hearing a suo motu case examining the regulatory framework governing air pollution, a Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana also expressed concern over “bumper-to-bumper” traffic in Delhi-NCR.
“We keep talking and sometimes make statements and suggestions, but the point is that AQI is already touching 400,” the CJI said.
The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad.
“Look at the roads in Delhi and the roads connecting Delhi with the NCR. Take a look at any road and the kind of vehicles moving on it. That is the major problem,” the CJI said.
The Bench said the poor people are the real sufferers, as they are on the roads, and moreover, the festival time is the only period when they earn a livelihood.
On stubble burning, the Bench stressed the need to educate farmers about using machines instead of resorting to farm fires.
On the plea seeking closure of schools or running them in hybrid mode for students of all age groups if the air quality index (AQI) rises above a certain mark, the bench said it will go by experts’ opinion.
Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre and other authorities, referred to the regulatory framework covering five major sectors: industrial emissions, vehicular pollution, construction and demolition dust, road dust and stubble burning.
She told the Bench that several measures had been introduced, including restrictions on the entry of certain vehicles, geo-tagging of pollution under control (PUC) certificates and action against visibly polluting vehicles through complaints received on applications and social media.
Ms. Bhati told the Bench that stubble burning accounted for 14% of Delhi’s pollution on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The Bench said it will pass some orders and take up the plea on November 16 after the court reopens following the Diwali vacation.
A thick layer of smog hung over the national capital on Friday (November 6, 2026) as the air quality deteriorated sharply and edged closer to the ‘severe’ category, with the overall AQI settling at 391.
Of the 59 monitoring stations across the city, 30 recorded ‘severe’ air quality at 9 a.m., while the remaining were in the ‘very poor’ category.
Rohini recorded the worst AQI at 475, followed by IIT Delhi at 472, official data showed.
